title: Treat a transaction the person split or excluded with a reason as already decided when the ingest evaluates
description:
## What changes for the user
The app's rules look at each new transaction once: they either put it on a budget line by themselves or
ask the person about it in the weekly review. They leave a transaction alone when the person has already
put it on a line. But two other things the person can do to a transaction are not treated as a decision:
dividing it into parts with a line each, and leaving it out of the budget with a reason. Today, if the
person does either before the rules have looked at the transaction, the rules look anyway. A divided
purchase can come back as a question in the weekly review, and while that question waits its parts stop
counting in the budget; a purchase left out with a reason can come back as a question too, and the month
cannot be closed until it is answered, although the purchase counts for nothing. After this lands, a
transaction the person divided or left out with a reason is never asked about and never put on a line by
the rules.

## Outcome
The ingest treats a transaction that has two or more split parts, or an exclusion with a reason, as
already decided, exactly as it treats one that is on a line or waiting in the queue: it writes no line,
queues no review and adds no history step, and counts it among the transactions already decided.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ingest* (`internal/ingest`) takes
each new snapshot of the bank's data into the app's database. Its last step *evaluates* each transaction
the rules have not looked at yet (`evaluateOne` in `internal/ingest/evaluation.go`): it asks the
classification rules (`classrules.Decide`) and then either stores a line by rule (with a history step
"Regra classificou como ..."), or stores a *pending review*, which puts the transaction in the weekly
queue, or leaves it. A transaction is a candidate while its index row's `evaluated` flag is 0; the flag
is set when it is evaluated, whatever the outcome, so each transaction is looked at once. A *split* is the
person dividing a purchase into parts, each with its own amount and optionally a line; fewer than two
parts is no split. An *exclusion* leaves a transaction out of the budget: it is stored as a text, where
no text at all means the transaction counts, an empty text means the switch is on but no reason was given
yet (which still counts in the budget), and a non-empty text is an exclusion with a reason, which takes
effect.

**What the code does today.** Before writing anything, `evaluateOne` asks `alreadyDecided`, which reads
what is kept about the transaction and answers true only when it is on a line or has a pending review
(`state.Line != nil || state.PendingReason != ""`). Its comment gives the purpose: "a decision the person
took in the minutes before a tick is never touched". The split parts (`AuthoredTransaction.Split`) and
the exclusion (`TransactionState.Exclusion`) are read by the same call and not looked at. The rules
themselves never see a transaction's own split or exclusion; they see those only on the examples they
learn from.

**What follows, read in `budgetrules.Dispose` (`internal/budgetrules/dispose.go`) and
`internal/api/pending.go`.** The budget decides what a transaction counts for in a fixed order: excluded
with a reason, then waiting for review, then split, then the rest.
- A split purchase the rules queue is "waiting" before it is "split": while the question waits, its parts
  add to no line. A line the rules store on a split purchase is kept and ignored, since the parts are
  what counts, and the history shows a rule step on a purchase the person had divided.
- An excluded purchase the rules queue still counts for nothing, but what is pending is decided by the
  stored review alone (`pendingTransactions` has no test for an exclusion), so it shows in the weekly
  queue, and closing its month, or any later month, is refused with "Resolva as pendências do mês antes
  de fechar." until the person answers.

**When the order "the person first, the rules later" happens.** A write's lookup creates the index row of
a transaction it has never met with `evaluated = 0`, so a transaction the person touches before any
evaluation is still a candidate. The ingest evaluates only in a month whose budget has at least one line,
from the month the database was created on. So everything the person divides or leaves out in a month
that has no budget yet is evaluated on the day that month gets its first line: the ingest runs right after
a budget is saved. That is the ordinary first day of use. The other window, the minutes between a new
snapshot and the next run of the ingest, is being closed by separate work that makes the ingest run before
a write; this item does not depend on it.

**What was decided, and what lost.**
- *Divided, or left out with a reason, counts as decided.* Leaving it as it is was rejected: an explicit
  decision should not come back as a question, and for a split the budget is wrong while the question
  waits.
- *An exclusion with no reason yet does not count as decided.* It does not take effect in the budget
  either; the transaction is still an ordinary one and the rules look at it.
- *Decided once is decided.* The `evaluated` flag is set as it is today for any transaction the ingest
  finds already decided, so the rules do not come back if the person later removes the split or the
  exclusion; the transaction then shows without a line and is placed by hand. Keeping such a transaction
  unevaluated so the rules return later was considered and left out: it changes what the flag means for
  one case only.
- *The queue's definition is not touched.* A review stored before this change on an excluded transaction
  stays in the queue until answered; no stored row is rewritten.

**Tests that exist.** `TestWhatThePersonDecidedBeforeTheLockIsLeftAlone` in
`internal/ingest/decide_test.go` pins the two cases the code knows, a line and a pending review. The
ingest's tests run over a harness (`internal/ingest/harness_test.go`: `world.night` writes the next
snapshot, `world.run` runs the ingest, `world.asPerson` records a change as the person, `world.kept`
reads what is kept about a transaction). The counts a run answers have a field for what was already
decided (`AlreadyDecided` in `internal/ingest/counts.go`), and a comment there says which counts add up
to the transactions evaluated. Splitting and excluding as examples are covered by
`internal/ingest/decide_inputs_test.go`, which is another path and does not change.

## Steps to Reproduce
Over invented data; no test does this today.
1. A month has no budget. A snapshot lists two purchases of establishments the rules have never seen. The
   person divides the first into two parts and leaves the second out with a reason.
2. The person saves a first budget for that month, with the lines the parts name; the ingest runs.
3. Expected: neither purchase has a pending review or a line by rule. Actual: each is evaluated; with no
   examples to go by, each gets a pending review, the weekly queue lists both, the first purchase's parts
   add to no line, and closing the month is refused.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The sequence above exists as a test in `internal/ingest/decide_test.go`, was seen failing on the code
as it stands, and passes: after the run neither purchase has a pending reason, a line, or a history step, and both have
`evaluated` set.
- [ ] A purchase with two parts and five examples of its establishment on one line, which today the rules
would put on that line, keeps no line of its own after the run and gains no history step.
- [ ] A transaction whose exclusion is switched on with an empty reason is evaluated as today: the same
test with an empty reason ends with the pending review or the line the rules give.
- [ ] A transaction with one stored part is not a split and is evaluated as today.
- [ ] The run counts each of them under `AlreadyDecided`, and the counts that the comment in
`internal/ingest/counts.go` says add up still add up.
- [ ] `TestWhatThePersonDecidedBeforeTheLockIsLeftAlone` passes unchanged.
- [ ] Each rule was seen failing once, by breaking it on purpose, and the pull request names the test that
failed for each: the split not consulted; the exclusion not consulted; an empty reason treated as a
decision; one part treated as a split.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is
empty.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: a transaction the person divided or left out with a reason comes out of an ingest run
with nothing written about it by the rules, and one with an empty reason or a single part is evaluated
as before.

## Tests
- Integration, in `internal/ingest` over the harness: the sequence of the steps above; the purchase with
five examples; the empty reason; the single part; the counts of the run.
- Unit, in `internal/ingest`: the condition itself, over what is kept about a transaction (a line, a
pending reason, two parts, one part, a reason, an empty reason, nothing).
- Golden: none moves.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ingest/evaluation.go`, `internal/ingest/decide_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ingest/harness_test.go`, `internal/ingest/counts.go`,
`internal/ingest/decide_inputs_test.go`, `internal/authored/transaction_reads.go`,
`internal/budgetrules/dispose.go`, `internal/api/pending.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `bin/ci`

One condition in one function of the ingest, and its tests. The rules package, the store, the queue's
definition and the budget's order are read to understand the consequence and are not edited.

## Recovery path
Nothing stored changes shape and no row is rewritten. Reverting the pull request brings the old condition
back; transactions skipped in the meantime keep their `evaluated` flag and are not asked about, which is
the state a transaction on a line is in as well.
close_reason: The ingest treats a transaction that has two or more split parts, or an exclusion with a non-empty reason, as already decided: it writes no line, no review and no step, marks it evaluated and counts it among those already decided. An empty reason and a single part are still evaluated. Verified by the gate on the branch, by the reproduction as a test that failed on the earlier code, by a table test over everything that can be kept about a transaction, and by ten deliberate breaks, four by the author of the change and six in review, each failing a named test. No golden file moved.

title: Store the classifier's threshold and minimum of examples, the card's label and its closing setting in the app's database, each answered with its default until it is set
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing the person sees changes with this piece. Today the settings screen's slider for how sure the
app must be before it files a purchase by itself, the field for how many examples it needs, the card's
label and the choice of a manual closing day all answer that the app is read-only, because the app has
nowhere to keep them. This piece is that place: a table in the app's own database that holds each of
the five settings, refuses a value outside its range by itself, and answers the value the app starts
with for anything never set. The handlers that let the person change the settings, and the card that
follows the closing day, are the next piece. If this were wrong the person would later find a setting
gone after a restart, a value the screen could never have sent stored anyway, or the undo of a first
change leaving something other than the default.

## Outcome
Migration `0004_settings` adds `settings(key, value)` to the app's database, registered in the
recorder's registry. `internal/authored` has store functions that write each of the five settings
through the recorder and read each of them with its default when nothing is stored, and the authored
view offers the same reads, the empty view answering the defaults. `authoredtest` has a builder that
sets any of the five in an invented authored state. No answer of the API changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database* is
`finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against
it; the server has one only when started with `--db`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave. *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored` through which every change to the app's
database is written; *the journal* is what it writes (one row per change in `changes`, one per effect in
`change_effects`); *undo* is the inverse of a change's recorded effects. *The authored view* is the
read-only view of the app's database a request handler is given.

**What earlier work provides.** None of it is in the repository when this text is written; each piece is
delivered before this bead starts, and its interfaces are to be read in the code as that work left them.

- The app's database (finwise-9h2: opening, recognising and migrating `finwise.db`): a migration is an SQL
  file embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`, recorded by name and checksum in
  `schema_migrations` once applied; at start every file not recorded is applied in name order, each in one
  transaction, after a copy of a database that already holds data is taken beside it
  (`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>`). A recorded name whose checksum differs from the embedded file, or a
  recorded name the binary does not have, is refused at start, so once a migration has been applied to a
  database that matters its file is frozen. Migration names are fixed in advance, one owner each: this
  work owns `0004_settings` and no other. Every SQL statement over the database is a registered constant:
  one test prepares each against the migrated schema and another fails on a statement that is not
  registered.
- The recorder and undo (finwise-wi4: the journal and the undo engine): a closed, hand-written registry of the
  journaled tables, each entry saying the table's shape, its key columns and how a key and a row are
  written as canonical JSON. An *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts per key, and an
  effect is one column changing; a restore is computed for the whole row and written once. The registry
  says which of two kinds an attribute table is: one of *optional facts*, where every column has a default
  and a row whose columns are all at their defaults is the same as no row, or one of things *created
  whole*, where creating the row is itself a unit. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing. A
  table in neither the registry nor the named list of tables deliberately not journaled fails a test, and
  so does a statement that inserts, updates or deletes in an authored table outside the recorder.
  `changes.undo` restores every `before` of a change and is refused with `refused` / `stale_change` when a
  later change still in force touched the same unit.
- The views (finwise-jzw: one snapshot of each store per request): the authored view is one read-only
  transaction; on a server without `--db` it is an empty view that answers "nothing authored", so read
  code has one path. Each slice adds to that view the reads of the tables it owns.
- `internal/authored/authoredtest` (finwise-fst: the write conformance harness and its invented authored
  states): builders of invented states of the app's database, one per group of tables, added by the slice
  that owns the tables, used by the conformance cases of `internal/api`.

**What the code is today (each point read in the file named).**

- `internal/api/settings_defaults.go` states the defaults the settings answer today, "the values the
  stand-in starts with": `defaultConfidenceThreshold` 85, `defaultMinExamples` 5,
  `defaultManualClosingDay` 28, `defaultClosingMode` `"auto"`; `internal/api/messages.go` holds
  `defaultCardLabel` `"Físico"`. `internal/api/settings.go`'s `readSettingsOverview` answers them.
- `web/src/api/contract/settings.ts` exports the bounds: `THRESHOLD_RANGE` 50 to 99,
  `MIN_EXAMPLES_RANGE` 1 to 50, `CLOSING_DAY_RANGE` 1 to 28; `web/src/api/contract/card.ts` has
  `ClosingMode = 'auto' | 'manual'`.
- `web/src/api/fake/settings.ts` keeps the five as fields of its state; `web/src/api/fake/settings-rules.ts`
  rounds and clamps the three numbers before storing them. Rounding and clamping are the API's work, in
  the next piece; the store receives values already in range and the database refuses any other.

**The schema: migration `0004_settings`.** One table, `settings(key, value)`, one row per setting that
the person has set. Its keys are a closed set of five: the confidence threshold, the minimum of
examples, the card label, the closing mode and the manual closing day (the spelling of each key is the
implementer's). It is an attribute table in the recorder's registry, keyed by `key`, whose fact is
`value`. The table declares its primary key and `NOT NULL` where a value is required, and `CHECK`s for
every closed set: the key is one of the five; the mode is `auto` or `manual`; the threshold is a whole
number from 50 to 99, the minimum from 1 to 50, the manual day from 1 to 28. How `value` is typed for a
number and for a text, and whether the registry treats the table as one of optional facts or of things
created whole, are the implementer's, under the criteria below. The table holds no amount of money, so
the obligation every migration's owner has, a test in which the database itself refuses a duplicate, an
invalid value and a negative amount, is met with a duplicate key, an unknown key, a mode outside the two,
a number outside its range, and a negative number for each numeric setting. A column this work proves it
needs may be added, in this file only.

**The store functions.** For each of the five settings: a write that records through the recorder, and a
read that answers the stored value or the default when nothing is stored. The defaults are the five
above, stated once in `internal/authored`, because the rules that classify new transactions run in
`internal/ingest` (finwise-82m: the job that brings a new snapshot in), which depends on `internal/authored`
and not on `internal/api`; making `internal/api` use them instead of its own constants is the next
piece's (finwise-suc). A write whose value is the one already stored records no effect, so the handler can
answer an empty change; whether writing a value equal to the default when nothing is stored writes a row
is the implementer's, and the choice is pinned by a test. The closing mode and the manual day are two
facts, written together by the one handler that sets them; the store offers whatever makes that one
change. The undo of the first write of a setting brings its read back to the default and the canonical
dump of the journaled tables back to what it was. The authored view offers the five reads; the empty view
answers the five defaults.

**Known next users, not built here:** the four write handlers, the settings overview and the card's reads
(finwise-suc: the API side of the settings and the card following the closing day); the rules that decide a
transaction's line, which read the threshold and the minimum (finwise-9gz: the pure classification rules;
finwise-82m).

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`): the spelling of the keys and the typing
of `value`, under the `CHECK`s; the registry kind of the table; whether a default written when nothing is
stored writes a row; the names of the functions and files.

**Privacy and conventions.** Nothing here needs a real ledger. Fixtures are invented, and no value from a
real snapshot (an amount, a description, a name, a document, an id) is ever printed, logged or copied
into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request. Work in your own git worktree, on your own branch, and
stop at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a
bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; the
float guard in `internal/api/reais_test.go` already covers `internal/authored`. Every SQL statement over
the app's database is a registered constant. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else
is English. A design value in a component comes from a token; this work touches no component.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A database that held only the earlier migrations gains `settings` when opened; the migration is
recorded once under the name `0004_settings`; opening it again applies nothing.
- [ ] From a test, directly against the migrated schema with no Go validation in the way, the database
refuses: a second row for one key; an unknown key; the mode `weekly`; a threshold of 49 and of 100; a
minimum of 0 and of 51; a manual day of 0 and of 29; a value of -1 for each of the three numeric keys.
It accepts each bound (50, 99, 1, 50, 1, 28) and both modes.
- [ ] Every statement this work adds is a registered constant prepared by the existing test; `settings`
is in the recorder's registry; no statement writes it outside the recorder.
- [ ] On a freshly migrated database and on the empty view, the five reads answer 85, 5, `"Físico"`,
`auto` and 28.
- [ ] Each write, recorded in a change, is answered by its read afterwards and by the authored view of a
later transaction; the closing mode and the manual day written together are one change with an effect on
each.
- [ ] Writing the value already stored adds no row to `change_effects`.
- [ ] Undoing the first write of each setting answers the default again and returns the canonical dump of
the journaled tables to the one taken before; undoing a second write answers the first value.
- [ ] An `authoredtest` builder sets any subset of the five in an invented authored state, and a test
reads them back through the authored view.
- [ ] No file outside `internal/authored/` changes, and no answer of the API changes (`git diff --stat`
over the branch).
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the final report:
each `CHECK` dropped in turn; the primary key dropped; a default changed; the empty view answering zero
values; the write that leaves a value as it is recording an effect.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the database refuses every invalid row above by itself, and
each of the five settings is written, read with its default and undone through the recorder.

## Tests
- Unit, over a temporary migrated database (`internal/authored`): the schema's refusals and acceptances,
  with no Go validation in the way.
- Unit (`internal/authored`): each read with nothing stored, on the database and on the empty view; each
  write then read; the no-effect write; undo of a first and of a second write through the recorder, with
  the canonical dump compared.
- Unit (`internal/authored/authoredtest`): the builder over any subset of the five.
- The existing statement-registry and recorder-registry tests, which now cover `settings`.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/migrations/0004_settings.sql`, `internal/authored/`,
`internal/authored/authoredtest/`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/settings_defaults.go`, `internal/api/messages.go`,
`web/src/api/contract/settings.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/card.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/settings.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/settings-rules.ts`, `bin/ci`

One migration, one store file with its test in `internal/authored`, the registry entry and the reads
added to the authored view wherever the recorder and the views put them, and one builder file in
`authoredtest`. One module. Nothing in `internal/api` changes here.

## Recovery path
The migration only adds one table. If it fails, its transaction rolls back and the server exits; when
the database already held data, the copy the migration runner took before migrating is beside it
(`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>`). To go back: stop the server; check the copy (`PRAGMA
integrity_check`, the application id); put it in place of the database with no `-wal` or `-shm` file
beside it; start a binary that does not carry this migration, since a database that holds a migration the
binary does not know is refused at start. Once the migration has been applied to a database that matters
its file is frozen; a correction is a new migration, never an edit.
close_reason: Migration 0004_settings adds the journaled settings table (one row per setting set; the table itself refuses an unknown key, a second row, a wrong type and an out-of-range value); the five reads answer their defaults, stated once in internal/authored, on a fresh database and on the empty view; writes through the recorder, an equal value recording nothing, the closing mode and day as one change; authoredtest builds a state with any subset set. bin/ci green. Review: three independent mutations, all failing tests; the two commits reordered so each builds alone. The implementer's twenty breaks each failed a test, one staying green by design (NOT NULL behind the type checks).

title: Describe the API contract as a machine-readable manifest
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing visible. Today the only description of what the screens expect from a backend is TypeScript that a Go program cannot read, so a real backend that misspells or forgets a field would show up as a blank on screen, or as a total that is silently missing a part. After this lands that description also exists as a file both sides read, and the gate can catch the mismatch before anyone sees it.

## Outcome
Every method of the interface's API contract is classified, and one generated, versioned file describes the whole contract for a non-TypeScript reader: each method's route, class, argument schemas and result schema, plus the error envelope. The gate fails when that file is stale.

## Context
The interface talks to its backend through one TypeScript interface, `FinwiseApi` in `web/src/api/types.ts`, with 13 domains and 82 methods declared in `web/src/api/contract/`. Today an in-memory stand-in (`web/src/api/fake/`) implements it. A Go backend is being built to implement the same contract; it will be read-only at first: reads answer, every write is refused with one error.

**Why a classification.** Nothing in the types says which methods change state. The server needs that to refuse writes without a handler per write, and tests need it to prove none was forgotten. Four classes:
- `session`: the PIN gate itself, `session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock`.
- `read`: returns data and changes nothing.
- `evaluate`: takes a draft, computes a result and stores nothing (`budget.evaluateScenario`).
- `write`: changes state. `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are writes.

The classification lives beside the contract as a constant checked by a mapped type over `FinwiseApi`, so a method that is added, removed or renamed without being classified is a type error, not a runtime surprise.

**Why an error type.** The contract has none: failures are `null`, a result union for the PIN, or prose comments saying "Refused". A backend that refuses writes needs one representation. Kinds: `locked` (no valid session), `read_only` (a write or an evaluation was refused), `ledger_unavailable` (the bank data cannot be read), `bad_request`, `unknown_method`, `internal`, and `network` (client side only: the request never got an answer). On the wire an error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`.

**The wire, decided.** One route per method, `POST /api/<domain>/<method>`, whose body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in declaration order and whose answer is the method's result as JSON (`null` for a method that returns nothing). An optional trailing argument may be omitted or `null`. Rejected: resource-style REST, which needs 82 hand-written mappings on each side for no other consumer.

**The manifest.** A script under `web/scripts/` writes `internal/contract/contract.json` with: a format version; for every method its domain, name, route, class, an array schema for its arguments and a schema for its result; the shared definitions; and the schema of the error envelope. Object schemas forbid properties the contract does not declare. The file is versioned and never edited by hand, like `web/src/styles/tokens.css`; the freshness check compares the generated output with the file on disk, not with git, because a built but uncommitted change must not fail the gate that runs before the commit.

**The generator and its risk.** `ts-json-schema-generator` 2.10.0 (MIT, supports TypeScript from 5.9 below 7; the repository is on 6.0.3) is the first choice. It may not resolve a mapped or conditional type that extracts arguments and results from `FinwiseApi`. Settle that first: if it cannot, walk the methods with the TypeScript compiler API, which is already a dependency, and use the generator only for named types. Either way no schema may come out as the empty schema.

**Proving the schema can fail.** The stand-in is type-checked against the contract, so every answer it gives must validate. A test calls every `read` method of the stand-in over the prototype dataset and validates each answer against its result schema with `ajv`. If an answer does not validate the schema is wrong. The same test mutates one answer (a number turned into a string, a required field removed, an unknown field added) and expects each mutation to be rejected.

Dependencies are pinned to exact versions, as everywhere in `web/package.json`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Removing one method's entry from the classification makes `npm --prefix web run typecheck` fail, and so does adding an entry for a method that does not exist.
- [ ] `internal/contract/contract.json` lists every method of `FinwiseApi` exactly once, each with a route of the form `/api/<domain>/<method>`, a class, an arguments schema and a result schema.
- [ ] `session.status`, `session.unlock` and `session.lock` are `session`; `session.changePin` and `changes.undo` are `write`; `budget.evaluateScenario` is `evaluate`.
- [ ] No arguments schema and no result schema in the manifest is the empty schema or accepts any value.
- [ ] Every answer of every `read` method of the stand-in, over the prototype dataset, validates against its result schema.
- [ ] A number turned into a string, a required field removed and an unknown field added are each rejected by validation.
- [ ] `bin/ci` fails with a message naming the manifest when `contract.json` on disk differs from what the script generates, and passes after the script is run.
- [ ] `ApiError` and its kinds are exported from the contract, and the error envelope's schema is in the manifest.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and editing any contract type without regenerating the manifest makes it fail.

## Tests
- Unit: the manifest covers the classification one to one; route format; no empty schema.
- Conformance: every stand-in answer against its schema, and the three mutations rejected.
- Unit: the freshness check fails on a stale file and passes on a fresh one.
- The type-level guard is broken once on purpose and the compiler error quoted in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/errors.ts`, `web/src/api/types.ts`, `web/scripts/contract-manifest.mjs`, `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts`, `web/package.json`, `web/package-lock.json`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `bin/ci`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/api/contract/`

Two new contract files, one script with its test, one generated file, and one new step in the gate. No screen, no store and no stand-in rule changes; `web/src/api/types.ts` only gains exports.
close_reason: Every method of FinwiseApi is classified under a mapped type (removing or inventing an entry fails typecheck with TS2741 / TS2353). internal/contract/contract.json lists 82 methods (3 session, 23 read, 1 evaluate, 55 write) with route, class, argument and result schemas and the error envelope; contract:check exits 1 on a stale file and bin/ci names the manifest. Every read answer of the stand-in validates with ajv and the three mutations are rejected. bin/ci: CI green. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%.

title: Derive the review's warnings from the subscriptions, let one be dismissed for good, and answer null for the approvals and warning actions nothing produces yet
description:
## What changes for the user
On the Semanal tab of Revisão, the "Avisos" card is always empty against real data: it says "Sem avisos.
Aumentos de preço, renovações e cobranças estranhas aparecem aqui quando forem detectados." even when a
subscription the person keeps just got more expensive, a yearly plan is about to renew, or a subscription
they marked to cancel charged the card again. After this lands each of those three shows there as one
sentence ("Preço subiu: … de R$ 19,90 para R$ 21,90", "Renovação anual em 9 dias: … · R$ 166,80",
"Marcada para cancelar e cobrou de novo: …"); clicking it opens that subscription, and the × dismisses it
with "Aviso dispensado." and a "Desfazer". A dismissed warning stays dismissed on every visit, while a new
price rise of the same subscription shows again, and a warning whose reason went away (the price came
back, the renewal passed, the status changed) disappears by itself. The "Aguardando seu ok" card keeps
saying nothing is waiting, and is now honest about it: nothing in the app proposes changes yet. If this
were wrong the person would not get an error: a warning they dismissed would keep coming back, or a second
price rise would stay hidden because they dismissed the first.

## Outcome
`review.weekly` answers its `warnings` derived from the subscriptions kept in the app's database and from
the card's charges in the ledger: one warning per subscription and kind that holds now (a price rise, a
renewal within thirty days, a charge after cancelling), each with a stable id, a fixed Portuguese sentence,
its subscription and no action, minus the ones dismissed. `review.dismissWarning` stores the id of an
active warning as a recorded change that `changes.undo` takes back, and answers null for anything else.
`review.runWarningAction`, `review.approve`, `review.refuse` and `review.propose` have handlers that answer
null and record nothing. The five names leave the list of writes without a handler.

## Context
**The app and its words.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite
*snapshot* that a separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app opens it read-only and never
writes to it. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, a second SQLite file the server opens when it is started
with `--db`; everything the person authors lives there. *The contract* is the TypeScript description of the
82 methods the interface calls (`web/src/api/contract/`); *the manifest*, `internal/contract/contract.json`,
is that contract generated for Go (route, class, argument and result schemas of each method) by
`npm --prefix web run contract`, versioned and never edited by hand. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake
backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of
how writes behave, and where this bead does not say otherwise its behaviour is the rule. *The journal* is
the record of every change made to the app's database (tables `changes` and `change_effects`), with its
author, from which a change is undone. A *golden file* is a recorded answer under
`internal/api/testdata/golden/` that a test compares the live answer with.

**What exists today (checked in the code).**
- `internal/api/review.go`: `registerReview` registers `review.weekly` and `review.payday`.
  `readWeeklyReview` checks its one month argument (`onlyMonthArgument`), requires a readable ledger and
  answers `queue.items`, `approvals` and `warnings` as empty lists (`weeklyReview.Warnings` is `[]any`).
  `review_test.go` pins that answer for both invented ledgers (`emptyWeeklyReview`) and holds the read
  cases `review.weekly ["2026-03"]` and `review.payday ["2026-03"]`; the golden file is
  `testdata/golden/{full,empty}/review.weekly.2026-03.json`.
- The five writes `review.approve`, `refuse`, `propose`, `dismissWarning` and `runWarningAction` (and every
  other write) are of class `write` in `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts` and are refused with
  `read_only` today.
- The contract (`web/src/api/contract/review.ts`): `ReviewWarning` is `{id, text, subscriptionId: string |
  null, actions: {id: WarningActionId, label}[]}`, where a null `subscriptionId` opens the list;
  `WarningActionId` is `'accept-suggestion' | 'reject-suggestion' | 'silence-pair'`; `dismissWarning(id)`
  answers `ChangeResult | null`, `runWarningAction(id, action)` `WarningActionResult | null`, `approve(id)`
  `Approved | null` ("Null when nothing by that id is waiting"), `refuse(id)` `ChangeResult | null`,
  `propose(id)` `ChangeResult | null` ("Null when it is unknown or already waiting"). `WeeklyReview` says
  the month limit and the week guide are read for the month asked and "the queue and the rest are the
  account's now". No contract type changes in this work.
- The stand-in seeds five warnings in `web/src/api/fake/review-data.ts` (`prototypeReview`), with the kinds
  of `WarningKind` in `review-model.ts`: `preco` (`price`, "Preço subiu: Spotify de R$ 19,90 para R$ 21,90",
  subscription `sp`), `nova` (`new-recurring`, with the actions "Sim" and "Não"), `sobre` (`overlap`, with
  "Silenciar este par"), `renov` (`renewal`, "Renovação anual em 9 dias: Amazon Prime · R$ 166,80",
  subscription `ap`) and `cobrou` (`charged-after-cancel`, "Marcada para cancelar e cobrou de novo: Editor
  de fotos", subscription null). Every space in those three texts is a plain space (U+0020). It also seeds
  four proposals and three waiting for approval. `visibleWarnings` in `review-rules.ts` hides the
  `new-recurring` warning once the suggestion was answered. In `review.ts`, `dismissWarning` answers null
  for an id it does not hold and otherwise deletes the warning from its state; `runWarningAction` acts on
  an offered action; `approve`, `refuse` and `propose` act on the seeded proposals. `review.test.ts` pins
  all of that under "the warnings" and "the changes waiting for approval".
- The marks of a subscription, in the stand-in (`marksOf` in `web/src/api/fake/subscription-rules.ts`):
  `Preço subiu` when the previous amount is lower than the amount; for a cycle of twelve months or more,
  when the whole days from today to the next charge are 0 to 30 (`RENEWAL_NOTICE_DAYS`), `renewalText`
  gives `Renova hoje` for 0, `Renova em 1 dia` for 1 and `Renova em N dias` otherwise; `Cobrou após
  cancelar` from a stored flag.
- The interface needs no change. `web/src/screens/revisao/WarningsCard.vue` shows each warning's `text` as
  a button that opens `/assinaturas/<subscriptionId>` (or `/assinaturas` when it is null), draws one button
  per action, and its × calls `dismissWarning` and, when the answer is not null, announces "Aviso
  dispensado." with "Desfazer" (`useReviewActions`). With no warning it shows "Sem avisos. Aumentos de
  preço, renovações e cobranças estranhas aparecem aqui quando forem detectados."
  `web/src/screens/revisao/ApprovalsCard.vue` shows, with no approval, "Nada aguardando. Mudanças que
  precisam do seu ok aparecem aqui depois de cada sincronização ou do relatório do mês."
- `internal/api/messages.go` opens with "Everything a person reads that the server writes lives in this
  file, in Brazilian Portuguese. The wording follows the stand-in's." No function of the Go code writes an
  amount as text today: `api.Reais` writes JSON numbers (`19.99`) from integer cents.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.** None of it is in the repository when this is written;
read it as it landed.
- The app's database (finwise-9h2): the package `internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against
  `finwise.db`; its migrations, recorded by name, and its rule that every SQL statement is a registered
  constant that a test prepares against the migrated schema.
- The recorder (finwise-wi4), the layer through which every change to a journaled table is written: a closed
  registry names each journaled table and its shape. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing,
  and an effect on it is one row appearing or disappearing. Undo restores a change's effects by inverse and
  refuses with `stale_change` when a later change still in force touched the same row.
- Write dispatch (finwise-2s5): a write that has a handler has its arguments validated against the method's
  schema from the manifest (a mismatch is `bad_request` before the handler runs), runs inside one immediate
  transaction with a recorder that writes the change's row lazily (with its first effect, or when the
  handler asks for the id; a handler that does neither leaves no trace in the journal), and is committed by
  the dispatcher. A write without a handler, or a server without `--db`, answers `read_only` before its
  body is read. A test walks the manifest and requires every write to have a handler or to be named in an
  explicit list, `writesWithoutHandler`, in a test file. `ledger_unavailable` is answered by a write
  exactly as by a read, through the same classifier.
- The write conformance harness (finwise-fst): every write has a case of exactly one mode (a recorded change,
  whose answer validates against the manifest, whose effects match a golden file under
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/` and whose undo returns a canonical dump of every journaled table
  to the dump taken before; or nothing to do, a null answer that adds no row to the journal); the package
  `internal/authored/authoredtest`, which builds invented states of the app's database; a third state for
  read conformance (the full invented ledger with an invented authored state, cases in
  `authoredReadCases`, golden files in `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`); and a test that runs
  every case and proves nothing it holds reaches the logs.
- Subscriptions (finwise-ot5): the table `subscriptions(id, establishment_key, created_from_tx_key,
  created_day, created_cents, name, line_id, status, status_day, review_on, note)` and its store, the pure
  package `internal/subrules` and the subscription reads. For each subscription `internal/subrules` derives,
  from the card's charges in the ledger (one charge per day, the stored creation day and amount standing in
  when no charge is left), the amount (the latest charge), the previous amount (the charge before it, if
  any), the cycle (`Mensal`, `Trimestral`, `Semestral`, `Anual` or `Bienal`, of 1, 3, 6, 12 and 24 months),
  the next charge (the latest charge's day plus the cycle's months) and which marks hold: `Preço subiu`
  when there is a previous amount lower than the amount; for a cycle of twelve months or more, a renewal
  when the whole days from today to the next charge are 0 to 30 (with those days); `Cobrou após cancelar`
  when the status is `Cancelar` and the latest charge's day is after `status_day` (never for the stored
  creation charge). A subscription's id is a decimal string (`"1"`), its `name` is the one stored at
  creation, and the list answers subscriptions in the order they were created.
- The review's migration and queue (finwise-rf3): the migration `0007_review`, which creates
  `closing_steps(month, step)`, `transfer_marks(month, transfer_key, done_on)` and `dismissed_warnings(id)`
  and enters them in the recorder's registry as set tables; the weekly queue and `review.acceptPending`,
  so `review.weekly` already reads the app's database when this starts. If the store functions that read
  and write `dismissed_warnings` are not there yet, they are part of this work, in the file of
  `internal/authored` that holds the review's tables; `0007_review` itself is not edited, because its
  checksum is recorded in every database that has started with it.

**The warnings, derived.** A warning is not stored anywhere: it is computed on every read of
`review.weekly` from what the subscription rules already derive, so that a warning holds exactly when the
corresponding mark is on the subscription's row. There are three kinds, named as the stand-in names them.
For every subscription in the app's database, whatever its status:

| kind | holds when | id | `text` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `price` | the subscription has a previous amount and it is lower than the amount (the `Preço subiu` mark) | `price:<subscription id>:<day of the latest charge>` | `Preço subiu: <name> de <previous amount> para <amount>` |
| `renewal` | the cycle is `Anual` or `Bienal` and the whole days from today to the next charge are 0 to 30 (the renewal mark) | `renewal:<subscription id>:<day of the next charge>` | `Renovação <anual\|bienal> hoje: <name> · <amount>` for 0 days; `Renovação <anual\|bienal> em 1 dia: <name> · <amount>` for 1; `Renovação <anual\|bienal> em <N> dias: <name> · <amount>` for 2 to 30 |
| `charged-after-cancel` | the status is `Cancelar` and the latest charge's day is after the status day (the `Cobrou após cancelar` mark) | `charged-after-cancel:<subscription id>:<day of the latest charge>` | `Marcada para cancelar e cobrou de novo: <name>` |

- `<subscription id>` is the decimal id the subscription reads answer; a day is `YYYY-MM-DD`; the parts are
  joined by `:` and nothing else (`price:1:2026-11-22`, `renewal:3:2026-04-20`,
  `charged-after-cancel:2:2026-11-11`). The id is the warning's kind, its subscription and what triggered
  it: the latest charge for a price rise and a charge after cancelling, the renewal day for a renewal. So
  it does not change while a renewal counts down from 30 days to 0, while its text does; and a price that
  rises again on a later charge is a new warning with a new id.
- `<name>` is the subscription's name as its row shows it. `<amount>` is the latest charge and
  `<previous amount>` the charge before it, both as the subscription rules give them (magnitudes in cents,
  tax included).
- The word after `Renovação` follows the cycle: `anual` for `Anual`, `bienal` for `Bienal`. The stand-in
  has only `anual`; `bienal` is the same sentence for the only other cycle the renewal applies to, so a
  two-year plan is not called yearly. The forms for 0 and 1 day follow the marks' own wording (`Renova
  hoje`, `Renova em 1 dia`).
- An amount in a sentence is written `R$`, one plain space (U+0020, as in `review-data.ts`), the whole
  reais with `.` between each group of three digits counted from the right, `,` and the two digits of the
  cents: 50 cents is `R$ 0,50`, 16680 is `R$ 166,80`, 119900 is `R$ 1.199,00`, 123456789 is
  `R$ 1.234.567,89`. It is computed from integer cents with integer arithmetic. The interface's own `brl`
  (`web/src/lib/format.ts`) puts a non-breaking space after the symbol; these sentences follow the
  stand-in's text instead, and the interface shows them as they come.
- Every warning answers `subscriptionId` with its subscription's id (the stand-in's `cobrou` has null; the
  server always knows the subscription) and `actions: []`: none of these kinds offers an action.
- Order: by kind, in the order the stand-in lists these three kinds (`price`, then `renewal`, then
  `charged-after-cancel`), and within a kind by subscription in the order the subscriptions were created
  (ascending id). One subscription can carry several warnings at once.
- Warnings are the account's now, as the contract says: they depend on today (the Brazil day of the
  request's instant) and not on the month `review.weekly` is asked for. Every month asked answers the same
  warnings.
- A warning whose id is in `dismissed_warnings` is left out.
- The sentences, the money text and the three kind names live in `internal/api/messages.go`, as that file
  requires. `internal/subrules` keeps answering values; it is read here, not edited.
- With no app's database (`--db` absent) there is no subscription and so no warning. With the snapshot
  missing, `review.weekly` answers `ledger_unavailable` as today.
- Kinds the stand-in has and this does not produce: `new-recurring` (it needs automatic detection of
  subscriptions) and `overlap` (it needs detecting two plans of one service); both are later work, and so
  are the actions they carry.

**`review.dismissWarning(id)`.** When `id` is the id of a warning that holds now and is not dismissed, it
adds the row `(id)` to `dismissed_warnings` through the recorder and answers `{changeId}`. For anything
else it answers null and records nothing: an id no warning has, an id of a warning that no longer holds,
an id already dismissed, the stand-in's ids (`preco`, `renov`). It reads the ledger to know which warnings
hold, so with the snapshot missing it answers `ledger_unavailable` and records nothing. `changes.undo` of
its change removes the row and the warning is shown again while it still holds. The row is never deleted
otherwise: once the warning stops holding, the row stays and does nothing; if the same id holds again
later (the same subscription, the same trigger) it stays dismissed. A non-string argument is
`bad_request`, checked by the dispatcher.

**The methods that answer null until something produces what they act on.** Each gets a handler that
validates nothing beyond what the dispatcher already checked, reads neither store, records nothing (no row
in `changes` or `change_effects`) and answers `null`, also with the snapshot missing:
- `review.runWarningAction(id, action)`: no warning offers an action; the kinds that would
  (`new-recurring`, `overlap`) do not exist yet. An `action` outside the three of `WarningActionId` is
  `bad_request` by the schema.
- `review.approve(id)`, `review.refuse(id)`, `review.propose(id)`: nothing produces a proposal until the
  nightly model call or a command-line client for agents does; both are later work. `review.weekly` keeps
  answering `approvals: []`.

**Where the server departs from the stand-in on purpose.** Each is pinned by a test whose name says what
departs; nothing else may differ.

| departure | stand-in | server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| where warnings come from | five seeded rows | derived from the subscriptions and the card's charges, on every read |
| kinds | five, two of them with actions | three, none with an action |
| `charged-after-cancel` | opens the list (`subscriptionId: null`) | opens its subscription |
| identity | a seeded short name (`preco`) | kind, subscription and trigger |
| dismissing | deletes the warning from the state | stores its id; a warning that no longer holds is gone by itself, and a new trigger is a new warning |
| `runWarningAction` | creates or rejects a suggestion, silences a pair | answers null |
| `approve`, `refuse`, `propose` | act on four seeded proposals | answer null; no approval is ever listed |
| undo | restores a snapshot of the whole state | by inverse, refused when overwritten since |

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

| decision | why | what lost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Warnings are derived on read, not stored | nothing would write them: there is no detector, and the marks already compute the same three facts | a table of warnings a job fills, which would need a producer and could disagree with the marks |
| A warning's id is its kind, its subscription and its trigger | a dismissal must silence that occurrence and nothing after it: a second price rise must show, a countdown must not reappear every day | dismissing a subscription's warnings for good, or by kind; an id made from the text, which changes every day of a renewal |
| The sentences are fixed and written by the server | the contract's warning carries its text, and the stand-in's sentences are the design's | texts built by the interface from structured fields, which would change the contract |
| Approvals, proposals and warning actions answer null | nothing produces a proposal or an actionable warning until the model or the command-line client does | inventing proposals without a rule |
| Where the result type allows null, an unknown target answers null | the screens already treat null as "nothing happened" | refusing every unknown id |

**Failure paths that touch this.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the snapshot is missing | `review.weekly` and `dismissWarning` answer `ledger_unavailable`, nothing is recorded; the four null methods answer null |
| a write fails halfway, or waits five seconds for the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; `internal` |
| an undo of a dismissal meets a later change of the same row | `stale_change`; nothing is restored |
| the subscription is undone or its charges leave the ledger | its warnings stop holding and are gone; dismissed rows stay and do nothing |
| the bank rewords the establishment so its key changes | later charges under the new key are not this subscription's; its warnings follow the charges it still has |
| two tabs dismiss the same warning at once | writes queue; the second finds it dismissed and answers null |
| the process stops between a write's commit and its answer | the change is stored; the interface says the result could not be confirmed and fetches again |

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Every fixture
here is invented; no proof of this work needs a real ledger. If one is opened to check a shape, it is opened
read-only, no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is printed, logged or copied into a
file, a commit or a pull request, a count may be shown to the person running the test and goes into no file,
and a test that touches it runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. A warning's text carries a
subscription's name and amounts: no test prints one from a real ledger, and the golden files are built from
invented ledgers only.

**Conventions.** Work in a git worktree of your own and end at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits,
no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer
cents and no float may appear on the money path; the float guard of `internal/api` covers the new files.
Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant in `internal/authored`; `internal/api`
executes none. New files in `internal/api` log nothing. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and
everything else is English. A design value in a component comes from a token (this work touches no
component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Unit: the money text answers `R$ 0,50`, `R$ 19,90`, `R$ 166,80`, `R$ 1.199,00`, `R$ 1.234.567,89`
for 50, 1990, 16680, 119900 and 123456789 cents, with U+0020 after `R$`, and imports no float type.
- [ ] Price rise: a subscription "Streaming Exemplo" with charges of 19.90 on 2026-09-22 and 2026-10-22 and
21.90 on 2026-11-22, read on 2026-11-22, answers exactly one warning `{"id":"price:<id>:2026-11-22",
"text":"Preço subiu: Streaming Exemplo de R$ 19,90 para R$ 21,90","subscriptionId":"<id>","actions":[]}`; a
fourth charge of 21.90 on 2026-12-22 makes it gone; a fourth charge of 23.90 instead gives one warning
`price:<id>:2026-12-22` reading `de R$ 21,90 para R$ 23,90`; prices that fell or stayed give none.
- [ ] Renewal: a subscription "Plano Anual Exemplo" with charges of 166.80 on 2024-04-20 and 2025-04-20
(cycle `Anual`, next charge 2026-04-20) answers `renewal:<id>:2026-04-20` with "Renovação anual hoje: Plano
Anual Exemplo · R$ 166,80" on 2026-04-20, "Renovação anual em 1 dia: Plano Anual Exemplo · R$ 166,80" on
2026-04-19 and "Renovação anual em 30 dias: Plano Anual Exemplo · R$ 166,80" on 2026-03-21, and no warning
on 2026-03-20 (31 days) and on 2026-04-21 (one day past).
- [ ] A `Bienal` subscription with charges on 2022-05-10 and 2024-05-10 read on 2026-05-01 answers "Renovação
bienal em 9 dias: <name> · <amount>"; a `Semestral` one whose next charge is 3 days away answers no renewal.
- [ ] Charged after cancelling: status `Cancelar` set on 2026-11-10 and a latest charge on 2026-11-09, on
2026-11-10 and on 2026-11-11 answer no warning, no warning, and `charged-after-cancel:<id>:2026-11-11` with
"Marcada para cancelar e cobrou de novo: <name>"; the same charge with status `Manter` answers none; a
subscription whose only charge is the stored creation charge answers none whatever its status.
- [ ] For every subscription of every test state, the kinds of its warnings are exactly the marks
`Preço subiu`, renewal and `Cobrou após cancelar` on its row from `subscriptions.list`.
- [ ] The renewal's id is the same on each of the 31 days from 30 to 0, and two reads of one state answer
byte-identical warnings.
- [ ] With three subscriptions each carrying a warning, and one carrying two, the warnings come by kind
(`price`, `renewal`, `charged-after-cancel`) and within a kind by ascending subscription id; `review.weekly`
for `2026-01` and for `2026-03` answers the same `warnings`.
- [ ] `review.dismissWarning` of an active warning answers 200 `{"changeId":"<n>"}`, `dismissed_warnings`
gains exactly that row, and the next `review.weekly` lacks that warning; after `changes.undo` of that id the
warning is listed again and the canonical dump of every journaled table equals the dump taken before.
- [ ] A dismissed warning stays out of `review.weekly` on two later reads and after the clock moves a day;
a later trigger of the same kind on the same subscription (the 23.90 charge above) is listed although the
first was dismissed.
- [ ] `review.dismissWarning` answers `null` and adds no row to `changes` or `change_effects` for: `"nope"`,
`""`, `"preco"`, an id already dismissed, and the id of a warning that held before a later charge and no
longer holds; `[7]` answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] With the snapshot file missing, `review.dismissWarning` answers 503 `ledger_unavailable` and records
nothing.
- [ ] `review.runWarningAction` with `["price:1:2026-11-22","silence-pair"]`, `review.approve`,
`review.refuse` and `review.propose` with `["teto"]` and `["nope"]` each answer `null` and add no row to
`changes` or `change_effects`, also with the snapshot missing; `runWarningAction` with the action `"pause"`
answers `bad_request`.
- [ ] Without `--db`, the five methods still answer `read_only` before their body is read, and
`review.weekly` answers `"warnings":[]` and `"approvals":[]`.
- [ ] The five names are gone from `writesWithoutHandler` and the manifest walk passes.
- [ ] The golden files of `full/` and `empty/` are unchanged; the `full-authored/` answer of `review.weekly`
is re-recorded, validates against the manifest, and holds exactly the warnings its invented subscriptions'
marks imply; `testdata/golden/writes/` gains the effects of `review.dismissWarning` (one row appearing in
`dismissed_warnings`).
- [ ] `web/src/api/fake/review.test.ts` and `web/src/screens/revisao/weekly.test.ts` pass unchanged and no
file under `web/` is edited.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the hand-off: the
renewal's id built from the days left instead of the renewal day; the price warning's id built without the
charge's day (a second rise then stays hidden); `≤ 30` written `< 30`; the dismissed filter removed from
`review.weekly`; `dismissWarning` storing an id that holds no warning; the money text without the thousands
separator; a null method asking the recorder for a change id.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, each of the three kinds is produced, dismissed, kept dismissed
and taken back by undo in a test over an invented ledger, and a warning whose reason went away is gone.

## Tests
- Unit, table, `internal/api`: the money text over the five amounts above; the three sentences, the 0-day,
  1-day and N-day renewal forms and both cycle words, character for character.
- Unit, table, over values from `internal/subrules` for invented charge histories: the price rise (up,
  down, equal, a later rise), the renewal at 30, 1 and 0 days, at 31 days and one day past, on `Anual`,
  `Bienal` and a shorter cycle, the charge before, on and after the cancelling day, the stored creation

- Property, over generated subscriptions and charges: the warning kinds of a subscription equal its marks;

- Integration (`httptest`), over ledgers built for the test with `ledgertest` and a scratch app's database
  seeded through `authoredtest`: `review.weekly` with the clock set to each day named above; dismissal,

- Conformance (writes), the harness's modes: a recorded change for `review.dismissWarning` with its effects'
  golden file and its undo; nothing to do for `review.dismissWarning` of an unknown id and for
  `runWarningAction`, `approve`, `refuse` and `propose`.
- Golden (read conformance): `review.weekly` in `authoredReadCases` re-recorded into `full-authored/` (added
  there if the case is not yet in that list); `full/` and `empty/` unchanged.
- The stand-in's tests and the review screen tests, unchanged, as the proof that the interface needs

- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the hand-off.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/review.go`, `internal/api/review_warnings.go`, `internal/api/review_approvals.go`,
`internal/api/messages.go`, `internal/api/review_warnings_test.go`, `internal/api/review_test.go`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `internal/authored/` (only the review's store file, and only if the
functions over `dismissed_warnings` are missing)
**Reads only:** `internal/subrules/`, `internal/api/subscriptions.go`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`,
`internal/ledger/ledgertest/`, `web/src/api/contract/review.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/review.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/review-rules.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/review-data.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/review-model.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/review.test.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/subscription-rules.ts`,
`web/src/screens/revisao/WarningsCard.vue`, `web/src/screens/revisao/ApprovalsCard.vue`,

One package of the HTTP layer and, at most, one store file of the app's database: a new file that derives

close_reason: review.weekly derives its warnings from the subscriptions' marks (a price rise, a renewal within thirty days, a charge after cancelling), each with an id that names what triggered it; review.dismissWarning stores one as an undoable change; runWarningAction, approve, refuse and propose answer null. title: Work out the card's bills and each pot's balance and yield
description:
## What changes for the user
The card page has to answer three questions: when does the bill close, which bill is this purchase on, and how much of what was already spent this month will only be charged next month and has to be set aside. The pots page has to say how much each pot holds and how much it yielded this month. Today those answers come from invented constants. After this lands they can be worked out from the bank's own records, and where the records cannot support an answer the app says it does not know instead of showing a zero.

## Outcome
Two Go packages of pure functions: `internal/cardrules` (the closing date, the bill a purchase falls on, the amount that falls on the next bill) and `internal/potrules` (a pot's identity over time, its latest balance, its yield for a month with the daily rows behind it), plus the ledger query for a pot's yield.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app over a SQLite ledger collected from the person's banks. `internal/ledger` already reads that ledger read-only and returns typed rows with amounts in integer cents; `internal/brday` gives a day and a month in Brazil time. This bead adds interpretation for the card and for savings pots. Apart from the one query it adds to the reader, it does no SQL and no I/O.

**The closing date is predicted from a table, never read from a forecast.** The provider's `creditCardMetadata.billForecastDate` carries only a month on the card in use and must not be read. For that card (C6) the closing date depends only on the weekday of the nominal due date, with no exception across the bills examined:

| the due date falls on | days from closing to due |
| --- | --- |
| Monday to Thursday | 6 |
| Friday | 7 |
| Saturday | 7 |
| Sunday | 8 |

Which table applies to a card is the caller's choice: the rules take the table as a parameter and export the one above; this package does not work out which bank an account belongs to. The ledger keeps the nominal due date. The bank moves a due date on a non-business day to the next business day for payment, and that does not change the closing date. The due day itself is read from the ledger, never written in code. A card of a bank with no such table (the Itaú cards show no single offset per weekday) has an unknown closing date: return unknown, do not guess.

**`bills.closing_date` is the first day of the next cycle.** A purchase dated, in Brazil time, on or after a bill's `closing_date` belongs to the next bill; the day before belongs to that bill.

**The bill of a purchase.** `creditCardMetadata.billId`, when present, joins `bills.id` and is the answer. When absent, the purchase belongs to the first bill whose closing date is after the purchase day; with no such bill yet, to the predicted next one.

**The amount that falls on the next bill.** The purchases of the month dated on or after the predicted closing date, plus those of the two days before it that have not received the closed bill's `billId` (a purchase made right before closing sometimes slips to the following bill).

**A manual closing day** is a setting the person can choose later; the rules take it as an optional parameter, and it moves the closing date while the due date stays fixed.

**Pots.** `reserved_balance_history` has one row per reserve entry of an account's latest sighting of a day. A pot is identified by `reserve_id`, valid only when `stable_identity = 1`; names repeat, so two pots with one name are two pots. A pot whose identity is not stable cannot be followed across days and is reported for its latest day only. The latest balance comes from the reader's existing query. A pot absent from the latest sighting of its account is closed.

**Yield is not the change in balance.** A deposit raises the balance and yields nothing. The collector's README has a query for it, `caixinha_yield` (near lines 339-555 at the time of writing): copy it into the reader with a citation and honour its `reason` column, which says when the yield of a day cannot be computed. When it cannot, the yield is unknown, not zero. Decided with the user: yield is shown per month and opens to its daily rows.

**Two bases.** Nubank reports yield net of tax and Mercado Pago gross. Whether to convert to one base is open; until then every yield figure carries its base, and two bases are never added together.

**Attributing a movement to a pot.** A deposit or withdrawal row sits on the account and does not name the pot. This package receives such movements as plain values (account, day, amount) and attributes one to a pot when the account has exactly one pot, or when exactly one pot's balance changed by that amount on that day; otherwise the movement stays on the account as unattributed and is counted.

**What the sources leave open.** For each, write the smallest safe rule, state it in a comment, and report how many rows it matched on a real ledger, as a count only: the bill of a purchase with no `billId`; movement attribution; one base for yield.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] For a due date of 2026-01-12 (Monday) the closing date is 2026-01-06; 2026-03-12 (Thursday) gives 2026-03-06; 2026-06-12 (Friday) gives 2026-06-05; 2026-09-12 (Saturday) gives 2026-09-05; 2026-04-12 (Sunday) gives 2026-04-04.
- [ ] A card of a bank with no table returns an unknown closing date.
- [ ] A purchase on a bill's `closing_date` belongs to the next bill, and one the day before belongs to that bill.
- [ ] A purchase with a `billId` belongs to that bill even when its date says otherwise.
- [ ] A fixture carrying a `billForecastDate` that contradicts the table changes no result.
- [ ] The amount for the next bill includes a purchase on the predicted closing date, includes one made the day before without the closed bill's `billId`, and excludes one made the day before that carries it.
- [ ] A manual closing day moves the closing date and leaves the due date unchanged.
- [ ] Two pots with the same name on one account are two pots with separate balances.
- [ ] A pot with `stable_identity = 0` is reported for its latest day and has no history.
- [ ] A day with a deposit and no yield reports a yield of zero for that day, not the deposit.
- [ ] A day the query marks as not computable makes the month's yield unknown.
- [ ] Yields of a net pot and a gross pot are never summed into one figure: the function that totals yields returns one total per base.
- [ ] A movement on an account with one pot is attributed to it; on an account with two pots it is attributed only when exactly one pot's balance changed by that amount that day; otherwise it is returned as unattributed.
- [ ] The yield query is prepared against the collector's real schema by the existing schema test.
- [ ] A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs the rules over a real snapshot and logs only counts: bills, purchases per bill source (`billId` or date), pots, months with known and unknown yield, movements attributed and unattributed.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run completes with counts and no error.

## Tests
- Unit: the closing table for each weekday and for year and month ends; bill assignment on both sides of a closing date; the next-bill amount.
- Unit: pot identity, closed pots, yield against deposits, unknown yield, the two bases, movement attribution.
- Golden: the yield query against the real schema file.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each rule is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield_test.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/card.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/card-rules.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/savings-rules.ts`, `bin/ci`

Two new packages of pure functions with their tests, and one new query in the reader: its statement joins the registry in `queries.go`, where a test requires every statement of the reader to live, and its code is a new file. No other reader file changes.
close_reason: internal/cardrules predicts a card's closing date from a weekday table passed in by the caller, places a purchase on its bill (the bill id wins; otherwise the first bill closing after the purchase day; unknown beyond the window or without a table), and sums what the month's spending puts on the next bill. internal/potrules follows a pot by its stable reserve id, reports a pot without one for its latest day only, gives a month's yield with its daily rows and its base, never adds two bases, and attributes a movement only when exactly one pot can claim it. The reader gains the collector's yield query, run as three statements over the same CTEs because the single statement does not prepare in this module's SQLite. bin/ci: CI green; the opt-in runs over a real snapshot completed with counts only. Review added a test for the closing day itself. Left for the reads: the yield query is slow when called once per pair of sightings, and a sighting with no pot returns no row.

title: Dispatch writes through the recorder with their arguments checked against the manifest, answer refusals with a reason, and serve undo
description:
## What changes for the user
Today every button that changes something answers "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado." No
button starts working with this piece alone: it is the machinery every one of them will run on, and the
actions themselves (the budget, the categories, the tags, the settings) arrive one group at a time after
it. What it settles is how a change behaves once it exists. A change is saved whole or not at all. A
change can be taken back, and when it can no longer be taken back because something was edited after it,
the app says so instead of quietly overwriting the newer edit. When the app has to say no (the month is
closed, the item no longer exists) the server gives the reason instead of a generic failure. A person
who starts the app without telling it where to keep their entries sees exactly what they see today. If
this piece were wrong the person would find a change half saved, a request the app should have turned
away accepted, or an undo that destroyed something they did later.

## Outcome
The router runs a handler for a write or an evaluation when the server has its own database and the
method has a handler, and refuses with `read_only` otherwise, still before the body is read. A write's
arguments are checked against the method's schema from the manifest before its handler runs; the handler
works inside one transaction through a recorder that the router commits, and any failure keeps nothing.
A handler's refusal is answered as `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"..."}}` with status 409.
`changes.undo` is the first write with a handler. A walk over the manifest replaces the test that
expected all 56 writes and evaluations to be refused.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database* is
`finwise.db`, owned by the package `internal/authored`; the server has one only when started with `--db`
/ `FINWISE_DB`, and without it runs as today's read-only server. *The contract* is the TypeScript
interface `FinwiseApi` under `web/src/api/contract/`; *the manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`,
generated from it and never edited by hand, which lists 82 methods: 3 of class `session`, 23 `read`, 1
`evaluate` (`budget.evaluateScenario`) and 55 `write`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave.

Four pieces this slice stands on, each described in plain words because it is another slice's:

- *The recorder and the undo engine* (finwise-wi4): the layer of `internal/authored` through which every
  change to the app's database is written and journaled, and the engine that reverses a recorded change.
  *The journal* is the pair of tables `changes(id, at, day, author, method, extended, undone_at)` and
  `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`. The recorder works from a closed
  registry of journaled tables of two shapes: an *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts
  per key, and an effect on it is one column changing; a *set table* holds rows that are facts by
  existing, and an effect on it is one row appearing or disappearing.
- *The per-request views* (finwise-jzw): a handler's third parameter is one value carrying a view of each
  store, opened for the request: the ledger's (one handle, one read-only transaction on the snapshot)
  and the app's database's (one read-only transaction, or an empty view when there is no database). The
  same slice made the clock a required part of the API's configuration.
- *The contract's side of refusals and the schemas* (finwise-our): the kind `refused` and a closed list of
  nine reasons in the TypeScript contract and in the manifest, and `internal/contract` handing out each
  method's argument schema with its definitions and the list of reasons.
- *The parsers* (finwise-po6): `ParseReais` and `Reais.UnmarshalJSON`, which read an amount from its decimal
  text into integer cents and refuse anything beyond one billion reais, and `ParseWholeNumber`.

**What the code is today in the files this slice changes (each point checked in the file named, as it
is before those four pieces land).**

- `internal/api/router.go`: `serve` checks, in order, the verb, the session, the method's class, the
  content type and the body. A `write` or `evaluate` method is answered `read_only` after the session
  check and before `readArguments`, so its body is never read. `readArguments` requires
  `application/json`, at most 1 MiB, a JSON array, and a length between the method's `MinArguments` and
  `MaxArguments`; nothing else about the arguments is checked. `checkRegistered` refuses a handler for
  any name that is not a `read` method.
- `internal/api/reads.go`: one `Registry`; `Register` panics on a second handler for a method;
  `NewReadRegistry` runs the twelve functions of `domainRegistrations`.
- `internal/api/errors.go`: six kinds with their statuses (`locked` 401, `read_only` 403,
  `ledger_unavailable` 503, `bad_request` 400, `unknown_method` 404, `internal` 500); `errorEnvelope`
  holds only a kind; `kindOfReadError` maps a handler's error by its class (`badArgumentsError`,
  `readOnlyError`, the ledger's errors, anything else `internal`) and never looks at its text.
- `internal/api/conformance_test.go` compiles every method's result schema with
  `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` (a direct requirement in `go.mod`), draft 7, and validates
  an answer decoded by the library's own `UnmarshalJSON`. No non-test file imports that library today.
- `internal/api/router_test.go`: `TestEveryWriteAndEvaluationIsRefusedWithASession` requires exactly 56
  write and evaluate methods and `read_only` for each over four bodies (`[]`, `not json`, empty,
  `{"a":1}`); `TestAWriteIsRefusedBeforeItsBodyIsRead` proves with a counting body, for
  `transactions.setLine` only, that the body is read zero times;
  `TestAHandlerCannotBeRegisteredForAWrite` expects `NewHandler` to refuse a handler for
  `transactions.setLine`, `budget.evaluateScenario`, `session.unlock` and `no.such`.
- `internal/api/budget.go`: `readBudgetView` answers `read_only` whenever it is given a draft, even a
  malformed one, and `TestTheBudgetViewRefusesAnyDraftAsAWriteIsRefused` (`budget_test.go`) pins that
  for the drafts `[]`, a one-group document, `0` and `"x"`.
- `internal/api/session_routes.go`: `sessionService.dispatch` knows `status`, `unlock` and `lock`.
  `session.changePin` is of class `write` in the manifest, and a test in `session_routes_test.go` expects
  it to answer `read_only` without the PIN comparison running.
- `web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`: the stand-in's `undo` restores a whole-state snapshot and throws a plain
  error for a change it does not know or has already undone (`writes.test.ts`, "refuses a change it does
  not know, or one already undone", which calls `undo('nope')`).

**1. The registry.** It takes handlers of every class except `session`. `checkRegistered` becomes: a
registered name must exist in the manifest and must not be of class `session`. `Registry.Register` and
`domainRegistrations` keep their names (the repository's `AGENTS.md` documents them); `changes.undo` is
registered by a new `registerChanges`, in a file of its own, listed there.
