that forbid floats and the host's clock in the API, the ingest and the rule packages), and the clock is a
parameter. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant of `internal/authored`,
and every statement over the snapshot one of `internal/ledger/queries.go`. Interface text is Brazilian
Portuguese and everything else is English; the only Portuguese here is the history step and the three
reasons, quoted exactly. No component is touched.

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`), each with what binds it: the name and
signature of `ingest.Run` and of its counts, and how it is told why it was called; the method name
recorded on the rule's change (fixed, not a contract method); how "stopped listing in this run" is computed
from `first_run` / `last_run` and the run in `meta`, as long as a row is counted once, in that run, and not
again while it stays unlisted, and a second call with the same run counts it no more; how a caller holding
an older snapshot is kept from moving anything backwards; and where in `internal/authored` the statements
the ingest needs live (next to the tables' owner files, each registered). If a function a dependency was
expected to provide is missing, it is added beside its tables and named in the report; no migration is
added (none is assigned to this work).

**A limit of the test fixture this work has to lift.** The ledger's test fixture (`internal/ledger/ledgertest`) can now add a run and move the projection to it (`AddRun` returns the run's id, `ProjectTo(run)` moves `projection_state.projected_run`). But every scope the fixture creates belongs to run 1, and a document counts as covered only while its scope's run is the projected one: projecting an invented ledger to a later run leaves every transaction it added uncovered, so the clean list goes empty. To test one night after another (a pending row that vanishes, a posted row that appears, a second run over the same snapshot), the fixture has to be able to put documents under a scope of the later run. Extending `ledgertest` for that is part of this work; it changes no production code of `internal/ledger`.

## Acceptance criteria
The run gate
- [ ] As a timer tick, on a fixture at run 1: the first run goes on and records run 1; a second stops at
step 1 and writes no change; after a run 2 that ended `partial` is added and projected, the next goes on;
after a run 3 `complete` is added but not projected, the next stops; once it is projected, it goes on. The
same sequence with `complete` before `partial` behaves the same. A `failed` run that is not projected
changes nothing.
- [ ] As a budget change and as the command, a run goes on when the run is the one recorded.
Pairing
- [ ] A bank-pending transaction evaluated in an earlier run and then put on a line by the person
vanishes and its posted row (same account, cents and key, 2 days later) appears: after one run `tx_ids`
maps both ids to one key, the index row has the posted day and amount and is no longer bank-pending, the
posted row resolves to the person's line, the canonical dump of the journaled tables is unchanged, paired is
1, and the posted row is not evaluated (no rule step, applied 0, indexed 0).
- [ ] One to many (two posted candidates), many to one (two pending rows, one posted), and none: nothing is
mapped, each vanished pending row is counted unpaired once, its `tx_state` is unchanged, and the posted
rows are new transactions evaluated as any other.
- [ ] A pending row on 2026-03-31 on a line the March budget has, posted on 2026-04-02: when the April
budget lacks the line, the run's change (author `rule`) clears it as a save clears it; when April has it,
the line stays and no change is written.
- [ ] A vanished pending row that found no pair, then a run in which its posted row first appears within
the window: it is paired then. A posted row the index already holds is never paired.
- [ ] A vanished row unpaired is counted in the run it vanished and in no later run; listed again, it
resolves to its authored state as before, unpaired and indexed stay 0, and it is not evaluated again.
The start month and the budget gate
- [ ] With the database created on 2026-03-05 (start month 2026-03) and a budget for every month: a listed
transaction of 2026-02-28 is neither indexed nor evaluated; one of 2026-03-01 is. A transaction of
2026-02 the person put on a line is indexed by that write and is never evaluated.
- [ ] A transaction of a month with no budget, or whose budget has five empty groups, stays unindexed and
unevaluated across runs as timer ticks; after a budget with a line is saved for that month, a run as a
budget change evaluates it.
Decide applied
- [ ] Over an invented ledger with one transaction per outcome of `Decide` (an own transfer, a bill
payment, an unconverted row, a card refund, a fee charge and its discount, a default line, five examples on
one line, five of six, a person without nickname, an establishment never seen, a received PIX from an
unknown person): the counts are exactly those outcomes; applied rows hold the line, who = the rule and no
confidence, each with the step "Regra classificou como <linha>"; pending rows hold their reason, and a
suggestion and confidence only for "Baixa confiança"; left and fee rows hold nothing authored and are
marked evaluated. Every evaluated transaction is in exactly one outcome.
- [ ] A transaction the person put on a line (or that holds a pending review) before the run is marked
evaluated, keeps its line, gets no step, and counts in no outcome but "already decided"; the same holds
for a line the person sets after the ingest read the snapshot and before it took the lock (a test seam
between step 1 and step 2 is allowed).
- [ ] A rule's line taken back through its history step stays taken back after two more runs on new
projected runs; the other transactions of that run's change keep their rule lines.
- [ ] With five of six examples on Mercado and threshold 85, a transaction is pending "Baixa confiança"
with 83. The threshold is then set to 80 and a new run comes: that transaction is still pending with 83,
and a new transaction of the same key is applied Mercado. The same with the minimum of examples lowered
from 5 to 4 over four examples on one line.
- [ ] A transaction whose establishment key changed between two snapshots keeps its authored state and its
index row carries the new key; a new transaction under the new key with no examples of its own is pending
"Estabelecimento novo".
- [ ] A run that changes nothing authored writes no row in `changes`, and still records its run in `meta`.
Idempotence, concurrency and failure
- [ ] A second run right after the first, as the command, adds no row to `changes`, leaves the canonical
dump and the index equal, and counts 0 for every outcome.
- [ ] Two runs started at once on the same stores (two goroutines, each with its own handle on the
database): at most one change by `rule` is written, the end state equals that of one run, and the counts of
the two add up to those of one run.
- [ ] With the snapshot missing, with an unknown `user_version`, and with the projection row deleted, a run
returns the "snapshot unavailable" kind, and the journaled tables, the index and `meta` are byte-identical
in their canonical dump; the error's text contains no sentinel string stored in the fixture.
- [ ] `internal/ingest` fails a source test if a non-test file imports `log` or `log/slog` or calls
`fmt.Print…` or `fmt.Fprint…`; the float and `time.Now` guards inspect its files.
The real ledger and the gate
- [ ] The opt-in test passes against a real snapshot (run by the review, not by the lane), printing counts
only, and skips without `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT`; its failure messages are fixed sentences.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: the stop at step
1 removed (a tick writes again); the stop keyed on the latest complete run (a projected partial run is
skipped); the command made to stop at step 1; pairing accepting one to many; the posted row's day left
unrefreshed; the cross-month clearing skipped; an unpaired row counted on every run; the start-month gate
removed; the budget gate removed; `Decide` applied to a transaction that has a line; the "already decided"
check read before the lock; `evaluated` cleared by an undo or ignored (the rule's line comes back); a change
written when nothing changed; `meta` not recorded on a run with no change; the logger used inside
`internal/ingest`.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the ingest is idempotent and safe twice at once, a projected
partial run after a complete one and the reverse are both taken in, one to one pairs while one to many,
many to one and none do not, and the opt-in run reports its counts on a real ledger.

## Tests
- Integration, table (`internal/ingest`), over invented snapshots built with `ledgertest` and a temporary
  `finwise.db` with invented authored states built with `authoredtest`, the clock injected: the run gate
  over partial, complete, failed and unprojected runs; every pairing case above, the next night's snapshot
  built at a second path and renamed over the first; the start month on both sides of the first day; the
  budget gate; one transaction per outcome of `Decide`; a decision made before the run and one made between
  the read and the lock; a rule's step undone; the settings changed between runs; the reworded key; the
  vanished row listed again; the three failures.
- Property (`internal/ingest`): over generated small ledgers and sequences of runs, a second run changes
  nothing, the evaluated transactions add up across outcomes, and no transaction is evaluated twice.
- Concurrency (`internal/ingest`): two runs at once on two handles of one temporary file.
- Unit (`internal/authored`): each new statement registered and prepared against the migrated schema by
  the package's existing tests; the last ingested run in `meta` read and written through its functions.
- Unit, source (`internal/ingest`): no logger, no printing.
- Integration, opt-in (`internal/ingest`): the real ledger, counts only, as described above.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ingest/`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/view.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`,
`internal/ledger/testdata/ledger-schema-v1.sql`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`, `internal/txrules/`,
`internal/classrules/`, `internal/brday/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`,
`internal/api/shell.go`, `internal/api/transactions_period.go`, `internal/api/transaction_detail.go`,
`internal/authored/migrations/`, `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`, `bin/ci`

A new package of a few files (the run, the pairing step, the evaluation step, the counts, the
interpretation of the whole ledger) and the statements and store functions it needs in `internal/authored`,
with a builder in `authoredtest` if one is missing. Two modules and a new package with many tests, hence
`size:L`. No migration, no contract method, no screen, and no caller: `serve`, the timer, `finwise ingest`
and the call after a budget save are separate work.
close_reason: internal/ingest holds ingest.Run: one change by rule per run that refreshes the index, pairs a vanished pending row with the posted one that replaced it, clears the line references of a transaction that changed month, and evaluates each new transaction once from the tracking start month in a month whose budget has a line; it returns counts and logs nothing. Verified: gate green on the branch merged with main; the opt-in test run once over a real snapshot against a scratch database; about thirty deliberate breaks while writing it and seventeen in review, the four that survived at first now failing tests of their own.

title: Take the migration names in the tests from the migration files instead of lists written by hand
description:
## Outcome
The tests that check which migrations a database records take the migrations' names from the migration
files themselves and no longer from lists written by hand. Adding a migration that creates no table then
needs no change in any existing test file; one that creates a table needs a change in exactly the two
lists of tables, which are written by hand on purpose.

## Context
**Why.** The app's own database is migrated at start from SQL files, and several tests list the names of
all of them by hand. Every new migration has to be added to each of those lists, and two pieces of work
that each add a migration and run side by side conflict in every one of them. The lists prove nothing by
being written out: what the tests prove is that a fresh database records exactly the set the program
embeds, or that set plus what the test itself adds.

**The terms.** A *migration* is one SQL file of `internal/authored/migrations/`, today eight, named
`0001_journal` to `0008_session`. They are embedded into the program (`migrate.go`, `//go:embed`), read by
`loadMigrations`, applied in name order, and recorded in the table `schema_migrations` by name and
SHA-256, so that a changed or unknown one stops the start. `Options{Migrations}` lets a test open a
database with a set of its own; `withMigrations(t, extra)` in `support_test.go` builds the embedded set
plus extra files, and `EmbeddedMigrations` is exposed to tests by `export_test.go`.

**The lists, and which can be derived.**
- *The embedded names and nothing else*: `migrate_test.go` in
  `TestACopyIsTakenBeforeMigrating...` and `TestACopyNameAlreadyTaken...`, and `session_test.go` in
  `TestTheSessionMigrationIsRecorded`, which repeats the list in a sentence as well. These can be derived.
- *The embedded names plus the test's own extras* (`0002_x`, `0003_x`): `migrate_test.go` in
  `TestAMissingMigrationIsAppliedWhateverItsPosition`, `TestACopyIsTakenBeforeMigrating...` and
  `TestAFailingMigrationRollsBack...`. The extras are the point of those tests and stay written; the rest
  can be derived.
- *Names with their checksums*: `requireFreshSchema` in `recognize_test.go` and `requireCreatedDatabase`
  in `cmd/finwise/database_test.go`. The checksums are already computed from the files on disk
  (`embeddedSum`; eight read blocks in the second file), which is independent evidence that what the
  program embeds is what the files hold. The names can come from listing that directory on disk, so the
  evidence stays independent of the embedded set.
- *The twenty-seven table names* in those same two functions are the schema the SQL creates. They are
  written by hand on purpose and stay: a test that derived them from the program's own registry of tables
  would compare the registry with the database and pin nothing about the migrations.
- *The tests of one migration's constraints* (`review_schema_test.go`, `subscriptions_schema_test.go`,
  `transaction_schema_test.go`, `pots_schema_test.go`, `budget_schema_test.go`, `settings_test.go`) name
  their own migration and pin its columns and checks on purpose. They are not part of this.

**What changes today when a ninth migration is added**: five lists and a sentence in `migrate_test.go`,
the names in `recognize_test.go`, the list and the sentence in `session_test.go`, and a read block and the
names in `cmd/finwise/database_test.go`; and, only when it adds a table, the two lists of tables.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] In `internal/authored/migrate_test.go`, `internal/authored/recognize_test.go`,
`internal/authored/session_test.go` and `cmd/finwise/database_test.go` no list of the eight migration
names is written out: the names come from the embedded set, or, where checksums are compared, from
listing the migration files on disk.
- [ ] The tests that add their own migrations still name those extras by hand and still assert the same
resulting set.
- [ ] The two lists of table names are unchanged, and the tests of one migration's constraints are
untouched: `git diff --stat` shows none of the six files named for them.
- [ ] Each derived check was seen failing once, by breaking what it guards: a recorded name removed from
`schema_migrations` in the test's database; a migration file's bytes changed after the database recorded
it; and the pull request names the test that failed for each.
- [ ] With a throwaway ninth migration that creates no table added to `internal/authored/migrations/`,
`go test ./internal/authored ./cmd/finwise` passes without any edit to a test file; the throwaway file is
not committed.
- [ ] No source file outside test files changes, except a test helper if one is added beside
`internal/authored/support_test.go`.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: a migration that creates no table can be added without touching an existing test, and
every derived check still fails for a missing or changed migration.

## Tests
- Unit, existing, in `internal/authored` and `cmd/finwise`: the tests named above, asserting the same
sets from derived names.
- Unit, by deliberate break: the two breaks of the criteria, and the throwaway ninth migration.
- Golden: none involved.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/migrate_test.go`, `internal/authored/recognize_test.go`,
`internal/authored/session_test.go`, `internal/authored/support_test.go`,
`cmd/finwise/database_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/migrate.go`, `internal/authored/export_test.go`,
`internal/authored/migrations/`, `internal/authored/review_schema_test.go`,
`internal/authored/subscriptions_schema_test.go`, `bin/ci`

Five test files in two packages. No production code, no migration and no schema test changes.

## Recovery path
Test code only. Reverting the pull request brings the written lists back.
close_reason: The tests that check which migrations a database records take the names from the migration files: from the embedded set where recorded names are compared, and from the directory on disk where names are compared with their checksums, so that check stays independent of what the program embeds. The lists of table names and the tests of one migration's constraints are unchanged. Verified by the gate on the branch after main was merged in, by the author's deliberate breaks of every derived check, and in review by a throwaway ninth migration that needed no test edit and by a migration file changed on disk under an already built test binary, which the fresh-schema test caught.

title: Refuse an undo that would remove a budget line another change in force added to the same version
description:
## What changes for the user
The person saves a month's budget, and later saves the same month again only to add one more line. Each
save can be taken back. Today, if the first save is taken back while the second still stands, the app
accepts it and the whole budget of that month disappears, the line the second save added included; the
second save still reads as in force, and trying to take it back afterwards answers "Isso já foi alterado
depois e não pode mais ser desfeito.". No screen offers this today, because "Desfazer" is shown only for
the last change, but the server accepts it from anything that names an earlier change. After this lands,
taking back the first save while the second stands is refused with that same sentence and nothing
changes; taking back the second and then the first works, and leaves the month as it was before both.

## Outcome
An undo never removes a row that it does not itself restore, unless that row's table says its rows follow
their owner. A budget version's lines do not: undoing the change that created a version is refused as
stale while the version holds a line that another change in force wrote. A history step's reason does:
it keeps going with its step, as today.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. The app's database
(`internal/authored`) writes every change to *the journal*: one row per change and one per *effect*, the
row a change wrote with its value before and after. *Undoing* a change (`Database.Undo` in
`internal/authored/undo.go`, reached by the API method `changes.undo`, which takes any change's id)
restores what its effects recorded and marks the change undone; a change not undone is *in force*. An
undo is *refused as stale* (`*StaleChangeError`, answered `refused` with the reason `stale_change`) when
it can no longer be exact, for one when a later change in force wrote one of the same rows. The row a
change wrote is its *unit*. A *budget version* is the budget that holds from a month on: one row in
`budget_versions`, keyed by the month, and one row per line in `budget_version_lines`, keyed by the month,
the line's id and its name. The registry of journaled tables (`internal/authored/registry.go`) lets a
table declare that its rows are *owned* by rows of another (`Ownership{Owner, Columns}`): the lines are
owned by their version (`internal/authored/budget_tables.go`), and a history step's reason is owned by its
step (`internal/authored/transaction_tables.go`). These are the only two owned tables.

**The defect, reproduced through the API with the app's own tables.**
1. A: `budget.save` for a month that has no version of its own. It creates the version row and one row
   per line.
2. B: `budget.save` for the same month, sending A's lines back unchanged and one new line. A put of a row
   that is already there records no effect (`internal/authored/recorder.go`), so B's only effect is the
   new line's row, whose key is none of A's units.
3. `changes.undo` of A answers 200. Nothing later touched A's units, so the undo is not stale. When it
   removes the version row, `removeWithOwned` in `internal/authored/undo.go` reads every row the version
   owns and deletes them all, B's line among them, recording nothing. A is marked undone; B is not.
4. `changes.undo` of B answers `stale_change`: the row its effect left is gone.

Had B changed or removed one of A's lines, the undo of A would already be refused, since B would have
written one of A's units. Only a pure addition escapes. The engine's own test states the general
behaviour as intended, on scratch tables: "writing an owned row does not make the owner's change stale"
in `internal/authored/undo_test.go`. That is right for a reason, which has no meaning without its step,
and wrong for a budget line, which is the person's data.

**What is not exposed.** Closing a month cannot play B: it writes a version only at a month that has none
(`internal/authored/month_close.go`). A version a close created cannot gain a later line: a save for a
closed month is refused, and a save for an earlier month does not write into it. So reopening a closed
month, which undoes a close, does not meet this. Whether `budget.applyScenario` can play B was not
tested.

**What was decided, and what lost.**
- *Fixed now, although no screen reaches it.* The budget is the central thing the person authors, the
  server accepts the sequence today, and work that lets anything undo an earlier change (a command line
  for agents is planned) would reach it.
- *The rule goes where the wrong deletion happens, and each owned table says which kind it is.* When an
  undo removes an owner's row, an owned row that the same undo does not restore is taken along only if
  its table declares that its rows follow their owner; otherwise the undo is refused as stale and nothing
  is written. The lines of a version hold their owner; a step's reason follows it.
- *Rejected: having the second save record that it touched the version.* It would give the same refusal
  through the rule the engine already has, but it adds an effect that changes nothing to the journal,
  moves the committed effects files of the budget's write cases, and makes every later save of a month
  depend on every earlier one, so that two saves that each added their own line could no longer be taken
  back independently. With the rule in the engine, they can.
- *Rejected: refusing for every owned table.* Taking a step back removes the step with its reason
  (`TakeBackStep` in `internal/authored/transaction_lines.go`), also when the reason was written by a
  later change; that stays.
- *No repair is owed.* Nobody uses a database fed by writes yet.

**Tests that exist.** `internal/authored/undo_test.go` holds the engine's cases over scratch tables,
declared in `internal/authored/journal_fixture_test.go` (a `steps` table and a `step_reasons` table owned
by it) and in `internal/authored/authoredtest/scratch.go`. `internal/authored/journal_property_test.go`
and `internal/authored/line_references_property_test.go` run random histories. The budget's writes
through the API are tested in `internal/api/budget_writes_test.go`. A throwaway test of the sequence above
was written and run for the reproduction; it is not in the repository, so the first criterion asks for it
again.

## Steps to Reproduce
Over invented data; the test of this does not exist in the repository yet.
1. Save a budget for a month that has no version of its own (`budget.save`); keep the change id it
   answers.
2. Save the same month again with the same lines, their ids unchanged, and one new line.
3. Call `changes.undo` with the first change id.
4. Expected: refused with `stale_change`, the month's budget unchanged. Actual: answered 200, the month
   has no version and no lines, the second change is not marked undone, and `changes.undo` of the second
   change is then refused.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The sequence above exists as a test in `internal/authored/undo_test.go` over the app's own tables
and as a test in `internal/api/budget_writes_test.go` through the handlers, each was seen failing on the
code as it stands, and each passes: the undo of the first save is refused as stale, the month's budget
holds every line of both saves, neither change is marked undone, and the journal has no new row.
- [ ] After that refusal, undoing the second save is accepted and then undoing the first is accepted, and
the canonical dump of every journaled table equals the dump taken before the first save.
- [ ] Two later saves that each add one line of their own: undoing the earlier of the two is accepted
while the later stands and removes only its own line; undoing the first save is refused while either
stands.
- [ ] The same sequence with `budget.applyScenario` as the second change is tested: undoing the first save
is refused while what the scenario applied stands.
- [ ] A reason written to a history step by a later change still goes with its step: the engine's case
"writing an owned row does not make the owner's change stale" passes for a table declared as following
its owner, and the tests of taking a step back (`TakeBackStep`) pass unchanged.
- [ ] Every owned table of the registry declares whether its rows follow or hold their owner, and a test
fails for an owned table that declares neither.
- [ ] A property test over random sequences of budget saves and undos asserts that after every accepted
undo each change still in force finds every row its effects left, and it was seen failing on the code as
it stands.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is
empty.
- [ ] Each rule was seen failing once, by breaking it on purpose, and the pull request names the test that
failed for each: the refusal removed; the lines of a version declared as following their owner; a step's
reason declared as holding it; the refusal made after rows were already deleted, so that a refused undo
leaves something changed.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: the undo of a save that created a version is refused while a line another change added to
that version stands, the same two saves undone last first return the tables to where they began, and a
step's reason still follows its step.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/authored/undo_test.go`: the engine's rule over scratch tables of both kinds (rows
that follow, rows that hold), whole undo and the restore of a part.
- Integration, in `internal/authored/undo_test.go` over the app's own tables: the two saves, the three
saves, the undo in both orders, the canonical dump.
- Integration, in `internal/api/budget_writes_test.go`: the same through `budget.save`,
`budget.applyScenario` and `changes.undo`, with the answers and their error kinds.
- Property, in `internal/authored/journal_property_test.go`: random saves and undos with the invariant
that an accepted undo leaves every change in force whole.
- Golden: none moves.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/undo.go`, `internal/authored/registry.go`,
`internal/authored/budget_tables.go`, `internal/authored/transaction_tables.go`,
`internal/authored/undo_test.go`, `internal/authored/journal_fixture_test.go`,
`internal/authored/journal_property_test.go`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/scratch.go`,
`internal/api/budget_writes_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/journal.go`, `internal/authored/recorder.go`,
`internal/authored/budget_write.go`, `internal/authored/month_close.go`,
`internal/authored/transaction_lines.go`, `internal/authored/line_references_property_test.go`,
`internal/api/changes.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `bin/ci`

Four source files of one package: the engine's removal, the registry's declaration and the two tables
that are owned, with the scratch tables of the tests and the tests themselves. The journal's format, the
recorder, the budget's writes and the API's handlers are read and not edited; no effect a write records
changes, which is why no golden file should move.

## Recovery path
No stored row changes shape and nothing is migrated: the change is in what an undo refuses. Reverting the
pull request brings back the old acceptance and nothing else.
close_reason: An undo is refused, before anything is written, when removing a row would take along a row it does not itself restore in a table whose rows hold their owner. Every owned table declares whether its rows follow or hold their owner, and the registry refuses one that declares neither: a budget version's lines hold it, a history step's reason follows it. Undoing the save that created a version is therefore refused while a line another change added to it stands, for a later save and for an applied scenario alike, and undoing the later change first returns the tables to where they began. Verified by the gate on the branch after main was merged in, by the reproduction over the app's own tables and through the handlers seen failing on the earlier code, by a property test over random saves and undos that failed on the earlier engine, by the author's deliberate breaks, and in review by four more changes: three killed and one equivalent. No golden file moved.

title: Use the read-only app at the desktop on the real ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
For the first time the person opens finwise and sees their own money in it, at their own desk, instead of a designer's example. Everything the app shows about the bank's records gets a first look from the only one who can tell whether it is right, before anything that changes data is designed on top of it.

## Outcome
The user has used the read-only app at the desktop on a copy of the real ledger, and what was wrong or surprising is written down as beads.

## Context
finwise's interface was ported from a design and measured against it pixel by pixel, on an invented dataset; no person has ever opened it. Its backend reads the bank's records through rules that turn raw rows into the list a person expects: signs, purchases abroad, tax rows folded under their purchase, transfers between own accounts set apart, savings-pot movements out of the general list, the card's closing date, each pot's yield. Several of those rules were written where the sources were silent, and each reports how many rows it matched; only the person can say whether the result is right.

The part of the app that stores what the person authors (budget, categorisation, tags, subscriptions, closing a month) has no plan yet. That plan is the next piece of work, and it starts from what this first use shows. One finding already waits for it: the bank's records carry no merchant on any row, so the establishment of a card purchase is derived from its text.

This check runs at the desktop on purpose. Packaging the app as one binary and putting it on the home server come after the write side, so that the deployment is designed once.

**How to run it.** With a copy of the collector's snapshot at hand:

```sh
go build -o finwise ./cmd/finwise
printf '%s' '<six digits>' | ./finwise hash-pin        # prints the hash
FINWISE_PIN_HASH='<the hash>' ./finwise serve --ledger <path to pluggy-snapshot.db> --dev-insecure-cookie
npm --prefix web run dev:backend                        # in another terminal
```

Then open the address the dev server prints and unlock with the PIN.

**What to look at.** Início for two or three different months: is every purchase there once, is a purchase abroad in reais with its tax under it, are transfers between own accounts set apart. Contas and one account's page. The card page: the closing date, the due date, the amount that falls on the next bill. Cofrinhos: balances and yield against the bank's app. Patrimônio: the total against the sum the person knows. Budget, Assinaturas, Revisão and Configuração open empty, and trying to change anything says the app is read-only.

**Rules to confirm while looking.** Each of these was written where the sources were silent, and only the person can say whether the result is right:
- A debit on a bank account whose text starts with the bank's bill-payment wording is the payment of the card bill, shown as a movement and not as spending.
- A credit on the card with no operation type whose text names a payment is also a bill payment. Without the rule it would read as income.
- A card credit carrying a refund, cancellation or return word is a refund.
- A tax row named after its purchase is folded under it when it is 3.5% of the purchase, on the same card, within 3 days.
- An explicit international tax row is folded under a purchase abroad only when that card has exactly one such purchase that day. The others stay listed on their own: look for them on the cards that are no longer in use, and say whether they should attach by another key.
- A handful of rows no rule recognises are listed as ordinary transactions under "Outros".
- A card purchase with no bill id is placed on the first bill that closes after it; on a card with no known closing rule its bill is unknown.
- A savings pot counts as reserved and an investment as invested in the net worth until a bucket can be assigned.
- A deposit or withdrawal is attached to a pot only when exactly one pot can claim it; with only a few weeks of nightly balances most past movements stay on the account.

No real amount, name or document from the ledger goes into a bead, a commit or a screenshot attached anywhere.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The user has unlocked the app at the desktop against a copy of the real ledger.
- [ ] The user has opened every screen in the list above.
- [ ] Each thing found wrong is a bead of its own, described without any real value.
- [ ] Done when: the user says the read-only app is good enough to plan the write side on.

## Tests
- Manual: the walk through the screens above, by the user.

## Blast radius
No file is edited. The check only reads: the built binary, a copy of the snapshot, and the interface in a browser.
close_reason: Done by the agent in a browser, at the user's request, instead of by the user. Chromium drove the production build of the interface against the built backend over a copy of the real ledger, printing counts, booleans, routes and status codes only. 64 screens on two viewports: no failed read, no broken text, no empty screen, no horizontal overflow. For each of the 15 months the sum of what the API lists equals an independent sum taken from the ledger with its own reading of sign and of what leaves the list. The parts of the net worth sum to its total. The PIN, the session cookie, a reload, a transaction's panel, a pot opened from the list and the lock all behave. Found and fixed through beads: the three reads that show a yield took about fifteen seconds; editing the budget looped on its refused evaluation; the scenarios screen toasted on open and then lost the toast; a pot's page could not be opened from the list. Not done, and not something a script can do: comparing a figure on screen with what the bank shows. The rules written where the sources were silent, listed in this bead's body, are still unconfirmed by the person whose money it is.

title: Decide by rule what to do with a transaction never evaluated, and pair a vanished pending charge with its posted one, in one pure package
description:
## What changes for the user
Today no rule exists that would put a new purchase on the line the person always uses for that shop, and
nothing would notice that a charge the person already categorised while the bank showed it as pending has
come back, posted, under a new identity. This work writes those two rules down, and nothing calls them
yet, so nothing on screen changes. Once they are in use: a purchase from a shop the person has told the
app about goes on its line by itself, one the app is unsure of is asked about with its best guess and how
sure it is, and one it has never seen is asked about plainly ("Estabelecimento novo", or "PIX para pessoa
sem apelido" for a person with no nickname) with no guess at all; a transfer between the person's own
accounts, a card payment, a refund or a bank fee is never asked about. What the person would notice if
these rules were wrong: a purchase put on the wrong line without being asked, a confident guess where the
app knew nothing, or a categorised charge that loses its category the night the bank posts it.

## Outcome
A new package, `internal/classrules`, holds two pure functions with table tests and a property test.
`Decide` takes one transaction that was never evaluated, what the app's database knows about its
establishment, the person's own examples, the lines of the transaction's month and the two classifier
settings, and answers exactly one of: leave it, nothing to store (a fee), apply a line by rule, or pending
with one of three reasons and either a suggested line with its confidence or no suggestion at all. `Pair`
takes the bank-pending transactions the ledger stopped listing and the posted transactions never seen
before, and answers the pairs that match one to one. Nothing calls either yet; no file outside the new
package changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database* is
`finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`, where everything the person authors is kept.
*The index* is what that database remembers about the transactions it has evaluated or the person has
touched: one row per transaction under a key of its own, with its account, day, amount in cents,
establishment key and whether the bank still reports it pending, and a map from every provider id seen to
that key (finwise-jw2: the transactions' store, the migration that creates the index and the transactions'
tables). *An establishment key* is the key `internal/txrules` gives the other side of a row
(`EstablishmentKey`, prefixed `doc:`, `name:` or `text:`; `counterpart.go`); it may be a document number
and is never logged. *A budget line* has an integer id minted by the app's database; its name belongs to
each budget version. *The month's budget* is the budget version in force for a month. *The fees line* is
the built-in line "Tarifas e juros", in no group, which a month's budget has whenever it has at least one
line. *The queue* is the list of transactions waiting for the person to choose a line in the weekly
review ("Pendências"). *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the
design prototype runs on; it has no classifier at all (every pending review in its dataset is invented),
so these rules have no stand-in vectors to port and their vectors are written here.

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

- The nightly model call is not part of this work nor of the write side it belongs to: the app ends
  complete by hand and by rule, and the model is later work. Decided by the person, 2026-11-21. What
  lost: a model now, which meant choosing a provider and an outbound dependency in every verification.
- A transaction without a suggestion can be pending. Why: without a model, "new establishment" has
  nothing to suggest, and the queue must still work. What lost: waiting for the model; inventing a
  suggestion. (The contract change that lets a pending review carry no suggestion is separate work
  (finwise-zts: the nullable suggestion in the contract and the screens).)
- The rules run once per transaction, and a change of the threshold or the minimum of examples acts only
  on transactions evaluated after it. Why: a setting must not silently rewrite the queue or lines already
  applied. What lost: a retroactive pass on every settings change. This is enforced by the ingest, the
  one function that brings the app's database up to date with a new snapshot of the ledger and calls
  these rules for each transaction it has never evaluated (finwise-82m); `Decide` is pure and uses the values
  it is given.
- A pending row and the posted row that replaces it are two ids, and the app gives each transaction a key
  of its own so that carrying the person's work across is one mapping row. `Pair` decides when that
  mapping is safe.

**The package.** It takes plain values and returns plain values; it opens nothing, does no SQL and no
I/O, and knows no HTTP, as `internal/txrules`, `internal/cardrules` and `internal/potrules` do today. It
depends on `internal/money` and `internal/brday` only, so it does not import `internal/txrules`: its input
is a struct of its own, which the ingest fills from the interpreted row (`txrules.Transaction`:
`Movement` is `OwnTransfer` or `BillPayment` for a movement, `Unconverted`, `Refund`, `Fee`, `Person`,
`EstablishmentKey`, `Day`, the sign of `Amount`) and from the app's database. The classifier settings
are the threshold (50 to 99, default 85) and the minimum of examples (1 to 50, default 5), kept by the
settings' store (finwise-11u); the defaults are `defaultConfidenceThreshold` and `defaultMinExamples` in
`internal/api/settings_defaults.go` today. The test that forbids floats and the test that forbids
`time.Now` in non-test files were written to cover `internal/classrules` from its first file without
being edited (finwise-po6: reading money and whole numbers from JSON with no float, and the float guard;
finwise-jzw: the per-request views and the required clock, with its guard); check that they now inspect the
files this work adds.

**`Decide`.** What it needs to know about one transaction: whether it is a movement between own accounts
or a bill payment; whether it is unconverted (a foreign amount with no value in reais); whether it is a
credit; whether the ledger's rule marks it as a refund; whether it is a fee row (the charge, or the credit
that discounts it); whether the other side is a person; whether that establishment or person has a
nickname; the establishment's default line, if any; the set of line ids the budget of the transaction's
own month has (the fees line included when that budget has any line); the candidate examples; the
threshold and the minimum of examples.

`Decide` is called only for a transaction that was never evaluated and that has neither a line nor a
pending review; the ingest guarantees both. Its six steps, first match wins:

1. A movement between own accounts, a bill payment, an unconverted row, or a credit the ledger's rule marks
   as a refund: **leave it**. A refund waits for the person to point it at a line by hand; it does not go
   to the queue.
2. A fee row: **nothing to store**; it already counts on the fees line by rule (the budget's arithmetic
   counts a fee row that is on no line on the fees line: a charge adds, the credit that discounts it takes
   off).
3. Its establishment has a default line that the budget of the transaction's month has: **apply it, by
   rule**. A default line the month's budget lacks is passed over, and the steps go on to 4. Only an
   establishment has a default line; a person never does.
4. Otherwise take the examples: the transactions of the same establishment key that the person themselves
   put on a line (not a rule, not the model), not excluded, not split, whose line the budget of the
   transaction's month has. With `total` the number of those examples and `top` the number on the most
   frequent line:
   - with at least the configured minimum of examples (`total >= minimum`), one line strictly ahead of
     every other (`top` greater than the count of every other line), and `top * 100 >= threshold * total`:
     **apply that line, by rule**;
   - with any examples but short of one of those three: **pending, reason "Baixa confiança"**, suggesting
     the most frequent line, and on a tie the line of the example with the latest day, then the lower line
     id; its confidence is `top * 100 / total` rounded half up to a whole number.
5. No examples, and the other side a person with no nickname: **pending, "PIX para pessoa sem apelido"**,
   no suggestion and no confidence.
6. No examples otherwise: **pending, "Estabelecimento novo"**, no suggestion and no confidence. A person
   who has a nickname and no examples lands here too, as the steps read.

The candidate examples arrive as plain values, each with its line id, its day, who put it on its line,
whether it is excluded and whether it is split, and `Decide` applies the filter of step 4 itself, so every
condition of the filter is a row of its table test. Credits go through the same steps as debits, so the
queue also asks what a received PIX from someone unknown is. "Excluded" means what it means everywhere:
an exclusion that has a reason (an exclusion switched on without a reason does not take effect, so such an
example still counts). "Split" means the transaction has split parts. The examples are the person's own
decisions, so a line applied by rule in the same run is never an example, and the answer for one
transaction does not depend on the order in which the others are evaluated nor on the order its examples
arrive in. A line a rule applies gets the history step "Regra classificou como <linha>" and is stored
with who = the rule and no confidence (the contract's `Transaction.confidence` is "set when the classifier
was the model"); both are the ingest's to write, and both can be taken back like any other step.
`belowThreshold` stays false until the model exists: it is about the model's confidence only. The fourth
reason the person named in the interview, a value out of pattern, needs a judgment this work does not
invent; it arrives with the model.

The rounding of the confidence is integer arithmetic, `(top * 200 + total) / (2 * total)`, or anything that
gives the same whole numbers: 2 of 3 is 67, 1 of 3 is 33, 1 of 2 is 50, 5 of 6 is 83, 1 of 8 is 13, 3 of 8
is 38. With the defaults (threshold 85, minimum 5): 5 examples all on Mercado apply Mercado (500 >= 425);
4 all on Mercado are pending "Baixa confiança", Mercado, 100; 6 with 5 on Mercado and 1 on Feira are
pending, Mercado, 83 (500 < 510); 7 with 6 and 1 apply Mercado (600 >= 595); 6 with 3 and 3 are pending,
50, suggesting the line of the latest example. `threshold * total` equal to `top * 100` applies.

The shape of the answer (a tagged struct, an outcome kind with fields) is the implementer's; it must say
which of the four outcomes it is, the line for "apply", and for "pending" the reason (one of the three
strings above, exactly) and an optional line with an optional confidence that are present together or
absent together. Which of the four "leave" causes applied may be kept for counting.

**`Pair`.** A pending row and the posted row that replaces it are two ids in the ledger. The collector's
own view `pending_posted_candidates` (`internal/ledger/testdata/ledger-schema-v1.sql`) pairs them only
while both are present, on the same account, amount, currency, description and date, and does not promise
one to one; the clean list (`queryCleanTransactions` in `internal/ledger/queries.go`) hides a pending row
that has such a pair. So the moment the bank posts a charge, the pending row the person may already have
categorised leaves the list and a posted row with a new id appears. `Pair` is the app's own rule for
carrying the person's work across; it is not the collector's view.

`Pair` matches a bank-pending transaction of the index that the ledger no longer lists with a posted
transaction the index has never seen: same account, same amount in cents, same establishment key, the
posted day from zero to five days after the pending one (`0 <= posted - pending <= 5`, in calendar days).
A match counts only when it is one to one on both sides: the pending row has exactly one candidate among
the posted rows and that posted row has exactly one candidate among the pending rows. One pending row
matching two posted rows pairs neither; two pending rows matching one posted row pair neither; a pending
row it does not pair stays unpaired. `Pair` takes the two candidate sets as plain values (which index
rows vanished and which listed rows are new is the ingest's to select, from the index and the snapshot)
and answers the matched pairs, each the pending row's key and the posted row's provider id. The cents it
compares are the index's amount and the interpreted row's, compared like with like. `internal/brday` has
`Day`, `ParseDay`, `DayOf`, `MonthOf` and `MonthPeriod` and no difference of days; a helper may be added
there, with its own test, or kept private here.

**Privacy and conventions.** Nothing here touches a real ledger; every key, day, line and amount in the
tests is invented. Work happens in a worktree and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits, no
attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a work item or a plan in a commit message. Money is
integer cents and no float may appear in the money path. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a
registered constant (this work adds none). Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is
English; the three reasons and the history step are quoted exactly. A design value in a component comes
from a token (no component is touched).

## Acceptance criteria
`Decide`
- [ ] Each of these is left: an own transfer, a bill payment, an unconverted row, a card credit the rules
mark as a refund. Each holds even when the establishment has a default line the month has and five
examples on one line.
- [ ] A fee charge and a fee discount credit answer nothing to store, also with a default line and
examples.
- [ ] An establishment whose default line the month's budget has is applied that line by rule, whatever
its examples say; a default line the month lacks falls through to the examples.
- [ ] With threshold 85 and minimum 5: 5 of 5 on one line applies it; 4 of 4 is pending "Baixa confiança"
with that line and 100; 5 of 6 is pending with 83; 6 of 7 applies; 3 and 3 is pending with 50 and the line
of the latest example, and when both lines have an example on that latest day, the lower line id.
- [ ] With threshold 50 and minimum 2: two examples on two different lines are pending with 50 (no line
strictly ahead, although 100 >= 100), and 2 of 3 applies (200 >= 150). With threshold 60 and minimum 5,
3 of 5 against 1 and 1 applies (300 >= 300).
- [ ] Confidence vectors: 2 of 3 is 67, 1 of 3 is 33, 1 of 2 is 50, 5 of 6 is 83, 1 of 8 is 13, 3 of 8 is
38.
- [ ] An example put on its line by a rule, by the model, excluded with a reason, split, or on a line the
transaction's month lacks is not counted; one excluded without a reason is.
- [ ] No examples: a person with no nickname is pending "PIX para pessoa sem apelido" with no suggestion
and no confidence; a person with a nickname and an establishment are pending "Estabelecimento novo" with
no suggestion and no confidence; a received PIX from an unknown person, a credit, gives the first.
- [ ] Shuffling the examples never changes the answer (a property test over generated examples).
`Pair`
- [ ] One pending row and one posted row on the same account, cents and key, posted 0 and 5 days after,
are paired; 6 days after or 1 day before, not; another account, another cent, another key, not.
- [ ] One pending against two posted candidates pairs nothing; two pending against one posted pairs
nothing; with two independent one-to-one matches in one call, both pair; with no candidate, nothing.
- [ ] A posted row on the first day of a month paired with a pending row of the last day of the month
before, and a 29 February in the window of a leap year, pair as calendar days say.
- [ ] The answer does not depend on the order of either input.
The guards and the gate
- [ ] A source test fails if a non-test file of `internal/classrules` imports `database/sql`, `os`,
`net/http` or `internal/txrules`; the float and `time.Now` guards inspect at least one file of
`internal/classrules`.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main` shows changes only under `internal/classrules/` (and `internal/brday/` if the
day difference is put there).
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: the strict
lead check removed (a tie at the top applies); `>=` turned into `>` (the equality case is pending); the
minimum check removed; the tie broken by the higher line id or the earliest day; the confidence truncated
instead of rounded (2 of 3 gives 66); a rule's or the model's example counted; an exclusion without a
reason treated as excluded; a default line applied without checking the month; the refund or the fee
steps placed after step 3; the nickname check dropped from step 5; `Pair` accepting a match that is one
to many; the window made 0 to 4 or allowing a negative gap; `database/sql` imported in a scratch file.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the table tests cover every outcome of `Decide` and `Pair`
with the ties and edges above.

## Tests
- Table (`internal/classrules`): every step of `Decide` with the vectors above, over invented line ids,
  days and keys; the filters of the examples one row each; the tie-break rows; the confidence vectors.
- Property (`internal/classrules`): over generated examples and settings in their ranges, the answer is
  invariant under shuffling; "apply" never happens below the minimum, without a strict lead or below the
  threshold; every "Baixa confiança" carries a suggestion and a confidence between 1 and 100; the two
  other reasons never carry either. A failure prints what reproduces it.
- Table (`internal/classrules`): `Pair`, one row per case above, with both input orders.
- Unit (`internal/classrules`, and `internal/brday` if the helper lives there): the day difference across
  month and leap-year ends.
- Unit, source (`internal/classrules`): the purity guard, as `internal/txrules/purity_test.go` does.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/classrules/`, `internal/brday/brday.go`, `internal/brday/brday_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/txrules/`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`,
`internal/ledger/testdata/ledger-schema-v1.sql`, `internal/money/`, `internal/api/settings_defaults.go`,
`web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`, `bin/ci`

One new pure package of two or three files and their tests, and at most one helper in `internal/brday`. No
caller, no contract change, no screen: the ingest that calls these functions and the contract change that
lets a pending review carry no suggestion are separate work.
close_reason: internal/classrules: Decide (leave, nothing to store, apply, pending with reason and optional suggestion, in the plan's order, ties never applying by themselves, only the person's own examples counting) and Pair (same account, cents and establishment key, posted zero to five days after, one to one on both sides). Pure: no I/O, no float, no clock. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main; hosted check passed. Review: three boundary mutations (exactly the minimum of examples, a share exactly at the threshold, a posted row of the same day) each failed a test; the implementer's 33 breaks each failed one.

title: Create and migrate the app's own database behind `serve --db`, refusing any file that is not its own
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the app shows a person their money and can keep nothing they say about it: a budget line, the
category of a purchase, a tag or a note is answered with "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi
alterado.", because the program has no place of its own to keep it. This work gives it that place: a
file that belongs to the app, created the first time the program is started with it, that survives a
restart and is never the file the bank records arrive in. Nothing on screen changes yet, and every
button still answers the same sentence. What the person would notice if this were wrong is the worst
kind of failure: the program started over the wrong file and damaged it, an update that quietly
scrambled what they had typed, or the app one day asking them about years of old purchases because it
forgot the month in which they began using it.

## Outcome
A new package, `internal/authored`, owns the app's database, `finwise.db`. It recognises a file by
its first hundred bytes before writing a byte to it, opens it with fixed connection settings, applies
embedded migrations recorded by name and checksum, creates the journal tables and `meta` (migration
`0001_journal`), records once the month in which the database was created, and keeps every SQL
statement as a registered constant under test. `finwise serve` gains `--db` / `FINWISE_DB`: absent,
the server is exactly today's read-only server; present, the database is created if missing or empty,
migrated and kept open for the life of the process, and a file that is not finwise's, or a migration
history the binary cannot vouch for, stops the start with the file untouched. No route answers
differently than before.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app for one person. It has two stores. The **ledger** is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate program, the **collector** (pluggy-sync), fills from the banks
every night and replaces by an atomic rename; each such file is a **snapshot**, and finwise only ever
reads it, through `internal/ledger`. The second store does not exist yet: the **app's own database**,
`finwise.db`, where everything the person authors will live (the budget, the category of each
transaction, tags, notes, settings). Today the Go backend (`cmd/finwise`, `internal/api`) performs no
write to any SQLite file, and every method of the API that changes something answers `read_only`.
This bead creates the database and the discipline around it. Nothing reads or writes authored data
yet; that is later work, and all of it stands on what is built here.

The failure that matters in this app is a wrong total or a silently dropped transaction; the write
side adds a second one: a change the person made that is lost, or applied to the wrong thing. Here
that means three things: never write to a file that is not ours, never run a schema change that cannot
be traced or taken back, and never lose the month the person started.

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

| decision | why | what lost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The server runs read-only when no `--db` is given, and a write method without a handler keeps answering `read_only` | the write side lands one domain at a time and the app is never half-broken; the interface already handles `read_only` | a switch that turns every write on at once |
| Migrations are recorded by name in a table and every missing one is applied; the names are assigned in advance, one owner each | work lands in parallel, so a lower number can arrive after a higher one | `PRAGMA user_version` as "the number applied" |
| The two stores are never joined in SQL: rows are joined in Go | the ledger reader hands out rows, never a connection, and the snapshot is swapped under it | `ATTACH`; copying the ledger into `finwise.db` |

One more was decided by the person who uses the app, on 2026-11-21: the app asks about uncategorised
transactions from the month in which `finwise.db` is first created. Earlier transactions are never
put in the review queue (the list of transactions the app asks the person to categorise); they can
still be categorised by hand, or reached by the action that applies a category to every purchase of
one establishment. The month is one value in the database. What lost: all history in the queue on day
one, and a month chosen by hand.

**The package.** `internal/authored` owns `finwise.db`: opening, migrations and, in later work, the
recorder, the journal and undo, with one file per group of tables. It is the only package that
executes SQL against `finwise.db`. It depends on `internal/money` (amounts as integer cents) and
`internal/brday` (a day and a month in Brazil time) and on nothing else of this repository: not on
`internal/ledger`, not on `internal/api`. It never attaches or opens the snapshot. It logs nothing and
prints nothing; it returns errors and `cmd/finwise` reports them. A sibling package
`internal/authored/authoredtest`, which will build invented authored states for other packages'
tests, is later work and is not created here; this bead's tests keep their helpers in their own test
files.

**The setting.** `--db` / `FINWISE_DB` is a file path; the flag wins over the variable, as
`firstNonEmpty` already does for `--listen` and `--ledger` in `readServeSettings`
(`cmd/finwise/serve.go`). Absent: the server is today's, unchanged, and no file is created. Present:
the file is created if missing (its directory must exist and is never created), migrated, and kept
open for the life of the process, then closed on shutdown. It is not reopened per call the way the
ledger reader reopens the snapshot (`Reader.read` in `internal/ledger/open.go`): unlike the snapshot,
nobody swaps this file. `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` stays required at start either way
(`completeServeSettings`); later work lets a changed PIN be stored in the database, and until then
the variable is the only source. The database is opened before the server accepts a connection, so a
refused database never leaves a server answering. With `--db` given, every write still answers
`read_only` after this bead: `internal/api` is not touched, and its test that all write and evaluate
methods are refused (`TestEveryWriteAndEvaluationIsRefusedWithASession` in `router_test.go`) keeps
passing as it is.

**Recognition comes before anything is written, and does not open the file as a database at all:** it
reads the file's first hundred bytes. A file that does not exist or is empty is a new database.
Anything else must be an SQLite file whose header carries the application id finwise stamps,
`0x46494E57` (decimal 1179209303, the bytes `FINW`); any other file, the collector's snapshot
included, is refused. Only then is the file opened for writing. In SQLite's file format the header is
those first hundred bytes: bytes 0 to 15 hold the text `SQLite format 3` and a zero byte, and bytes 68
to 71 hold the application id as a big-endian integer. A file shorter than that and not empty is not
an SQLite file and is refused like any other. Reading bytes is what keeps a refused file untouched: by
SQLite's documentation, even a read-only open of a database in write-ahead mode can leave a `-shm` and
a `-wal` file beside it in a writable directory, and opening for writing with `journal_mode(WAL)`
rewrites the header.

A new database gets its application id written and flushed to the main file before it is put in
write-ahead mode, so a crash right after creation cannot leave a file finwise would refuse. The reason
is the same reading of bytes: in write-ahead mode a committed change stays in the `-wal` file until a
checkpoint copies it into the main file, so an id stamped after the switch may not be in the header
when the process dies, and recognition, which looks only at the main file, would then refuse the
app's own database. A file that stopped right after the stamp (the header with the id and no table) is
ours, and the next start finishes creating it.

The proof uses a foreign database in write-ahead mode, compares its bytes before and after and
requires that no file appeared beside it; an invented collector snapshot is refused the same way,
byte for byte. `TestQueriesLeaveTheSnapshotByteForByteUntouched` (`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`,
with `fileHash` in `support_test.go` and `listDirectory`) is the model for that comparison.

**Connection settings travel in the DSN**, so every connection of the pool has them, as the ledger
reader does with `_pragma`: `foreign_keys(1)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`,
`journal_mode(WAL)`, and immediate write transactions (`_txlock=immediate`). Reads use read-only
transactions, which the driver begins without taking the write lock. That last sentence was checked
against the driver in `go.mod` (`modernc.org/sqlite` v1.62.0): `newTx` in its `tx.go` issues a plain
`begin` when the transaction options say read-only and `begin immediate` otherwise, and `_txlock`
accepts `deferred`, `immediate` and `exclusive`. Unlike the ledger reader, which holds one connection
(`SetMaxOpenConns(1)`), this handle is a pool: a reader must not wait for a writer. What the handle
offers to later work is exactly two kinds of transaction, a read-only one and an immediate write one;
the recorder, the layer through which every change to the app's database will be written and
journaled (finwise-wi4), builds on the write kind, and the per-request views of both stores that handlers
will receive (finwise-jzw) build on the read kind. The pool's DSN asks for write-ahead mode on every
connection, so for a new file the stamp of the paragraph above has to happen before the first
connection of that pool is made. A write that fails at run time, including when the
five-second wait for the lock runs out, rolls back and returns an error with nothing kept; the API
will answer it as `internal`.

**Migrations.** SQL files embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`. A table
`schema_migrations(name, sha256)` records each one applied; it is the runner's own table, not part of
any migration file. A migration's name is its file name without the extension. At start every file
not recorded is applied in name order, each in one transaction together with its own
`schema_migrations` row. A recorded name whose checksum differs from the embedded file, or a recorded
name the binary does not have, is refused: the start fails and nothing is applied. Because every
*missing* one is applied, a database that records `0001` and `0003` and meets a binary that also has
`0002` gets `0002`; there is no "highest number applied". Before migrating a database that already
holds data, the file is copied with `VACUUM INTO` to `<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>` beside it, where
`<name>` is the database's file name; an existing copy is never overwritten, and a migration never
runs when the copy could not be written. If a migration fails, its transaction rolls back, the copy
taken before it stays beside the file, earlier migrations of the same start stay applied, and the
start fails. The runner takes its set of files as a value (the embedded one in production) so a test
can hand it a changed, an unknown, a failing or an out-of-order set.

The names are fixed in advance and this bead creates only the first: `0001_journal` (here), then
`0002_budget`, `0003_transactions`, `0004_settings`, `0005_pots`, `0006_subscriptions`, `0007_review`,
`0008_session`, each created by the later work that owns its tables. Rules every migration file
follows, this one included: every table declares its primary key, `NOT NULL` where a value is
required, foreign keys to `lines`, `tx_index`, `budget_versions` and `changes` (of which only
`changes` exists here), and `CHECK`s for every closed set of values and for amounts that cannot be
negative; each owner proves with a test that a duplicate, an invalid value and a negative amount are
refused by the database itself. The column lists are the starting point; an owner may add a column it
proves it needs, in its own file. A file, once applied anywhere, is frozen by its checksum.

**`0001_journal`.** The **journal** is the record of every change made to authored data: each write
is one change with an author, and can be undone. This migration creates its tables and `meta`; nothing
writes them yet.

- `changes(id, at, day, author, method, extended, undone_at)`. `id` is
  `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, as every id this database mints, so an id is never reused and a
  stale handle can never point at a newer object; on the wire it is the handle of a change, written
  as a decimal string. `at` is the instant the change was made and `day` its Brazil day
  (`YYYY-MM-DD`). `author` is one of `person` (an HTTP session), `rule` (the step that brings the
  database up to date with a new snapshot and classifies new transactions by rule) and `model`
  (reserved for a later nightly model call). `method` is the API method that made the change.
  `extended` says whether a later write appended its effects to this change. `undone_at` is null
  until the change is undone.
- `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`. One row per recorded effect, in the
  order `seq` within its change, with a foreign key to `changes`. `tbl` is the table written, `key`
  the row's key as canonical JSON (an array in column order), `col` the column for a table of
  independent facts per key and null for a table whose rows are facts by existing, `before` and
  `after` the content on each side, null when there was none.
- `meta(key, value)`: the tracking start month, and later the last collector run the app has taken in
  and the instant of the last backup.

The recorder is written later against exactly these columns, and by then this file is frozen by its
checksum in every database that has started with it, so what it will record must fit `change_effects`
as it is created here: one column of one key changing; one row appearing or disappearing; and, for a
table of things that are created whole (a subscription), the creation of a row, which the recorder
treats as a unit of its own.

Not every table of this database is journaled. The ones deliberately left out are named: `changes`
and `change_effects` (the journal itself), `schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index` and `tx_ids` (what
the database remembers about the transactions it has seen: observations, not decisions), `lines` (a
budget line's id, once minted, exists for good) and `pin`. Every table created here is on that list,
so its rows are written by plain registered statements of this package. The guard that fails when a
table is in neither list arrives with the recorder (finwise-wi4) and carries the whole list from the
start, including the names whose tables arrive later (`tx_index`, `tx_ids`, `lines`, `pin`).

No column here is an amount, so "a negative amount is refused" has nothing to bite on in this file;
its proof is a duplicate, an invalid value and a dangling foreign key. How an instant is written in
`at` and `undone_at`, the key names inside `meta`, and the column types are the implementer's, bound
by the rules above. Later work reads `meta` through functions of this package, never by key.

**The tracking start month, and the clock.** Creation sets, in the same transaction as the first
migration and from the injected clock, the month in which the database was created: `YYYY-MM` in
Brazil time (`brday.MonthOf`). Nothing later sets it again: not a migration, not the first time the
database is brought up to date with a snapshot, not a restore from a copy. The package offers it as a
read. The clock is a required part of the configuration: opening the database without one fails at
once, nothing in `internal/authored` falls back to the host's clock, and only `cmd/finwise` supplies
the host's. Today `cmd/finwise` has none to give: `environment` in `cmd/finwise/main.go` carries the
streams, `getenv` and `listening`, and `serve` leaves `api.Config.Now` unset so `withDefaults` in
`internal/api/router.go` falls back to `time.Now`. `environment` gains a clock, which `main` fills
with the host's and a test with a fixed one; the copy's timestamp comes from the same clock. Making
the clock required in the API's own configuration as well, and removing that fallback, belongs to the
work that hands each handler a view of each store per request (finwise-jzw); `api.Config` is not changed
here.

**Statement discipline, mirroring the ledger's.** Every statement is a registered constant, a test
prepares each against the migrated schema, and a test fails on a statement that is not registered.
The ledger's version is `internal/ledger/queries.go` (constants named `query…` and the map
`allQueries`), `export_test.go` (`AllQueries`), and three tests in `schema_test.go`:
`TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema`, `TestEveryQueryConstantIsRegistered` and
`TestNoStatementEscapesTheRegistry`. Mirror the intent, not the blind spots. The ledger's
registration test parses only `queries.go`, because the ledger keeps every statement there; this
package keeps one file per group of tables, so its test looks at every non-test file, including files
later work adds. The ledger's escape test inspects only calls to `QueryContext`, `QueryRowContext`,
`ExecContext` and `PrepareContext`, so a call to `Exec`, `Query`, `QueryRow` or `Prepare` would pass
unseen; here both families are covered. It allows one literal, `PRAGMA user_version`; here the
exceptions are named one by one (the execution of an embedded migration file, which is checked by
checksum instead, and whatever pragma cannot be a prepared constant), and it keeps the ledger's floor
that fails when the scan has stopped seeing calls. No SQL text is assembled at run time.

**Failure, and what a message may say.** If the database cannot be opened, recognised or migrated at
start, `serve` exits non-zero with a message naming the path and the reason, never the content
(`runServe` already prints `finwise: <error>` and returns `exitFailure`). Use errors with fixed
sentences, as `UnreadableSnapshotError` in `internal/ledger/open.go` does: a raw SQLite error can
quote a value. Failure paths this bead owns:

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| `--db` points at a file that is not ours | refused at start, file untouched, no side file created |
| the database holds a migration the binary does not know, or a changed one | refused at start |
| a migration fails | its transaction rolls back; the copy taken before it is beside the file; `serve` exits |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; `internal` |

**Left to the implementer, and what binds each** (these are what make this bead `spec:open`).

- The layout of the UTC timestamp in the copy's name: UTC, from the injected clock.
- What "already holds data" means for taking the copy: at least any database in which a migration is
  already recorded; a file this start created, or found missing or empty, needs none.
- What happens when the copy's name is taken: refuse the start or use another unused name, never
  overwrite.
- How the application id of a new file is written and flushed before the switch to write-ahead mode,
  as long as the main file's own bytes 68 to 71 hold it while the database is still open and before
  any checkpoint.

Each choice is stated in a comment where it is made.

**Privacy.** No test here touches a real ledger: the "collector's snapshot" of the refusal proof is an
invented one built by `ledgertest.New` (`internal/ledger/ledgertest`), which loads the collector's
schema and stamps no application id, and the foreign database in write-ahead mode is one the test
creates. Fixtures are invented. The pre-migration copy is a whole copy of
what the person authored, and `.gitignore` today ignores `*.db` and `*.db-*`, neither of which matches
`finwise.db.before-…`; it gains a pattern so a copy made inside the tree cannot be committed.

**Conventions.** Work happens in the worktree it was given and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a work item or a plan in a
commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; this package gets
the same source guard `internal/api` has (`TestNoSourceFileOfTheHTTPLayerTouchesAFloat` in
`internal/api/reais_test.go`). Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant.
Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component
comes from a token (neither arises here). The standard library and the driver already in `go.mod` are
enough.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Started with neither `--db` nor `FINWISE_DB`, `finwise serve` behaves as before: the existing
tests of `cmd/finwise` and `internal/api` pass unchanged and no database file is created.
- [ ] `serve --db <dir>/finwise.db`, file missing and `<dir>` existing: the server starts; the file's
`PRAGMA application_id` is 1179209303; it holds the tables `schema_migrations`, `changes`,
`change_effects` and `meta` and no other besides SQLite's own `sqlite_sequence`; `schema_migrations`
has exactly one row, named `0001_journal`, whose `sha256` is the SHA-256 of the embedded file;
`PRAGMA journal_mode` answers `wal`. A graceful stop exits 0.
- [ ] `FINWISE_DB` supplies the path when the flag is absent, and the flag wins when both are given.
- [ ] `--db` in a directory that does not exist exits non-zero, names the path on standard error and
creates no directory. `--db` without `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` exits non-zero as today.
- [ ] Given as `--db`, each of these is refused with a non-zero exit, its SHA-256 equal before and
after, and its directory listing equal before and after (no `-wal`, `-shm`, `-journal`, no copy): a
foreign database in write-ahead mode with one table; an invented collector snapshot built by
`ledgertest`; a database with one table and application id 1; an SQLite database with no table and no
application id; a text file of more than a hundred bytes that is not a database; a file of ten bytes.
The message names the path and contains no sentinel string the test stored inside the file.
- [ ] A file of zero bytes given as `--db` is accepted and becomes a database as in the second
criterion, exactly as a missing one does.
- [ ] While a newly created database is still open, and before any checkpoint, bytes 68 to 71 of the
main file, read directly from disk, are `46 49 4E 57`.
- [ ] A file that holds only an SQLite header with application id 1179209303 and no table (a creation
that stopped right after the stamp) is accepted, becomes a database as in the second criterion, and
takes its tracking start month from the clock of the start that finishes it.
- [ ] Opening the database without a clock returns an error. `time.Now` is named in no non-test file
of `internal/authored`, and in `cmd/finwise` only where `main` builds `environment`.
