- [ ] Created with the clock at 2026-12-01T01:30:00Z, the tracking start month reads `2026-11`.
Reopened with the clock at 2027-02-10T12:00:00Z it still reads `2026-11`, and it still does after a
start that applies a further, test-supplied migration.
- [ ] A second start with nothing pending applies nothing, leaves `schema_migrations` as it was and
creates no `.before-` file.
- [ ] A database recording `0001_journal` and a test migration `0003_x`, started with a set that also
has `0002_x`, ends with three recorded rows and `0002_x` applied.
- [ ] A set in which one byte of an applied file differs is refused; so is a database recording a
name the set lacks. In both, nothing is applied, `schema_migrations` is unchanged and no copy is made.
- [ ] A pending migration over a database that already records one: before it runs, a file named
`<database file name>.before-<UTC timestamp>` appears beside the database, carries application id
1179209303, answers `ok` to `PRAGMA integrity_check`, and does not record the pending name. A file
already at that name is byte-identical afterwards.
- [ ] A migration that fails (test-supplied) leaves its tables absent and its name unrecorded, leaves
earlier migrations of the same start applied, leaves the copy beside the file and makes the open fail;
through `serve` the exit is non-zero and names the path. When the first migration of a new file is the
one that fails, the next start with a correct set succeeds on that same file.
- [ ] On three connections held at once from each of two handles on one file, `PRAGMA foreign_keys`
answers 1, `busy_timeout` 5000, `synchronous` 2 and `journal_mode` `wal`.
- [ ] With two handles on one file: a `change_effects` row for a change that does not exist is refused
through each; a second write transaction begun while the first is open returns only after the first
commits; a read-only transaction begun on the other handle while a write transaction is open returns
at once and reads the state from before that write.
- [ ] The database itself refuses: a second `change_effects` row with the same `change_id` and `seq`;
a second `meta` row with the same key; a `changes` row whose `author` is not `person`, `rule` or
`model`; a `changes` row with `at`, `day`, `author` or `method` missing; an `extended` outside its two
values.
- [ ] After the highest row of `changes` is deleted, the next row gets a higher id, never the deleted
one.
- [ ] Every statement constant of `internal/authored` is registered and prepares against the migrated
schema. A constant left out of the registry fails a test; a statement executed from a non-test file
that is not a registered constant or a named exception fails a test, through the `…Context` methods
and through `Exec`, `Query`, `QueryRow` and `Prepare` alike; the scan fails when it inspects no call.
- [ ] A source test fails on `float64`, `float32`, `ParseFloat`, `FromFloat` or a float literal in a
non-test file of `internal/authored`.
- [ ] `git check-ignore` matches `finwise.db.before-x`.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api`, `internal/ledger` or `web/` is changed.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: recognition
done by opening the file as a database, or moved after the write-open (the byte and side-file
comparison fails on the foreign database in write-ahead mode); the application id stamped after the
switch to write-ahead mode (the main file's header lacks it while the database is open); the clock
defaulted to the host's when none is given; the checksum comparison removed;
the unknown-name check removed; the copy skipped; `foreign_keys` dropped from the DSN;
`_txlock=immediate` dropped (the second writer no longer waits at its begin); the tracking start month
written on every open; a statement constant left unregistered; a `float64` added.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, a foreign database in write-ahead mode and an invented
collector snapshot given as `--db` are each refused byte for byte with nothing appearing beside them,
and a changed or unknown migration stops the start.

## Tests
- Integration, `cmd/finwise` (the existing `runCommand`, `refusalVars`, `cancelledContext` and
`startServer` of `finwise_test.go`), over temporary directories: start with and without `--db`, the
environment variable, the missing directory, the refused files with hashes and directory listings,
the zero-byte file, a failing migration's exit.
- Unit, `internal/authored`, over temporary files: recognition case by case from the first hundred
bytes (missing, empty, ours, ours with no table yet, foreign in write-ahead mode, foreign with another
id, no id, not SQLite, too short); the header bytes of a new database read from disk while it is
open; the tracking start month with a fixed clock on both sides of midnight in Brazil; opening without
a clock.
- Table, `internal/authored`, over test-supplied migration sets: nothing pending, out of order, changed
checksum, unknown recorded name, failing migration, first migration failing, the copy and its checks,
a name already taken.
- Unit, two handles on one temporary file: the four pragmas on several pooled connections, the foreign
key on both, the waiting writer, the reader that does not wait.
- Unit, the migrated schema: each constraint of `0001_journal` refused by the database; ids not
reused.
- Unit, source scans: every statement registered and prepared; no statement outside the registry; no
float.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/`, `cmd/finwise/serve.go`, `cmd/finwise/main.go`,
`cmd/finwise/finwise_test.go`, `.gitignore`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/queries.go`, `internal/ledger/schema_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`, `internal/brday/`, `internal/money/`,
`internal/api/`, `bin/ci`

One new package (opening and recognition, the migration runner, the one migration file, the statement
registry, the read of the tracking start month, and their tests) and the wiring of one flag in
`cmd/finwise`, which also gains a clock in `environment`. About eight code files in two packages, and
the first schema of a new database, hence `size:L`. `internal/api` is read to see what must not
change and is not edited: handlers do not receive the database in this bead.

## Recovery path
The database is new, so there is nothing to convert and nothing this bead can lose but the file it
creates. To stop using it, start the server without `--db`: it is today's read-only server and the
file is left alone. To restore a database from a copy (the one a migration takes before it runs, or
any consistent copy): stop the server; check the copy (`PRAGMA integrity_check` answers `ok`, the
application id is 1179209303); put it in place of the database with no `-wal` or `-shm` file beside
it; start the server. A binary older than the database refuses it at start (it records a migration
that binary does not know) instead of guessing, so going back to an older binary means going back to
the copy taken before the migration. Deleting a database also deletes the month it was created in;
the next creation records a new one.
close_reason: finwise serve --db (or FINWISE_DB) creates, recognises and migrates the app's own database, and without it the server is the read-only server it was. Recognition reads the file's first hundred bytes and never opens a foreign file as a database: seven kinds of file that are not the app's (the collector's snapshot, another application id, no id, a text file, a short file, a write-ahead database with a pending -wal, a non-SQLite file carrying the id bytes) are refused by name and left byte for byte untouched with nothing appearing beside them. The application id is flushed to the main file before write-ahead mode. Migrations are recorded by name and checksum, applied whatever their position, refused when changed or unknown, with a copy taken before migrating a database that already records one. The tracking start month is the Brazil month of creation and is never rewritten. Connection settings hold on every pooled connection; a second writer waits and a reader does not. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main, run on a still tree; Review: five independent mutations; one survived at first (the SQLite magic not checked) and now has a test in both the unit and the serve refusals. The implementer's 29 breaks each failed a test.

title: Save a transaction's split, its exclusion from the totals and its refund mark, and count each where the budget looks
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the transaction panel offers "Dividir em linhas" for a purchase that was for two things, a "Não
conta" switch with a reason for a purchase that is not really the person's (a company expense, a
purchase made for someone else), and "Marcar como estorno" with the line it reduces for money that came
back; the list offers "não conta" for a whole selection. Every one of them answers that the app is
read-only, so a supermarket bill that was half pharmacy stays whole on one line, a company purchase
inflates the month, and a refund counts as income. After this lands each of those is kept and survives a
restart: a split shows what it still lacks or exceeds while the person types the parts and puts each
part on its own line, an exclusion takes the transaction out of every total once it has a reason (and
not before), a refund reduces the line it was pointed at, and turning a refund or an exclusion off
leaves a step in the purchase's history that can be taken back. A selection marked "não conta" can be
taken back from its toast as one change. If this were wrong the person would see a month's spending that
silently counts a purchase twice, drops the part of a split, or keeps counting what they excluded.

## Outcome
Six methods of the API stop answering `read_only` when the server runs with its own database and are
answered by handlers: `transactions.setSplit`, `setExcluded`, `setExclusionReason`, `excludeMany`,
`setRefund` and `setRefundLine`. Each is one recorded change that `changes.undo` takes back exactly.
The reads of the list and the detail answer what these writes stored (the split and its parts, what it
still lacks, the exclusion and whether it counts, the refund and its line, the history steps three of
them write), and the function that says what a transaction counts for places each transaction where
these fields say, with the two invariants of the totals holding after every one of these writes over
every month of the invented ledger. The first payload the panel sends when a split is switched on (the
whole amount on the transaction's line, then a part of zero) is accepted for every purchase whose panel
shows the split.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and the file may be swapped
under it at any time. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`,
where everything the person authors is kept; the server has one only when started with `--db`, and
without it every write answers `read_only`, as today. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave, and its behaviour is the rule here except where this text says the server departs from it. *The
manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated description of every API method (route,
class, argument and result schemas, error envelope). *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored`
through which every change to the app's database is written, and *the journal* is what it writes: one
*change* per write (author, method, instant, Brazil day) and its *effects*; `changes.undo(changeId)`
applies the inverse of a change's effects and is refused with `refused` / `stale_change` when something
it would overwrite was changed since. *The index* is the pair of tables `tx_index` and `tx_ids` in which
the app's database remembers the transactions it has seen: the bank's id of a transaction can change (a
pending row is replaced by a posted one), so the database mints a key of its own, `tx_key`, and maps
every provider id seen to it; everything authored about a transaction hangs on `tx_key`, never on the
provider's id. A *budget line* has an integer id minted by the app's database and a name that belongs to
a budget version; the budget *in force for a month* is the latest version starting at or before that
month (a month before the first version uses the first). The built-in *fees line* is in no group, has a
fixed id and the fixed name `Tarifas e juros`, and can be named in a write in any month whose budget has
at least one line. A *disposition* is the one place the function that says what a transaction counts
for puts a listed transaction (below). A *golden file* is the exact, committed answer of one call over
an invented fixture. A *purchase* here is a debit that is not a movement between own accounts or a bill
payment: what the panel calls spending and shows the split and the reimbursement for.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.**

- The recorder, the journal and the undo engine (finwise-wi4). A journaled table has one of two shapes. An
  *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts per key; an effect is one column changing; in a
  table of optional facts (a transaction's state) every column has a default, a row whose columns are
  all at their defaults is the same as no row, and the first fact written about a transaction creates
  its row without owning it. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing (a split part, a
  history step); an effect is one row appearing or disappearing. No statement may insert, update or
  delete in an authored table outside the recorder; a test fails if one does. The recorder also offers
  the inverse of a chosen part of a change, performed inside another open change, and a read-only
  check that says whether that inverse would be refused: these are what taking one history step back
  is made of.
- A handler receives one value carrying a view of each store for the request (finwise-jzw): the ledger view
  is one handle and one read-only transaction, so every ledger query of a request sees the same
  snapshot; the clock comes from the request's context and is never the host's.
- Money coming in (finwise-po6): `ParseReais` turns a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal text,
  exponent form included, with no float, rounding half away from zero beyond two places and refusing
  anything that is not a finite number within one billion reais; `Reais` gains `UnmarshalJSON` on top
  of it, so a split part's amount decodes directly. It refuses `null`, so an absent amount never reads
  as zero. A negative amount is accepted by the parser; the handler that takes an amount that cannot be
  negative answers `bad_request` for one.
- Write dispatch (finwise-2s5): the registry takes handlers of class `write`; the router validates the
  arguments against the method's schemas from the manifest before the handler runs (a mismatch is
  `bad_request`), hands the handler a recorder that already holds one immediate transaction and the
  facts of the change (author `person`, the method, the instant, the Brazil day), commits when the
  handler returns, and rolls everything back on any failure. A handler refuses with the kind `refused`
  and one reason of a closed list (HTTP 409); the two this slice produces are `not_found` ("Esse item
  não existe mais.") and `unknown_line` ("Essa linha não existe no budget desse mês."); the interface
  shows the sentences. The change's id, a decimal string, is the `changeId` every one of these methods
  answers. A test file keeps an explicit list of the writes that still have no handler,
  `writesWithoutHandler`; a method leaves it when its handler lands. A domain's handlers are
  registered by a `register<Domain>` function in a file of its own, listed once in
  `domainRegistrations` (`internal/api/reads.go`).
- The write conformance harness and `internal/authored/authoredtest` (finwise-fst): every write has cases in
  a mode. For a *recorded change* the answer validates against the manifest, the change's effects
  match a golden file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`, and undoing it returns a canonical
  dump of every journaled table to the dump taken before. A *refusal* case expects 409, its reason, and
  no table changed at all. Reads over the full invented ledger with an invented authored state have
  their own list of cases, `authoredReadCases`, and golden files under `testdata/golden/full-authored/`.
  The test that proves no handler logs what it reads runs every write case. A list in the test file
  names the refusal reasons that have no producer yet; the slice that first produces a reason removes
  it from that list and adds its case.
- The budget's tables and the line menu (finwise-ef7): lines with stable ids, budget versions per month, the
  fees line, closed months, and one function of "the lines a month's budget has" that resolves a line's
  name in the budget in force for a given month to its id, or says the month's budget does not have it.
- The function that says what a transaction counts for (finwise-305: `internal/budgetrules` with
  `Dispose` and its invariants): `budgetrules.Dispose` puts every listed transaction in exactly one
  disposition, with a property test of the two invariants and a check of them that tests can run.
- The transactions' store (finwise-jw2: the migration `0003_transactions`, the index, the map of provider
  ids, the recorder's registry entries and the fixture builders): among others,
  `tx_state(tx_key, line_id, classified_by, confidence, pending_reason, pending_line_id,
  pending_confidence, ask_reason, note, exclusion, refund, refund_line_id, reimbursable, expected_cents,
  credit_tx_key unique, credit_cents)` (an attribute table of optional facts, one row per transaction),
  `tx_split_parts(tx_key, position, line_id, cents)` (a set table), `history_steps(id, tx_key,
  change_id, kind, text, day)` and `history_step_reasons(step_id, reason)`, each registered with the
  recorder, and the `authoredtest` builders for them. In `tx_state`, `exclusion` is null for "counts",
  empty for "switched on, no reason yet" and a text for the reason; `refund` is null for "as the
  ledger's rule says" and 0 or 1 for what the person set. No migration is added here: if a column proves
  missing, say so in the report instead of adding a migration file, because migration names are
  assigned in advance, one owner each.
- The transactions' API side (finwise-tsr: the lookup of the transaction a write names, the merged list,
  detail and filter reads, the function that gives the name to show for an establishment key, and the
  third golden state): the function that resolves the transaction a write names and creates or
  refreshes its index row, and the reads of the transaction list, the transaction detail and the filter
  options answering from the store's tables.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named).**

- `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts` classes the six methods as `write`.
  `web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts` and `transactions.ts` give their signatures; every one
  answers `Promise<ChangeResult>`, so the result cannot be null and an unknown target is refused, never
  answered null. `SplitPart` is `{ line: string | null; amount: number }`.

**The rules common to the six writes.**

1. *The target.* A write resolves the transaction it names through the same interpreted ledger read the
   API lists transactions with (the one `transactions.detail` uses for its target), in the request's
   ledger snapshot, through the lookup of the transaction a write names (finwise-tsr): an id that read does
   not list (an unknown id, a tax row folded into its purchase, a pot movement) is refused with
   `refused` / `not_found` and nothing is recorded. This departs from the stand-in, whose `change()` in
   `transaction-edits.ts` answers a change id for a transaction that does not exist. The lookup then
   creates or refreshes the transaction's index row (the index records observations, is not journaled
   and is not undone). Use that one lookup, never a second copy in a handler file.
2. *One change.* Each call is one change by `person`. A write that leaves every stored value as it was
   (the same parts, the same reason, the same mark, the same line) records an *empty change*: it answers
   the change's id, the change has no effect, writes no history step, and its undo is a no-op. The
   stand-in writes a history step for `setRefund`, `setRefundLine` and `setExcluded(…, false)` even when
   nothing changed; here a step is written only when the change has an effect on that transaction, which
   follows from the empty change.
3. *The snapshot.* When the ledger snapshot is missing the write answers `ledger_unavailable`, through
   the same classifier a read uses, and nothing is recorded. A write that fails halfway, or waits out
   the database's five-second lock, keeps nothing and answers `internal`.
4. *No month is closed to these.* Closing a month freezes its budget, not its transactions (a decision
   the person made, and what lost was refusing every transaction write in a closed month, which would
   need a way to reopen one): none of these writes is refused because the transaction's month is
   closed.
5. *A line belongs to the transaction's own month.* A split part's line and a refund's line are
   resolved by name in the budget in force for the transaction's own Brazil month, through the function
   of the lines a month's budget has (finwise-ef7), and stored by id. A name that budget lacks is refused with
   `unknown_line` and nothing is recorded, even when the current month's budget has it. The fees line is
   accepted under its fixed name in a month whose budget has at least one line and refused with
   `unknown_line` in a month whose budget has none. A read shows the name the line has in the budget of
   the transaction's own month. Clearing these references when a later budget save removes a line is
   later work (finwise-oib: a save clears the references of the transactions whose month lost a line; a split
   part keeps its place and loses its line), not this slice's.
6. *Kinds the panel does not show a section for.* The panel shows the split only for a purchase and the
   refund only for a credit, but the stand-in stores a split, an exclusion or a refund mark on any
   listed transaction, and nothing in the rules refuses them. Store them likewise; the dispositions
   below decide what they count for (a split is read only on a debit, a refund mark only on a credit),
   so a split on a credit or a refund mark on a debit is kept and changes no total.

**The split.** `setSplit(id, parts)`, stored in `tx_split_parts`, one row per part with its position, its
line (or none) and its amount in cents.

- `null`, an empty list or a list of one part removes the split: no part row is left.
- Two or more parts replace the stored ones whole, in the order sent. A part's `line` may be null. A
  part's amount is zero or more (the panel starts a new part at zero); a negative amount is
  `bad_request` and nothing is recorded. Two parts may name the same line. Nothing forces the parts to
  add up while the person is typing them.
- A list equal to the stored one (same lines, same amounts, same order) is an empty change.
- The transaction's own line, who put it there and its pending review are not touched: removing the
  split later brings the transaction back to its line.
- The detail answers `splitParts` as the stored parts in order, each with its line's name and its amount
  in reais, or `null` when there is no split; `splitRemaining` is the transaction's amount in magnitude
  less the sum of the parts, in cents, positive for what is missing and negative for what exceeds, and
  zero when there is no split. The list and the detail answer `split: true` exactly when parts are
  stored. Vectors from the stand-in's `panel-writes.test.ts`, on a purchase of R$ 180,00:
  `[Transporte 100, (none) 0]` gives `split: true` and `splitRemaining: 80.00`; `[Transporte 100, Lazer
  90]` gives `-10.00`; `[Transporte 100, Lazer 80]` gives `0.00`; `[Transporte 180, (none) 0]` then
  `null` gives `split: false`, `splitParts: null`, `splitRemaining: 0.00`.
- The panel's first payload must be accepted. For a purchase whose detail names its line, that name was
  answered by the read from the budget of the transaction's own month, so the write resolves it in the
  same month; for one with no line the first part's line is null. The part of zero is valid. The amount
  is the detail's amount in magnitude, a JSON number in reais that `ParseReais` turns back into exactly
  the transaction's cents.
- Splitting a purchase that has a linked reimbursement is refused with `split_with_reimbursement`
  ("Uma compra dividida não pode ter reembolso ligado."). No purchase can have a linked reimbursement
  until the reimbursement writes land (finwise-ilt: marking a purchase reimbursable, linking a received PIX
  to it, its candidates over the whole ledger and the credit's side), and that work adds this refusal
  to `setSplit` together with its reverse; this slice does not.

**The exclusion.** Stored in `tx_state.exclusion`. Exclusion takes effect only once it has a reason;
switching it on without one keeps the transaction counting, and the interface says so.

- `setExcluded(id, true)` stores the empty reason (switched on, no reason yet), whatever was stored
  before: on a transaction already excluded with a reason it empties the reason, as the stand-in does.
  The interface sends `true` only when the exclusion is off. No history step.
- `setExcluded(id, false)` stores null (counts) and writes the history step `Você voltou a contar esta
  transação` when the exclusion was on (with or without a reason). Taking that step back restores what
  the exclusion was, reason included.
- `setExclusionReason(id, reason)` stores the reason trimmed, whatever the switch: a reason given to a
  transaction whose exclusion was off switches it on with that reason, as the stand-in does; a reason of
  only spaces stores the empty reason and the transaction keeps counting. No history step.
- `excludeMany(ids, reason)` stores the reason as sent on every transaction of the list, as the stand-in
  does (it does not trim; the interface sends `Marcada em lote`). It validates the whole list before
  changing anything: a repeated id counts once, and one unknown id refuses the call with `not_found`,
  nothing recorded and no table changed (the stand-in skips the ids it does not find; bulk writes all or
  nothing is a departure). An empty list, or a list where every transaction already has that reason, is
  an empty change. No history step. Its undo restores each transaction's exclusion as it was, so a
  transaction that already had that reason keeps it.
- The list and the detail answer `excluded: true` exactly when the stored reason is non-empty;
  `countsInTotals` is false for a movement, an unconverted row and an excluded one; the detail answers
  `exclusion` as `{reason}` (the stored text, empty included) or `null`. Vectors from the stand-in: on
  `setExcluded(true)` the detail answers `exclusion: {reason: ""}`, `excluded: false`,
  `countsInTotals: true`; after `setExclusionReason("Compra da empresa")` it answers
  `exclusion: {reason: "Compra da empresa"}`, `excluded: true`, `countsInTotals: false`.

**The refund.** Stored in `tx_state.refund` and `tx_state.refund_line_id`. `refund` shows what the person
set, or the ledger's rule (`txrules`, card credits only) when they set nothing.

- `setRefund(id, on)` stores 1 or 0 and writes the step `Você marcou como estorno` or `Você desmarcou o
  estorno`. Storing the value already stored is an empty change; storing the value the ledger's rule
  already gives, over a null, is a real change (the column goes from null to a value) and writes its
  step. Switching it off keeps the line chosen for it.
- `setRefundLine(id, line)` resolves the name in the transaction's own month (rule 5), stores it by id
  and writes the step `Você definiu que o estorno abate <linha>`, with the name as resolved. It does not
  require the mark to be on, as in the stand-in. The detail answers `refundLine` with the line's name,
  whether the mark is on or off, and `refund` with the effective mark.
- Vectors from the stand-in, on a received PIX that the rules had put on an income line: `setRefund(true)`
  then `setRefundLine("Mercado")` leaves the history, newest first, `Você definiu que o estorno abate
  Mercado`, `Você marcou como estorno`, before any older step; after `setRefund(false)` the newest step
  is `Você desmarcou o estorno` and the line no longer reduces Mercado.

**What these writes count for.** The dispositions are delivered by finwise-305 with this table; the rows this
slice feeds are 3, 5 and 8, and the rest is reproduced so the order is clear. Amounts are magnitudes in
cents; the first matching row wins.

| # | disposition | condition | counts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | unconverted | the ledger has no value in reais for it | nothing |
| 2 | movement | a movement between own accounts or a bill payment | nothing |
| 3 | excluded | excluded with a reason | nothing |
| 4 | waiting | pending review | nothing |
| 5 | split | a debit with two or more parts | each part with a line adds its amount to that line; the rest (the amount less those parts, which is negative when they exceed it) is unassigned |
| 6 | fee | a fee row, charge or discount, that is on no line (posted, as the existing fees rule defines it) or that the person put on the fees line | a charge adds to the fees line; the credit that discounts it takes off |
| 7 | reimbursement | a credit linked to a purchase | no line; the smaller of its amount and the purchase's is applied inside the purchase, and any excess counts nowhere |
| 8 | refund | a credit that is a refund | reduces its refund line by its amount; with no refund line, nothing |
| 9 | income | a credit on a line of the income group | received on that line |
| 10 | other credit | any other credit | nothing |
| 11 | on a line | a debit with a line | its amount less the applied reimbursement |
| 12 | uncategorised | a debit with no line | nothing; its amount less the applied reimbursement is unassigned |

Two invariants guard the totals. For every debit of dispositions 5, 11 and 12: what it adds to lines,
plus what is unassigned, plus the applied reimbursement, equals its amount. For every month: every
listed transaction is in exactly one disposition, so the dispositions' counts add up to the number of
transactions the API lists and their amounts to the sum of the listed magnitudes. Vectors from the
stand-in, on the R$ 180,00 purchase: split `[Transporte 100, Saúde 80]` adds 100 to Transporte and 80 to
Saúde; `[Transporte 100, (none) 80]` adds 100 to Transporte and leaves 80 unassigned; `null` puts it back
on its own line (or uncategorised). An exclusion with a reason moves the transaction to disposition 3;
one without a reason leaves it where it was. A credit marked as a refund with a refund line reduces that
line by its amount; marked with no line it counts for nothing (it no longer counts as income); unmarked
it is income again if it is on an income line.

**History steps, and who owns what.** A step is a row of `history_steps` of the kind that records what
its change did to the transaction, tied to that change, with its text and the Brazil day of the change;
the detail lists the steps newest first. Taking one back (`transactions.undoHistoryStep(id, stepId)`)
opens a new change that applies the undo's inverse to the units of that one transaction that the step's
change touched, then deletes the step; a step whose columns were changed again since is refused, and
`HistoryEntry.undoable` is computed with the same comparison. Because effects are per column, taking
back `Você marcou como estorno` leaves a refund line chosen after it untouched. The history list of the detail with its `undoable` comes with the reads that merge what the person
authored (finwise-tsr: the transaction list, detail and filter options over both stores); the handler of
`undoHistoryStep` and the function that appends a step come with the line writes (finwise-yfu: setting, confirming and explaining a transaction's line, its
history and the undo of one step), which land in parallel with this slice, on the recorder's inverse of
a part (finwise-wi4). If the tree has no function that appends a step when this work starts, write it once in
`internal/authored` beside the tables and use it, never a copy in a handler file; if the detail does not
yet answer the history from the table, complete it under the rule above. The steps this slice writes
must be undoable by that mechanism, and the vectors below are proved here at the store level, through
the recorder's inverse of a part and its read-only check; whichever of this slice and the line writes
lands second adds the same vectors through `undoHistoryStep` to its tests.

- From the stand-in's "taking a step back": after `setRefund(true)` and `setRefundLine("Mercado")`,
  taking back the mark's step leaves `refund` as it was before the mark and `refundLine: "Mercado"`;
  the mark's step is gone from the history and the line's step stays.
- After an exclusion with the reason `Compra da empresa` and `setExcluded(false)`, taking back `Você
  voltou a contar esta transação` brings back `exclusion: {reason: "Compra da empresa"}` and
  disposition 3.
- After `setRefund(true)`, taking its step back gives `refund` as before; `changes.undo` of the change
  that took it back gives `refund: true` again.
- A refund line set by `setRefundLine("Tarifas e juros")` on a transaction with no refund line, taken
  back, answers `refundLine: null`.
- A step whose column was changed by a later change still in force is not undoable, and taking it back
  is refused with nothing changed.

**What the plan of this work leaves open, and what constrains it** (this is why the bead is `spec:open`).

- *An unconverted purchase.* Its amount is in a foreign currency, so a split's `splitRemaining` against it
  mixes units. It counts for nothing (disposition 1 comes first), so no total is affected. Whether
  `splitRemaining` is computed as for any other purchase or answered otherwise is the implementer's; it
  must never be summed anywhere, and one test pins what it answers.
- *How a split part's position is numbered* and whether parts that did not change are kept or rewritten
  when the list is replaced, within the rule that the effects golden files are deterministic and that
  undo restores the parts exactly, order included.
- *File and function names.*

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. The rule
in full: a real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document,
id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown
to the person running a test and goes into no file; a test that touches a real ledger runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Nothing in this slice needs a real ledger. Every fixture is
invented, and `-update` of the golden files refuses to run while `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set. New
files in `internal/api` log nothing; the no-leak test's list of strings must cover what the new write
cases carry (an exclusion reason, a line's name, an amount).

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path: amounts arrive through
`ParseReais` and leave through `Reais`, and the test that forbids floats in `internal/api` must keep
passing. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant, prepared against the
migrated schema by a test. Interface text and history texts are Brazilian Portuguese, quoted exactly as
above, and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (this slice
touches no component). Register the handlers in a registration function of this slice's own file,
listed once in `domainRegistrations`, instead of adding lines to `registerTransactions` in
`transactions.go`, which the sibling slices landing in parallel would edit too. Each departure from the
stand-in named above (unknown targets refused, bulk all or nothing, no step for a change that changed
nothing, a step changed since not undoable, money in cents) is pinned by a test, and the final report
names the test beside the departure.

title: Count a linked credit as a reimbursement only while the ledger lists its purchase
description:
## What changes for the user
When someone pays the person back for a purchase, the person links the PIX they received to that purchase.
From then on the PIX is shown as a reimbursement, it is not counted as income, and its amount is taken off
the purchase. Today, if the bank later stops listing that purchase (a pending charge it cancelled, for
one), the PIX keeps its "Reembolso" badge and keeps being left out of income, while there is no purchase
any more for its amount to come off. That money then counts nowhere in the month's figures, and nothing on
screen can undo the link, because the link is undone from the purchase's panel and the purchase is gone.
After this lands, a PIX whose purchase is no longer listed goes back to being an ordinary received amount:
it loses the badge, counts as income when it is on an income line, and otherwise shows as uncategorised so
the person can place it. If the bank lists the purchase again, the PIX is its reimbursement again, without
the person doing anything.

## Outcome
A credit is treated as the reimbursement of a purchase only while the snapshot the request reads lists the
purchase that names it. While it does not, every read disposes the credit as it would an unlinked credit
and answers `reimbursementIncome: false` for it. The stored link is not touched and applies again when
the purchase is listed again.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger snapshot* is a file a
separate collector fills from the banks; the app only reads it, and a transaction it *lists* is one the
current snapshot holds and the app's interpretation shows. *The app's database* keeps what the person
authors, under a key of the app's own per transaction (`TxKey`); it keeps rows for transactions the
ledger no longer lists. *A link* is the purchase's stored statement that a credit paid it back: the
purchase's row names the credit's key and the amount (`LinkReimbursement` in
`internal/authored/transaction_reimbursement.go`); one credit pays one purchase. *A disposition* is what a
transaction counts for in a month's budget, decided by `budgetrules.Dispose`
(`internal/budgetrules/dispose.go`) from an input the API builds per transaction.

**What the code does today.** In `internal/api/transactions_authored.go`:
- `linkedCreditsOf` decides which listed credits are reimbursements. For each listed credit it asks the
  store whether some stored purchase names it (`PurchaseLinkedTo`, which answers the purchase's key). It
  never asks whether that purchase is listed; its comment says only that the purchase may be in a month
  the answer does not cover.
- That map feeds two things: `disposable` sets `LinkedToPurchase` from it, which makes `Dispose` answer
  `Reimbursement` for the credit, a disposition that adds to no line, leaves nothing unassigned and takes
  nothing off anything; and `transactionOf` sets the wire field `reimbursementIncome` from it, which the
  interface shows as the "Reembolso" badge.
- The purchase's side is separate and already careful: `appliedCredit` takes a credit's amount off its
  purchase only while the ledger lists the credit, "so the purchase never vanishes from the totals for
  money nobody can see arriving". The listed credits come from one reading of the whole ledger
  (`linkedCreditRows` and `readListedCredits` in `internal/api/reimbursement_candidates.go`), made only
  when a purchase of the answer names a credit.

So when the purchase is no longer listed and the credit is, the credit is still a `Reimbursement`, and
no purchase takes its amount off: the amount is in no income figure and in no spending figure. The person
cannot repair it: unlinking resolves the purchase through the list and answers `not_found` for one the
list does not show, the credit's own panel has no reimbursement section, and the credit is kept out of
the candidates of other purchases because a stored purchase still names it.

**What reads the result.** Every month figure starts from `disposeMonth`
(`internal/api/month_dispositions.go`), which uses the same input: the budget view (what an income line
received), the budget's establishments, the variable limit shown on the home and in the weekly review,
and the closing view's planned against actual. The list and the transaction panel show the badge. The
ingest's rules do not look at links, so nothing changes there.

**What an unlinked credit counts for**, which is what such a credit becomes: a refund when it is one; income
when it is on a line of the income group; otherwise an "other credit", which adds to no line and shows in
the list without a line. Linking a credit settled its pending review, so it is not asked about again by
itself; the person places it by hand.

**What was decided, and what lost.**
- *The credit follows the purchase's listing, as the purchase already follows the credit's.* Leaving it
  was rejected: it is money missing from the totals with no way out on screen.
- *The link is kept.* It is the person's statement and the purchase may come back (a pending charge
  posted late); nothing is written by a read.
- *Whether the purchase is listed is read from the snapshot the request reads*, not from the marks the
  ingest leaves on the index, which are only as fresh as its last run.
- *No new control.* A way to unlink from the credit's panel was considered and left out. For the same
  reason the candidates rule is not changed: a credit whose unlisted purchase still names it stays out of
  other purchases' candidates.
- *The whole ledger is not read where it was not read before.* Learning whether purchases are listed
  takes a reading of the whole ledger and one lookup of keys. It is made only when a listed credit of the
  answer is named by a stored purchase, and it shares the reading `linkedCreditRows` makes when both are
  needed.

**Tests that exist.** `TestALinkAppliesOnlyWhileTheLedgerListsItsCredit` in
`internal/api/reimbursement_candidates_test.go` runs the mirror case over three snapshots (the credit
listed, not listed, listed again) built by `reimbursementLedger(t, without...)`, which builds the invented
ledger without the rows named; its fixture has a dinner (`tx-dinner`), a lunch and a PIX (`tx-pix-ana`).
It checks the wire fields, the dispositions, the two invariants of a month's totals (`monthInvariants`),
that the stored link is unchanged and that the journal did not move. Those invariants do not catch this
defect: a `Reimbursement` credit passes both. No test has a linked credit whose purchase is not listed.
The committed golden files that show a linked credit have both rows listed, so none should move. The
stand-in backend of the interface cannot have a purchase missing while its credit stays, so it does not
change.

## Steps to Reproduce
Over invented data; no test does this today.
1. A snapshot lists a dinner and a received PIX. The person marks the dinner reimbursable and links the
   PIX to it.
2. The next snapshot lists the PIX and no longer lists the dinner.
3. Read the list of the PIX's month and the budget view of that month.
4. Expected: the PIX answers `reimbursementIncome: false` and is disposed as an unlinked credit. Actual:
   it answers `reimbursementIncome: true`, its disposition is `Reimbursement`, and its amount is in no
   line of the month.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The sequence above exists as a test beside `TestALinkAppliesOnlyWhileTheLedgerListsItsCredit`, over
three snapshots (the dinner listed, not listed, listed again), was seen failing on the code as it stands,
and passes.
- [ ] With the dinner not listed: the PIX answers `reimbursementIncome: false` in the list and in its
detail, and its disposition is the one an unlinked credit of the same facts gets (`OtherCredit` with no
line).
- [ ] With the dinner not listed and the PIX on a line of the income group: the PIX is disposed `Income`
and the budget view's received figure of that line includes its amount, to the cent.
- [ ] With the dinner listed again: the PIX is disposed `Reimbursement`, answers
`reimbursementIncome: true`, and the dinner's effective amount has the PIX's amount taken off, exactly as
before the dinner vanished.
- [ ] Across the three snapshots the stored link is unchanged and the journal gains no row.
- [ ] The purchase and its credit in different months: the purchase is listed, in a month the read does
not cover, and the credit is still disposed `Reimbursement` (a credit is not judged by the rows of the
answer alone).
- [ ] A read whose listed credits are named by no stored purchase makes no reading of the whole ledger for
this, shown by a test that counts the readings or by the code path being the one `linkedCreditRows`
already has for that case; the pull request says which.
- [ ] `monthInvariants` answers nothing wrong in each of the three snapshots, and a new assertion in the
test says what the invariants cannot: with the dinner not listed, the PIX's amount is either on an income
line or shown without a line, never a reimbursement of nothing.
- [ ] The existing mirror test and `TestACreditTheLedgerStoppedListingIsNoOnesToLinkAndListedAgainIsStillTaken`
pass unchanged.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is
empty.
- [ ] Each rule was seen failing once, by breaking it on purpose, and the pull request names the test that
failed for each: the listing of the purchase not consulted; the purchase judged by the rows of the answer
instead of the whole ledger; the link cleared when the purchase vanishes.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: over a snapshot that no longer lists a linked purchase, its credit counts as an ordinary
credit in every read and figure, and counts as the reimbursement again when the purchase returns, with
the stored link never written.

## Tests
- Integration, in `internal/api/reimbursement_candidates_test.go`: the three snapshots through the read
handlers (list, detail, budget view), with the wire fields, the dispositions, the invariants, the stored
link and the journal.
- Unit, in `internal/api`: the function that decides which listed credits are reimbursements, over a
purchase listed in the answer, listed in another month, and not listed.
- Golden: none moves.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/transactions_authored.go`, `internal/api/reimbursement_candidates.go`,
`internal/api/reimbursement_candidates_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/month_dispositions.go`, `internal/api/transaction_reimbursement_writes.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_reimbursement_writes_test.go`, `internal/api/transaction_count_invariants_test.go`,
`internal/authored/transaction_reads.go`, `internal/authored/transaction_reimbursement.go`,
`internal/budgetrules/dispose.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `bin/ci`

Two source files of one package and one test file. It stops at the read: no write, no store function, no
rule of `budgetrules`, no contract type, nothing of the interface or the stand-in is edited. The size
label is `size:M` for the tests it owes, not for the code.

## Recovery path
Nothing stored changes: the fix is in how a read interprets a link that is already kept. Reverting the
pull request brings the old reading back and loses nothing.
close_reason: A credit linked to a purchase counts as its reimbursement only while the snapshot the request reads lists the purchase; otherwise it is disposed as an unlinked credit, and it is the reimbursement again when the purchase returns. The stored link is never written by a read, and the purchase's listing is read from the whole ledger, only when a stored purchase names a credit of the answer. Verified by the gate on the branch after main was merged in, by the reproduction over three snapshots seen failing on the earlier code, by tests of an income line and of a purchase in another month, by the author's four deliberate breaks, and in review by four more changes: two killed, one that showed a missing test for a failed reading of the ledger, since added and now failing under it, and one equivalent. No golden file moved.

title: Keep the classifier's threshold and minimum of examples, the card's label and its closing setting, and let a manual closing day place only the bills the bank gave no closing date
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the settings screen shows a slider for how sure the app must be before it files a purchase by
itself, a field for how many examples it needs to learn an establishment, a label for the card, and a
choice between the bank's closing day and one of the person's own; moving any of them answers that the
app is read-only, and the screen goes back to the default. After this lands each of them is kept, is
still there after a restart, and can be taken back. A manual closing day fills in where the bank sent no
closing date for a bill, so a card whose bank never says when its bill closes gets a closing date, a
best purchase day and a figure for what this month's purchases put on the next bill; a bill the bank
did date keeps the bank's date, and the "bank's day" the screen shows next to the choice stays the
bank's. The calibration chart keeps saying there is nothing to judge yet, because nothing classifies
with a confidence until the nightly model exists. What the person would notice if this were wrong: a
closing date the bank reported moved by a setting, the pay-ahead figure counting the wrong purchases, a
threshold typed as 72.6 kept as something other than 73, or a setting that is gone after a restart.

## Outcome
Migration `0004_settings` adds `settings(key, value)` to the app's database. `settings.setThreshold`,
`settings.setMinExamples`, `settings.setCardLabel` and `settings.setClosing` have handlers: each parses
its arguments without a float, holds a number to the contract's range, and is one recorded change that
`changes.undo` takes back exactly. `settings.overview` answers the stored threshold, minimum of
examples, card label, closing mode and manual day (the defaults where nothing is stored), the bank's
closing day computed as if no manual day were set, and the calibration as five bands with no figure and
no suggested threshold. The card's reads (`card.overview`, the pay-ahead of `home.summary`, the card
bill of `review.closing`) place every bill the bank gave no closing date by the manual day when the mode
is manual, through the one rule `cardrules` already has, and never move a closing date the bank
reported. The threshold and the minimum are readable by the rules that classify new transactions,
which arrive later and act only on what they evaluate after a change.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and the file may be swapped
under it at any time. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`,
where everything the person authors is kept; the server has one only when started with `--db`, and
without it every write answers `read_only`, as today. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave, and its behaviour is the rule here except where this text says the server departs from it. *The
contract* is the TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/contract/`); *the manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it, with a schema for every method's arguments and
result. *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored` through which every change to the app's
database is written; *the journal* is what it writes (one row per change in `changes`, one per effect in
`change_effects`); *undo* is the inverse of a change's recorded effects. *The current month* and *today*
are the Brazil month and day of the instant in the request's context, never the host's clock. *A golden
file* is the committed, exact answer of one call over an invented fixture. *The gate* is `bin/ci`, the
exact checks CI runs.

**What earlier work provides.** None of it is in the repository when this text is written; each piece is
delivered before this bead starts, and its interfaces are to be read in the code as that work left them.

- The app's database ({{F1}}: opening, recognising and migrating `finwise.db`): a migration is an SQL
  file embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`, recorded by name and checksum in
  `schema_migrations` once applied; at start every file not recorded is applied in name order, each in one
  transaction, after a copy of a database that already holds data is taken beside it
  (`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>`). A recorded name whose checksum differs from the embedded file is
  refused at start, so once a migration has been applied to a database that matters its file is frozen.
  Every SQL statement over the database is a registered constant: one test prepares each against the
  migrated schema and another fails on a statement that is not registered.
- The recorder and undo ({{F2}}: the journal and the undo engine): a closed, hand-written registry of
  the journaled tables. An *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts per key, and an effect is
  one column changing; a restore is computed for the whole row and written once. The registry says which
  of two kinds an attribute table is: one of *optional facts*, where a row whose columns are all at
  their defaults is the same as no row, or one of things *created whole*. A *set table* holds rows that
  are facts by existing. A test fails when a statement inserts, updates or deletes in an authored table
  outside the recorder. `changes.undo(changeId)` restores every `before` of a change and is refused with
  `refused` / `stale_change` when a later change still in force touched the same unit.
- The views ({{F3b}}: one snapshot of each store per request): a handler's third parameter is one value
  carrying a view of each store, opened for the request. The authored view is one read-only transaction,
  so an answer is wholly before or wholly after a concurrent write; on a server without `--db` it is an
  empty view that answers "nothing authored", so read code has one path. Each slice adds to that view the
  reads of the tables it owns.
- Numbers in ({{F4b}}: the parsers of money and whole numbers): `ParseWholeNumber(raw) (int, error)` in
  `internal/api` reads a JSON number with no float, rounds to the nearest whole number with a half going
  up (72.5 becomes 73, -72.5 becomes -72), and answers an error, which becomes `bad_request`, for
  anything that is not a JSON number or whose result is beyond one billion in magnitude. The clamping and
  the ranges are this slice's.
- Write dispatch ({{F4c}}: writes run through the recorder with their arguments checked against the
  manifest): a write that has a registered handler, on a server with the app's database, has its
  arguments validated against the method's schema in the manifest (a mismatch is `bad_request`), then
  runs inside one immediate transaction with a recorder that holds one open change (author `person`, the
  method's qualified name, the instant, the Brazil day); the dispatcher commits, and any failure rolls
  everything back and answers `internal`, including a wait of five seconds for the lock that runs out.
  Where the result cannot be null, as for every method here, a write that changes nothing records an
  *empty change*: it answers a change id, the change has no effect, and its undo is a no-op. A test walks
  the manifest: every write has a handler or is named in an explicit list, `writesWithoutHandler`; a
  method leaves the list when its handler lands.
- The write conformance harness ({{F5}}: write cases by mode, `authoredtest`, the new golden
  directories): for a *recorded change* the answer validates against the manifest, its effects match a
  golden file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`, and undoing it returns a canonical dump of
  every journaled table to the dump taken before. `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds invented states
  of the app's database, one builder per group of tables, added by the slice that owns the tables. Reads
  over the full invented ledger with an invented authored state have their own list of cases,
  `authoredReadCases`, with golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`; their type
  and constructor are their own so that the interface's equality test, which finds the read cases by the
  written shape ``readCase{"domain.method", `[...]`}``, does not take them for reads over the empty
  ledger. The test that proves no handler logs what it reads runs every write case.

**What the code is today (each point read in the file named).**

- `web/src/api/contract/settings.ts`: `setThreshold(percent: number)`, `setMinExamples(count: number)`,
  `setCardLabel(label: string)` and `setClosing(mode: ClosingMode, manualDay: number)`, each answering
  `Promise<ChangeResult>` (never null). The bounds are exported there: `THRESHOLD_RANGE` 50 to 99,
  `MIN_EXAMPLES_RANGE` 1 to 50, `CLOSING_DAY_RANGE` 1 to 28. `ClosingMode` is `'auto' | 'manual'`
  (`web/src/api/contract/card.ts`), an enum in the manifest; `CardClosing` is `{mode, bankDay: number |
  null, manualDay}`. `web/src/api/contract/classification.ts` classes the four as `write`.
- `internal/api/settings.go`: `readSettingsOverview` answers `CardLabel: defaultCardLabel`,
  `Categorization: defaultCategorization()` and `Closing: {Mode: defaultClosingMode, BankDay:
  bankClosingDayOf(card), ManualDay: defaultManualClosingDay}`. `bankClosingDayOf` takes the day of the
  month of `card.openBillOf().closing`. `defaultCategorization` builds five bands from
  `calibrationFirstBand` (50) by `calibrationBandWidth` (10), the last reaching `calibrationTop` (100),
  each with a null `correctionPercent`, and no suggested threshold.
- `internal/api/settings_defaults.go`: `defaultConfidenceThreshold` 85, `defaultMinExamples` 5,
  `defaultManualClosingDay` 28, `defaultClosingMode` `"auto"`, with a comment saying the backend has
  nowhere to keep a change, which stops being true here. `internal/api/messages.go` holds
  `defaultCardLabel` `"Físico"`.
- `internal/api/settings_test.go`: `TestTheSettingsHoldTheDefaultsWhereThePersonHasChosenNothing`,
  `TestTheCalibrationBandsTileTheRangeOfTheThresholdAndAreAllUnjudged` and
  `TestTheSettingsShowTheCardAndTheDayTheBankClosesItsBill` (bank day 28 over the full invented ledger, 3
  over `c6Ledger` at 2026-03-20, null with no card) pin today's answers and keep passing unchanged on a
  server without the app's database.
- `internal/cardrules/cycle.go`: `cardrules.Card` already has `ManualClosingDay int`. Its comment: "when
  not zero, replaces the table for every closing date the ledger does not carry. A closing date the
  ledger does carry is what the bank did, and a setting made now does not rewrite it."
  `predictedClosing` (unexported) applies it: `ManualClosingDate(due, day)` when it is set, the bank's
  `Table.ClosingDate(due)` otherwise; `ledgerCycles` uses a bill's own `Closing` when the ledger carries
  one and `predictedClosing` only when it does not, and `cycles` predicts three more cycles after the
  latest bill the same way. `PlacePurchase` and `AmountOnNextBill` go through those cycles.
  `ManualClosingDate` (`closing.go`) is the latest such day strictly before the due date, held to the
  month's last day in a shorter month.
- `internal/api/card.go`: `loadCard` builds `cardrules.Card{Bills, Table}` and never sets
  `ManualClosingDay`. `(*cardView).closingOf(placement)` answers the bill's own `ClosingDate` when the
  placement names a ledger bill that has one, and otherwise `card.rules.Table.ClosingDate(placement.Due)`
  directly: it is the one place that computes a closing without going through the rule above, so with a
  manual day set the open bill would be placed by the manual day and then shown with the table's date,
  or with none. `openBillOf` (the open bill, its closing and due), `billWire` (a past bill's `closedOn`)
  and through them `overview`, `mayFallBefore` and `pastBills` use it. `loadCard` is called by
  `readCardOverview`, `readHomeSummary` (`home.go`, the pay-ahead), `readClosing` (`review_closing.go`,
  the card bill) and `readSettingsOverview`.
- The stand-in: `web/src/api/fake/settings.ts` (the four writes: `setThreshold` and `setMinExamples` and
  the day of `setClosing` through `clampThreshold`, `clampMinExamples`, `clampClosingDay` of
  `settings-rules.ts`, which round with `Math.round` and then clamp, a non-finite value becoming the
  minimum; `setCardLabel` stores `label.trim()`; `setClosing` stores the mode and the clamped day
  together), `settings.test.ts` (groups "confidence threshold", "card closing", "calibration") and
  `card-rules.ts`, whose `closingDayOf` uses the manual day for every bill whenever the mode is manual.
- The interface already sends these writes and refetches the overview after each (`ConfigScreen.vue`
  watches the revision counter): `CategorizationSection.vue` sends `setThreshold` when the slider is
  released and `setMinExamples` with `Number(input.value)`; `CardSection.vue` sends
  `setClosing(mode, closing.manualDay)` when a mode is chosen and `setClosing('manual', Number(value))`
  when the day changes; `NicknamesSection.vue` sends `setCardLabel(text)`. No file under `web/` changes in
  this slice.

**The schema: migration `0004_settings`.** One table, `settings(key, value)`, one row per setting that
the person has set. Its keys are a closed set of five (the threshold, the minimum of examples, the card
label, the closing mode, the manual closing day; the spelling of each key is the implementer's). It is
an attribute table in the recorder's registry, keyed by `key`, whose fact is `value`. The table declares
its primary key and `NOT NULL` where a value is required, and `CHECK`s for every closed set: the key is
one of the five; the mode is `auto` or `manual`; the threshold is a whole number from 50 to 99, the
minimum from 1 to 50, the manual day from 1 to 28. How `value` is typed for a number and for a text, and
whether the registry treats the table as one of optional facts or of things created whole, are the
implementer's, under what the criteria observe. The table holds no amount of money, so the obligation
every migration's owner has, a test in which the database itself refuses a duplicate, an invalid value
and a negative amount, is met here with a duplicate key, an unknown key, a mode outside the two, a
number outside its range, and a negative number for each numeric setting. A column this work proves it
needs may be added, in this file only.

**The four writes.** Each is one change by `person`, its effects only on `settings`. None reads the
ledger, so each succeeds when the snapshot file is missing.

- `setThreshold(percent)`: `ParseWholeNumber`, then held between 50 and 99. Vectors from the stand-in's
  "holds the value between 50 and 99 and to whole numbers": 10 becomes 50, 100 becomes 99, 72.6 becomes
  73; the stand-in's `NaN` cannot arrive in JSON.
- `setMinExamples(count)`: the same, between 1 and 50 (0 becomes 1, 80 becomes 50, 12 stays 12).
- `setClosing(mode, manualDay)`: the mode is the manifest's enum, so anything else is `bad_request`
  before the handler runs; the day is `ParseWholeNumber`, then held between 1 and 28 (31 becomes 28, 0
  becomes 1). Both are stored in the same change, whatever the mode: in `auto` the manual day is kept and
  shown, as the stand-in keeps it, and undo restores both (the stand-in's "takes back with the change":
  after `setClosing('manual', 10)` and its undo the closing reads `{mode: 'auto', bankDay: 28,
  manualDay: 28}` over its dataset).
- `setCardLabel(label)`: the label is free text, stored trimmed; an empty result is stored as the empty
  text and answered as `""`, as the stand-in does, not as the default. The label is shown only by the
  settings screen; the card names in `home.summary` and `review.closing` come from the card account and
  are not touched.
- A value that the JSON does not hold as a number (a string, `null`, a boolean) is `bad_request`, and so
  is a number beyond one billion in magnitude (`ParseWholeNumber`'s bound): `setThreshold(1000)` is 99,
  `setThreshold(2e9)` is refused.
- A write that leaves the stored value as it is (the threshold set to the value it already holds, the
  same mode and day again, the same label) records an empty change. Whether setting a value equal to the
  default when nothing is stored writes a row or records an empty change is the implementer's: both
  answer the same everywhere, and the effects golden file pins the choice.

**What the reads answer.** `settings.overview` answers the stored threshold, minimum, card label, mode
and manual day, and the defaults (85, 5, "Físico", `auto`, 28) for what is not stored, as today. Without
`--db` every read answers byte for byte what it answers today. The threshold and the minimum of examples
are also read by the rules that classify new transactions ({{R1}}: the pure function that decides "apply
this line", "pending" or "leave" for one transaction; {{R2}}: the job that brings a new snapshot in and
runs it), so the authored view offers one read of each that answers the stored value or the default.
Those rules run once per transaction, and a change of threshold or of minimum acts only on transactions
evaluated after it: the settings writes start no pass, touch no transaction, and record nothing outside
`settings`. Why: a setting must not silently rewrite the queue or the lines already applied. Rejected: a
retroactive pass on every settings change. The stand-in's test "moves which classifications are marked
as unsure, and takes back with the change" is not ported: on the server `belowThreshold` is about the
model's confidence only and stays false until the model exists, which is the rules' work.

**The card follows the closing setting, and never rewrites the bank.** When the mode is `manual`, the
card's rules receive the stored manual day through the field `cardrules.Card.ManualClosingDay`; when it
is `auto`, they receive zero, whatever day is stored. The rule is the one `cardrules` already states:
the manual day decides the closing of a bill for which the ledger carries no closing date, and of the
cycles predicted after the latest bill; a closing date the bank reported is what the bank did, and a
setting made now does not rewrite it. Why: the existing rule is deliberate and its comment says why.
Rejected: overriding the bank's dates with the setting, which is what the stand-in's `closingDayOf` does
and where the server departs from it on purpose. `closingOf` in `card.go` is brought under that rule, so
every closing the card shows (the open bill's `closesOn` and `bestPurchaseDay`, a past bill's
`closedOn`, the window of `mayFallOnNextBill`, the pay-ahead) comes from the same cycles that placed the
bill. Doing that needs `cardrules` to answer the closing of a due date without a ledger date (what
`predictedClosing` computes), so an exported way to ask it is added there; its name and shape are the
implementer's, the rule and the comment in `cycle.go` stay as they are, and nothing in `card.go` calls
`Table.ClosingDate` directly afterwards. `home.summary`'s pay-ahead and `review.closing`'s card bill read
the same `cardView` and follow without further rules.

**The bank's day stays the bank's.** The settings screen's `closing.bankDay` is computed without the
manual day: the day of the month on which the open bill closes as the ledger and the bank's table say,
exactly as `bankClosingDayOf` answers it today, and null when they cannot say, whatever the mode and the
manual day stored. So over the full invented ledger it stays 28 and over `c6Ledger` it stays 3 with any
manual day; over a card of a bank with no table and no ledger date it stays null even when a manual day
places the bill.

**Calibration.** It stays as the read side answers it today: the contract's five bands, 50–59, 60–69,
70–79, 80–89 and 90–100, each with `correctionPercent: null`, and `suggestedThreshold: null`, with any
authored state and after any write. Lines applied by a rule never count as the model's; the figures
arrive with the nightly model, which is later work. This is a departure from the stand-in, which shows
the prototype's seeded percentages (46, 31, 18, 7, 2) and suggests 80; the port of
`calibrationBands` and `suggestedThreshold` is not part of this work.

**Where this departs from the stand-in on purpose,** each pinned by a test that the final report names:
the manual day places only the bills the bank gave no closing date (the stand-in applies it to every
bill); calibration has no figures; a number beyond one billion is refused instead of clamped (the
stand-in clamps any number); the threshold does not move `belowThreshold`.

**Failure paths that touch this work.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the migration fails | its transaction rolls back; the copy taken before it is beside the file; `serve` exits naming the path and the reason, never the content |
| the database holds a migration the binary does not know, or a changed one | refused at start |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; `internal` |
| an undo meets a later change of the same setting | `refused` / `stale_change`; nothing is restored |
| the process stops between a write's commit and its answer | the change is stored; the interface says the result could not be confirmed and refetches |
| the snapshot is missing | the four writes succeed; `settings.overview` and the card's reads answer `ledger_unavailable`, as today |

**Known next users, not built here:** the rules that classify new transactions read the threshold and the
minimum ({{R1}}, {{R2}}); the pots' bucket and linked lines ({{S2}}) and the establishments and people of
the settings overview with their two writes ({{S3}}) add to `settings.overview` and to the settings
writes beside this work; the last backup in the overview's data section is another slice's ({{F7}}).

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`), each with what constrains it: the
spelling of the five keys and how `value` is typed, under the `CHECK`s above; the registry kind of the
table, as long as the undo of the first write of a setting brings the read back to the default and the
canonical dump back to what it was; whether a value equal to the default with nothing stored writes a
row; the name and shape of the exported closing method in `cardrules`; how `cardView` keeps the bank's
view for the bank day beside the one with the manual day; the names of the new files.

**Privacy and conventions.** Nothing here needs a real ledger. A real ledger is a person's whole financial
history and this repository is public: fixtures are invented, and no value from a real snapshot (an
amount, a description, a name, a document, an id) is ever printed, logged or copied into a file, a
commit, a bead or a pull request. Work in your own git worktree, on your own branch, and stop at local
commits: atomic, Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a
plan in a commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; a test
already forbids floats in `internal/api` and covers `internal/authored`. Every SQL statement over the
app's database is a registered constant. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is
English; this work adds no Portuguese. A design value in a component comes from a token; this work
touches no component. Register the four handlers in a registration function of this slice's own file,
listed where write dispatch lists them, so the sibling settings slices add their own files instead of
editing these lines. New files in `internal/api` log nothing: the request log holds the verb, the route,
the status, the duration and the error kind, never an argument, a body or a label.

## Acceptance criteria
The invented ledgers run on a clock fixed at 2026-03-20 unless a criterion says otherwise.

Schema
- [ ] A database that held only the earlier migrations gains `settings` when opened; the migration is
recorded once under the name `0004_settings`; opening it again applies nothing.
- [ ] From a test, directly against the migrated schema with no Go validation in the way, the database
refuses: a second row for one key; an unknown key; the mode `weekly`; a threshold of 49 and of 100; a
minimum of 0 and of 51; a manual day of 0 and of 29; a value of -1 for each of the three numeric keys.
- [ ] Every statement this work adds is a registered constant prepared by the existing test, and
`settings` is in the recorder's registry.

The writes (with `--db`)
- [ ] `settings.setThreshold` with 10, 100, 72.6, 72.5, 72.4 and 1000 makes `settings.overview` answer
`categorization.threshold` 50, 99, 73, 73, 72 and 99; with `"73"`, `null` and `2e9` it answers 400
`bad_request` and the canonical dump is unchanged.
- [ ] `settings.setMinExamples` with 0, 80 and 12 makes the overview answer `minExamples` 1, 50 and 12.
- [ ] `settings.setClosing("manual", 31)` makes the overview answer `closing` `{"mode":"manual",
"bankDay":28,"manualDay":28}` over the full invented ledger; `setClosing("manual", 0)` answers
`manualDay` 1; `setClosing("auto", 12)` answers `{"mode":"auto","bankDay":28,"manualDay":12}`;
`setClosing("weekly", 10)` answers 400 `bad_request`.
- [ ] After `setClosing("manual", 10)` and `changes.undo` of its change, the overview answers
`{"mode":"auto","bankDay":28,"manualDay":28}` and the canonical dump is the one taken before.
- [ ] `settings.setCardLabel("  Virtual ")` makes the overview answer `"cardLabel":"Virtual"`;
`setCardLabel("   ")` answers `""`; undoing the first, on a database with nothing else set, answers
`"Físico"`.
- [ ] Each of the four answers 200 `{"changeId":"<decimal id>"}` that validates against the manifest, is
one change with author `person` and its own qualified method name, has effects on `settings` only, and
undoing it returns the canonical dump of every journaled table to the one taken before; none of the four
remains in `writesWithoutHandler`.
- [ ] `setThreshold(73)` after `setThreshold(72.6)`, and `setClosing` with the stored mode and day, each
answer a change id whose change has no row in `change_effects`; its `changes.undo` succeeds and changes
nothing.
- [ ] With the snapshot file missing, each of the four succeeds and its effect is stored.
- [ ] On a server without the app's database the four answer 403 `read_only` before their body is read,
and `settings.overview`, `card.overview`, `home.summary` and `review.closing` answer byte for byte what
they answered before; the existing tests of `settings_test.go`, `card_test.go`, `home_test.go` and
`review_closing_test.go` pass unchanged.

The card
- [ ] Over `noTableLedger` (a bank with no closing table and bill `bill-it` due 2026-03-25 with no closing
date) in mode `auto`, `card.overview` answers `closesOn`, `dueOn`, `bestPurchaseDay` and
`payAhead.amount` null, as today; after `setClosing("manual", 22)` it answers `closesOn` and
`bestPurchaseDay` `"2026-03-22"`, `dueOn` `"2026-03-25"` and `payAhead.amount` `0.00`, while
`settings.overview` answers `bankDay` null.
- [ ] Over `c6Ledger` at 2026-03-20, after `setClosing("manual", 25)`: the past bill `bill-jan`, whose
closing date the ledger carries, keeps `closedOn` `"2026-02-04"`; `bill-feb`, which the ledger gives no
closing date, has `closedOn` `"2026-02-25"` (it is `"2026-03-04"` by the bank's table in mode `auto`);
the open bill has `closesOn` `"2026-03-25"` and `dueOn` `"2026-04-10"`; `settings.overview` still answers
`bankDay` 3.
- [ ] Over the full invented ledger, whose open bill `bill-mar` carries the closing date 2026-03-28,
`setClosing("manual", 10)` leaves `card.overview`'s `closesOn` `"2026-03-28"` and the whole answer of
`card.overview` byte for byte as in mode `auto`, and `bankDay` 28.
- [ ] Over a ledger built for the test with card purchases on and after a manual closing day of the
current month and none the ledger dates, `home.summary`'s `payAhead.amount` and `review.closing`'s card
bill equal `card.overview`'s `payAhead.amount` in mode `manual`, and are null and absent in mode `auto`
over the same ledger with no bank table.
- [ ] No non-test file of `internal/api` calls `Table.ClosingDate` after this work (a source check or a
test), and `cycle.go`'s comment on `ManualClosingDay` is unchanged.

Calibration and the rules' inputs
- [ ] Over the full invented ledger, with an authored state that sets every one of the five settings,
`categorization.calibration` is exactly the five bands 50–59, 60–69, 70–79, 80–89, 90–100 with
`correctionPercent` null, and `suggestedThreshold` is null.
- [ ] The authored view answers the threshold and the minimum of examples as stored, and 85 and 5 with
nothing stored, and 85 and 5 on the empty view of a server without `--db`.

The harness and the gate
- [ ] The write conformance harness has a recorded-change case for each of the four writes, with its
golden effects file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`.
- [ ] `authoredReadCases` holds `settings.overview` over an authored state that sets all five settings to
values other than the defaults, with its golden file under
`internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`, not written in the shape the interface's equality test
scans for.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` or `empty/` changes, and
`web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` passes untouched.
- [ ] The test that proves no handler logs what it reads passes over the new write cases, with the card
labels of those cases among the strings it looks for, and fails when a handler of this slice is made to
log its argument.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the final report:
the clamp removed from each of the three numeric writes; rounding half to even instead of half up;
`setClosing` storing only the mode; the label stored untrimmed; `closingOf` left calling the table
directly (the `noTableLedger` and `c6Ledger` criteria fail); the manual day applied over a date the
ledger carries (`bill-jan` moves); the bank day computed with the manual day (`bankDay` moves); the manual
day passed in mode `auto`; one `CHECK` of the schema dropped.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
