- [ ] The coverage test fails for a registered write or evaluation with no case in its mode, and for a
case naming a method with no handler; `changes.undo` and `session.changePin` are the only two methods
named as exempt.
- [ ] The reasons test accounts for all nine: `stale_change` by a case, the eight others by the explicit
list; it fails when a reason is in neither and when one is in both.
- [ ] The file of a recorded-change case is `testdata/golden/writes/<domain>.<method>[.<slug>].json` by
the rule of `goldenName`, and a test fails when two cases name the same file.
- [ ] `authoredReadCases` has a type and a constructor of its own and at least one case; it is answered
over the full invented ledger and an invented authored state, validates against its result schema and
equals its file in `testdata/golden/full-authored/`.
- [ ] `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` has a check that no call of `authoredReadCases` is among the
calls it collects; the check was seen failing once, with an authored case that makes a call no entry of
`readCases` makes spelled as a `readCase{...}` literal; `npm --prefix web test` passes.
- [ ] Every case of `readCases`, over both invented ledgers, answered by a router with a freshly created
      app's database that holds nothing authored, equals its golden file in `full/` or `empty/`. The list
      of cases allowed to differ is empty, and a name put in it whose two answers are equal fails the
      test. Seen failing once with a read handler made to answer differently when its authored view is not
      the empty one.
- [ ] `TestEveryGoldenFileHasACase` fails for a stray `.json` file placed in each of `full/`, `empty/`,
`full-authored/` and `writes/`, and for one in a directory of any other name.
- [ ] No commit of this slice changes a file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` or
`internal/api/testdata/golden/empty/`.
- [ ] An update of the files of `writes/` or of `full-authored/` is refused while
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set: a test shows it.
- [ ] The no-leak test runs every write case and every authored read case, and fails when a test handler
is made to log one of its arguments through the default `slog` logger and through the standard `log`.
- [ ] `internal/api/testdata/golden/README.md` describes the four directories, the naming of a file in
each and the update command of each.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the breaks listed in the criteria above, plus the dump against a registry entry left out of it.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, a deliberately broken undo fails the harness in a test
that stays in the suite, and no file of `full/` or `empty/` was changed by this slice.

## Tests
- Unit (`internal/authored/authoredtest`): a built database is migrated and deterministic; the creation
  instant decides the tracking start month.
- Unit: the canonical dump, equal for equal states and different for one column and for one row, over
  scratch tables of both shapes.
- Conformance, over the full invented ledger of `fixtures_test.go` and a database built by
  `authoredtest`, with handlers registered only in the test and writing to scratch tables: one case per
  mode (a recorded change, nothing to do, an evaluation, an extension) and one refusal case.
- Unit, in the pattern of `TestTheConformanceCheckRejectsAnAnswerThatDoesNotMatch`: each check fed its
  broken inputs (three broken undos, an extension undone to the wrong state, a non-conforming answer,
  changed and reordered effects, a journal row after a null answer, a table changed by an evaluation, a
  row left by a refusal).
- Unit: the coverage test, the reasons test and the test that two cases do not share a file, each with
  a test of the test, in the pattern of `TestTheCoverageCheckFailsWhenAHandlerIsMissingOrInvented`.
- Golden: the seeded authored read case in `full-authored/`; the 59 files of each of `full/` and `empty/`
  untouched by this slice.
- Unit: `TestEveryGoldenFileHasACase` over the four directories; the update refusal for the new ones.
- Unit: the no-leak test over write cases and authored read cases, with a handler that logs.
- Unit (vitest, `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`), over the Go test sources, the golden files of
  `empty/` and the stand-in's empty ledger: the new check that the authored list is left out, and the
  existing equality still holding.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/authoredtest/`, `internal/api/conformance_test.go`,
`internal/api/golden_test.go`, `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`, `internal/api/harness_test.go`,
`internal/api/fixtures_test.go`, `internal/api/write_conformance_test.go`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/README.md`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`, `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/empty/`, `internal/api/reads_coverage_test.go`,
`internal/api/router_test.go`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`,
`web/src/test/replay.ts`, `bin/ci`

Test code and one test-support package: about ten files, in `internal/api`'s tests, the new
`authoredtest` and one test of the interface that gains one check; no production file of `internal/api`
and no screen. It stays one bead although it reaches three places, because its parts share
`golden_test.go` and the README, and because `authoredtest` has no user but this harness when it lands.
`write_conformance_test.go` is new and may be split in two if the cases and the checks read better
apart. `internal/authored` is used as delivered; the one change this slice may make there is bringing
the canonical dump to the rule of point 2. The golden files of `full/` and `empty/` are read and not
changed; `testdata/golden/writes/` gains its first file only with the first real recorded write, which
belongs to a later slice, so the directory may not exist in the tree when this lands.

It is labelled critical although it changes no production code: every later write is accepted on this
harness's word, so a check here that cannot fail lets a wrong undo through in silence. Only `bin/ci`
proves it whole, because a mistake in how a Go case is spelled is caught by a test of the interface.
close_reason: The conformance harness covers writes by mode (recorded change, extension, nothing to do, evaluation, refusal), with coverage of every registered write and of the nine refusal reasons, a third read state over invented authored data, the check that an empty database answers what no database answers, and the no-leak test over write and authored cases. full/ and empty/ untouched. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main. Review: four independent mutations on the harness's own checks; three survived at first and now fail a table of fourteen inputs each only one check can refuse. The implementer's thirty breaks each failed a test, three after a fix of the suite.

title: Let the interface talk to a real backend
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the interface can only run on the invented dataset bundled with it. After this lands the same interface, built for real use, talks to the backend: the PIN is checked by the server, the screens show what the server answers, and three things that used to fail silently now say something. Trying to change anything shows one message that the app is read-only for now and leaves the screen as it was. A session that expired brings back the PIN screen. A request that fails shows a message with a button to try again instead of a blank page.

## Outcome
An HTTP implementation of the interface's API contract beside the in-memory stand-in, chosen when the interface is built, and one place that turns every failure of the API into what the person sees.

## Context
finwise's interface reaches its backend through one TypeScript interface, `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/types.ts`). `web/src/main.ts` provides an implementation with `app.provide(apiKey, createFakeApi())`, and everything else calls `useApi()` (`web/src/api/context.ts`). The only implementation is the in-memory stand-in under `web/src/api/fake/`, which serves the design prototype's dataset; the parity check that measures every screen against the design depends on that dataset.

A generated manifest, `internal/contract/contract.json`, lists every contract method with its route (`/api/<domain>/<method>`) and its class (`session`, `read`, `evaluate`, `write`). The contract also exports `ApiError` with a `kind`: `locked`, `read_only`, `ledger_unavailable`, `bad_request`, `unknown_method`, `internal`, and `network` for a request that got no answer. A Go backend serves those routes: `POST`, the body is the JSON array of the method's arguments in order, the answer is the result as JSON (`null` for nothing), an error is `{"error":{"kind":"<kind>"}}`, and the session is a cookie the server sets. That backend is read-only: every `write` and `evaluate` method answers `read_only`.

**The client.** Built by iterating the manifest, not as an open-ended proxy, so it has exactly the contract's methods and a call to a method that does not exist cannot become a request. Each method posts its arguments with `credentials: 'same-origin'`, returns the parsed result (`undefined` for a method that returns nothing), and throws `ApiError` with the kind the server sent, or `network` when `fetch` itself fails.

**Chosen at build time.** `vite build` produces the interface for real use, with the HTTP client. `vite build --mode prototype` produces it with the stand-in; the parity scripts build in that mode. `npm --prefix web run dev` keeps the stand-in, PIN `123456`. A new `dev:backend` script runs the dev server with the HTTP client and proxies `/api` to `127.0.0.1:8080`. The stand-in and its dataset are loaded with a dynamic import so they are not in the bundle for real use, and the gate proves it by searching the built files for a sentinel string that exists only in the prototype dataset.

**Why failures need one place.** Nothing in the interface handles a rejected call today. A write is called in seven different patterns (the transaction panel's `write`, `useLineChange`, `actOnSelection`, `useSettingsWrites`, the `announce` helpers of the review and the subscriptions, the closing actions and the budget save, and the PIN form), about sixty call sites, with no shared wrapper; a rejected write becomes an unhandled rejection and a rejected read leaves a blank screen. Rewriting those call sites belongs with the part of the app that will make writes real. Here one function receives every `ApiError`, wired to both `app.config.errorHandler` and the window's `unhandledrejection` event:
- `read_only`: one toast, "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.", and `useRevisionStore().bump()`, so every screen fetches again and shows the server's state instead of an optimistic one.
- `locked`: the session store becomes locked, which brings the PIN screen back.
- `ledger_unavailable`: a toast, "Dados do banco indisponíveis no momento.", with the action "Tentar de novo".
- anything else: a toast, "Não foi possível carregar os dados.", with the action "Tentar de novo".

"Tentar de novo" bumps the revision counter, which makes the screens fetch again. The toast is the existing one (`useOverlayStore().showToast(message, actions)`); the design has no error variant and none is added. An error that is not an `ApiError` is not swallowed.

**Tests at the right boundary.** The client's own tests stub `fetch`, which is its boundary. Tests of screens keep the repository's rule: the backend is faked with `createFakeApi`, here wrapped by a small test helper that makes every `write` and `evaluate` method of the classification reject with `read_only`, so each write pattern is exercised through a real screen.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The client exposes exactly the methods of the manifest, and each one posts to its route with a JSON array body and `credentials: 'same-origin'`.
- [ ] A 403 answer carrying `read_only` rejects with an `ApiError` of that kind; a rejected `fetch` rejects with kind `network`; a `null` answer to a method that returns nothing resolves to `undefined`.
- [ ] The files produced by `vite build` do not contain the prototype dataset's sentinel string, the files produced by `vite build --mode prototype` do, and `bin/ci` fails if the first ever does.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] For each of the seven write patterns, a refused write through a mounted screen shows exactly one toast with the read-only text, bumps the revision counter once, shows no undo toast, and leaves no unhandled rejection.
- [ ] A call rejected with `locked` shows the PIN screen.
- [ ] A read rejected with `ledger_unavailable` shows its toast, and its "Tentar de novo" makes the screen fetch again and render once the read succeeds.
- [ ] A thrown error that is not an `ApiError` still reaches the console and shows no toast.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run dev` unlocks with `123456` on the stand-in; `dev:backend` sends `/api` to `127.0.0.1:8080`.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` describes the two builds and the two dev scripts.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and the seven refused-write tests pass.

## Tests
- Unit: the client against a stubbed `fetch`: routes, bodies, results, each error kind.
- Unit: the failure function for each kind, and for a non-API error.
- Component: one refused write per write pattern through a mounted screen; a locked answer; a failed read and its retry.
- Build check in the gate: the sentinel string absent from the bundle for real use.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/http/`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/main.ts`, `web/src/stores/session.ts`, `web/src/test/`, `web/vite.config.ts`, `web/package.json`, `web/scripts/parity/`, `bin/ci`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/stores/overlay.ts`, `web/src/stores/revision.ts`

A new client directory, one new module for failures, the provisioning line in `main.ts`, a lock entry point on the session store, a test helper, the build modes and the gate's bundle check. No screen component and no write call site is edited.
close_reason: web/src/api/http builds the client by iterating the manifest and posts each method to its route with same-origin credentials; the implementation is chosen by a build constant, and the gate proves the build for real use carries neither the stand-in nor the prototype dataset. One function wired to Vue's error handler and to unhandledrejection turns read_only into one toast and a revision bump, locked into the PIN screen, and any other failure into a toast with a retry; no write call site was edited. bin/ci: CI green, 839 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. Each of the seven write patterns has a refused-write test. Known and left: after a refused month close the closing step collapses, which needs an edit to that screen.

title: Compare smaller local models with the outside model for nightly categorisation
description:
## What changes for the user
Every night, the transactions that fixed rules cannot classify are sent to an outside provider's
model: their descriptions, amounts and counterpart names leave the home server, and each call is
billed. The user accepted that for now and asked to know whether a smaller model running at home
could do the same job. Once this lands they have that answer in numbers taken from their own
transactions: which home-run model came closest, how far it trails or beats the outside one, and
whether switching would mean correcting more transactions by hand.

## Outcome
A committed report compares at least three models that run on the user's own hardware against the
outside model on the same set of transactions the user has already confirmed or corrected, and
ends with one recommendation: switch, keep the outside model, or send only the uncertain rows
outside.

## Context
The app assigns each transaction to a budget line, which is one row of the user's monthly budget
(groceries, transport and so on). Fixed rules do most of it: a company that always lands on the
same line is mapped once. What the rules cannot place goes to a language model in a nightly job
that runs with nobody present. The model's answer is applied by itself only when its confidence
is at or above a threshold the user sets, called the auto-apply threshold here; below it the
transaction waits in a queue for the user to decide.

It was decided that the backend reaches the model by calling an HTTP API directly, in the chat
format that outside providers and local model runtimes both accept, so that changing model is a
matter of two configuration values, the base URL and the model name. This bead is the test of
that claim as much as of the models: if a local model needs a different request, the claim is
false and the report must say so.

The user's words when asking for this: outside providers are fine "por enquanto", with a bead to
"avaliar/testar modelos locais menores". Privacy is one reason and cost the other. One guard
already holds on every path: a personal tax number (CPF) is never part of a request, because it
does not help classification.

Two constraints shape the work and are easy to break by accident:

- **The repository is public and the evaluation set is real financial data.** The labelled set
  and every per-row output stay outside the repository, in a directory git ignores. The report
  publishes aggregates only: no description, no counterpart name, no amount per row. Test
  fixtures are synthetic.
- **Which models to try is decided when the work runs, not here.** The set of small models that
  are worth trying changes from month to month, so naming them now would date the bead. The
  criteria fix how many and how they are compared instead.

The evaluation tool may be a script outside the backend, in Python, since it is run by hand a few
times and never deployed. The user was told this and did not object. It must send the same
request the nightly job sends, which is why this bead cannot start before that job exists.

It cannot start yet for a second reason: there is nothing to evaluate against until the user has
used the app long enough to confirm or correct a few hundred categorisations. Both waits are on
work that has no bead at the time of writing, so the bead is parked as blocked with a comment, to
be replaced by dependency edges when the categorisation work is written up.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The evaluation set holds at least 300 transactions whose budget line the user confirmed or
      corrected, spanning at least 3 calendar months, with every CPF removed. The report states
      its size and month span.
- [ ] At least 3 models running on the user's own hardware are measured, at no fewer than 2
      different sizes, beside the outside model in use on that day as the baseline. The report
      names each one with the exact version or tag that was run.
- [ ] Every arm receives the request the nightly job builds, byte for byte except the base URL
      and the model name. The report states this, or lists each difference a model required.
- [ ] For each arm the report gives four figures over the whole set: the share of rows whose
      budget line matches the user's; the share of rows answered at or above the auto-apply
      threshold in force (coverage); the share of matches among those rows; and the share of
      answers that were not valid against the response schema.
- [ ] For each local arm the report records the host's CPU, memory and GPU, and the peak memory
      the model used.
- [ ] Seconds per nightly batch, median of three runs per arm with the arms interleaved, are
      measured **by the review** rather than by whoever implements this, and recorded in the
      report.
- [ ] No file under version control contains a transaction description, a counterpart name or a
      per-row amount from the evaluation set: `git grep` for three descriptions sampled from the
      set returns nothing.
- [ ] The report ends with exactly one recommendation (switch, keep, or route by confidence) and
      the two figures it rests on.
- [ ] Done when: the report is committed at `docs/evaluations/local-models.md` and a reader can
      tell from it alone, without rerunning anything, which local model did best and by how many
      percentage points it trails or beats the baseline at the threshold in force.

## Tests
- Unit: the scoring functions (match share, coverage, match share above the threshold, invalid
  answer share) over a synthetic labelled fixture with known expected values, including a row
  with an invalid answer and a row exactly at the threshold.
- Unit: the loader refuses a set that still carries a CPF-shaped value.
- Manual check: the three measured runs per arm, standing in for an end-to-end test that cannot
  run in CI because the models and the labelled set exist only on the user's machines.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `tools/model-eval/`, `docs/evaluations/local-models.md`
**Reads only:** the backend code that builds the nightly categorisation request

A new, self-contained tool directory (the script, its scoring module and their tests) and one
report. Nothing in the backend or the interface changes; the request builder is read so the tool
sends the same request, and is not edited. If the comparison argues for switching, the switch
itself is a configuration change and belongs to a separate bead.

comments.author: gabriel
comments.text: Blocked on work that has no bead yet: the nightly categorisation job whose request this evaluation must reuse, and a few hundred categorisations confirmed or corrected by the user. When that work is written up as beads, replace this status with dependency edges (br dep add finwise-g82 <bead>) and set the status back to open.

title: Let a closed month be reopened from the closing screen, by undoing the change that closed it
description:
## What changes for the user
Today, when the person closes a month, the app keeps that month's budget exactly as it stood and stops
accepting changes to it. The dialog that confirms the close says so, and from then on nothing on screen
takes the close back. If, days later, they notice that a planned amount of that month was wrong, they
cannot correct it: the month's budget has no edit button any more, and the only way back is to look up an
identifier in the database file and call the server by hand. After this lands, a month the person closed
shows a button that reopens it, behind a confirmation. Reopening puts the month back as it was before the
close, so its budget can be edited again, and the month can be closed again afterwards. When reopening is
no longer possible, because something changed later that depends on the close, the person reads a sentence
that says so and the month stays closed.

## Outcome
The read that feeds the closing screen answers, for a month that a close is holding closed, the identifier
of the change that closed it, and nothing for any other month. On the eighth step of the closing screen of
such a month a button "Reabrir mês" appears; confirmed, it undoes that change through the undo the server
already has. No new write is added to the contract. The stand-in backend behaves the same way.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. Everything the person authors is kept in
the app's own database, and every change to it is written to *the journal*: one row per change (its
author, its method, its instant, and whether it was undone) and one row per *effect* (the table and key it
touched, with the value before and after). A change has an identifier, *the change id*, which is a decimal
string on the wire. *Undoing* a change restores what its effects recorded and marks the change undone; the
method `changes.undo(changeId)` does it. A change that was not undone is *in force*. The server refuses an
undo with the error kind `refused` and the reason `stale_change` when the change is unknown or already
undone, when a later change in force touched the same rows, or when a check finds that the restored state
would be wrong; the interface shows that reason as "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser
desfeito.". *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend that answers with the design prototype's dataset
(`web/src/api/fake`); the build for real use talks to the Go server instead. *The manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from the TypeScript contract types and never edited by hand.
*Golden files* are the committed answers of every read over invented data, under
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`. *Parity* is the script that compares each ported screen, pixel by pixel,
with the design prototype.

**What closing a month does today.** The closing screen is the route `/revisao/fechamento`; its eighth
step closes the selected month. The button is disabled while a transaction of that month or an earlier one
waits for review. A click opens a confirmation ("Fechar {mês}? O budget deste mês fica guardado e não muda
mais.", confirm label "Fechar o mês"). The write `review.closeMonth(month)` records, as one change, a row
in the table of closed months and, when the month had no budget version starting at it, a copy of the
budget in force as a version of the month's own. It answers `{changeId}`. From then on saving or applying
a budget for that month is refused with "Esse mês já está fechado."; the month's transactions stay
editable. The interface discards the answered id (`web/src/screens/revisao/useClosingActions.ts`, whose
comment says that closing carries no toast because the screen itself shows the result), and no read gives
it back, so the close cannot be undone from any screen. On the server the undo of a close is already
exact and tested (`internal/api/review_close_test.go`): it removes the closed row and the copied version,
and the month can then be closed again under a new change id.

**What was decided, and what lost.**
- *A control on the closed month, not a toast after the close.* A toast with "Desfazer" lasts eight
  seconds and the confirmation already guards against a wrong click; the regret this is for comes days
  later. The close keeps having no toast, and reopening has none either: the screen shows the month open.
- *Reopening is the undo of the close's change, not a new write.* A method `review.reopenMonth` was
  considered and rejected: it would add a method to the contract, a handler, conformance cases and a
  stand-in implementation for something the journal already does and its tests already hold.
- *The change id travels in the closing read.* `review.closing(month)` gains one nullable field,
  `closeChangeId`. It is the id of the change that is in force, whose method is `review.closeMonth`, and
  whose effects wrote the closed-months row of that month; otherwise it is null. The method filter is
  load-bearing: a closed row can be written by a change that did more than close. The invented state of
  the conformance suite closes January inside its one seed change, and the stand-in starts with a month
  already closed that no change of its log wrote; undoing either would undo far more than a close, so
  both answer null and show no button. A wrong id here is silent and expensive: `changes.undo` undoes
  whatever id it is given.
- *The button lives in step eight of the closed month*, where the close button was, and not in the list
  "Meses fechados": the rows of that list are whole-row buttons that select a month, and the list's
  entries would each need the id.
- *The sentences about closing stay as they are.* "não muda mais" and "só para leitura" remain true while
  the month is closed. Reopening shows no new refusal reason: `stale_change` and its sentence are reused.

**What the journal offers for the lookup.** No existing read goes from a table and key to the change that
wrote it, so one new SQL statement is needed. Every statement of `internal/authored` is a constant
registered in `statements.go`, and three tests of `source_test.go` fail for one that is not. The closest
existing statement is the one behind `TransactionsSettledBy` in `internal/authored/review.go`, which joins
changes to effects, keeps changes in force, filters on the effect's table and reads the key with
`json_extract`. An effect's key is a JSON array; for the closed-months table it is `["<month>"]`.
`internal/api` holds no SQL: the handler asks the store.

**What a new field of a read obliges.** The TypeScript type `ClosingView`
(`web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`) gains the field and the manifest is regenerated with
`npm --prefix web run contract`. The Go wire type is `closingViewWire` in `internal/api/review_closing.go`.
Eight golden files hold an answer of this read: two under `full/`, two under `empty/` and four under
`full-authored/` (months 2026-01 to 2026-04), rewritten by
`go test ./internal/api -run TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile -update` and
`go test ./internal/api -run TestEveryAuthoredReadCaseAnswersAndMatchesItsGoldenFile -update`; each diff is
read, not accepted by running the command. An inline expectation in `internal/api/review_closing_test.go`
(`closingOf`) pins the whole answer and needs the key. The stand-in must answer the field too:
`web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts` validates its answers against the manifest, and
`web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` compares it with the `empty/` golden files field by field.

**How a refusal reaches the person.** Call sites do not catch. A failed call ends in
`web/src/api/failures.ts`, which for `refused` toasts the reason's sentence with no action and bumps the
revision counter, so the screen refetches and shows what the server holds. A screen test makes one method
fail with `failingOne` and refuses every write with `readOnlyApi` (both in `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`);
`mountWithFailures` there installs the failure handlers.

**Parity.** The closing screen has states in `web/scripts/parity/states.mjs`, two of them with a closed
month. By their steps neither shows the body of step eight for a month that carries a close id: one
selects the stand-in's month that was closed from the start, which answers null, and the other folds
every step after closing. That is read from the step lists and not measured, so the parity run is a
criterion below. The design prototype has no reopen control; nothing about its reference changes.

**Not known, and settled by a test here.** No test undoes a close after a transaction of the closed month
was put on a line. The close's change shares no row with such a write, so the undo should be accepted; a
criterion below proves it. A known refusal, which stays: after a close, a budget save for an earlier month
that removes a line a transaction of the closed month is on makes the undo of the close refuse until that
save is undone.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `ClosingView` has `closeChangeId: string | null`, the manifest is regenerated, and the gate's check
that the manifest is current passes.
- [ ] For a month closed through `review.closeMonth`, `review.closing(month).closeChangeId` equals the
`changeId` that close answered. After `changes.undo` of that id the same read answers `closed: false` and
`closeChangeId: null`. After the month is closed again it answers the new id, which differs from the first.
- [ ] For an open month the field is null. For a month whose closed row was written by a change of another
method it is null while `closed` is true: `full-authored/review.closing.2026-01.json` shows exactly that.
- [ ] With two months closed by two closes, each month answers its own close's id, and undoing one of them
reopens that month only.
- [ ] A month is closed, a transaction of that month is then put on a line its budget has, and the close
is undone: the undo is accepted and the transaction keeps its line.
- [ ] The lookup is one statement constant registered in `internal/authored/statements.go`;
`go test ./internal/authored` passes, and no file of `internal/api` holds SQL.
- [ ] The eight golden files of `review.closing` change by the new key alone, and no other golden file
changes: `git diff --stat` over `internal/api/testdata/golden/` lists those eight files with one added
line each.
- [ ] On the closing screen, step eight of a closed month whose `closeChangeId` is not null shows a button
"Reabrir mês". With null it shows none: the stand-in's month that is closed from the start has no button.
- [ ] A click on "Reabrir mês" opens a confirmation with the message "Reabrir {mês}? O budget deste mês
volta a poder ser editado." and the confirm label "Reabrir mês". Declining calls no method. Confirming
calls `changes.undo` once, with exactly the id the read gave, and afterwards step eight shows the button
"Fechar o mês" again and the list "Meses fechados" no longer holds the month.
- [ ] A successful reopen shows no toast, and a close still shows none.
- [ ] With `changes.undo` made to fail as `refused` with `stale_change`, confirming shows the toast "Isso
já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito." with no action, the month still shows as closed, and
the composable has no `catch`. With every write refused as read-only, confirming shows "Somente leitura por
enquanto. Nada foi alterado." and the month still shows as closed.
- [ ] The stand-in keeps the change id of each close it performs, answers it in `closing`, answers null
after that change is undone, and `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts` and `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`
pass.
- [ ] Each rule was seen failing once, by breaking it on purpose, and the pull request names the test that
failed for each: the lookup without the filter on changes in force (an undone close's id is answered);
without the filter on the method (January answers the seed change's id); without the filter on the month
(another month's id is answered); the button shown when the id is null; the undo called before the
confirmation is accepted.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` passes on both viewports with no limit raised and no state removed,
and its output is in the pull request body.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: a person can reopen, from the closing screen, a month they closed and edit its budget
again; the server's tests show the id of a close going out in the read and coming back to undo exactly
that close; and a reopen the server refuses leaves the month closed with its sentence on screen.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/authored`: the lookup over months closed by a close in force, by a close that was
undone, by a change of another method, and over an open month; two closed months answered apart.
- Integration, in `internal/api` (`review_close_test.go`, `review_closing_test.go`): the id answered by
the close equals the id the read gives; undo, then null; close again, a new id; the undo of a close after
a line was set on a transaction of the month.
- Golden: the eight `review.closing` files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, each diff read.
- Unit, with the screen mounted, in `web/src/screens/revisao/closing.test.ts`, over `createFakeApi`: the button present and
absent, the confirmation accepted and declined, the call and its argument, the screen after a reopen, the
refusal through `failingOne`, the read-only backend through `readOnlyApi`.
- Unit, in `web/src/api/fake/closing.test.ts`: the stand-in's id per close, null after the undo, null for
the month closed from the start.
- End to end, by hand: the parity script's run over the closing screen's states in a real browser, with its
output kept.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/closing.go`, `internal/authored/statements.go`,
`internal/api/review_closing.go`, `web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`,
`internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/api/fake/closing.ts`,
`web/src/screens/revisao/StepClose.vue`, `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`,
`web/src/screens/revisao/useClosingActions.ts`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`,
`internal/api/review_close_test.go`, `internal/api/review_closing_test.go`,
`web/src/screens/revisao/closing.test.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/closing.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/journal.go`, `internal/authored/undo.go`,
`internal/authored/review.go`, `internal/authored/month_close.go`, `internal/api/changes.go`,
`internal/api/review_close.go`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`,
`web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `web/src/stores/overlay.ts`, `web/scripts/parity/states.mjs`,
`design/README.md`, `web/src/api/contract/manifest.test.ts`, `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`, `bin/ci`

Nine code files in four places (the store, the API, the contract with its stand-in, one screen), with four
test files, a test beside the store's read and the golden files, which is why this is `size:L` although each edit is small. It
stops at the closing screen: the list of closed months, the header's seal, the budget screen and the undo
engine itself are not edited. No migration and no new table: the id is read from the journal as it is.
The seam is not split in two because the contract field without the screen leaves an id nobody uses, and
both halves share the contract type and the stand-in.

## Recovery path
Nothing is migrated and no stored row changes shape: the field is derived at read time and the control
calls an undo that already exists. Reverting the pull request removes both, and a month reopened in the
meantime stays open as any undone change does; it can be closed again from the screen.
close_reason: A month the person closed can be reopened from the closing screen: the closing read answers the id of the change that closed it, only while the month reads closed and only for a change in force of the method that closes a month whose effects wrote that month's row, and a button in step eight, behind a confirmation, undoes that change. The stand-in keeps the id of each close it performs. Verified by the gate and the design parity on the branch after main was merged in, by tests of the id going out in the read and coming back to undo exactly that close, of two closed months, of a close undone after a line was set in the month, of the screen's button, confirmation, call and refusals, by the author's fifteen deliberate breaks, and in review by four more, each failing a named test. The eight golden files of the closing read gained the new key and nothing else moved.

title: Give the ledger reader a view that runs every query on one handle and one read-only transaction
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing the person sees changes with this piece, and no answer of the app changes. The app builds a
screen by asking the bank's records several questions, one after another, and a separate collector
replaces those records every night; a screen opened at the moment of the replacement can today be put
together half from yesterday's records and half from today's. This piece gives the part of the app that
reads those records a way to answer many questions from one state of them. The piece after it uses that
for every screen. It also carries every question the app asks today, so if it were wrong the person
would see it at once: a screen that fails to open, or a figure that is no longer what it was.

## Outcome
`internal/ledger` has a view of the snapshot: one handle and one read-only transaction that every one
of the 13 query methods can run on, so that all the queries made through one view see the same snapshot
even when the collector swaps the file meanwhile. The reader's own 13 methods are kept, each as a
wrapper that opens a view for that one call, so no file outside `internal/ledger` changes and every
existing test passes untouched.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate collector (pluggy-sync) fills from the banks every night and
replaces by an atomic rename; the app only reads it, and "the snapshot" below is that file. *The
reader* is `ledger.Reader`, the type through which the HTTP backend (`internal/api`) and the tests of
the rule packages ask the snapshot for accounts, transactions, bills, pots and so on. A *read handler*
is the function of `internal/api` that answers one method of the API.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named).**

- `internal/ledger/open.go`: a `Reader` holds only a path and `New` does not touch the file. Every
  public query goes through `read`, which opens a fresh handle with `openReadOnly` (it stats the file,
  opens it with `mode=ro`, `query_only(1)` and `busy_timeout(5000)` in the DSN, one connection), begins
  one read-only transaction, checks `PRAGMA user_version` with `requireSupportedVersion`, runs one
  function, passes its error through `asUnreadable` and closes. The package comment says why: the
  snapshot is replaced by an atomic rename and nothing promises what an open handle sees across the
  swap, so every call opens the file, runs and closes.
- There are 13 public query methods on `*Reader`, in 11 files: `Accounts` (`accounts.go`), `Bills`
  (`bills.go`), `BalanceHistory` and `ReserveHistory` (`history.go`), `Identities` (`identities.go`),
  `InvestmentPrincipals` (`investment_principal.go`), `Investments` and `InvestmentHistory`
  (`investments.go`), `Pots` (`pots.go`), `PotYields` (`pot_yield.go`), `SyncState` (`sync.go`),
  `CleanTransactions` (`transactions.go`), `YieldHistory` (`yield_history.go`). Each runs its
  statements inside the function it hands to `read`, which receives the `*sql.Tx` (`Accounts`, for
  example, calls `queryAccountRows(ctx, tx)` there).
- A read handler makes several of those calls, so it opens the snapshot several times and can see two
  snapshots across the swap: `readShellOverview` (`internal/api/shell.go`) calls `Accounts`,
  `SyncState` and `CleanTransactions`.
- The typed errors: a missing file is `fs.ErrNotExist` wrapped by `openReadOnly`; another schema
  version is `UnsupportedVersionError`; a file SQLite cannot read as a database, or a damaged one, is
  `UnreadableSnapshotError`. `internal/api/errors.go` answers all three as `ledger_unavailable`.
- Every SQL statement over the snapshot is a registered constant of `queries.go`, and
  `TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema` (`schema_test.go`) prepares each against the
  collector's schema.
- `internal/ledger/safety_test.go` pins the package's promises: every query refuses an unsupported
  version; the open path refuses writes; `TestQueriesLeaveTheSnapshotByteForByteUntouched` (the file's
  hash and its directory's listing are the same after every query);
  `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` (a call after a rename sees the new file); a missing file is
  an error; a file that is not a database, or a damaged one, is unreadable. `everyQuery` in
  `support_test.go` walks 12 of the 13 queries; `PotYields` has its own tests in `pot_yield_test.go`.
- Who holds the reader: 21 source files of `internal/api` that call its methods or pass it on,
  `cmd/finwise/serve.go` (which only builds it), and test files of `internal/ledger`, `internal/api`,
  `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and `internal/txrules`.
- `internal/api/pots_yield_guard_test.go` scans every non-test file under `internal/` and `cmd/` for
  the identifier `PotYields` (the collector's slow reference statement, which no request may reach)
  and exempts only `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go` and `queries.go`, by path.

**What changes.**

1. *The view.* The package gains a view of the snapshot: one handle and one read-only transaction, the
   version checked once, kept for as long as the view is open and released when it is closed. Every
   one of the 13 queries can run on it. Every query made through one view sees the same snapshot even
   when the collector renames a new file over the path meanwhile; a view opened after the rename sees
   the new file. The open path stays read-only twice over (`mode=ro` and `query_only`), the statements
   stay the registered constants of `queries.go`, and each query's error still passes through
   `asUnreadable`.
2. *The reader's methods stay, as wrappers.* Each of the reader's 13 methods becomes a wrapper that
   opens a view, runs that one query on it and closes it: exactly what a call does today. Twelve of
   them are gathered in one new file, so that the slice that removes them later deletes one file. The
   thirteenth, the reader's `PotYields`, stays in `pot_yield.go` beside the view's own, because the
   guard described above fails on that name in any other file. For the same reason nothing outside
   `pot_yield.go` may name `PotYields`, an interface that lists the view's methods included.
3. *Nothing outside the package changes.* No file of `internal/api`, of the rule packages or of
   `cmd/finwise` is edited, and no existing test file of `internal/ledger` is edited: they all keep
   calling the reader and keep passing, `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` among them, because a
   wrapper still opens the file that is there now. The view's own promises are proved in a new test
   file.

**Who uses the view next, so the design can be checked against real use.** The slice after this one
(finwise-jzw: every read handler receives a view of each store, opened for its request, and the reader's
wrappers are removed) hands one ledger view to each request and closes it when the request ends,
whether it answered, failed or panicked. Two things it needs constrain this slice. A request that never
asks the ledger anything must not fail because the snapshot is missing, so it must be possible to hold
a view that has not touched the file yet, or to open one only when first needed; whether that lives in
the view (opened at its first query) or in its caller is the implementer's, as long as all the queries
of one view see one snapshot. And the errors of a view are the same typed errors as today, returned by
whichever call first touches the file, so the API's answers do not change. Later the job that brings a
new snapshot into the app's own database reads the run that produced the rows and the rows themselves
through one view, for the same reason.

**Left to the implementer.** The names of the view type, of what opens it and of the wrapper file.

**Why it is done this way, and what lost.** Ledger rows are handed out as rows, never as a connection,
and the snapshot is swapped under the reader; what a request needs is one snapshot for all its queries.
A fresh handle per query, which is what the code does today, lost: it is exactly what lets one answer
mix two snapshots. Changing the reader and every caller in one step also lost, to this slice and the
next: the callers are some sixty files in five packages, and a view that lands first, with the old
methods still answering, can be proved on its own with no caller touched.

**The failure path this slice prepares.** The snapshot is swapped during a request: the request
finishes on the snapshot it opened, and the next one sees the new one. Here it is proved for a view;
the next slice makes it true for a request.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Nothing
in this slice needs a real ledger and the opt-in test that reads one
(`internal/ledger/realsnapshot_test.go`) is not edited. The rule stands all the same: a real snapshot
may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed,
logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person
running the test and goes into no file; such a test runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a
file. Fixtures are invented (`internal/ledger/ledgertest`), and no `.db` file is opened by hand.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; this slice changes how rows
are fetched, not how an amount is decoded. Every SQL statement over the snapshot stays a registered
constant, as every statement over the app's own database must be. Interface text is Brazilian
Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (this slice
touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] On one view over the `populated` fixture, each of the 13 queries returns what the reader's method
of the same name returns.
- [ ] A view answers `Accounts`; a second invented snapshot holding a different account is renamed over
the path; the same view then answers `Accounts` and `CleanTransactions` from the first snapshot; a view
opened after the rename answers from the second.
- [ ] A view kept open across all 13 queries leaves the file's hash and its directory's listing as they
were: no `-journal`, `-wal` or `-shm` file appears.
- [ ] Through a view, a snapshot with `user_version` 2 is `UnsupportedVersionError`, a file that is not
a database and a damaged database are `UnreadableSnapshotError`, and a missing file satisfies
`errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist)`; none of them yields a row.
- [ ] A query on a closed view is an error, not a fresh open of the file.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main -- . ':(exclude)internal/ledger'` is empty, and among the test files of
`internal/ledger` the diff against `main` shows only added files.
- [ ] `git diff main -- internal/ledger/queries.go` is empty and
`TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema` passes.
- [ ] Both `PotYields` methods are in `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, and
`go test ./internal/api -run TestNoReadHandlerReachesTheCollectorsYieldStatement` passes.
- [ ] `go test ./...` passes with no test edited, the golden comparison of `internal/api`
(`TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile`) included, without `-update`.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the final
report: the swap test against a view that reopens the file for each query; the closed-view test against
a view that reopens after it was closed; the untouched-file test against a handle opened without
`mode=ro`; the parity test against one query left running on a handle of its own.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, a snapshot swap between two queries on one view is not
seen in a test that was seen failing, and no file outside `internal/ledger` differs from `main`.

## Tests
- Unit, over two invented snapshots built with `ledgertest` (`ledgertest.NewAt` at a second path and
  `os.Rename`, as `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow` builds them): a view keeps its snapshot
  across the swap for every later query; a new view sees the new file.
- Unit, over the `populated` fixture of `support_test.go`: the 13 queries on one view against the
  reader's 13 methods; the file and its directory untouched after a long-lived view.
- Unit, over the same fixture with its version changed (`SetUserVersion`), over a text file and over a
  database with its pages overwritten (as `TestADamagedDatabaseIsUnreadableToo` builds one), and over a
  missing path: the view's typed errors.
- Unit: a query on a closed view.
- The existing tests of `internal/ledger`, `internal/api` and the rule packages, unedited, as the proof
  that the wrappers answer as the methods did; golden, the 59 files of each of
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` and `empty/`, unchanged.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/accounts.go`, `internal/ledger/bills.go`,
`internal/ledger/history.go`, `internal/ledger/identities.go`, `internal/ledger/investment_principal.go`,
`internal/ledger/investments.go`, `internal/ledger/pots.go`, `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`,
`internal/ledger/sync.go`, `internal/ledger/transactions.go`, `internal/ledger/yield_history.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/queries.go`, `internal/ledger/schema_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `internal/ledger/support_test.go`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/`,
`internal/api/`, `internal/cardrules/`, `internal/potrules/`, `internal/txrules/`,
`cmd/finwise/serve.go`, `bin/ci`

One package: `open.go` and the 11 files that hold the 13 queries change, and three files are new (the
view, the reader's twelve wrappers, the view's tests). It is labelled large for the count of files, not
for the reach: nothing outside `internal/ledger` is edited, no existing test is edited, and the
statements of `queries.go` are not touched. The callers in `internal/api`, the rule packages and
`cmd/finwise` are read only to confirm they still compile and pass.
close_reason: ledger.View runs all thirteen queries on one handle and one read-only transaction opened by its first query; a snapshot renamed over the path is not seen by an open view and is seen by the next; the first open's result, success or failure, is what every later query gets; a closed view refuses. The reader's methods remain as wrappers, so no caller and no golden file changed. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main; hosted check passed. Review: three independent mutations; one survived at first (a failed open retried by the next query) and now has its own test. A new test shows the connection mode alone refuses a write with query_only lifted.

title: Change the PIN on the server, count a wrong current PIN in the same lockout as the PIN screen, and end every other session
description:
## What changes for the user
Today "Trocar PIN" in Configurações answers "Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado." against the
real server: the PIN is the one whose hash was put in the server's configuration, and only someone editing
that configuration and restarting the server can change it. After this lands the person types the current
PIN and the new one twice, and from that moment the new PIN is the one that opens the app, also after a
restart, and the old one no longer does. Every other browser or tab that was open goes back to the PIN
screen at its next request; the one where the PIN was changed stays open. Typing the current PIN wrong counts
against the same three attempts as the PIN screen: twice the form says "PIN atual incorreto", and the third
time the app returns to the PIN screen, which says how long to wait. If this were wrong the person would not
see an error: the old PIN would keep opening the app, someone holding an open session could guess the
current PIN without limit, or a session opened by somebody else would survive the change meant to shut it
out.

## Outcome
The migration `0008_session` creates `pin(id, hash, changed_at)`, one row at most. `session.changePin`,
on a server started with `--db`, is answered by the session service: it verifies the current PIN under the
shared lockout, checks the new PIN, stores the new hash in the app's database, makes the running server
verify against it at once, removes every session but the caller's, and answers. The third wrong current PIN,
and any attempt while the hold runs, removes the caller's session and answers `locked` with exactly one
`Set-Cookie` header, the one that clears the cookie. At start, a stored hash is the one that opens the app,
and `finwise serve` says so in one log line. Nothing of it is a recorded change; no log line, error or row of
the journal holds a PIN. Without `--db` the method keeps answering `read_only`.

## Context
**The app and its words.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person, behind a six-digit PIN. *The
ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads
it, and changing the PIN never touches it. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, a second SQLite file the
server opens when started with `--db` / `FINWISE_DB`; everything the person authors lives there. *The
contract* is the TypeScript description of the 82 methods the interface calls (`web/src/api/contract/`);
*the manifest*, `internal/contract/contract.json`, is that contract generated for Go, with each method's
route, class (`session`, `read`, `evaluate`, `write`) and argument schema. *The stand-in* is the in-memory
fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement
of how writes behave. *The journal* is the record of every change made to the app's database (tables
`changes` and `change_effects`), from which a change is undone. *The lockout* is the server's count of wrong
PINs: three in a row hold every attempt for 300 seconds, globally, because there is one user.

**What exists today (checked in the code).**
- `internal/api/session_routes.go`: `sessionService` holds `store` (the sessions), `lockout`, `verifyPIN
  func(attempt string) bool` and `cookie`. `recognise` looks the request's cookie up and, for a live
  session, sends the cookie again (`cookie.issue`) so its lifetime follows the sliding expiry; the router
  calls it on every request before anything else but the verb. `dispatch` knows `status`, `unlock` and
  `lock`, and answers `internal` for any other name. `unlock` decodes one string and calls
  `lockout.Attempt(func() bool { return service.verifyPIN(attempt) })`: `OutcomeUnlocked` opens a session
  and answers `{"ok":true}`, `OutcomeHeld` answers `{"ok":false,"reason":"locked-out","retryAfterSeconds":N}`,
  a wrong PIN `{"ok":false,"reason":"wrong-pin"}`. `lock` removes the caller's session, then
  `w.Header().Del("Set-Cookie")` with the comment that recognise already renewed the cookie and "two
  Set-Cookie lines for one name leave the outcome to whichever a client reads", then `cookie.clear`.
- `internal/api/lockout.go`: `Lockout.Attempt(verify)` holds its mutex across `verify` (so parallel attempts
  cannot each get a guess). While a hold runs it answers `OutcomeHeld` with the seconds left and never calls
  `verify`. A right attempt sets the count to zero and answers `OutcomeUnlocked`. A wrong one adds one: below
  three it answers `OutcomeWrongPIN`; at three it sets the count back to zero, holds for `lockoutDuration`
  (300 s) and answers `OutcomeHeld` with 300. `RetryAfterSeconds` is what `session.status` reports. There is
  one `Lockout` per handler, built in `newSessionService`.
- `internal/api/sessions.go`: sessions live in memory, keyed by a SHA-256 digest of the token; `Create`,
  `Touch` and `Remove` exist, and nothing removes every session but one.
- `internal/api/cookie.go`: the cookie is `__Host-finwise-session` (`finwise-session` with
  `--dev-insecure-cookie`), `Path=/`, `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Secure` unless insecure; `issue` sets
  `Max-Age` to the session's idle lifetime, `clear` sets `MaxAge = -1` (written `Max-Age=0`) with no value.
- `internal/api/pinhash.go`: `ValidPIN` (exactly six ASCII digits); `NewPINHash(pin)` derives
  `pbkdf2-sha256$600000$<salt>$<key>` with a fresh 16-byte salt and a 32-byte key; `ParsePINHash`; `Verify`
  compares in constant time. `ErrMalformedPINHash` carries no part of the value it rejected.
- `internal/api/router.go`: `Config.VerifyPIN` is required (`withDefaults` fails without it). `serve` checks
  the verb, then the session (`recognise`; only `session.status` and `session.unlock` answer without one),
  then the class: every `write` and `evaluate` answers `read_only` before its body is read; then the body
  (`readArguments`: JSON content type, at most 1 MiB, an array whose length is within the method's bounds),
  then session methods go to `sessions.dispatch`. `session.changePin` is of class `write`, so today it never
  reaches the session service.
- `cmd/finwise/serve.go`: `completeServeSettings` requires `FINWISE_PIN_HASH`, parses it with
  `api.ParsePINHash`, and refuses to start with a message that names neither the value nor the hash;
  `serve` builds the handler with `VerifyPIN: settings.pinHash.Verify` and logs with `log/slog` to standard
  output ("listening", and a warning for the insecure cookie).
- `internal/api/session_routes_test.go`: `TestChangePinIsReadOnlyAndComparesNothing` expects `read_only`,
  zero PIN comparisons and the PIN unchanged; `newTestEnv` (`helpers_test.go`) counts every comparison in
  `pinTries`. `internal/api/logging_test.go` holds the sentinels test for the request log, and
  `handler_silence_test.go` fails when any file of `internal/api` other than `logging.go` and `router.go`
  logs or prints.
- The stand-in (`createFakeApi` in `web/src/api/fake/index.ts`) checks in this order: the current PIN
  (`wrong-current`), then the new one against `/^\d{6}$/` (`invalid-new`), then the repeat (`mismatch`),
  and then replaces its PIN. It has no lockout on this path and no sessions. `session.test.ts` pins the
  order ("reports the wrong current PIN before the other two faults") and the cases `12345`, `1234567`,
  `12345a` and `''` for `invalid-new`.
- The contract (`web/src/api/contract/session.ts`): `changePin(current, next, repeat)` answers
  `{ok: true}` or `{ok: false, reason: 'wrong-current' | 'invalid-new' | 'mismatch'}`; "After a change the
  old PIN no longer opens the app." No contract type changes here.
- The form, `web/src/screens/config/PinSection.vue`, shows "PIN atual incorreto", "O novo PIN precisa ter 6
  dígitos" and "Os dois campos do novo PIN não conferem" for the three reasons, and on `{ok: true}` closes
  and toasts "PIN alterado.". It does not catch: any rejection goes to the central failure handler, so a
  `locked` answer brings the PIN screen back. `web/src/screens/config/config.test.ts` ("PIN section") and
  `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts` ("the PIN form") test it; neither changes here.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.** None of it is in the repository when this is written;
read it as it landed.
- The app's database (finwise-9h2): the package `internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against
  `finwise.db`, opened once for the life of the process with immediate write transactions; migrations
  embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`, recorded by name and checksum in `schema_migrations`,
  every missing one applied at start in name order, each in one transaction, and the file copied with
  `VACUUM INTO` to `<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>` before a database that holds data is migrated; every SQL
  statement a registered constant that a test prepares against the migrated schema. `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` stays
  required at start whether or not `--db` is given.
- The recorder (finwise-wi4), the layer through which every change to a journaled table is written, with a guard
  that fails when a statement changes an authored table outside it. Its list of tables deliberately not
  journaled already names `pin`: changing the PIN is not a recorded change and has no undo, so `pin` is
  written by plain registered statements of `internal/authored`, outside the recorder.
- Write dispatch (finwise-2s5): the router's `write`/`evaluate` branch answers `read_only` before the body is
  read when the server has no app's database or the method has no implementation; otherwise it reads the
  arguments and validates them against the method's argument schema compiled from the manifest
  (`bad_request` on a mismatch) before anything runs. A test walks the manifest and requires each write to
  have exactly one implementation (a registered handler or, for `session.changePin` alone, the session
  service) or to be in an explicit list `writesWithoutHandler`; the walk fails if the registry ever holds a
  handler for `session.changePin`, which sits in that list until this work.
- The interface's handling of refusals and of `locked` (finwise-diw): `markLocked()` in
  `web/src/stores/session.ts` brings the PIN screen back at once and then loads `session.status` for the
  hold alone, so a PIN screen brought back by a `locked` answer shows "Muitas tentativas. Tente de novo em N
  minutos." with the keypad held, and a failure of that status call shows nothing; and a test helper beside
  `readOnlyApi` in `web/src/test/readOnly.ts` that makes one named method of a `FinwiseApi` reject with a
  chosen kind.

**`0008_session`.** One migration file, `internal/authored/migrations/0008_session.sql`. The name is fixed;
migrations are recorded by name, so it may be applied to a database that already holds a higher-numbered one.

| column | holds | constraint |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `id` | always 1: there is one PIN | primary key, `CHECK (id = 1)` |
| `hash` | the stored form `pbkdf2-sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<key>` that `NewPINHash` writes | not null |
| `changed_at` | the instant of the change, from the request's clock, written as the app's database writes its instants | not null |

No row exists until the first change; writing the PIN replaces the one row. The table is not journaled and
no row of `changes` or `change_effects` is ever written for it. The store offers two functions, reading the
stored hash (or "none") and writing it with its instant in one immediate transaction; both are registered
statements of `internal/authored`, in a file of its own for the session's table.

**The operation, in this order.** `session.changePin(current, next, repeat)` with a live session, on a
server with an app's database:

1. The router reads and validates the arguments against the schema (three strings). A mismatch is
   `bad_request`, with no PIN compared and the lockout's count unchanged.
2. Verify `current` under the lockout: the same `Lockout` value `session.unlock` uses, through `Attempt`, with
   the verifier the server uses now.
   - `OutcomeWrongPIN` (the first and the second wrong PIN of a row): answer
     `{"ok":false,"reason":"wrong-current"}`, status 200. The session stays, and the answer carries the
     renewed cookie like any request with a session.
   - `OutcomeHeld`, which is the third wrong PIN of a row (the count is set back to zero and the hold of
     300 s starts) and also any attempt while a hold already runs, the right PIN included (the verifier is
     then not called at all): remove the caller's session from the store; take back the renewed cookie
     `recognise` had already put on the answer (`w.Header().Del("Set-Cookie")`, as `lock` does); clear the
     cookie (`cookie.clear`); answer 401 `{"error":{"kind":"locked"}}`. The answer carries exactly one
     `Set-Cookie` header, the clearing one: the cookie's name, no value, `Max-Age=0`. Only the caller's
     session is removed; other sessions stay as they are.
   - `OutcomeUnlocked`: the count is now zero, and it stays cleared even if the new PIN is then rejected.
3. `next` must be exactly six ASCII digits (`ValidPIN`, which agrees with the stand-in's `/^\d{6}$/`):
   otherwise `{"ok":false,"reason":"invalid-new"}`.
4. `repeat` must equal `next`: otherwise `{"ok":false,"reason":"mismatch"}`. A new PIN equal to the current
   one is accepted, as in the stand-in.
5. Derive the new hash (`NewPINHash`) and store it with its instant in `pin`, in one immediate transaction
   that is committed before anything below happens.
6. From that moment the running server verifies every PIN (unlock and the next change) against the new
   hash: the session service's verifier is replaced in memory by the new hash's `Verify`.
7. Drop every session but the caller's (a new function of the session store that removes all tokens except
   one).
8. Answer `{"ok":true}`, with the caller's renewed cookie.

The wrong-current check comes first whatever the other two arguments are, as in the stand-in: `["000000",
"12","34"]` is `wrong-current`. A failure at step 5 (the hash cannot be derived, the write fails, the
five-second wait for the database's write lock runs out) answers 500 `internal`; the old hash stays the
one the server verifies against and in the database, and every session stays as it was, because steps 6 and
7 run only after the commit. A change and an unlock that run at the same time each verify against either
the old hash or the new one, never anything else, and once `{"ok":true}` is answered the hash the server
verifies against and the stored row are the same; how the session service serialises steps 2 to 6 against
each other is the implementer's, as long as it does not hold the lockout's mutex while waiting on the
database. The method needs no ledger: it works while the snapshot file is missing. It is not a recorded
change and has no undo; `changes.undo` knows nothing of it.

**Without an app's database** (no `--db`), `session.changePin` answers 403 `read_only` before its body is
read, with no PIN compared, as every write does there. Without a session it answers 401 `locked`, as today.

**At start.** `finwise serve` with `--db` reads the stored hash after the database is opened and migrated.
When there is one, it is the hash that opens the app and the environment's is ignored; `cmd/finwise` logs
one line at start, at level info, with exactly the message `the PIN stored in the database opens the app;
FINWISE_PIN_HASH is ignored` and no attribute holding either hash. When there is none, the environment's hash
is the one, and no such line is logged. `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` stays required and is still parsed at start
either way, with the messages it has today. A stored hash that `ParsePINHash` refuses stops the start with a
message that names the database's path and the reason and never the value, as a database that cannot be
opened or migrated does; the server never falls back to the environment's hash silently.

**Where it is wired.** The router hands `session.changePin` to `sessionService` together with the app's
database: it is not a generic write handler, because it needs what only the session service has (the
caller's token, the lockout, the session store), and it does not go through the recorder. `dispatch` gains
the method, or the router calls a method of the service directly; that is the implementer's. The name leaves
`writesWithoutHandler`, and the manifest walk counts it as implemented by the session service: removing it
from the list without the router handing it over makes the walk fail, and registering a handler for it in
the registry still makes the walk fail. How the service reaches the store (a field of `Config`, an
interface the service owns) is the implementer's; a test must be able to make the write of step 5 fail.

**What the interface does with it, and what does not change.** Nothing in the interface is edited. The form
already shows the three faults and the success. A `locked` answer reaches the central failure handler,
which brings the PIN screen back, and the PIN screen loads the hold and shows the wait (finwise-diw). Other tabs
answer `locked` at their next request and return to the PIN screen the same way. The stand-in stays as it is:
it has no lockout on this path and no sessions to drop, and the contract does not change; it follows the
contract's type changes and nothing else.

**PINs in logs, errors and the journal.** The request log stays as it is (verb, route, status, duration,
error kind) and never carries an argument. No new file of `internal/api` logs or prints. No answer and no
error text carries a PIN: the error envelope has a kind and nothing else, and `ErrMalformedPINHash` and the
start messages name no value. No row of `changes` or `change_effects` is written by this method. The only
trace of the new PIN in the database is its hash in `pin.hash`.

**Where the server departs from the stand-in on purpose.** Each is pinned by a test whose name says what
departs.

| departure | stand-in | server |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a wrong current PIN | answers `wrong-current` every time | counts in the shared lockout; the third locks |
| while a hold runs | compares as usual | removes the caller's session and answers `locked`, comparing nothing |
| other sessions | none exist | all but the caller's are removed |
| where the PIN lives | in memory | its hash in the app's database, the one that counts from then on and after a restart |

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

| decision | why | what lost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A wrong current PIN counts in the same global lockout as a wrong unlock, and the third locks | an open session must not become a way to guess the PIN without limit | a separate count for the form; refusing without a limit |
| The third wrong attempt removes the caller's session and answers `locked` | the person lands on the PIN screen with the wait, which explains the hold; the same session could otherwise keep trying after it | a form that only says "wait", while the session stays open |
| Every other session is dropped | a PIN is changed to shut someone out, and their open session would otherwise survive it | keeping other tabs open |
| The stored hash wins over the environment's once it exists, said in one log line | the person changes the PIN in the app and must not have to edit the server's configuration | the environment as the only source; refusing to start while both exist |
| `FINWISE_PIN_HASH` stays required at start | a database without a stored PIN must still be openable | starting without any PIN source |
| Not a recorded change, no undo | an undo would bring back a PIN the person meant to retire, through a handle that lives in a toast | changing the PIN as a journaled write |
| Order: verify, store, swap, drop, answer | a failure of the store leaves everything as it was | swapping in memory first, which a failed write would leave out of step with the database |
| `changePin` answers `read_only` without `--db` | there is nowhere to store the hash | changing the PIN in memory until the next restart |

**Failure paths that touch this.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the write of the hash fails or waits out the lock | `internal`; the old PIN still opens the app; every session stays |
| the process stops between the commit and the answer | the new PIN is stored and counts at the next start; the interface says the result could not be confirmed (finwise-diw); other sessions in memory are gone with the process anyway |
| a stored hash cannot be parsed at start | the start fails naming the path and the reason, never the value |
| the snapshot is missing | nothing changes for this method |
| two tabs change the PIN at once | each is verified against the hash in force when it runs; the last committed one counts, and the server's verifier and the row agree |

**Privacy and secrets.** The repository is public. Every fixture is invented and no proof here needs a real
ledger. A PIN, a hash or a cookie value is never printed by a test, logged, or written into a file, a commit
or a pull request; a test that checks logs and answers searches them for the PINs it typed and fails if one is
there.

**Conventions.** Work in a git worktree of your own and end at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits,
no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer
cents and no float may appear on the money path (this work touches none). Every SQL statement over the app's
database is a registered constant in `internal/authored`; `internal/api` executes none. Interface text is
Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English, log messages included. A design value in a component
comes from a token (this work edits no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A database opened after this lands records `0008_session` in `schema_migrations`, and the database
itself refuses a row with `id` 2, a second row with `id` 1, and a row with a null `hash` or a null
`changed_at`; every new statement is registered and prepared by the statement test.
- [ ] With an app's database, `["123456","135790","135790"]` (the current PIN right) answers 200
`{"ok":true}`; `pin` then holds one row whose `hash` `ParsePINHash` accepts and whose `changed_at` is the
test clock's instant; `changes` and `change_effects` gained 0 rows.
- [ ] After that change, with no restart: `session.lock` then `session.unlock` with `135790` answers
`{"ok":true}` and with `123456` answers `{"ok":false,"reason":"wrong-pin"}`; a second change must give
`135790` as the current PIN.
- [ ] Of three sessions opened before the change, the caller's still answers `session.status` with
`locked: false` after it, and the other two answer 401 `locked` on any route.
- [ ] `["000000","135790","135790"]` and `["000000","12","34"]` answer `{"ok":false,"reason":"wrong-current"}`;
`["123456","12345","12345"]`, `1234567`, `12345a` and `""` answer `invalid-new`; `["123456","135790","135791"]`
answers `mismatch`; none of these changes `pin` or any session.
- [ ] Two wrong current PINs answer `wrong-current` twice and the session still answers reads; the third
answers 401 `{"error":{"kind":"locked"}}` with exactly one `Set-Cookie` header, whose name is the session
cookie's, whose value is empty and which carries `Max-Age=0`; the caller's cookie then answers 401 `locked`,
another session opened before still answers reads, and `session.status` reports `retryAfterSeconds` 300.
- [ ] While that hold runs, a change from another live session with the right current PIN answers 401
`locked` with one clearing `Set-Cookie`, calls the PIN comparison 0 times, and removes that session; after the
clock moves 300 seconds a change with the right current PIN works.
- [ ] The lockout is shared: two wrong unlocks then one wrong current PIN answer `locked`; two wrong current
PINs then one wrong unlock answer `{"ok":false,"reason":"locked-out","retryAfterSeconds":300}`; a wrong current
PIN, then the right one with an invalid new PIN, then two wrong unlocks answer `wrong-pin` twice and hold
nothing.
- [ ] Arguments `["123456",135790,"135790"]` and an array of two answer `bad_request` with the PIN comparison
called 0 times and the lockout's count unchanged.
- [ ] When the write of the hash is made to fail, the answer is 500 `internal`, `pin` is as before, the old PIN
still unlocks, the new one does not, and every session opened before still answers reads.
- [ ] With the snapshot file missing, a change works and answers `{"ok":true}`.
- [ ] Without `--db`, `session.changePin` answers 403 `read_only` with its body read 0 times and the PIN
comparison called 0 times; without a session it answers 401 `locked`.
- [ ] `session.changePin` is gone from `writesWithoutHandler`, the manifest walk passes, and it fails when the
router stops handing the method to the session service.
- [ ] Restart, at the command level: `finwise serve --db <scratch>` with the hash of `123456` in
`FINWISE_PIN_HASH`, a change to `135790`, then a new `serve` over the same database and the same environment:
the log holds the line `the PIN stored in the database opens the app; FINWISE_PIN_HASH is ignored` once,
`135790` unlocks and `123456` answers `wrong-pin`. A `serve` over a fresh database logs no such line and
`123456` unlocks. A `serve` over a database whose `pin.hash` is not a valid hash exits non-zero, and neither
its message nor the log holds that value.
- [ ] A test that makes changes with distinctive PINs as current, new and repeat (right and wrong ones, the
locked case and the failed write included) finds none of them in the request log, in any answer body or in
any error text, and finds no row added to `changes` or `change_effects`; `TestOnlyTheRequestLogWritesAnything`
passes with no new file allowed to log.
