- [ ] Screen test: with the whole app mounted and unlocked over the stand-in, a hold running in the stand-in
(three wrong unlocks), and `session.changePin` refused with `locked` through the test helper, saving the PIN
form brings the PIN screen back with its keys disabled and the message "Muitas tentativas. Tente de novo em 5
minutos.", no toast, and nothing unclaimed.
- [ ] The existing PIN tests of `web/src/screens/config/config.test.ts`, `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`
and `web/src/api/fake/session.test.ts` pass unchanged; under `web/` the only change is the new file
`web/src/screens/config/pin-lockout.test.ts`.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the hand-off: the
verifier left on the old hash after a change; the other sessions left alive; the caller's session dropped
too; the renewed cookie left beside the clearing one (two `Set-Cookie` lines); the hold not counted for a
wrong current PIN; the swap made before the store, with the store failing; the stored hash ignored at start;
`CHECK (id = 1)` removed.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, a PIN changed through the API opens the app at once and after a
restart while the old one and every other session are shut out, and the third wrong current PIN answers
`locked` with one clearing cookie and lands on the PIN screen with its wait.

## Tests
- Unit, `internal/authored`, a migrated scratch database: the refusals of `pin` by the database itself; read
  and write of the stored hash; the statements registered and prepared.
- Unit, `internal/api`: the session store's removal of every session but one (the kept one live, the others
  gone, an unknown kept token removing all).
- Integration (`httptest`), `internal/api`, a scratch app's database in the test's temporary directory and
  the injected clock: success and its effects; the three faults and their order; the shared lockout in both
  directions; the third wrong current PIN and the attempt during a hold, with the `Set-Cookie` header
  counted; `bad_request`; the failed write; the snapshot missing; no `--db`; no session; the immediate effect
  on unlock; the sessions dropped and kept.
- Unit, the manifest walk with `session.changePin` implemented by the session service.
- Integration, `cmd/finwise`, on a free port as `TestServeStartsWithoutASnapshotAndTheHashUnlocks` does: the
  restart with a stored hash, the log line, a fresh database, a stored hash that does not parse.
- Unit, logs and answers: the distinctive PINs absent from the request log, the answers and the errors; the
  journal untouched.
- Screen test (vitest, a new file beside the settings screen's tests): the PIN form answered `locked` during a
  hold lands on the PIN screen with the wait, through the helper over `createFakeApi`.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the hand-off.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/migrations/0008_session.sql`, `internal/authored/session.go`,
`internal/api/session_routes.go`, `internal/api/sessions.go`, `internal/api/router.go`,
`cmd/finwise/serve.go`, `internal/api/session_routes_test.go`, `internal/api/sessions_test.go`,
`internal/api/change_pin_test.go`, `cmd/finwise/finwise_test.go`, `internal/authored/session_test.go`,
`web/src/screens/config/pin-lockout.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/lockout.go`, `internal/api/cookie.go`, `internal/api/pinhash.go`,
`internal/api/logging.go`, `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`, `internal/api/logging_test.go`,
`internal/api/helpers_test.go`, `cmd/finwise/main.go`, `web/src/api/fake/index.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/session.test.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/session.ts`,
`web/src/screens/config/PinSection.vue`, `web/src/screens/config/config.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/api/failures-on-screen.test.ts`, `web/src/stores/session.ts`,
`web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `AGENTS.md`, `bin/ci`

Six source files in three places: one migration and one store file in the package that owns the app's
database; the session service, the session store and the router's hand-over in the HTTP layer; and the
start in `cmd/finwise`. That is a schema change across three modules, hence `size:L`, and each change is
small. The tests follow, plus one new screen test that edits no screen. The test file holding
`writesWithoutHandler` changes by one name. The lockout, the cookie and the PIN hash are used as they are.
The contract, the manifest, the stand-in and every component are not touched. `AGENTS.md` still says "The
PIN is never stored" after this; that sentence is left to the work that brings `AGENTS.md` up to date with
the write side (finwise-59d), which follows this one.

## Recovery path
The migration adds one table and changes no existing one, and the collector's snapshot is never written. Before
a database that already holds data is migrated, the runner copies it with `VACUUM INTO` to
`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>` beside it and never overwrites an existing copy; a migration that fails rolls
back its own transaction and `serve` exits naming the path and the reason. To go back to that copy: stop the
server; check the copy (`PRAGMA integrity_check` answers `ok`, the application id is `0x46494E57`); put it in
place of the database with no `-wal` or `-shm` file beside it; start the binary that goes with it. A binary
that does not carry `0008_session` refuses a database that records it instead of guessing, so going back to
an older binary means going back to that copy, and what was typed after the copy was taken is lost with it.

A PIN that was changed and then forgotten, with the server stopped: delete the one row of `pin` with the
`sqlite3` shell on the stopped server's database (`DELETE FROM pin;`), then start the server; the hash in
`FINWISE_PIN_HASH` opens the app again, and no start line about the stored PIN is logged. Nothing else in the
database depends on that row.
close_reason: session.changePin is answered by the session service on a server with --db: the current PIN checked under the lockout the PIN screen shares, the faults in a fixed order, the new hash stored in a one-row table before the verifier is swapped, every other session ended; at start a stored hash opens the app and the environment's is ignored, and one that does not parse stops the start. No PIN in a log, an answer, the journal or an error. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main. Review: four independent mutations; two survived at first (the mutex that serialises two changes; the store not cancelled with the request) and each now fails a test built for it. The implementer's fifteen breaks each failed a test.

title: Show a pot's day with an unknown yield as unknown
description:
## What changes for the user
A savings pot's month opens into the days behind its yield. When the bank's records cannot support one of those days, the month's total rightly reads as unknown, but the day itself is simply missing from the list, so nothing on screen says which day broke the month. After this lands that day is listed with a dash.

## Outcome
A pot's daily yield row can carry an unknown amount in the contract, the backend answers such a day instead of leaving it out, and the pot's page shows a dash for it.

## Context
finwise's interface reaches its backend through a TypeScript contract (`web/src/api/contract/`), described for Go by a generated manifest the gate keeps current (`npm --prefix web run contract`). The convention in `AGENTS.md`: a field the ledger cannot always answer is nullable in the contract and a screen shows its absence as a dash; a zero is for a figure that is truly zero.

The backend computes a pot's yield per pair of nightly sightings (`internal/potrules`), and a pair it cannot support gets a row whose yield is unknown, with a reason. `savingsPots.detail` puts the known rows in `yield.days`. The contract's `PotYieldDay.amount` is a required number, so the handler in `internal/api/pots_detail.go` leaves an unknown row out, and the month's total is `null`.

No pair on the real ledger examined so far was unknown, so the case is not on screen today.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] In the contract, `PotYieldDay.amount` is nullable and the manifest is regenerated.
- [ ] Over a fixture pot whose month has a day the rules cannot support, `savingsPots.detail` lists that day with a `null` amount, in order among the others, and the month's total is `null`.
- [ ] The pot's page shows a dash for that day and no "R$ 0,00"; a test mounts it over the stand-in with such a day.
- [ ] Over the prototype dataset nothing changes: `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] The backend's golden files for the pot detail are re-recorded from the fixture ledgers and its answers still validate against the schema.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and an unknown day shows a dash.

## Tests
- Unit: the handler over a month with an unknown day.
- Component: the pot's page over the stand-in with an unknown day.
- Conformance: the stand-in's and the backend's pot answers against the regenerated schema.
- Golden: the pot detail's answers.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/savings-pots.ts`, `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/`, `web/src/api/fake/savings-rules.ts`, `web/src/test/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/api/pots_detail.go`, `internal/api/pots_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`
**Reads only:** `internal/potrules/`, `web/src/lib/format.ts`, `AGENTS.md`, `bin/ci`

One field of one contract type becomes nullable, one screen and one handler follow, and the generated manifest and the pot detail's golden files are refreshed.
close_reason: PotYieldDay.amount is nullable in the contract and the manifest is regenerated. The pot detail handler lists a day whose yield is unknown, in order, with a null amount, and the month's total is null; a day with a deposit and no yield stays a known zero. The pot's page shows a dash for such a day and for the total; the stand-in can carry an unknown day and its answers validate against the schema as a new state. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main, 940 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. No golden file changed: neither recorded ledger holds an unknown day, so the case is covered by the handler's test.

title: Mark a purchase reimbursable and link it to a received PIX from anywhere in the ledger, so the purchase counts for what is left and the PIX for nobody's income
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the transaction panel of a purchase offers "Reembolsável", a field "Espero receber R$" and "Ligar a
um PIX recebido", the list of received PIX that could pay it back; the switch answers that the app is
read-only and the list is always empty. So when the person pays a dinner for two and the friend sends
their half by PIX a week later, the month counts the whole dinner as spending and the PIX as income,
and nothing ties the two together. After this lands the person marks the dinner reimbursable (the app
expects half back until told otherwise), sees every received PIX of the ledger that could be the
payment, whatever month it arrived in, and links one: the dinner then counts only for what is left, the
PIX stops counting as income and leaves the review queue if it was waiting there, and the history says
which PIX paid it. A PIX can pay one purchase only, a purchase never counts for less than nothing even
when the PIX was larger, and a purchase that is split into lines cannot also have a PIX linked, with a
sentence that says so. If this were wrong the person would see the same money counted twice, a month
that seems to have earned what was only paid back, or a purchase that silently vanished from the totals.

## Outcome
Four methods of the API stop answering `read_only` when the server runs with its own database and are
answered by handlers: `transactions.setReimbursable`, `setExpectedReimbursement`, `linkReimbursement`
and `unlinkReimbursement`. Each is one recorded change that `changes.undo` takes back exactly; linking
and unlinking write a history step. The detail of a purchase answers its reimbursement (the expected
amount and the link) and the candidates, every received PIX of the whole ledger that may pay it back,
newest first; the candidates are derived from the ledger and so appear even without the app's database,
which changes nine golden files of the full invented ledger in that one field. The credit's side is
answered: a linked credit says it is reimbursement income, counts as nobody's income, and its pending
review is settled by the link. A purchase's effective amount is its amount less the smaller of the two
amounts, never past zero; a link applies only while the ledger lists its credit. An undo that would
give one credit two purchases is refused as stale. `setSplit` refuses to split a purchase with a linked reimbursement and
`linkReimbursement` refuses a split purchase, both with `split_with_reimbursement`.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and the file may be swapped
under it at any time. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`,
where everything the person authors is kept; the server has one only when started with `--db`, and
without it every write answers `read_only`, as today, while every read answers from the ledger with an
empty authored view. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the
design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes behave, and its behaviour is
the rule here except where this text says the server departs from it. *The manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated description of every API method (route, class,
argument and result schemas, error envelope). *The recorder* is the layer of `internal/authored` through
which every change to the app's database is written, and *the journal* is what it writes: one *change*
per write (author, method, instant, Brazil day) and its *effects*; `changes.undo(changeId)` applies the
inverse of a change's effects and is refused with `refused` / `stale_change` when something it would
overwrite was changed since. *The index* is the pair of tables `tx_index` and `tx_ids` in which the
app's database remembers the transactions it has seen: the bank's id of a transaction can change (a
pending row is replaced by a posted one), so the database mints a key of its own, `tx_key`, and maps
every provider id seen to it; everything authored about a transaction hangs on `tx_key`. The *tracking
start month* is the month in which `finwise.db` was created; the rules that classify new transactions
only look at transactions from then on, so a transaction older than that may never have been indexed. A
*purchase* is a debit that is not a movement between own accounts or a bill payment: what the panel
shows the split and the reimbursement for. A *received PIX* is a credit whose kind is `pix`. A *pending
review* is a transaction waiting in the queue for the person to choose its line. A *golden file* is the
exact, committed answer of one call over an invented fixture.

**The decision, and what lost.** A purchase cannot be both split and linked to a reimbursement. Why: the
stand-in silently ignores the reimbursement of a split purchase (its `contributions` in `rules.ts`
returns the parts and never looks at the link), and sharing a reimbursement over the parts is arithmetic
nobody asked for. What lost: proportional allocation over the parts. The refusal is `refused` /
`split_with_reimbursement`, HTTP 409, whose sentence in the interface is "Uma compra dividida não pode
ter reembolso ligado.".

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.**

- The recorder, the journal and the undo engine (finwise-wi4): an *attribute table* holds one row of
  independent facts per key and an effect is one column changing; in a table of optional facts (a
  transaction's state) every column has a default and a row at its defaults is the same as no row. No
  statement may write an authored table outside the recorder. The recorder offers the inverse of a
  chosen part of a change, performed inside another open change, and a read-only check that says
  whether it would be refused: this is what taking one history step back is made of. The undo engine
  also owns this rule: a restore that the database's own constraints refuse means the state it would
  bring back is no longer possible, and the undo is answered `refused` / `stale_change` with nothing
  changed, exactly like an undo that a later change made stale. This slice relies on it (below) and
  does not implement it; if the engine in the tree does not yet answer a constraint refusal that way,
  say so in the report rather than mapping the error in a handler.
- A handler receives one value carrying a view of each store for the request (finwise-jzw): the ledger view
  is one handle and one read-only transaction, so every ledger query of a request sees the same
  snapshot; the clock comes from the request's context and is never the host's.
- Money coming in (finwise-po6): `ParseReais` turns a JSON number into integer cents with no float,
  rounding half away from zero beyond two places and refusing anything that is not a finite number
  within one billion reais. An amount that cannot be negative (an expected reimbursement) is
  `bad_request` when it is; the handler applies that rule.
- Write dispatch (finwise-2s5): the router validates arguments against the manifest's schemas, hands the

- The write conformance harness and `authoredtest` (finwise-fst): recorded-change cases with effects golden

- The function that says what a transaction counts for (finwise-305: `internal/budgetrules` with

- The transactions' store (finwise-jw2: the migration `0003_transactions`, the index, the map of provider

**The rules common to the four writes.** They are T4's, restated. The purchase is resolved through the
same interpreted ledger read the detail uses for its target, in the request's snapshot, and an id it
does not list (unknown, a tax row folded into its purchase, a pot movement) is refused with `not_found`,
nothing recorded; its index row is created or refreshed. A write that leaves every stored value as it
was records an empty change: it answers its id, has no effect and no history step, and its undo is a
no-op. A missing snapshot answers `ledger_unavailable` with nothing recorded; a write that fails halfway
or waits out the five-second lock answers `internal` with nothing kept. A closed month refuses none of
these (closing freezes a month's budget, not its transactions). `setReimbursable` and
`setExpectedReimbursement` store on any listed transaction, as the stand-in does; only a purchase can be
linked, and the dispositions read a reimbursement only on a purchase.

**Marking.**

- `setReimbursable(id, true)` stores `reimbursable` on, the expected amount as half the transaction's
  amount in magnitude, in cents, half rounded up (`(|cents| + 1) / 2` in integer arithmetic: 18000 gives
  9000, 18001 gives 9001, 12345 gives 6173, 1 gives 1), and no link. The amount is the one the list
  shows, tax included. As in the stand-in, this holds whatever was stored before, so marking a purchase
  already marked starts over at half and drops its link; the interface sends `true` only when the
  purchase is not marked. No history step.
- `setReimbursable(id, false)` stores `reimbursable` off, the expected amount null and no link. No
  history step. The credit it was linked to becomes a candidate again.
- `setExpectedReimbursement(id, amount)` stores the amount in cents, or null when the field was cleared,
  only while the transaction is marked; on one not marked it is an empty change. A negative amount is
  `bad_request` and nothing is recorded. The link is kept. No history step.
- The detail answers `reimbursement` as `{expected, link}` while marked (expected in reais or null) and
  null otherwise. Vectors from the stand-in's `panel-writes.test.ts`, on a purchase of R$ 180,00:
  marking answers `{expected: 90.00, link: null}`; `setExpectedReimbursement(120)` answers
  `expected: 120.00`; unmarking answers `reimbursement: null`.

**The candidates.** A candidate is a received PIX from anywhere in the ledger that is not a movement
between own accounts, not unconverted, not excluded, not a refund (by the effective mark: the person's,
or the ledger's rule when they set nothing), and not already linked to another purchase; newest first.
"Excluded" means excluded with a reason, the list's `excluded`: an exclusion takes effect only once it
has a reason, so a credit switched to "não conta" without one still counts and is still a candidate.
A payroll credit is not a PIX and so never one; a received PIX already on an income line still is, as in
the stand-in, which is how a reimbursement first filed as income gets attached to its purchase. The
candidates are interpreted over the whole ledger in one pass, as the card's read does, so they reach
credits of other months and credits older than the tracking start that were never indexed; the
detail's own target keeps the month it is interpreted in today. Each candidate answers the credit's
provider id as listed, the name to show for its establishment key, its day and its amount in reais. The
detail answers the candidates for a transaction whose panel shows the reimbursement section, whether or
not it is marked, and an empty list otherwise. Because the candidates come from the ledger, the detail
answers them without `--db` too: in the full invented ledger the nine details named above answer
`reimbursementCandidates` with `tx-salary` then `tx-stale`, and nothing else in `full/` changes.

This departs from the stand-in, whose filter keeps every PIX credit not on the line `Salário` and not
claimed: movements, refunds, excluded and unconverted rows are left out here. And where the stand-in
leaves out a credit claimed by any purchase, the purchase's own linked credit included, the rule here
leaves out only one linked to another purchase; the panel shows the candidates only while the purchase
has no link, so nothing visible differs.

**Linking.** `linkReimbursement(id, creditId)`:

1. The purchase is resolved as above; an unknown one is `not_found`.
2. Linking needs a purchase already marked: on any other transaction (one not marked, a credit, a
   movement) it answers its change and does nothing, an empty change, as the stand-in does.
3. A split purchase is refused with `split_with_reimbursement`, nothing recorded.
4. The credit must be among the purchase's candidates; anything else (an unknown id, a debit, a payroll
   credit, a movement, a refund, an excluded credit, a credit linked to another purchase) is refused with
   `not_found`, nothing recorded.
5. Otherwise, in one change: the credit's index row is created or refreshed (it may never have been
   indexed); the purchase stores `credit_tx_key` (the credit's key) and `credit_cents` (the credit's
   amount in cents as the ledger lists it now); the credit's pending review, if it had one, is cleared
   (`pending_reason`, `pending_line_id`, `pending_confidence`), which settles it; and the purchase gets
   the step `Você ligou ao PIX de <nome> · R$ <valor>`, where the name is the name shown for the
   credit's key and the value is the credit's amount written as `brl` writes it in
   `web/src/lib/format.ts`: `R$`, a no-break space (U+00A0), then the magnitude with `.` between
   thousands and `,` before two decimals (`R$ 150,00`, `R$ 1.500,00`), as `brazilianDecimal` already
   writes it; the `·` is U+00B7 with a space on each side. The text is stored as written then.
6. Linking the credit the purchase already has is an empty change. Linking another credit to a purchase
   that has one replaces the link, as in the stand-in; the old credit becomes a candidate again.

Because `credit_cents` is the credit's amount as listed, and the index carries a pending row to its
posted replacement only when the amount in cents is equal, the stored figure and the listed one agree
for as long as the credit is listed under that key.

**Unlinking.** `unlinkReimbursement(id)` drops the link (both columns) and keeps the mark and the
expected amount, writing `Você desfez a ligação com o PIX`. On a transaction with no link it is an empty
change with no step (the stand-in writes the step anyway). The credit becomes a candidate again; its
pending review is not brought back, and since a transaction the rules have evaluated is never evaluated
again, it does not return to the queue by itself.

**Taking the steps back, and undo.** The history steps and their undo are the line writes' (finwise-yfu:
`undoHistoryStep` takes one step back by applying the undo's inverse to the units of that one
transaction that the step's change touched, refused when one of them was changed since). Two
consequences of that rule for this slice, to be pinned and not "fixed": taking back the link's step
restores the purchase's link columns only, so the link goes and the credit's settled review stays
settled, while `changes.undo` of the link's change restores both; and the stand-in's vector holds (after
marking and linking, taking the link's step back answers `{expected: 90.00, link: null}`). Whichever of
this slice and the line writes lands second adds that vector through `undoHistoryStep` to its tests;
here it is proved through the recorder's inverse of a part. One case meets the database: unlink a
purchase, link the same credit to another purchase, then undo the unlink. No later change touched the
first purchase's columns, but restoring its link would give one credit two purchases, which the unique
`credit_tx_key` refuses. By the undo engine's rule (finwise-wi4), a restore the database's own constraints
refuse means the state it would bring back is no longer possible: the undo is answered `refused` /
`stale_change` ("Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito."), nothing changes, and both
purchases keep what they had. The same holds for the undo of an unmarking, of a replaced link, and for
taking back the unlink's step, whenever the credit has since been linked elsewhere.

**What the purchase and the credit answer.**

- The purchase: `reimbursed` is true exactly when it has a link. `reimbursement.link` is
  `{transactionId, name, day, amount}`: the credit's provider id as listed, the name shown for its key,
  its day and `credit_cents` in reais; finding the credit's id, name and day needs the whole-ledger pass
  the candidates already make. `effectiveAmount` is the amount less the applied reimbursement, the
  smaller of the credit's amount and the purchase's magnitude, so it never changes sign: a purchase of
  R$ 180,00 answers `-30.00` with a credit of R$ 150,00, `0.00` with one of R$ 180,00 and `0.00` with one
  of R$ 200,00 (whose link still answers `amount: 200.00`).
- A link applies only while its credit is listed. The same principle as "pending means listed now": a
  transaction the ledger stops listing keeps its authored rows and counts nowhere until it is listed
  again. So when the ledger stops listing a linked credit, the link stays stored (`credit_tx_key` and
  `credit_cents` are not touched, and no change is recorded), but it is not applied: the purchase
  answers `reimbursed: false`, `reimbursement.link: null` (its mark and expected amount unchanged) and
  `effectiveAmount` equal to its amount, and the dispositions apply nothing inside it, so it counts its
  whole amount. The stored credit is still "linked to another purchase" for every other purchase's
  candidates and for the unique key. If the credit is listed again under the same key, the link applies
  again with no write. The stand-in answers the link null and still takes the stored amount off, which
  disagree with each other; the server departs from it here.
- The credit: `reimbursementIncome` is true exactly when a purchase is linked to it, in the list and the
  detail; its `pending` is null once linked; its amount and effective amount are its own.
- What they count for, from the dispositions delivered by finwise-305 (first match wins; amounts are
  magnitudes in cents): disposition 7, *reimbursement*: a credit linked to a purchase counts on no line;
  the smaller of its amount and the purchase's is applied inside the purchase, and any excess counts
  nowhere; it comes before refund (8) and income (9), so a linked credit is nobody's income even on an
  income line. Disposition 11, *on a line*: a debit with a line adds its amount less the applied
  reimbursement. Disposition 12, *uncategorised*: a debit with no line adds nothing, and its amount less
  the applied reimbursement is unassigned. Dispositions 1 to 4 (unconverted, movement, excluded with a
  reason, waiting for review) come first for either side. The invariant for every debit of
  dispositions 5, 11 and 12: what it adds to lines, plus what is unassigned, plus the applied
  reimbursement, equals its amount; and for every month every listed transaction is in exactly one
  disposition, the counts adding up to the number listed and the amounts to the sum of the listed
  magnitudes. A split purchase (5) never has an applied reimbursement, by the refusal above.
- Vectors from the stand-in, on the R$ 180,00 purchase and a PIX of R$ 150,00 from a person named Ana on
  2026-11-12: after marking and linking, the link is `{transactionId: <the PIX>, name: "Ana", day:
  "2026-11-12", amount: 150.00}`, `effectiveAmount: -30.00`, `reimbursed: true`, the newest step is
  `Você ligou ao PIX de Ana · R$ 150,00`, and the purchase's line receives 3000 cents instead of 18000;
  after unlinking, the line receives 18000 again, the newest step is `Você desfez a ligação com o PIX`
  and `reimbursement` is `{expected: 90.00, link: null}`; after linking again and unmarking, the PIX is
  a candidate of another purchase again.

**The split refusal, both ways.** `linkReimbursement` refuses a split purchase (step 3 above), and this
slice adds to `setSplit` (in the split writes' file, finwise-9je) the refusal of two or more parts on a
purchase that has a linked reimbursement, with `split_with_reimbursement` and nothing recorded.
Removing a split (`null`, an empty list or one part) is never refused, and a purchase marked
reimbursable without a link can be split. This slice is the first producer of
`split_with_reimbursement`: it removes the reason from the harness's list of reasons with no producer
and adds its refusal cases.

**What the plan of this work leaves open, and what constrains it** (this is why the bead is `spec:open`).

- *The order of the checks* between a split purchase and a credit that is not a candidate in
  `linkReimbursement`, and between `split_with_reimbursement` and `unknown_line` in `setSplit`. Either
  order refuses with nothing recorded; one test per pair pins the order chosen.
- *The order of candidates within one day.* Newest first is fixed; within a day the recommendation is
  the list's order (`newestFirst`), which keeps the ledger's order. Deterministic either way, pinned by
  a test with two candidates on one day.
- *An unconverted purchase.* Its amount is not in reais, so taking a credit in reais off it mixes units;
  it counts for nothing (disposition 1). Whether linking it is an empty change, as for a transaction that
  is not a purchase, or a link whose `effectiveAmount` is left equal to the amount, is the implementer's,
  with the constraint that no figure ever combines the two currencies. One test pins it.
- *File and function names.*

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. The rule
in full: a real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document,
id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown
to the person running a test and goes into no file; a test that touches a real ledger runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Nothing in this slice needs a real ledger. Every fixture is
invented (the name `Ana` above is the stand-in's), and `-update` of the golden files refuses to run while
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set. A candidate's establishment key may be a document number; it is never
logged. New files in `internal/api` log nothing; the no-leak test's list of strings must cover what the
new write cases carry (an amount, a credit's id, a name).

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path: the half is computed on
cents, the minimum is taken on cents, amounts arrive through `ParseReais` and leave through `Reais`.
Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant, prepared against the migrated
schema by a test. Interface text and history texts are Brazilian Portuguese, quoted exactly as above,
and live in `internal/api/messages.go`; everything else is English; a design value in a component comes
from a token (this slice touches no component). Register the handlers in a registration function of
this slice's own file, listed once in `domainRegistrations`. Each departure from the stand-in (unknown
purchases refused; the candidates' filter; the own link still a candidate; a reimbursement that never
exceeds its purchase; a link not applied while its credit is not listed; linking settling the credit's
review; no step for an unlink that unlinked nothing; a split purchase refused both ways) is pinned by a test, and the final report names the test beside the
departure. The nine golden files of `full/` that change are rewritten with `-update` and each diff is
read in review: only `reimbursementCandidates` may differ.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] With `--db`, each of `transactions.setReimbursable`, `setExpectedReimbursement`,
`linkReimbursement` and `unlinkReimbursement` answers 200 with `{"changeId": "<decimal id>"}` that
validates against the manifest; none of the four remains in `writesWithoutHandler`; without `--db` each
still answers `read_only` before its body is read.
- [ ] Each of the four has a write-conformance case in the recorded-change mode whose effects equal its
golden file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/` and whose undo returns the canonical dump to

title: Read which collector run produced the snapshot's current rows, on the ledger's view, and let invented ledgers advance it
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing on screen changes. This work lets the app tell one night's bank records from the next: the
collector that fills the ledger records which of its runs produced the rows the app reads, and the app has
never looked at that. Once the app can read it, the job that brings each night's records into the app's own
database can do its work once per new night instead of on every tick, and can tell a night whose run
stopped halfway but was still taken in from one that was never taken in at all. What the person would
notice if this were wrong, later: purchases from a night that never reach the review queue, or the same
night taken in again and again.

## Outcome
`internal/ledger` gains one registered statement that reads `projection_state.projected_run`, a query
method `ProjectedRun` on `ledger.View` beside the others, and its wrapper on `Reader` in
`internal/ledger/reader_queries.go`, so the view's existing tests cover it with the other thirteen queries.
A snapshot with no projection row answers a typed error with a fixed sentence. `ledgertest` can add a run
and advance the projection to it. No other package changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate program, *the collector* (pluggy-sync), fills from the banks every
night and replaces by an atomic rename; each such file is *a snapshot*, and the app only reads it, through
`internal/ledger`. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, a separate file where everything the person
authors is kept. *The ingest* is the function that will bring the app's database up to date with each new
snapshot (finwise-82m: it indexes new transactions, carries a pending charge's work to its posted row and
classifies by rule); this work gives it the one fact it reads first.

**What the code is today (each point read in the file named).**

- `internal/ledger/view.go`: a `View` is one handle and one read-only transaction on the snapshot,
  opened by its first query (`(*Reader).View()`, then `view.read`), so every query made through one view
  sees the same snapshot even when the collector renames a new file over it meanwhile; a view whose first
  open failed keeps that error; a closed view answers `ErrViewClosed`. Every query method is a method of
  `*View` in its own file (`View.SyncState` in `sync.go`, `View.Accounts` in `accounts.go`, …), and
  `internal/ledger/reader_queries.go` keeps the reader's methods as wrappers that open a view for one call.
  Separate work removes those wrappers once nothing calls them (finwise-qet); until then every query has one.
- `internal/ledger/sync.go`: `View.SyncState` reads the latest complete run's finish
  (`queryCompleteRunFinishes`), the latest run whatever its outcome (`queryLatestRun`) and the
  connections. No statement reads `projection_state`.
- `internal/ledger/testdata/ledger-schema-v1.sql`: `projection_state(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY CHECK (id =
  1), projected_run INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id), code_version TEXT NOT NULL)` records which run
  produced the current rows. `runs.outcome` is one of `running`, `complete`, `partial`, `failed`,
  `interrupted`, `migrated`, so a run can end `partial`, and the run that produced the rows is not always
  the latest complete one nor the latest one.
- `internal/ledger/queries.go`: every statement is a `query…` constant registered in `allQueries`;
  `schema_test.go` prepares each against the collector's schema
  (`TestEveryQueryPreparesAgainstTheCollectorsSchema`), fails on a constant missing from the registry
  (`TestEveryQueryConstantIsRegistered`) and on a statement executed outside it
  (`TestNoStatementEscapesTheRegistry`). The collector's README is cited in a comment where a statement
  mirrors one of its queries.
- `internal/ledger/view_test.go`: the interface `ledgerQueries` lists what a `Reader` and a `View` both
  answer, and `everyAnswer` asks all 13 queries. `TestEveryQueryOnOneViewAnswersAsTheReaderDoes` fails
  when a query answers the same over the populated ledger (`viewLedger`) and over an empty replacement,
  because then the swap could not show a stray handle; other tests use `everyAnswer` to check that a view
  keeps its snapshot after a rename, leaves the file byte for byte untouched, and answers an unusable
  snapshot with the typed errors.
- `internal/ledger/ledgertest/ledgertest.go`: `newFixture` inserts run 1 and then `projection_state` once,
  with `projected_run = 1`. `AddRun(Run{Outcome, FinishedAt})` appends a run, returns nothing, and never
  touches `projection_state`. `NewWithFirstRunOutcome` makes a fixture whose only run ended with a given
  outcome.

**What to build.**

- A statement `queryProjectedRun` reading `projected_run` from `projection_state` where `id = 1`,
  registered in `allQueries`.
- `func (view *View) ProjectedRun(ctx context.Context) (int64, error)`, in `sync.go` beside `SyncState`
  or in a file of its own, running on `view.read` like every other query, so its error passes through the
  same classification (`asUnreadable`; a missing file, a file that is not a database, an unknown
  `user_version` answer the errors the other queries answer). A snapshot with no `projection_state` row
  answers a typed error of its own (for example `NotProjectedError`, with an `Is…` helper like
  `IsUnsupportedVersion`) whose text is a fixed sentence and carries no value from the file. It is never
  answered as run 0.
- `func (reader *Reader) ProjectedRun(ctx context.Context) (int64, error)` in `reader_queries.go`, written
  as the other wrappers are, and `ProjectedRun` added to `ledgerQueries` and to `everyAnswer` in
  `view_test.go`, whose counts (13) become 14. For the swap test to keep its guard, the populated ledger it
  uses must answer a projected run the empty replacement does not: `viewLedger` (or `populated`) adds a
  run and advances the projection to it.
- In `ledgertest`: `AddRun` returns the id of the run it added (callers that ignore it still compile), and
  a method advances the projection to a given run (for example `ProjectTo(run int64)`), refusing, through
  the fixture's usual `t.Fatalf`, a run that does not exist (the schema's foreign key says so too).

The outcome of a run is never consulted by this statement: what it answers is which run produced the
rows, so a run that ended `partial` and was projected is answered, and a run that was added but not
projected is not. Neither `LastCompleteSync` nor `LatestRun` of `SyncState` is a substitute, and neither
changes.

**Privacy and conventions.** No test here touches a real ledger; every fixture is invented with
`ledgertest`. If the implementer runs the existing opt-in tests over a real snapshot
(`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT`), no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is printed,
logged or copied anywhere, and a run id from a real ledger is such a value. Work happens in a worktree and
ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a
work item or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path.
Every SQL statement over the snapshot is a registered constant of `queries.go`. Everything here is
English.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `queryProjectedRun` is in `allQueries`, and the existing preparation, registration and escape
tests pass with it; removing it from the registry fails `TestEveryQueryConstantIsRegistered`.
- [ ] On a new `ledgertest` fixture `ProjectedRun` answers 1, through a view and through the reader.
- [ ] After `AddRun` of a `partial` run 2 and the projection advanced to 2, it answers 2; after `AddRun`
of a `complete` run 3 without advancing, it still answers 2; once advanced to 3, it answers 3. On
`NewWithFirstRunOutcome(t, "partial")` it answers 1.
- [ ] A fixture whose `projection_state` row was deleted answers the typed error, whose text contains no
sentinel string the test stored in the file; a missing file, a file that is not a database and an
unsupported `user_version` answer the same errors the other queries answer.
- [ ] `ledgerQueries` and `everyAnswer` include `ProjectedRun`; `TestEveryQueryOnOneViewAnswersAsTheReaderDoes`
asks 14 queries and passes; on one view, `ProjectedRun` asked after a newer snapshot was renamed over the
file answers the run of the first snapshot, and a view opened after the rename answers the new one.
- [ ] `ProjectTo` of a run that does not exist fails the test that calls it.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main` shows changes only under `internal/ledger/`.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: the statement
reading `MAX(id) FROM runs` instead (the unprojected run 3 is answered); the missing row answered as 0;
the query run on a handle of its own instead of the view's transaction (the rename is seen); `ProjectTo`
left as a no-op.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and a view answers the projected run of its own snapshot,
advanced by `ledgertest`, partial runs included.

## Tests
- Unit (`internal/ledger`, over `ledgertest` fixtures): the projected run on a new fixture, after runs are
  added and projected, after a run is added and not projected, on a fixture whose only run ended partial,
  and with the row deleted.
- Unit (`internal/ledger/view_test.go`): `ProjectedRun` among the view's queries in the swap test, the
  kept-snapshot test, the byte-for-byte test and the typed-errors test.
- Unit (`internal/ledger/schema_test.go`): the new constant prepared, registered and seen by the escape
  scan, as every other.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/queries.go`, `internal/ledger/sync.go`, `internal/ledger/reader_queries.go`,
`internal/ledger/view_test.go`, `internal/ledger/ledgertest/ledgertest.go`, and a test file of the package
for the new cases
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/view.go`, `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/schema_test.go`,
`internal/ledger/testdata/ledger-schema-v1.sql`, `internal/ledger/support_test.go`, `bin/ci`

One statement, one query method and its wrapper, one fixture helper and the tests that cover them, all in
one module: `size:M`. No caller is added: the ingest reads it later. `internal/api` is not touched.
close_reason: A view of the ledger answers which collector run produced the rows it reads (projection_state.projected_run, a registered statement), whatever that run's outcome; a snapshot with no projection answers a typed error; ledgertest.AddRun returns the run's id and ProjectTo moves the projection. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main; hosted check passed. Review: two independent mutations each failed a test; the implementer's eight breaks each failed one. Note for the ingest: projecting an invented ledger past run 1 uncovers the fixture's documents, whose scopes belong to run 1.

title: Close a month only when it is due and nothing of it waits for review, keep its budget as a version of its own, undo the close exactly, and list closed months in the shell
description:
## What changes for the user
Today "Fechar o mês" at the end of the closing tab answers that the app is read-only, the sidebar never lists a
closed month, and nothing keeps a month's budget from changing after the month is over. After this lands the
person closes a month once its reviews are answered: the month is sealed on the day it was closed, it appears
in the list of closed months and in the sidebar, its budget is kept exactly as it stood and no later save can
change it, while its transactions can still be corrected. A month that has not arrived yet cannot be closed,
and a purchase of the current month waiting for review no longer stops the person from closing last month;
what stops a close is a review still waiting from that month or an earlier one. A close can be taken back,
which reopens the month on whatever budget is in force before it. Taking back an earlier change that would move
a closed month's budget is refused with "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito." and changes
nothing. If this were wrong the person would see a closed month whose budget moved, a month closed with a review
still open, a month that refuses to close because of next month's purchase, or, after taking a close back, a
budget that is not the one in force before it.

## Outcome
`review.closeMonth(month)` has a handler. It refuses a month already closed (`month_closed`), a month after
the current one (`future_month`) and a month while a transaction of that month or an earlier one is pending
(`pending_reviews`). Otherwise it records, as one change, the closed month with today's day and, when no
budget version starts at that month, a version there holding exactly the budget in force for it; it answers
the change's id, and `changes.undo` of it removes exactly what it wrote, unless a check of the undo engine
refuses it. This slice registers one such check with the undo engine: after a restore, every month that is
closed must have exactly the budget it had before the undo; an undo that fails it is rolled back whole and
answered `refused` / `stale_change`. `shell.overview` answers the closed months from the app's database, oldest
first. On a server without the database both answer what they answer today.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and every request reads one
snapshot of it. *The app's own database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the package `internal/authored`, the only
package that executes SQL against it; the server has one only when started with `--db` / `FINWISE_DB`. *The
stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it and its
tests are the only existing statement of how writes behave, and its behaviour is the rule wherever this text
does not say otherwise. *The contract* is the TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` under `web/src/api/contract/`;
*the manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it and never edited by hand. *The journal*
is the record of every change to authored data; *undo* is the inverse of a change's recorded effects. *A month*
is `YYYY-MM` and *a day* `YYYY-MM-DD`, in Brazil time (`internal/brday`; a month's end is
`brday.MonthPeriod(month).Last`); "today" and "the current month" are the Brazil day and month of the instant in
the request's context, never the host's clock. *A budget version* is a budget document valid from a month on;
*the budget in force* for a month is the latest version that starts at or before it, a month before the first
version uses the first, and with no version at all a month has no budget (five empty groups).

**What earlier work provides.** None of the following is in the repository when this text is written; each is
delivered before this slice starts and is used here as it landed.

- The app's database and its statement registry (finwise-9h2); the recorder and undo (finwise-wi4): every change to a
  journaled table is written through the recorder as one recorded change; a *set table* holds rows that are
  facts by existing and an effect is one row appearing or disappearing; a version and its lines are a parent
  and its children, restored together whatever their order. `changes.undo(id)` collapses the change's effects
  per unit (a table and a key), refuses with `refused` / `stale_change` and changes nothing when the change is
  unknown or already undone or when a later change still in force has an effect on any of those units (the
  journal's order decides, not the value), and otherwise restores every `before` and marks the change undone;
  an undo is not itself undoable. Before an undo commits, the engine runs the checks other packages have
  registered with it, inside the undo's own transaction and after the restore; a failing check rolls the undo
  back whole and answers `refused` / `stale_change`. An undo never repairs anything by itself: it restores
  recorded effects or it is refused.
- The per-request views (finwise-jzw) and write dispatch (finwise-2s5): arguments validated against the manifest, one
  immediate transaction with a recorder holding one open change (author `person`, method
  `review.closeMonth`, the instant and the Brazil day), committed by the dispatcher, any failure rolled back as
  `internal`; without the database, or without a handler, `read_only` before the body is read; the error kind
  `refused`, HTTP 409, `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"<reason>"}}`; the manifest walk with
  `writesWithoutHandler`.
- The write conformance harness (finwise-fst): a case per write as a *recorded change* (the answer validates against
  the manifest, its effects match a golden file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`, and undoing it
  returns a canonical dump of every journaled table to the dump taken before); one refusal case per reason, the
  reasons with no producer yet named in a list in a test file; `internal/authored/authoredtest`; the third read
  state with cases in `authoredReadCases` and golden files in `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`.
- The budget's tables and its save (finwise-ef7): `budget_versions(from_month)` and `budget_version_lines(from_month,
  group_key, position, line_id, name, cents, flag)` (set tables), `closed_months(month, closed_on)` (a set table
  that nothing writes before this slice), stable line ids with names owned by each version, the function of the
  version in force for a month, and the save's month rule: a save for M is refused with `month_closed` when M is
  closed; for every closed month later than M, a version that already starts at it is left exactly as it is (it
  appears in no effect) and one is written there holding what was in force for it otherwise; every other later
  version is removed; the document is written at M; and it is written again at the month after each later
  closed month unless that month is closed too. The store function that writes "a version at a month holding
  exactly what was in force for it" exists for that rule; this slice uses it.
- The clearing of line references (finwise-oib): a save clears, in its own change, every transaction's reference to
  a line its month's budget no longer has (its own line goes back to nobody, a split part keeps its amount with
  no line, a refund's line and a pending suggestion are cleared); one undo restores them. A closed month that
  keeps its own version loses no line, so its transactions keep theirs. The same work registers the undo
  engine's second check: after a restore, no transaction may be left on a line that the budget in force for
  its month lacks (what counts as "on a line" is that work's, as it defines the references it clears).
- The one definition of pending (finwise-rf3): a transaction is pending when it has a pending review in
  `finwise.db`, the ledger lists it now, and its month's budget has at least one line; one function answers
  them, optionally only those dated up to a given day.
- The closing view (finwise-ysr): `review.closing(month)` reads `closed_months` for `closed` and `closedOn`, shows a
  closed month with every step done and none markable and every contribution made, counts in its first step the
  pending transactions dated up to the month's end (the same ones the close looks at), and lists closed months
  newest first; `review.markStepDone` answers null for a closed month.

**What the code is today (each point read in the file named).**

- `web/src/api/fake/closing.ts`: `closeMonth(month)` throws when the month is already closed, throws when
  `pendingCount(state) > 0` (every pending transaction of the state, whatever its month), and otherwise appends
  `{month, closedOn: state.shell.today}` to `state.shell.closedMonths` under one change. It writes no budget
  version: a closed month keeps its budget only because `saveFrom` (`budget-versions.ts`) recomputes what was in
  force for every later closed month at each save. It has no check for a future month.
- `web/src/api/fake/closing.test.ts`, group "closing the month": refused while anything waits; closes on today
  once the queue is empty and the shell reports `[{2026-10, 2026-11-02}, {2026-11, 2026-11-28}]`, the closing
  view `closed: true` with every step done and its list newest first; the budget of the month is then read-only
  (`budget.view(...).closed` true, `budget.save` refused); refused for a month already closed; taken back by its
  change, which reopens the month.
- `web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`: `ClosingApi.closeMonth(month): Promise<ChangeResult>`, commented
  "Refused while anything is waiting for review, and for a month already closed."; `ClosedMonthEntry` is
  `{month, closedOn}`. The result is not nullable. The manifest carries no method-level comment (its method
  entries have only domain, name, route, class, arguments and result), so changing that comment leaves the
  manifest unchanged.
- `internal/api/shell.go`: `readShellOverview` answers `ClosedMonths: []closedMonth{}` with the comment "Nobody
  has reviewed or closed anything yet"; `closedMonth` is `{month, closedOn}`. `internal/api/shell_test.go`
  (`TestShellOverviewOverTheFullLedger`) expects `[]`, and the golden files `full/shell.overview.json` and
  `empty/shell.overview.json` hold `"closedMonths": []`. The shell's `pendingCount` is not this slice's (finwise-tui).
- The interface: `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue` asks "Fechar <mês>? O budget deste mês fica guardado
  e não muda mais." before calling `useClosingActions().closeMonth`, which bumps the revision and shows no toast,
  so the interface offers no "Desfazer" for a close; a close is taken back through `changes.undo` with its id.
  `StepClose.vue` disables the button while `pendingCount > 0` and reads "Tudo pronto. Depois de fechado, o mês
  fica só para leitura." That sentence is the prototype's and stays as it is, although a closed month's
  transactions stay editable. The month selector never offers a month after the current one, so the future-month
  refusal is reached only by a client that sends one. A refusal ends in `web/src/api/failures.ts` like every
  other write, with the sentences below (finwise-diw, the work that teaches the interface the reasons).

**1. `review.closeMonth(month)`, in order.** The month is checked against the manifest and parsed (`2026-13` is
`bad_request`). Then, first match wins:

| # | condition | answer | what the person reads |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `closed_months` has the month | 409 `refused` / `month_closed` | "Esse mês já está fechado." |
| 2 | the month is after the current month | 409 `refused` / `future_month` | "Esse mês ainda não chegou." |
| 3 | (the snapshot is read here; missing, `ledger_unavailable`) a pending transaction is dated on or before the month's end | 409 `refused` / `pending_reviews` | "Resolva as pendências do mês antes de fechar." |

The server sends only the kind and the reason; the sentences are the interface's. Rows 1 and 2 need no ledger,
so a closed month answers `month_closed` even with the snapshot missing. Row 3 counts the pending transactions
of the month and of every earlier month, under the one definition, exactly the ones the closing view's first
step counts: a pending row the ledger no longer lists does not block, and blocks again once it is listed; a
pending review in a month whose budget has no line does not block. The current month can be closed; so can any
earlier month, in any order. A refusal changes nothing and adds no row to the journal. Lost with these rules:
the stand-in's global count, under which a purchase of November waiting for review blocks the close of October,
and the absence of a future-month check.

Otherwise, in the one change:

1. `closed_months` gains `(month, today)`.
2. When no version starts at the month, a version is written there holding exactly what is in force for it at
   that moment: the same line ids, names, amounts, flags, groups and positions, read before anything is
   written, through the same store function a save uses for a later closed month. When a version already
   starts there it is not touched and appears in no effect. When the month has no budget at all, the version
   written is the five empty groups. So what a closed month keeps is a row, not a computation.
3. Answer `{"changeId": "<id>"}`.

Writing that version changes the budget of no month: it is a copy of what was already in force at the month, and
every month that took its budget from the same earlier version now takes the same content from the copy (a
month before the first version took the first, and now takes the copy, which is the same). So the close does not
call the rules that classify new transactions, which a budget save calls after its commit, and it clears no
line reference. It writes no history step. It does not touch the closed month's transactions: closing freezes
the budget of the month, not its transactions, so they can still be recategorised, split, excluded and linked;
a pending review can even come back to a closed month later (a row the bank posts late in that month, which
the rules then cannot decide), and it then blocks the close of every later month until it is answered.

**2. Its undo.** `changes.undo` of the close removes exactly what it wrote: the row of `closed_months` and, when
it wrote one, the version and its lines. The month reopens and falls back to whatever budget is in force before
it: the latest version that starts before it, or the first version when none does. Nothing later can have
touched what a close wrote while the month stays closed (a save for the month is refused, and a save across it
leaves its version alone), so the units of a close are never stale; a second undo of the same change is, by the
undo engine's rule. What can still refuse it is the second check below: when the budget the month falls back to
lacks a line one of its transactions is on, the undo is refused with `stale_change` and changes nothing (example
D). After an undo the month can be closed again, which records a new change.

**3. The check this slice registers with the undo engine.** After the restore and before the undo commits: for
every month that is closed once the restore is done, the budget in force for it must equal the budget in force
for it before the undo, compared as `budget.document` would answer it, line by line: the same lines, in the same
groups and order, with the same names and amounts (and, since they are the same rows, the same flags). If any
closed month differs, the check fails, the undo engine rolls the undo back whole and answers `refused` /
`stale_change`, and nothing is changed or marked undone. A month that the undo itself reopens (the undo of its
close) is not closed once the restore is done, so its fall-back is allowed. The check reads only the app's
database, through registered statements of `internal/authored`, and runs for every undo the engine performs.
Where it is registered (the budget's store in `internal/authored` is the natural owner) and how the "before" is
taken (read before the restore, compared after it, in the same transaction) are the implementer's, within the
undo engine's mechanism (finwise-wi4). The person reads the sentence of `stale_change`, "Isso já foi alterado depois e
não pode mais ser desfeito.": the close came after, and the change cannot be taken back while it stands.

The second check, registered by the clearing of line references (finwise-oib), is used here as delivered: after the
restore, no transaction may be left on a line the budget of its month lacks. Neither check repairs anything; an
undo that would need a repair is refused, and the person takes back the later change first.

**4. A save before a close, across a close, and the undo of each, worked.** All of it invented. Clock
2026-03-20. Two lines: Mercado (line id 4) and Delivery (line id 5). The starting state Z: one version from
2026-01 holding Mercado 400,00 and Delivery 200,00; a transaction Tf of 2026-02-10 and a transaction Tm of
2026-03-05, both on Delivery; nothing closed, nothing pending. "V@M" is the version that starts at M.

*A. Closing a month that has no version of its own.* `C = closeMonth(2026-02)` writes the closed row
`(2026-02, 2026-03-20)` and V@2026-02 = {Mercado 400,00; Delivery 200,00}. Every month answers the same
budget as before. Undoing C removes both and gives Z.

*B. A save for the month, then its close.* `S = save(2026-02, {Mercado 500,00; Delivery 200,00})` writes
V@2026-02. `C = closeMonth(2026-02)` finds a version starting there and writes only the closed row.

| order | first undo | then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| undo C, then S | succeeds: February is open, on V@2026-02 (Mercado 500,00) | S's undo succeeds (nothing is closed): Z |
| undo S while C stands | refused, `stale_change`, nothing changed: S's units were touched by no later change, but removing V@2026-02 would answer the closed February from V@2026-01 (Mercado 400,00), and the closed-month check fails | undo C, then S: Z |

The close wrote nothing on the version S wrote, so only the check stops S's undo. Lost with the check: taking
back a save made before a close without first taking back the close.

*C. A save for an earlier month, then a close.* `S = save(2026-01, {Mercado 450,00; Delivery 200,00})` rewrites
V@2026-01. `C = closeMonth(2026-02)` finds no version at February and writes V@2026-02 = {Mercado 450,00;
Delivery 200,00} with the closed row.

| order | after the first undo | after the second |
| --- | --- | --- |
| undo C, then S | February reopens on V@2026-01 (Mercado 450,00) | Z |
| undo S, then C | succeeds, the check passes (February's budget is its own row and does not move): V@2026-01 is back to Mercado 400,00; February, closed, keeps V@2026-02 (450,00); March, which takes the latest version at or before it, now takes V@2026-02 and also answers 450,00 | Z |

Here the closed month is protected by its own row. The consequence to know: once a close wrote a version, it is
also the budget of every later month that has no version of its own, so undoing a save made before the close no
longer reaches those months; a save for March sets them.

*D. A close, then a save across it that removes a line.* `C = closeMonth(2026-02)` writes V@2026-02 = {Mercado
400,00; Delivery 200,00} and the closed row. `S = save(2026-01, {Mercado 450,00})`, with Delivery removed: the
closed February has its own version, which is left exactly as it is; V@2026-01 becomes {Mercado 450,00}; the
document is written again at the month after February, V@2026-03 = {Mercado 450,00}. The months that lose
Delivery are January and March onwards, so in S's own change Tm loses its line (finwise-oib); Tf, in the closed
February, keeps Delivery.

| order | first undo | then |
| --- | --- | --- |
| undo S, then C | succeeds, both checks pass: V@2026-01 is back to {Mercado 400,00; Delivery 200,00}, V@2026-03 is gone, Tm is back on Delivery, a line March's budget has again; February is still closed on its own version | C's undo succeeds: February reopens on V@2026-01, which has Delivery, so Tf is on a line of its month: Z |
| undo C while S stands | refused, `stale_change`, nothing changed: February would reopen on V@2026-01 as S left it, {Mercado 450,00}, and Tf would be left on Delivery, a line February's budget lacks, so the line check fails | undo S, then C: Z |

The same close and save with no transaction of February on Delivery (Tf left out of the state): undoing C while
S stands succeeds, both checks pass, and February reopens on {Mercado 450,00}; undoing S then gives Z. The undo
of a close is refused only when the month it reopens would hold a transaction on a line its fall-back budget
lacks; it never clears that reference itself.

*E. A close, then a save for a later month.* `C = closeMonth(2026-02)`, then `S = save(2026-03, {Mercado
600,00; Delivery 200,00})` writing V@2026-03. Their units are disjoint and neither undo moves a closed month's
budget or strands a transaction, so either undo succeeds in either order; undoing C alone reopens February on
V@2026-01, where Tf's Delivery is, and leaves March on V@2026-03.

*F. Closing a month with no budget, or before the first version.* With no version at all, closing 2026-02 writes
V@2026-02 with five empty groups; a later save for 2026-03 then makes January take V@2026-02 (the first version)
and stay without lines, where without the close it would have taken the March budget. With only V@2026-03,
closing 2026-02 writes V@2026-02 as a copy of V@2026-03, and January, which took the first version, still answers
the same budget.

**5. Closed months in the shell.** `shell.overview` answers `closedMonths` as every row of `closed_months`,
`{month, closedOn}`, oldest first by month, as the shell lists them today; the closing view lists the same rows
newest first (finwise-ysr). Without the database the list is empty, as today. Nothing else of the shell changes here.

**6. The contract's comment.** `ClosingApi.closeMonth`'s comment in `web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`
becomes true again: refused for a month already closed, for a month after the current one, and while a
transaction of that month or an earlier one waits for review. The manifest does not change. The stand-in does
not change: it follows only the contract's type changes, and this slice has none.

**Where the server departs from the stand-in on purpose,** each pinned by a test the final report names: the
close looks at the pending transactions of that month and earlier ones, listed now, instead of the global count;
a future month is refused; the refusals are typed reasons instead of thrown errors; closing writes the month's
budget as a version of its own (the stand-in writes none and recomputes a closed month's budget at every save);
an undo that would change a closed month's budget is refused (the stand-in's snapshot restore would put back
whatever the snapshot held); undo is by inverse instead of restoring a snapshot.

**Failure paths that touch this slice.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the snapshot is missing while closing an open month | `ledger_unavailable`; nothing is recorded |
| the close fails halfway, or waits out the five-second lock | one transaction: neither the closed row nor the version is kept; `internal` |
| two tabs close the same month | the writes queue; the first closes it, the second answers `month_closed` |
| a pending row of the month vanished from the ledger | it does not block; its authored rows stay; if it is listed again it blocks the close of every later month until answered |
| the process stops between the close's commit and its answer | the close is stored; the interface says the result could not be confirmed and refetches |
| the undo of a close after a save across it that removed a line one of the month's transactions is on | refused, `stale_change`, nothing changed; the person takes back the save first (example D) |
| the undo of a save made before a close of the same month | refused, `stale_change`, nothing changed; the person takes back the close first (example B) |
| a registered check fails while an undo is being committed | the whole undo is rolled back; nothing is restored, nothing is marked undone, nothing is repaired |

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. Nothing in this
slice needs one: every ledger and authored state here is invented. If one is opened to check a shape, it is
opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is printed, logged, or copied into
a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person running the test and goes into no
file; a test that touches it runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. New files of `internal/api`
log nothing.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of your own and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional
Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer
cents and no float may appear in the money path. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered
constant of `internal/authored`. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English. A design
value in a component comes from a token; this slice changes no component. A golden file changes only with `go
test ./internal/api -run TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile -update`, which refuses to run while
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set, and every changed golden file is read before it is committed.

## Acceptance criteria
The clock is 2026-03-20 unless said; the budget is the state Z of section 4 unless said.

Refusals and their order
- [ ] With pending reviews on transactions dated 2026-02-27 and 2026-02-28 (an instant of 2026-03-01 at 02:30
UTC, which is 23:30 of the 28th in Brazil), `closeMonth(["2026-02"])` answers 409
`{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"pending_reviews"}}` for each alone; with only one dated 2026-03-01 (03:00
UTC, midnight in Brazil) it closes February; with one dated in January it is refused for February.
- [ ] A pending review whose transaction the snapshot does not list does not block; over a second snapshot that
lists it again, the same database refuses with `pending_reviews`. A pending review in a month whose budget has no
line does not block.
- [ ] `closeMonth(["2026-04"])` answers `future_month`, also when a transaction of March is pending;
`closeMonth(["2026-03"])` closes the current month.
- [ ] `closeMonth` of a month already closed answers `month_closed`, also when a pending review of that month
exists and also with the snapshot file missing; with the snapshot missing an open month answers 503
`ledger_unavailable`; `2026-13` answers 400 `bad_request`; on a server without the database it answers 403
`read_only` with its body read 0 times.
- [ ] Every refusal leaves the canonical dump of the journaled tables and the row counts of `changes` and
`change_effects` as they were.

The close and its undo
- [ ] Example A: the close answers a change id; `closed_months` holds `(2026-02, 2026-03-20)`;
`budget_versions` holds 2026-01 and 2026-02, and the lines of 2026-02 equal those of 2026-01 in line id, name,
amount, flag, group and position; `budget.document` answers the same for 2025-12, 2026-01, 2026-02 and 2026-03 as
before the close; undo returns the canonical dump to the one taken before.
- [ ] Example B: `changes.undo` of S while C stands answers 409
`{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"stale_change"}}`, the canonical dump of every journaled table is the one taken
before the attempt, S is not marked undone, and `budget.document(["2026-02"])` still answers Mercado 500.00; after
undoing C, the same undo of S succeeds and the state is Z. Undoing C then S also ends at Z.
- [ ] Example C in both orders gives the states of its table, including March answering 450,00 after S's undo
while February is closed, and ends at Z.
- [ ] Example D: after S, Tm has no line and Tf keeps Delivery; `changes.undo` of C while S stands answers 409
`stale_change` with the dump unchanged, C not marked undone and `closed_months` still holding 2026-02; undoing S
then C succeeds and ends at Z. In the same state without Tf, undoing C while S stands succeeds and February
reopens on {Mercado 450,00}; undoing S then gives Z.
- [ ] Example E: both undos succeed in either order. Example F: closing a month with no version writes a version
with no line, and closing a month before the first version writes a copy of the first.
- [ ] The closed-month check, tested on its own: an undo that would change, for a closed month, a line's amount, a
line's name, the order of two lines, or which lines the budget has, is refused with `stale_change` and changes
nothing; an undo that changes only the budget of an open month, or of the month it reopens, passes it.
- [ ] After a close, `budget.save` and `budget.applyScenario` for that month answer `month_closed`, a save for an
earlier month leaves the closed month's version without any effect on it, `review.closing` answers `closed` true
with `closedOn`, and `review.markStepDone` for it answers null.
- [ ] After a close, a transaction of the closed month can still be put on a line of that month's budget.
- [ ] A second `changes.undo` of a close answers `stale_change`; closing the month again after the undo answers a
new change id.
- [ ] The close calls no ingest: the number of changes by the author `rule` is the same before and after it.

The shell
- [ ] With 2026-02 and 2025-12 closed (in that order), `shell.overview` answers `closedMonths`
`[{"month":"2025-12",...},{"month":"2026-02",...}]` with their days, and `review.closing` lists them the other way
round.
- [ ] On a server without the database `shell.overview` answers byte for byte what it answers today over both
invented ledgers; `TestShellOverviewOverTheFullLedger` passes unchanged; no file under `testdata/golden/full/` or
`empty/` changes.

Harness and guards
- [ ] `review.closeMonth` has write-conformance cases as a recorded change for example A (a version written) and
for a month that already has its version (only the closed row), each with golden effects under
`testdata/golden/writes/`; refusal cases for `future_month` and `pending_reviews`, both removed from the list of
reasons without a producer (and `month_closed`'s case kept); it leaves `writesWithoutHandler` and the manifest walk
passes.
- [ ] `authoredReadCases` gains `shell.overview` with two closed months, with its golden file under
`testdata/golden/full-authored/` (or the existing case of the shell there gains them).
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run contract:check` passes with the new comment: the manifest is unchanged.
- [ ] No non-test file added or changed here contains a float or a call to `time.Now`.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the final report: the pending
check made global; the check's last day taken as the month's first; the listing condition dropped; the future check
removed; the checks reordered so a closed month answers `pending_reviews`; the version not written when none starts
at the month; the version written over one that exists; a copy that loses a flag or a position; the undo leaving the
version behind; the shell listing newest first; the closed-month check left unregistered (example B's undo of S
succeeds); the check comparing amounts only (a rename of a closed month's line passes); the check applied to the
month the undo reopens (example D without Tf: the undo of C is refused).
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the manifest walk passes without `review.closeMonth` in its list, and
examples A to F of section 4 are each a passing test that reproduces every state of its table.

## Tests
- Integration with `httptest`, `internal/api`, over ledgers built with `ledgertest` and authored states built with
  `authoredtest`: each refusal and their order; the Brazil-day boundary of the month's end; the vanished pending row
  across two snapshots; the close with and without a version to write; examples A to F with both undo orders,
  comparing `budget.document`, `budget_versions`, `budget_version_lines` and `tx_state` after each step.
- Unit, `internal/authored` over a migrated scratch database: writing a closed month and the copy of the version in
  force; every new statement registered and prepared.
- Table, `internal/authored` (or wherever the check is registered): the closed-month check over before-and-after
  budgets that differ in an amount, a name, an order, a line added or removed, and that do not differ; a month the
  undo reopens; refused undos leave the dump unchanged and the change not undone.
- Write conformance (the harness): two recorded-change cases with golden effects and their undo to the dump taken
  before; the refusal cases of the two reasons first produced here.
- Golden (read conformance, third state): `shell.overview` with closed months; `full/` and `empty/` unchanged.
- Contract: `contract:check` after the comment changes.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the final report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/review_close.go`, `internal/api/review_close_test.go`, `internal/api/shell.go`,
`internal/api/shell_test.go`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`, `web/src/api/contract/review-closing.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/fake/closing.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/closing.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/budget-versions.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/rules.ts`, `internal/api/review_closing.go`,
`internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`,
