`web/src/screens/revisao/useClosingActions.ts`, `web/src/screens/revisao/StepClose.vue`,
`web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`, `bin/ci`

One new handler file (the name is a proposal) and its test; the shell's closed months read from the authored
view; in `internal/authored`, the write of a closed month (the table and the version copy already exist with the
budget's store), the closed-month check registered with the undo engine, and their statements; one comment of the
contract. The undo engine's check mechanism and the line check are used as delivered, not changed. About four code files in three places, hence
`size:L` by the module count though the code is small. The budget's save, the clearing of references, the pending
function, the closing view, the shell's pending count, the stand-in and the screens are used or read, not changed.
close_reason: review.closeMonth closes a month that has come and has nothing waiting for review up to its last day, keeps its budget as a version of its own, and is undone exactly; a second check of the undo engine refuses any undo that would move a closed month's budget; shell.overview lists the closed months. Every write of the contract now has a handler. Verified: gate green on the branch merged with main; twenty-three deliberate breaks while writing it and four in review, the two that survived at first now failing cases of their own.

title: Work out the budget's figures on the server in integer cents, for the month's budget and for a draft, and weigh a scenario against the month by line id
description:
## What changes for the user
Today, over their real bank data, the budget screen shows five empty groups and nothing else: whatever
budget the person keeps, no line says how much was spent on it, the income is zero and the investment
rate is a dash; pressing "Editar budget" and changing any amount ends the edit at once with the message
that the app is read-only, and the scenarios screen sends the person back to the budget the moment it
opens. After this lands the budget screen shows, for the month on screen, what was received on each
income line, what was spent on each fixed and variable line and what is left of it, which variable line
went over its cap, the balance of the savings pot a provision or a reserve is linked to, the fees the
banks charged, what is left to invest and its share of the income. While editing, every change is
weighed at once, with a renamed line keeping what was spent on it and a new line starting at nothing;
the scenarios screen says how much a scenario would invest and which of its amounts differ from the
month's budget; and opening a line lists the places that make it up, biggest first. If this were wrong
the person would see a total that does not add up to the purchases behind it, a line that loses its
spending when renamed, a pot balance shown under a line that is not linked to that pot, or a scenario
that marks an untouched amount as changed.

## Outcome
The pure package `internal/budgetrules` gains `View` and `ScenarioImpact`, which compute every figure of
`BudgetView` and `ScenarioImpact` in integer cents from plain values: the groups of a budget with each
line's id, name, amount and flag; what each line id received or spent in the month, from the
dispositions; the balance of the pot each line is linked to; whether the month is closed; and the
investment "made". `budget.view(month)` answers the budget in force for the month from the app's
database, `budget.view(month, draft)` answers the same figures for a draft, with its arguments validated
against the manifest before the handler runs, `budget.evaluateScenario(month, draft)` has a handler, and
`budget.establishments(month, line)` groups the month's contributions to a line by establishment. A negative
amount in a draft is `bad_request`. On a server without the app's database `budget.view` without a draft and `budget.establishments` answer exactly
what they answer today, and no golden file under `full/` or `empty/` changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, through `internal/ledger`.
*The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`, where everything the
person authors is kept (a budget, a transaction's line, a link between a budget line and a pot); the
server has one only when started with `--db`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it and its tests are the only existing statement
of how the budget's figures behave, and its behaviour is the rule wherever this text does not say
otherwise. *The contract* is the TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` under `web/src/api/contract/`; *the
manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it, versioned and never edited by hand,
which gives Go each method's route, class (`read`, `evaluate`, `write`, `session`) and the schemas of its
arguments and result. *A budget* is a list of versions, each valid from a month on; the budget in force
for a month is the latest version at or before it, and a month before the first version uses the first.
It has five groups a person edits, by key: income (`rec`), fixed (`fix`), variable (`var`), provisions
(`prov`, money set aside every month for a bill that comes once in a while) and reserves (`res`, money set
aside for something wanted). *A line* has an integer id minted once in the app's database, a name that
belongs to the budget version, an amount in cents and an optional flag such as "Não garantida". *The fees
line* is the built-in line "Tarifas e juros": it belongs to no group and no document and has a fixed id.
*A draft* is a budget document the person is still editing; it is sent to be weighed and never stored by
this work. *A pot* is what the pots screens list: a reserve entry of a bank account (id
`reserve:<account>/<reserveId>`), an investment (id `investment:<id>`) or, when the bank does not keep an
entry's identity stable, a slot (id `slot:<account>/<n>`). *A month* is `YYYY-MM` and *a day*
`YYYY-MM-DD`, both in Brazil time (`internal/brday`); "the current month" is the Brazil month of the
instant in the request's context, never the host's clock. *A golden file* is the committed, exact answer
of one call over an invented fixture. *The gate* is `bin/ci`, the exact checks CI runs.

**What earlier work provides.** None of the following is in the repository when this text is written;
each is delivered before this bead starts, and its interfaces are to be read in the code as that work
left them.

- The per-request views (finwise-jzw): a handler's third parameter is one value carrying a view of the
  ledger (one handle and one read-only transaction on the snapshot, so every ledger query of the request
  sees the same snapshot) and a view of the app's database (one read-only transaction, or an empty view
  that answers "nothing authored" on a server without `--db`, so read code has one path). The clock is a
  required part of the configuration and `nowOf` never reads the host's clock. A handler that asks the
  ledger nothing is answered normally when the snapshot file is missing.
- Write dispatch (finwise-2s5): the registry takes handlers of every class but `session`; a write or an
  evaluation that has a handler, on a server with the app's database, has its arguments validated against
  the method's argument schema in the manifest before the handler runs (a mismatch is `bad_request`, the
  handler is not called, and the arguments are checked from the bytes that arrived so no number passes
  through a float). Without the database, or without a handler, a write or an evaluation answers
  `read_only` before its body is read. An evaluation receives the same read-only views as a read and stores
  nothing. A test walks the manifest and requires every write and evaluation to have a handler or to be
  named in the list `writesWithoutHandler`, where `budget.evaluateScenario` stands until this work. Reads
  are not validated by schema; they keep their own strict decoding (`decodeArgument` in `arguments.go`).
  `budget.view`'s draft is the one exception that work left for this one: until now it refuses any draft
  with `read_only`.
- Money in (finwise-po6): `ParseReais` turns a JSON number into integer cents from its decimal text, with no
  float, rounding half away from zero beyond two places and refusing anything that is not a finite number
  within one billion reais; `Reais` decodes through it; an amount that cannot be negative, a budget line's
  among them, is `bad_request` when it is.
- The write conformance harness (finwise-fst): every write and evaluation has a case in its mode, and an
  *evaluation* case passes only if no table of the app's database changes at all.
  `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds invented authored states, one builder per group of tables.
- The contract's line id (finwise-m9q): `BudgetLineDoc` carries an optional `id`, a decimal string, which the
  interface's draft keeps through copying, renaming, moving and editing; a new line has none.
- The budget's tables (finwise-ef7): `lines(id, builtin)`, `budget_versions(from_month)`,
  `budget_version_lines(from_month, group_key, position, line_id, name, cents, flag)`, `scenarios` and
  `closed_months(month, closed_on)`, with the read of the budget in force for a month and the one function
  that says which line ids a month's budget has (its lines, and the fees line when it has at least one).
  Its decoder of a budget document (groups by key, each line with its optional id, its amount as `Reais`
  and its flag, an empty flag being no flag) is the one this work uses for drafts; its validation
  (`invalid_budget`) is not, because a draft is not validated beyond its shape.
- The transactions' store (finwise-jw2): the migration `0003_transactions` with `tx_index`, `tx_ids` (every
  provider id mapped to the transaction's own key) and `tx_state` (a transaction's line, split parts,
  exclusion, refund and its line, reimbursement and its linked credit, pending review), and the
  `authoredtest` builders for them.
- The transactions' API side (finwise-tsr): the lookup of a transaction, the merged reads (a listed
  transaction joined in Go, by its key, with its authored state, inside one request that sees one snapshot
  of each store), the one function that answers the name to show for an establishment key (the nickname
  when the person gave the key one, else the ledger's name), and the third read state: read conformance
  run over the full invented ledger with an invented authored state, with golden files in
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/` (the directory finwise-fst added) and cases in a list of their
  own, `authoredReadCases`, with a type and constructor of their own so that the interface's equality test
  does not find them.
- The dispositions (finwise-305): the pure package `internal/budgetrules` with `Dispose`, the function that
  says what a transaction counts for, and its two invariants (every listed transaction in exactly one
  disposition; for every debit, what it adds to lines plus what is unassigned plus the applied
  reimbursement equals its amount). It takes one listed transaction with its authored state merged in and
  answers its disposition and the amounts it adds to which line ids. This work adds the view to that same
  package. Amounts are magnitudes in integer cents; the first condition that matches wins:

  | # | disposition | condition | adds |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 | unconverted | the ledger has no value in reais for it | nothing |
  | 2 | movement | a movement between own accounts or a bill payment | nothing |
  | 3 | excluded | excluded with a reason | nothing |
  | 4 | waiting | pending review | nothing |
  | 5 | split | a debit with two or more parts | each part with a line adds its amount to that line; the rest is unassigned |
  | 6 | fee | a fee row, charge or discount, on no line (posted, as the existing fees rule says) or put on the fees line by the person | a charge adds to the fees line; the credit that discounts it takes off |
  | 7 | reimbursement | a credit linked to a purchase | no line; the smaller of its amount and the purchase's is applied inside the purchase |
  | 8 | refund | a credit that is a refund | takes its amount off its refund line; with no refund line, nothing |
  | 9 | income | a credit on a line of the income group | adds its amount to that line (received) |
  | 10 | other credit | any other credit | nothing |
  | 11 | on a line | a debit with a line | adds its amount less the applied reimbursement |
  | 12 | uncategorised | a debit with no line | nothing |

  A row the bank still reports as pending is listed and counts like any other; only the fee rule keeps
  counting posted fee rows alone.
- The pots' store (finwise-rju): the migration `0005_pots` with `pot_lines(line_id, pot_id)`, a line linked to
  at most one pot, and `pot_settings(pot_id, bucket)`, with the authored view's read of the links. That is
  all this work needs of the pots' work: the reads and writes that use a pot's effective bucket
  (finwise-7ss) and the screens that follow them (finwise-xu2) are not needed, since a balance cell shows the pot's
  balance and not its bucket. The write that toggles a link arrives with them; here a link exists only in
  a fixture built with `authoredtest`.

**What the code is today** (each point read in the file named).

- `internal/api/budget.go`: `registerBudget` registers `budget.document`, `budget.view`,
  `budget.establishments` and `budget.scenarios` (by then finwise-ef7 has replaced the first and the last).
  `readBudgetView` parses the month with `monthArgument` (`fresh_install.go`), refuses any second argument
  that is not `null` with `readOnlyError` ("evaluating one is the budget's arithmetic, which belongs to the
  part of the app that is not built"), and answers `budgetView{Month, Groups: emptyBudgetGroups(fees)}`
  with `fees` from `feesOfMonth`. `readBudgetEstablishments` checks two arguments and answers `[]`.
  `budgetView` has `InvestmentRate any`, written as `null`.
- `internal/api/budget_view.go`: `editableGroupNames` (the five keys with the names in
  `internal/api/messages.go`: "Receita", "Fixos e essenciais", "Variáveis", "Provisões", "Reservas de
  desejo"); the wire types `budgetGroupView`, `budgetLineView` (`Cells [3]any`, `Marks []any`, `Bar
  any`), `noneCell`, `moneyCell`, `percentCell`; `emptyBudgetGroups` (fixed and variable carry
  `subtotalSpent` 0.00, the others null; then Rainy Funds, `feesGroup` and `investmentGroup`);
  `feesOfMonth`, which reads the month as the transaction list does (`loadContext`, then
  `interpretPeriod` widened by the tax pairing window and cut back, in `transactions_period.go`) and sums
  `spentOnFees`: posted fee rows that are not movements and not unconverted, charges positive and the
  discounts taken off.
- `internal/api/messages.go` holds every text the server writes for a person; it has the group names,
  `budgetGroupRainyFunds` "Rainy Funds", `budgetGroupFees` "Tarifas e juros" and `budgetGroupInvestment`
  "Investimento", and not yet "Estourou" or "Budget maior que a receita".
- `internal/api/budget_test.go`: `TestTheBudgetAnswersAsAFreshInstallOverBothLedgers` (the full ledger
  holds one 25.00 fee in March); `TestTheBudgetViewNamesTheMonthItWasAskedForAndOnlyCountsItsFees`;
  `TestTheBudgetViewRefusesAnyDraftAsAWriteIsRefused`, which expects `read_only` for the drafts `[]`, a
  one-group document, `0` and `"x"`; `TestTheBudgetMethodsRefuseArgumentsThatAreNotWhatTheyTake`;
  `TestSpentOnFeesCountsWhatWasChargedNetOfDiscounts` (seven rows, 3200 cents). Its `readCases`, in the
  written shape ``readCase{"budget.view", `["2026-03",null]`}``, are found by
  `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`, which scans the Go test sources for that shape and requires the
  stand-in to answer each case exactly as the golden file of `empty/` does.
- The manifest: `budget.view` is of class `read`, arguments `[YearMonth, BudgetDoc | null]`, one or two;
  `budget.evaluateScenario` is of class `evaluate`, arguments `[YearMonth, BudgetDoc]`;
  `budget.establishments` is a `read` of `[YearMonth, string]`. `BudgetGroupDoc` and `BudgetLineDoc` have
  `additionalProperties: false`; `EditableGroupKey` is an enum of the five keys; a line's `amount` is a
  number.
- The stand-in: `web/src/api/fake/budget-view.ts` (`buildView`, `editableGroup`, `incomeLine`,
  `outgoingLine`, `provisionLine`, `wishLine`, `rainyFundLine`, `investmentLine`, `investmentMade`,
  `establishmentsOf`, `scenarioImpact`), `rules.ts` (`contributions`, `spentByLine`, `groupTotalOf`,
  `plannedInvestmentOf`, `percentOfIncome`), `budget.ts` (`view` and `evaluateScenario` pass the draft
  through `cleanDraft`, which turns an amount that is not a finite number into zero), and the tests
  `budget.test.ts` (groups "budget figures", "the establishments of a line", and the `evaluateScenario`
  cases of "scenarios") and `rules.test.ts` ("contributions", "spentByLine"). The stand-in joins
  everything by a line's name, reads spending from a seeded baseline (`spentByLine` moves it only in the
  current month), finds a line's pot by the pot's name, rounds money with `Math.round(x * 100) / 100` and
  draws fractions as bars.
- The interface: `web/src/screens/budget/BudgetScreen.vue` asks `budget.view(month, draft)` after every
  change of the draft (each committed name or amount field, each line added, removed or moved), with no
  debounce, keeps only the latest answer, and ends the edit when that call answers `read_only`.
  `ScenariosScreen.vue` asks `budget.evaluateScenario(month, draft)` after every change of its draft, with
  no debounce, and returns to the budget when that answers `read_only`. Both draw `impact.changed` by the
  position of each group and line of the draft they sent. The amount inputs are `type="number"` and send
  `Number(typed) || 0`, so a field left blank or holding something that is not a number becomes 0, and a
  typed negative number is sent as it is, until separate work turns it into 0 at the source (finwise-lhk: the
  two amount inputs never put a negative amount in a draft).

**The decisions this work carries, with what lost.**

- Spending is looked up by line id, never by name: a draft's renamed line keeps its spending and a line
  the draft has just added (no id) has none. Lost: the stand-in's join by name, under which renaming a
  line silently drops its history from every total.
- Spending and income received are summed from the ledger for the month asked, by Brazil day, through the
  dispositions. Lost: the stand-in's seeded baseline, which has no rule behind it and no rule at all for
  income received.
- A provision or reserve line's pot is the pot the line is linked to in `pot_lines`, never a pot of the
  same name. Lost: the join by name, under which renaming a line or a pot silently moves a balance.
- `ScenarioImpact` compares each scenario line with the line of the same id in the budget of the month
  asked, instead of by position; a line without an id is changed. Lost: comparing by position, which marks
  every line after an inserted one as changed and compares a moved line with its neighbour.
- Every percentage the server computes is a whole number rounded half up, as the existing reads already
  answer `fill` and `progress`. Lost: the stand-in's fractions (a bar of 77.0 for 308 of 400 happens to be
  whole; 290 of 900 would be 32.22).
- A draft being edited is not validated beyond its shape: an empty or repeated name, a name equal to the
  fees line's and an id that names no line are all weighed as typed. Only the save validates (finwise-ef7).
- Pot targets (Rainy Funds) get no control in this plan of work, a decision of the person: the Rainy Funds
  group is answered empty.
- The investment's "made" follows the month's "Investimento" transfer of the payday review, which does
  not exist yet (finwise-66k: the payday transfers derived from the budget and marked by month). Until then it
  is answered as not made.
- The next charge of a provision has no source yet: it is answered as the contract's "no date".

**The figures.** Every amount is integer cents (`money.Cents`) from the budget's `cents` column and the
dispositions to the wire, where `api.Reais` writes it. The only divisions are the two percentages, rule
(P). `View` is a pure function of plain values: it opens nothing, knows no HTTP and reads no clock, as
`internal/txrules`, `internal/cardrules` and `internal/potrules` do today. Its inputs, for a month M:

- `G`: the groups of the budget in force for M (or of the draft), each line with its id (absent for a
  draft's new line), its name, its amount `a ≥ 0` and its flag;
- `F(id)`: for every line id, the sum of what `Dispose` adds to that id over the transactions the API
  lists whose Brazil day is in M, signed as the table says (a refund takes off, an income credit adds to
  its income line). The transactions of M are read as `feesOfMonth` reads them today, widened by the tax
  pairing window and cut back to M, so a purchase is placed exactly as the list shows it. `F` of an id
  nothing touched, and of a line without id, is 0;
- `P(id)`: for a line id linked in `pot_lines`, the pot's balance now, as `loadPots` builds it (`potEntry.
  balance`; the pots are needed for the balance alone, so they are loaded without the yield, as `home.go`
  does), counted only while the ledger lists that pot now and the pot is open; otherwise absent. The
  balance is today's whatever month is asked, as in the stand-in. The same rule, "a link counts only while
  its pot is listed and open", is the one the payday transfers will use (finwise-66k), so it is one function;
- `closed`: whether M has a row in `closed_months`;
- `made`: the amount the investment line shows as made. This work always supplies 0; it is an input so
  that the payday work (finwise-66k) can feed it (the residual once the month's "Investimento" transfer is
  marked, or when the month is closed) without changing `View`.

Numbered, each in cents:

1. `T(k) = Σ a(l)` over the lines of group k, for each of the five keys. A group a draft leaves out has
   no lines and `T = 0`.
2. `income = T(rec)`.
3. `outgoing = T(fix) + T(var) + T(prov) + T(res)`.
4. `investment = income − outgoing`. It can be negative.
5. `allocated = outgoing + investment`, as the stand-in computes it (it equals `income` by construction,
   and a test says so).
6. `rate = null` when `income = 0`; otherwise `round½↑(investment × 100 / income)`, by rule (P). This is
   also `investmentRate` and the third cell of the investment line. The residual (4) and the rate (6) are
   functions of their own that `View` calls, because the payday review and the net worth's investment rate
   (finwise-66k) take them "exactly as the budget view answers them".
7. Rule (P), whole percent rounded half up: for `x = n × 100 / d` with `d > 0`, `round½↑(x) = ⌊(200·n + d)
   / (2·d)⌋`, with a floor division, not Go's `/`, which truncates toward zero and gives the wrong answer
   for a negative `n`. Half goes toward positive infinity, as JavaScript's `Math.round`: 12.5 → 13, −12.5
   → −12, −184.67 → −185. One function, in `internal/budgetrules`, serves every percentage of this work
   and of the work after it (the weekly fill, the contribution's progress).
8. `share(part, whole) = 0` when `whole = 0`; otherwise `round½↑(part × 100 / whole)` held between 0 and
   100. The upper bound is the stand-in's `Math.min(100, …)`; the lower bound is the contract's ("`bar` is
   the share of the amount reached, 0 to 100"), which a negative `part` (refunds larger than the purchases
   on a line) would otherwise break; the stand-in has no lower bound and answers a negative bar there.
9. An income line l: cells `[money a(l), money F(l), none]`; marks `[{text: flag, tone: "neutral"}]` when
   it has a flag, else `[]`; `over` false; `bar` null; `expandable` true.
10. A fixed or variable line l: `done = F(l)`, `left = a(l) − done`, `over = left < 0` (strictly above
    the amount). Cells `[money a(l), money done, difference left]`; `expandable` true. A fixed line: marks
    `[]`, `bar` null. A variable line: marks `[{text: "Estourou", tone: "bad"}]` when `over`, else `[]`;
    `bar = share(done, a(l))`.
11. `potCell(l) = money P(l)` when `P(l)` is present, else `none` (the stand-in answers money 0 for a line
    with no pot of its name; here a line with no counted link has no balance to show).
12. A provision line l: cells `[money a(l), potCell(l), next-charge null]`, the contract's
    `{"type":"next-charge","charge":null}`; marks `[]`, `over` false, `bar` null, `expandable` false.
13. A reserve line l: cells `[money a(l), potCell(l), money F(l)]`; marks `[]`, `over` false, `bar` null,
    `expandable` true.
14. An editable group k: `subtotal = T(k)`; `subtotalSpent = Σ F(l)` over its lines for `fix` and `var`
    (0.00 when it has no line), `null` for the other three; `over = (k = var) ∧ subtotalSpent > T(var)`,
    strictly; its lines in the version's (or the draft's) order within the group.
15. Rainy Funds: `{key: "rf", name: "Rainy Funds", subtotal: 0.00, subtotalSpent: null, over: false,
    lines: []}`.
16. Fees: `fees = F(fees line)`. Group `{key: "tar", name: "Tarifas e juros", subtotal: fees,
    subtotalSpent: null, over: false}` with one line "Tarifas e juros", cells `[money fees, none, none]`,
    marks `[]`, `over` false, `bar` null, `expandable` true. The fees line counts by rule in every month,
    with or without a budget. With nothing authored this equals today's `spentOnFees` for the month.
17. Investment: group `{key: "inv", name: "Investimento", subtotal: investment, subtotalSpent: null, over:
    investment < 0}` with one line "Investimento", cells `[money investment, money made, percent rate]`,
    `over = investment < 0`, marks `[{text: "Budget maior que a receita", tone: "bad"}]` when over, else
    `[]`, `bar` null, `expandable` false.
18. The view: `{month: M, closed, income, allocated, investmentRate: rate, groups}`, the groups in the
    order `rec`, `fix`, `var`, `prov`, `res`, `rf`, `tar`, `inv`, the five editable ones always present,
    with the fixed names the server owns, whatever names or order a draft sends.

Both new texts, "Estourou" and "Budget maior que a receita", are the stand-in's and go to `messages.go`.

**The scenario's impact** (`budgetrules.ScenarioImpact`), for a month M and a draft S:

19. `current = {investment: investment(C), rate: rate(C)}` by (4) and (6), where C is the budget in force
    for M. A month with no version has no lines: `{0.00, null}`.
20. `scenario = {investment: investment(S), rate: rate(S)}`.
21. `difference = investment(S) − investment(C)`.
22. `changed[g][i]`, for every group g of S in the order it was sent and every line i of it in the order
    sent (the screen draws it by those positions): `true` when the line has no id, or C has no line with
    that id, or that line's amount in C is not `a(S, g, i)`; `false` otherwise. Only the amount is
    compared: a renamed or moved line with the same id and amount is not changed.

An evaluation reads nothing from the ledger, so it answers when the snapshot is missing.

**The establishments of a line** (`budget.establishments(month, name)`):

23. The name is resolved in the budget in force for the month: "Tarifas e juros" is the fees line in any
    month, as the view shows it in any month; any other name is the line that version gives that name. A
    name the month's budget does not have answers `[]`.
24. A transaction listed in the month is in the list when `Dispose` reports at least one addition to that
    line id, even of zero; it adds the sum of its additions to that id (two parts of one split on the
    line add together) and counts once.
25. Grouped by establishment key (`txrules.Transaction.EstablishmentKey`, `doc:`, `name:` or `text:`; a
    person has one too): `amount = Σ` of its transactions' sums, signed (a refund takes off), `count` the
    number of its transactions, `name` the name to show for the key. Order: `amount` descending, then
    `key` ascending.
26. Invariant: the amounts of a line's establishments add up to `F(line)`, the figure the view shows for
    that line in the same month, and the counts to the number of transactions that add to it.

The name to show is the one the function of the transactions' API side gives for the key (finwise-tsr): the
nickname when the person gave the key one, else the ledger's name. This work calls it and computes no name
of its own.

**`budget.view` with a draft, and its arguments.** The router validates `budget.view`'s arguments against
its argument schema in the manifest before the handler runs, as it does for every write and evaluation
with a handler, and only for this read: every other read keeps its own decoding. So over HTTP the drafts
`0` and `"x"`, a group key outside the five, a line with a field the contract does not have and a line
without `amount` are 400 `bad_request` with the handler not called; `null` and an empty array `[]` (a
document with no groups) pass. The handler then parses what a schema cannot say: the month
(`bad_request` for `2026-13`), each amount through `Reais` (`bad_request` for a negative amount, one beyond
one billion reais, or `1e400`). Then it builds the view of the draft with (1) to (18), reading from the app's
database only the closed month and the links, and from the ledger the month's transactions and the pots.
It stores nothing: a read runs in a read-only transaction.

On a server without the app's database `budget.view` is still a read, so a draft is weighed against an
empty authored view (no line has spending, no link exists) and answered; `budget.evaluateScenario` is of
class `evaluate` and keeps answering `read_only` there, before its body is read. Over the interface this
means: on a server without `--db` the edit mode of the budget no longer ends at the first change, and
saving keeps answering `read_only`, which keeps the edit as today; the scenarios screen keeps returning to
the budget.

**A negative amount.** A negative amount in a draft stays `bad_request` on the server: a budget line's
amount cannot be negative. From the screens it is stopped at the source by separate web work (finwise-lhk): the
amount inputs of the budget's edit mode and of the scenario editor put 0 in the draft where a negative was
typed, so the person's edit never gets stuck on a draft every evaluation refuses. That work may land
before or after this one; this one changes no component and keeps the refusal for any other client.

**What the stand-in does that is not ported** (each pinned by a test named in the report of the work):
the seeded spending baseline and its freeze outside the current month; the join by name of spending, pots
and the scenario's comparison; the pot's next charge; the Rainy Funds built from pots named "RF ..."
with a target; the investment counted as made in a closed month (it arrives with the transfers); the
fractional bars; `cleanDraft`'s zero for an amount that is not a number, which has no wire form (JSON has
no `NaN`, and a `null` amount is refused by the schema); the establishments' order on a tie, which the
stand-in leaves to insertion.

**The cost of an evaluation.** The interface asks for a draft's figures after every change, with no
debounce, so one evaluation is one ledger read of the month widened by the pairing window, one load of the
pots without yield and a few authored reads. Its time on a real ledger is measured by the review, not by
this work, and recorded on the pull request beside the time of `budget.evaluateScenario`; whether a
debounce is then needed in the interface is the review's decision, and this work adds none. Reading the
whole ledger on every call is accepted for now and is deferred work that will read this measurement.

**Failure paths that touch this work.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the snapshot is missing | `budget.view` (with or without a draft) and `budget.establishments` answer 503 `ledger_unavailable`; `budget.evaluateScenario` answers, as it reads no ledger |
| the snapshot is swapped during a request | the request finishes on the snapshot its ledger view opened |
| a save commits while a view is being computed | the view's authored read is wholly before or wholly after it |
| a line is renamed, reordered or moved between groups | its id holds, and so do its spending and its pot |
| a line is linked to a pot the ledger no longer lists, or to a closed pot | its balance cell is `none` |
| a draft sends a negative amount | 400 `bad_request`, the handler's parse of the amount; once finwise-lhk has landed the screens never send one |
| a server without the app's database | `budget.view` and `budget.establishments` answer as today; a draft is weighed against nothing authored; `budget.evaluateScenario` answers `read_only` |

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. A real
snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever
printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the
person running the test and goes into no file; a test that touches a real ledger runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Fixtures are invented. The review's timing of an evaluation on a
real ledger records durations only, never a figure the evaluation answered. A line's name and an
establishment's name are the person's own words: new files of `internal/api` log nothing, and the request
log keeps to verb, route, status, duration and error kind.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional
Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is
integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; the test that forbids floats covers
`internal/api` and the rule packages. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant
of `internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against `finwise.db`; this work should need no
new one beyond what finwise-ef7 and finwise-rju added, and any it adds is registered and prepared by the existing
test. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English. A design value in a component
comes from a token; this work changes no component. A conformance case that carries a draft or needs
authored data is in `authoredReadCases`, never in `readCases` in the shape the interface's equality test
scans for: that test replays each such case on the stand-in over an empty ledger and requires the same
answer, and for a draft's provision or reserve line the stand-in answers money 0 where the server answers
`none`, since no pot is linked. A golden file changes only
with `go test ./internal/api -run TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile -update`, which refuses to run while
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set, and every changed golden file is read before it is committed.

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`), with what constrains each:

- the signatures of `View` and `ScenarioImpact` and the shape of their inputs: plain values in, plain
  values out, amounts as `money.Cents`, no float, no clock, no I/O; `internal/api` turns the result into
  the wire types of `budget_view.go`;
- what a draft in which one group key appears twice gives: either every line of both is kept, in document
  order, or the lines are placed as the save places them (finwise-ef7 made that choice for the save and pinned
  it). No line may be dropped silently, and `changed` still has one entry per group and line as sent; a
  test pins it;
- whether `feesOfMonth` and `spentOnFees` survive: if nothing calls them after this work, remove them, and
  keep the seven rows of `TestSpentOnFeesCountsWhatWasChargedNetOfDiscounts` as a test of the fees figure
  (16), which must still give 3200 cents;
- where the exception that validates `budget.view`'s arguments lives in the router: one place, naming
  that one read, with a test that it applies to no other read.

title: Add the transactions' tables to the app's database, keeping each transaction under a key of its own and mapping the bank's ids to it
description:
## What changes for the user
Nothing on screen changes with this piece. Everything the person will later decide about a transaction (the
budget line it goes on, its tags and note, a nickname for the shop, a split, "não conta", a refund, a
reimbursement, and the history of what was done to it) needs a place to be kept that survives a restart and
is never the bank's own file. This work is that place. What the person would notice if it were wrong,
later: a correction made on a purchase that vanishes when the bank replaces the pending charge with the
posted one, a reason typed in "Por quê?" that blocks taking the line change back, or one PIX accepted as the
reimbursement of two purchases.

## Outcome
Migration `0003_transactions` adds nine tables to the app's database: the index of transactions seen
(`tx_index`, `tx_ids`), each transaction's state (`tx_state`), its tags and split parts, each
establishment's row and fixed tags, and the history steps with the reasons the person gave. The seven
journaled ones are entered in the recorder's registry with their shapes; the two index tables are on the
list of tables deliberately not journaled. `internal/authored` gains one function that mints or refreshes a
transaction's index row and maps a provider id to its key inside a write's transaction, and the reads of
these tables that the authored view of a request offers. `internal/authored/authoredtest` gains builders
for every new table. No answer of the API changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database* is
`finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against it;
the server has one only when started with `--db`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave. *A provider id* is the id the bank gives a transaction; a bank-pending row and the posted row that
replaces it carry two different provider ids. *A budget line* has an integer id minted by the app's
database (table `lines`). *An establishment key* is the identity of an establishment or a person, a text
with the prefix `doc:`, `name:` or `text:` (`internal/txrules/counterpart.go`); under `doc:` it is a
document number and is never logged.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.** None of it is in the repository when this text is
written; read each in the code as that work left it.

- The app's database (finwise-9h2, through the recorder's work): `internal/authored` recognises, opens and
  migrates `finwise.db`. A migration is an SQL file embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`, recorded
  by name and checksum in `schema_migrations`; every file not recorded is applied at start in name order,
  each in one transaction, after a copy of a database that already holds data is taken beside it with
  `VACUUM INTO` (`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>`); a recorded name whose checksum differs, or one the binary
  does not have, is refused at start. Every SQL statement over the database is a registered constant: a
  test prepares each against the migrated schema and another fails on a statement that is not registered.
  Connections carry `foreign_keys(1)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`, WAL and immediate write
  transactions; reads use read-only transactions.
- The recorder, the journal and undo (finwise-wi4): the journal is `changes(id, at, day, author, method,
  extended, undone_at)` and `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`. Every change to
  an authored table goes through a recorder that works from a closed, hand-written registry. Each entry says
  which of two shapes the table has, its key columns, how a key and a row are written as canonical JSON, and
  which registered statements read and write it. An *attribute table* holds one row of independent facts
  per key and an effect is one column changing; in a *table of optional facts* every column has a default
  and a row at its defaults is the same as no row, so the first fact written about a key creates the row
  without owning it. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing and an effect is one row appearing
  or disappearing; a set row can keep its key while its other columns change, and a row with a minted id is
  restored under the same id. A table can be *owned* by another: writing an owned row is an effect on its
  own unit and on no unit of the change that made the owner, so neither undo nor extension of that change
  is refused because of it; removing the owner removes its owned rows and records them as effects of the
  same change. A statement that inserts, updates or deletes in a registered table outside the recorder fails
  a test, and every table of the schema is either registered or on the named list of tables deliberately
  not journaled, which already names `tx_index` and `tx_ids`; writes to those happen in the same
  transaction as the change they accompany and are not effects, so undoing the change leaves them.
- The write conformance harness (finwise-fst): `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds an invented, migrated
  database in a test's temporary directory from a clock handed in, one builder per group of tables, added by
  the slice that owns the tables. A builder goes through the package's own functions and the recorder and
  must not need an exemption from either guard. The canonical dump of every journaled table, taken from the
  registry, is a function of `internal/authored`; a row of a table of optional facts at its defaults is the
  same as no row in it.
- The budget's tables (finwise-ef7): migration `0002_budget` with `lines(id, builtin)` (the fees line seeded with
  a fixed id), budget versions and their lines, scenarios and closed months, in the registry; this
  migration's foreign keys to `lines` point there.
- The views handed to handlers (finwise-jzw, before the harness above): a request's authored view is one
  read-only transaction on the app's database, and each slice adds to it the reads of the tables it owns.
  Without `--db` it is an empty view that answers "nothing authored".

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

- `finwise.db` gives each transaction its own key and maps the provider's ids to it. Why: a pending row is
  replaced by a posted row under a new id; with a key of its own, carrying the person's work across is one
  mapping row instead of rewriting every table. Rejected: the provider's id as the key.
- `finwise.db` keeps a small index of the transactions it has seen (account, day, amount, establishment
  key), used for identity, guards and the rules' examples, never as the source of a figure shown or summed.
  Ledger rows and authored rows are joined in Go, by key. Rejected: `ATTACH`; copying the ledger into
  `finwise.db`; a fresh ledger handle per query.
- Every minted id comes from a column declared `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, so an id is never reused
  and a stale handle can never point at a newer object.
- Migrations are recorded by name; names are assigned in advance, one owner each. This work owns
  `0003_transactions` and no other.

**The schema: migration `0003_transactions`.** The columns are the starting point; a column this work proves
it needs may be added, in this file only. Every table declares its primary key, `NOT NULL` where a value is
required, foreign keys to `lines`, `tx_index` and `changes`, and a `CHECK` for every closed set of values and
for every amount that cannot be negative. The proof includes a test in which the database itself, with no
Go validation in the way, refuses a duplicate, an invalid value and a negative amount.

| table | columns | kind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tx_index` | `tx_key` (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`), `account_id`, `day` (`YYYY-MM-DD`, Brazil), `cents`, `establishment_key`, `bank_pending` (0 or 1), `first_run`, `last_run`, `evaluated` (0 or 1) | not journaled |
| `tx_ids` | `provider_id` (primary key), `tx_key` (references `tx_index`) | not journaled |
| `tx_state` | `tx_key` (primary key, references `tx_index`), `line_id`, `classified_by`, `confidence`, `pending_reason`, `pending_line_id`, `pending_confidence`, `ask_reason`, `note`, `exclusion`, `refund`, `refund_line_id`, `reimbursable`, `expected_cents`, `credit_tx_key` (unique, references `tx_index`), `credit_cents` | attribute table of optional facts |
| `tx_tags` | `tx_key`, `tag`, `position` | set |
| `tx_split_parts` | `tx_key`, `position`, `line_id` (nullable), `cents` (zero or more) | set; a part can keep its place and lose its line |
| `establishments` | `key` (the establishment key), `nickname`, `default_line_id` | attribute table of optional facts |
| `establishment_tags` | `key`, `tag`, `position` | set |
| `history_steps` | `id` (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`), `tx_key`, `change_id` (references `changes`), `kind` (a step or a note), `text`, `day` | set; restored under the same id |
| `history_step_reasons` | `step_id` (references `history_steps`), `reason` | set, owned by its step |

What the columns mean, as fixed already:

- `tx_state`: `line_id`, `pending_line_id` and `refund_line_id` reference `lines`. `classified_by` is who
  put the transaction on its line: the person, a rule, or the model (reserved for a later nightly call); null
  for nobody. `confidence` is the model's, a whole percent. A transaction is pending when `pending_reason`
  is set, and `pending_line_id` with `pending_confidence` is its suggestion (both may be null: a review
  without a suggestion is a state later work uses). `ask_reason` says the panel is asking "why". `note` is
  `""` by default. `exclusion` is null for "counts", empty for "switched on, no reason yet" and a text for
  the reason. `refund` is null for "as the ledger's rule says" and 0 or 1 for what the person set.
  `reimbursable` is 0 or 1. `expected_cents` is the amount the person expects back, or null when they
  cleared it. `credit_tx_key` is the credit linked to a reimbursable purchase, unique because one credit
  pays one purchase, and `credit_cents` is the credit's amount as the work that links reimbursements
  (finwise-ilt) stores it.
- A tag's `position` is the order it was added in and is never renumbered: removing a tag leaves the others
  where they were.
- `establishments.default_line_id` references `lines`; it is stored by id and belongs to no month.
- A history step's `kind` is a *step* (it records what its change did to the transaction) or a *note* (it
  records that something happened beside it). `day` is its change's Brazil day; `text` is the Portuguese
  sentence written at the time.
- The reason a person gives for a correction belongs to its step but is kept beside it, in
  `history_step_reasons`, owned by the step: giving a reason does not make the line change stale (so "apply
  to all purchases here" and the toast's "Desfazer" still work after it), and taking that change back takes
  its reason with it. The reason a transaction's detail answers is the one on its latest step that has one;
  it is stored nowhere else. A foreign key with a cascading action would delete rows the recorder never
  saw, so the owned rows are removed by the recorder, not by `ON DELETE CASCADE`.
- `first_run` and `last_run` are the collector runs in which the bank listed the row; no reader statement
  reads the collector's run yet, so they stay null until the work that brings the database up to date with
  each snapshot (finwise-82m) fills them. `evaluated` says the rules that classify new transactions have met the
  row, so they run once per transaction.

Which values `classified_by` and `kind` store, the exact keys of the set tables and how a position is
numbered are the implementer's, within the `CHECK`s and the rule that a position is never renumbered.

**The registry.** The seven journaled tables are entered with the shapes in the table: `tx_state` and
`establishments` attribute tables of optional facts; `tx_tags`, `tx_split_parts`, `establishment_tags` and
`history_steps` set tables; `history_step_reasons` a set table owned by `history_steps`. Each entry names
the registered statements that read and write it. `tx_index` and `tx_ids` stay on the list of tables not
journaled.

**The index.** `tx_index` and `tx_ids` are what the app's database remembers about the transactions it has
evaluated or the person has touched. They record observations, not decisions: they are not journaled, an
undo never removes an index row, and the index only grows. They serve four things: carrying the person's
work from a pending row to its posted replacement (the ingest, finwise-82m, maps the posted row's provider id to
the pending row's key, with no authored row rewritten); running the rules that classify new transactions
once per transaction (`evaluated`); knowing a transaction's month when a budget changes (the clearing of
lines a month lost, finwise-oib, reads the month from `tx_index.day` with no ledger read); and finding the
examples of an establishment. No amount shown or summed ever comes from the index.

This work writes the store half of the function every transaction write uses to find what it names; the
other half, which resolves a provider id in the ledger, is the merged reads' work (finwise-tsr). Given, inside a
write's transaction, a provider id and the row's current facts (account, Brazil day, cents, establishment
key, whether the bank still reports it pending), it answers the transaction's key: a provider id not in
`tx_ids` mints a new `tx_key`, writes its `tx_index` row and maps it; a known one refreshes `account_id`,
`day`, `cents`, `establishment_key` and `bank_pending` to the facts given (if the bank reworded the row the
index row takes the new key; nothing authored moves). It writes through what the recorder offers for a
table not journaled, records no effect, and does not by itself write a change's row. It leaves `evaluated`
at 0: when the rules later meet a row the person already decided they mark it and leave it alone. Which
interpreted amount `cents` holds is the caller's, as long as the ingest's pairing compares it the same way
on both sides.

**The reads the authored view gains.** Inside a request's read-only transaction, and inside a write's
transaction for a write: the key of each of a set of provider ids (absent for one never seen); for a set of
keys, their `tx_state` rows, own tags in position order, split parts in position order, and history steps
with their owned reasons and the id of the change behind each; for a set of establishment keys, their rows
and fixed tags in position order; every distinct tag in `tx_tags` and `establishment_tags`; for a credit's
key, the purchase that links it; and the Brazil day of a key from `tx_index`. Each is one registered
statement or a few, never one query per transaction of a list. On the empty authored view of a server
without `--db`, each answers nothing. Exact signatures are the implementer's; the merged reads (finwise-tsr) and
the transaction writes after it are their users.

**The builders.** `authoredtest` gains builders for every new table, through the recorder and the store
functions above, so that later tests can hold an invented state with: a line put by the person and one by
a rule; a pending review with and without a suggestion; a nickname; own and fixed tags; a note; a default
line; split parts with and without a line; an exclusion with and without a reason; a refund override and a
refund line; a reimbursable purchase with an expected amount and with a linked credit; history steps of
both kinds, with and without a reason, made by real recorded changes so that one can be overwritten by a
later change.

**Failure paths that touch this work.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the migration fails | its transaction rolls back; the copy taken before it is beside the file; `serve` exits naming the path and the reason, never the content |
| the database holds a migration the binary does not know, or a changed one | refused at start; so once `0003_transactions` has been applied to a database that matters, its file is never edited again |
| a write fails after indexing a transaction | one transaction: the index row rolls back with the change |
| a transaction disappears from the ledger | its authored rows and its index row stay; nothing is deleted |
| the bank rewords a row so its establishment key changes | the index row takes the new key; what is stored under the old establishment key stays |

**Privacy and conventions.** Nothing here needs a real ledger; every fixture is invented. A real ledger is
a person's whole financial history and this repository is public: a real snapshot may be opened read-only;
no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a
commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person running a test and goes into no file;
a test that touches a real ledger runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. The package logs
nothing. Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits,
no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer
cents and no float may appear in the money path (`internal/authored` has its float guard). Every SQL
statement over the app's database is a registered constant. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and
everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token (neither arises here).

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`): the stored values of `classified_by` and
`kind`, the keys of the set tables and the numbering of positions, within the `CHECK`s; the signatures of
the index function and of the reads; file and function names.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A database that held the journal's and the budget's tables gains the nine tables when opened; the
migration is recorded once under `0003_transactions`; opening it again applies nothing.
- [ ] From a test, directly against the migrated schema, the database refuses: a second `tx_ids` row for one
provider id; two `tx_state` rows linking the same `credit_tx_key`; the same tag twice on one transaction and
on one establishment; a split part of -1 cents; an `expected_cents` of -1; a `classified_by`, `kind`,
`refund`, `ask_reason`, `reimbursable`, `bank_pending` or `evaluated` value outside its set; a `line_id`,
`pending_line_id`, `refund_line_id`, split part line or `default_line_id` not in `lines`; a `tx_state`,
`tx_tags`, `tx_split_parts` or `history_steps` row whose `tx_key` is not in `tx_index`; a step whose
`change_id` is not in `changes`; a reason whose step does not exist.
- [ ] The seven journaled tables are in the recorder's registry with the shapes above,
`history_step_reasons` owned by `history_steps`; `tx_index` and `tx_ids` are on the list of tables not
journaled; the test that every table is classified passes, and fails when one entry is removed.
- [ ] The index function, for a provider id never seen, mints one `tx_key`, writes one `tx_index` row with
the facts given and `evaluated` 0, and one `tx_ids` row, and adds no row to `changes` or `change_effects`;
called again it mints nothing; called with a new day and a new establishment key it refreshes both on the
same key; two provider ids can map to one key.
- [ ] A recorded change that indexes a transaction and then fails leaves `tx_index` and `tx_ids` as they
were; one that commits keeps the index row, and `changes.undo` of it leaves the index row in place.
- [ ] A reason written for a step by a later change does not make the step's change stale: undoing that
change still succeeds and removes the step and the reason, and the canonical dump returns to the one taken
before it.
- [ ] Each read of the authored view answers, over a state built with the new builders, exactly what the
builders wrote, own tags and fixed tags in position order across a removal and its undo (add `#a`, `#b`,
`#c`, remove `#b`, undo: `#a`, `#b`, `#c`); on the empty view each answers nothing.
- [ ] Every new statement is a registered constant prepared against the migrated schema; no file of the
package uses a float; no file outside `internal/authored/` changes; `0001_journal.sql` and `0002_budget.sql`
are byte-identical to what they were.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the report: one `CHECK`
and one uniqueness rule of the migration dropped; the reason table left out of the owner relation (taking
the change back then leaves the reason, or giving a reason makes it stale); the index write recorded as an
effect; the index row minted twice for one provider id; a position renumbered on removal; a table left out
of both lists.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the migration refuses its invalid rows by itself, and a
transaction indexed inside a recorded change keeps one key for every provider id mapped to it.

## Tests
- Unit, over a temporary migrated database: the schema's refusals of a duplicate, an invalid value, a
  negative amount and a broken reference, with no Go validation in the way.
- Unit: the index function (mint, refresh, map a second id, no effect, rollback with a failed change, kept
  by an undo).
- Unit: the owned reasons against undo and extension of the step's change.
- Unit: each read of the authored view against the builders' state, and on the empty view.
- Unit, guards: every table classified; every statement registered and prepared; no write to a registered
  table outside the recorder; the float scan.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/migrations/`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/migrations/0001_journal.sql`, `internal/authored/migrations/0002_budget.sql`,
`internal/txrules/counterpart.go`, `web/src/api/fake/model.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/history.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/transaction-edits.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`,
`web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`, `bin/ci`

One migration; in `internal/authored`, the store of the nine tables in two or three files, their registry
entries and statements, the index function and the reads the authored view gains; one builder file in
`authoredtest`. `size:L` because it is a schema change. `internal/api` is not touched: nothing reads these
tables until the merged reads (finwise-tsr). The difficulty is `critical` because the transaction's identity and
the ownership of its reasons decide whether the person's work survives a pending charge being posted and
whether an undo can be taken.

## Recovery path
The migration only adds tables. If it fails, its transaction rolls back and the server exits; when the
database already held data, the copy the migration runner took before migrating is beside it
(`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>`). To go back: stop the server; check the copy (`PRAGMA integrity_check`, the
application id); put it in place of the database with no `-wal` or `-shm` file beside it; start a binary
that does not carry this migration, since a database that holds a migration the binary does not know is
refused at start. Once the migration has been applied to a database that matters its file is frozen; a
correction is a new migration, never an edit.

The database itself refuses every invalid row; IndexTransaction and AddHistoryStep on the recorder, the reads on the view; authoredtest builders and seed. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main (list conflicts with the pots and settings work resolved). title: Answer each request from one snapshot of the ledger and one of the app's database, and require the clock
description:
## What changes for the user
The app builds a screen by asking the bank's records several questions, one after another, and a separate
collector replaces those records every night. A screen opened at the moment of the replacement can be put
together half from yesterday's records and half from today's: a total that does not match the rows under
it, with nothing on screen saying so. After this lands a screen is always built from one state of the
records, the one that was there when it was asked for, and the next screen sees the new one. Nothing else
changes: every figure and every sentence the app shows today stays the same. It is also the ground the
rest of the work on saving stands on, because once the app keeps what the person types (a budget, a
category, a note) each screen has to show the bank's records and the person's own entries as they were at
one same moment. If this were wrong the person would see, for one refresh around the nightly update or
while another tab is saving, a figure that disagrees with its own breakdown, or a screen that fails to
open.

## Outcome
Every read handler of the HTTP backend receives, as its third parameter, one value that carries a view of
each store, opened for that request: the ledger's view (one handle and one read-only transaction on the
snapshot) and a view of the app's own database that is one read-only transaction, or an empty view that
answers nothing when the server runs without that database. No file of `internal/api` or of `cmd/finwise`
calls a query method of the reader any more, tests included: the queries are reached through the view. The
reader's own wrappers stay in place after this slice; removing them, and moving the tests of
`internal/ledger`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and `internal/txrules` onto the view, is the next
piece of work (finwise-qet: it deletes the reader's thirteen query methods, which only tests still call, and
makes those four packages' tests open a view instead). The clock is a required part of the API's configuration, supplied by
`cmd/finwise` alone; asking for "now" without one panics, and a source test keeps `time.Now` out of the
HTTP layer and of the packages that hold rules. No answer changes: every golden file is byte for byte
what it was.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite file,
`pluggy-snapshot.db`, that a separate collector (pluggy-sync) fills from the banks every night and
replaces by an atomic rename; the app only reads it, and "the snapshot" below is that file. *The ledger's
view* is delivered by finwise-gn5: a type of `internal/ledger` that is one handle and one read-only
transaction on the snapshot, on which each of the 13 query methods can run, so that all the queries made
through one view see one snapshot; that slice kept the reader's own 13 methods as wrappers that open a
view per call, twelve of them in one file of their own and `PotYields` in `pot_yield.go`. *The app's
database* is `finwise.db`, a second SQLite file that will hold what the person authors; unlike the
snapshot nobody swaps it, so it is opened once and kept open for the life of the process. It is owned by
the package `internal/authored`, delivered by finwise-9h2 (recognising the file, opening it with its
connection settings, the migrations table and runner, the first migration with the tables of the journal
that will record every change, the tracking start month, which is the month the database was first
created in and is kept as one value of the table `meta`, the registry of SQL statements, and the `--db`
/ `FINWISE_DB` setting of `finwise serve`). Without `--db` the server is today's read-only server. *The
manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated description of the 82 methods of the API,
of which 23 are of class `read`. A *read handler* is the Go function that answers one read method. The
*golden files* under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` and `empty/` (59 files each) are the exact
answers of every read over two invented ledgers, compared byte for byte by
`TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile`.

**What the code is today (each point checked in the file named; the ledger's view is the one thing
described from the slice that delivers it).**

- `internal/api/reads.go`: `ReadHandler` is `func(ctx context.Context, args []json.RawMessage, reader
  *ledger.Reader) (any, error)`. `Registry.Register` panics on a duplicate. `domainRegistrations` lists
  twelve `register<Domain>` functions that together make 23 registrations (22 functions:
  `subscriptions.candidates` and `subscriptions.recurring` share `readNothingListed`).
- `internal/api/router.go`: `serveRead` calls `handler(withNow(r.Context(), found.now), arguments,
  found.reader)`. `Config.Ledger` is a `*ledger.Reader`; `Config` has no field for the app's database.
  `withDefaults` sets `config.Now = time.Now` when the `Config` has none.
- A handler makes several calls to the reader, each of which opens the snapshot anew, so it can see two
  snapshots across the swap. `readShellOverview` (`shell.go`) calls `Accounts`, `SyncState` and
  `CleanTransactions`; `readSettingsOverview` (`settings.go`) calls `loadCard`, `loadPots` and
  `SyncState`. A handler that answers a fixed value still asks the ledger one question first,
  `requireReadableLedger` in `fresh_install.go`, so that it never answers over a snapshot that is gone.
  A handler that takes arguments checks them before its first ledger call.
- `internal/api/now.go`: `withNow` puts the clock function in the context and `nowOf` calls it; when the
  context has none, `nowOf` returns `time.Now()`. `nowOf` is called in `accounts.go`, `shell.go`,
  `card.go`, `pots_model.go` and `settings.go`. `cmd/finwise/serve.go` builds its `api.Config` without a
  clock, so the server's clock today is the default in `withDefaults`.
- `internal/api/errors.go`: `kindOfReadError` answers `ledger_unavailable` for a missing file
  (`fs.ErrNotExist`), an unreadable one (`fs.ErrPermission`, `ledger.IsUnreadableSnapshot`) and an
  unsupported version; anything else is `internal`. `internal/api/logging.go` recovers a handler's panic
  and answers `internal`.
- The reader's methods are called, outside `internal/api`, only by tests: 8 test files of
  `internal/ledger`, and `internal/cardrules/forecast_test.go`, `internal/cardrules/realsnapshot_test.go`,
  `internal/potrules/realsnapshot_test.go` and `internal/txrules/realsnapshot_test.go`.

**What changes.**

1. *One value per request.* The third parameter of a handler becomes one value carrying a view of each
   store, opened for the request. The router builds it for each read and closes it when the handler has
   returned, on every path: an answer, an error, a panic. Every ledger query of the request runs on the
   request's one ledger view, so it sees the same snapshot even when the collector swaps the file
   meanwhile.
2. *The authored view.* For the app's database a handler never holds the connection pool. The router
   opens one read-only transaction per read (and, once evaluations are dispatched, per evaluation) and
   hands the handler a view of it, so an answer is wholly before or wholly after a concurrent write. A
   write handler will instead receive the recorder, the layer through which every change to the app's
   database is written and journaled (finwise-wi4); wiring that in is the write dispatch (finwise-2s5: the router
   running a handler for a write inside one transaction and one recorded change), not this slice.
   Without `--db` the authored view is an empty one that answers nothing, so read code has one path: no
   handler ever asks whether a database is configured. This is the standing rule for every read method a
   later slice adds to the view: on the empty view it answers "nothing authored", the contract's empty
   value. `Config` gains the app's database and `cmd/finwise/serve.go` passes the one it opened.
3. *The signature change.* All 23 registrations change signature in one commit that lands alone.
4. *The reader's wrappers stay.* With no handler left on the reader, its 13 wrappers have no caller in
   `internal/api` or `cmd/finwise`; the tests of `internal/api` that called them (the opt-in real-ledger
   tests, `pots_yield_reference_test.go`, `review_payday_test.go` and the test helpers) open a view instead.
   The wrappers themselves are not touched here: the wrapper file, the reader's `PotYields` in
   `pot_yield.go` and the tests of the four packages outside `internal/api` that still call them are the
   next piece of work (finwise-qet), so no file of `internal/ledger`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules`
   or `internal/txrules` is edited by this slice.
5. *The clock.* "Today" and "the current month" are the Brazil day and month of the instant in the
   request's context. The clock is a required part of the API's configuration: building the handler
   without one fails at once, and only `cmd/finwise` supplies the host's clock. The router always
   installs it; `nowOf` without one panics instead of reading the host's clock; and a source test forbids
   `time.Now` in the non-test files of `internal/api`, `internal/ingest` and the rule packages
   `internal/budgetrules`, `internal/classrules` and `internal/subrules`.

**What is left to the implementer, and what constrains each choice.**

- *Names.* The per-request value and the authored view are named by the implementer. `Registry.Register`
  and `domainRegistrations` keep their names: the repository's `AGENTS.md` documents them.
- *When the snapshot is opened.* Whether the request's ledger view touches the file when the request
  starts or at the handler's first query is the implementer's. Three things constrain it. A request must
  see one snapshot for all its queries. A handler that asks the ledger nothing must not fail because the
  snapshot is missing: the write side needs this (undoing a change touches no snapshot, and a write
  answers `ledger_unavailable` only when the snapshot it needs is missing), and the router's own tests
  already run handlers on a `Config` with no ledger at all (`newTestEnv` in `helpers_test.go`,
  `withRead`, `returnsNothing`). And no existing answer may change: a missing or unreadable snapshot is
  still `ledger_unavailable` through `kindOfReadError`, and malformed arguments are still `bad_request`.
- *What the authored view can read.* The read methods of the authored view are added by the slices that
  own each group of tables. When this lands the only table with content is `meta`, so the view needs
  just enough to make its own proof observable: one read of a value another connection can change. The
  tracking start month is the natural one; which value it is stays the implementer's.
- *One instant or one clock per request.* Today the context carries the clock function and `nowOf` calls
  it on every use. Reading the clock once per request, so a request cannot see two days around midnight,
  is consistent with the rule in point 5 and is the implementer's to adopt. What is required is the
  failure at construction, the panic and the source test.
- *The packages that do not exist yet.* `internal/ingest` and the three rule packages are created by
  later slices. The source test must already name them, so each is covered from its first file without
  anyone editing the test. How a directory that is not there yet is treated is the implementer's, but a
  missing directory must not fail the gate and a present one must not be skipped. The three rule packages
  that exist (`internal/txrules`, `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules`) name no `time.Now` today and
  may be added to the list at no cost; that is allowed, not required.

**What follows from the code and is not optional.**

- The `time.Now` default in `withDefaults` (`router.go`) goes: the source test has no exemption inside
  `internal/api`. `NewHandler` returns an error for a `Config` with no clock, as it already does for one
  with no PIN verifier, and `cmd/finwise/serve.go` hands in the host's clock; if `cmd/finwise` already
  carries a clock of its own for creating the app's database, it is that same one.
  `TestAHandlerCannotBeRegisteredForAWrite` and `TestNewHandlerNeedsAPINVerifier` (`router_test.go`)
  build a `Config` without `Now`: give them a clock, or they will keep passing for the wrong reason.
- `PotYields`, the collector's slow reference statement, stays in `internal/ledger/pot_yield.go`, the
  reader's wrapper beside the view's method: `internal/api/pots_yield_guard_test.go` scans every package for
  that name and exempts that file and `queries.go` by path. This slice adds no other mention of it in a
  non-test file, and the tests of `internal/api` that read yields (`pots_yield_reference_test.go`, the
  opt-in `pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go` and `pots_yield_months_realsnapshot_test.go`) are test files,
  which that scan does not read.
- The tests of `internal/ledger` (among them `TestEachCallSeesTheFileThatIsThereNow`, which is true only
  while the wrappers open the file on every call), of `internal/cardrules`, `internal/potrules` and
  `internal/txrules` are not edited here and keep passing, because the wrappers still answer as before.
- `TestAReadHandlerGetsTheContextTheArgumentsAndTheReader` (`router_test.go`) asserts the old third
  parameter and is rewritten to assert the new one. Every hand-written handler in `router_test.go`,
  `logging_test.go` and `helpers_test.go` changes signature with the rest.
- Test code that calls a helper directly (`loadPots`, `loadCard`, `loadContext`) must pass a context with
  a clock, as `card_test.go` and `net_worth_test.go` already do with `withNow`. The opt-in tests that
  read a real ledger are skipped in the gate, so a bare context there would panic only when someone runs
  them: check those by reading.
- `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go` allows only `logging.go` and `router.go` to name a logging
  package. Any new file of `internal/api` logs nothing.
- The per-request value and the handler signature carry no `net/http` type: a later command-line client
  is expected to call the handlers as plain functions, outside HTTP.
- The recorder (finwise-wi4) is being built in `internal/authored` at the same time as this slice. Keep this
  slice's additions to that package in a file of their own, so the two do not edit the same lines.

**Why it is done this way, and what lost.** Ledger rows and authored rows are joined in Go, by key,
inside one request that sees one snapshot of each store, because the reader hands out rows, never a
connection, and the snapshot is swapped under it. Three alternatives lost: attaching the snapshot to the
app's database connection with `ATTACH`; copying the ledger into `finwise.db`; and a fresh ledger handle
per query, which is what the handlers do today and is exactly what lets one answer mix two snapshots. The
app's database is not reopened per call because, unlike the snapshot, nobody swaps it.

**The failure path this slice owns.** The snapshot is swapped during a request: the request finishes on
the snapshot it opened, and the next one sees the new one. Its named proof: a request that pauses
between two ledger queries while the snapshot is swapped answers wholly from the first snapshot.

**Why the signature change is one commit.** The package compiles only when the handler type, the
registry, the router's call and every handler agree, and the proof of this slice is that no golden file
changes. A commit that holds only the mechanical change can be reviewed by that one property.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. This slice
edits the plumbing of the opt-in tests of `internal/api` that read a real ledger (`realsnapshot_test.go`,
`realsnapshot_money_test.go`, `fresh_install_realsnapshot_test.go`, `pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go` and
`pots_yield_months_realsnapshot_test.go`), so the rule applies in full: a real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document,
id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown
to the person running the test and goes into no file; those tests run only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Fixtures are invented, and no `.db` file is opened by hand.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path. Every SQL statement over the
app's database is a registered constant, as every statement over the ledger already is. Interface text is
Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from a token
(this slice touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The third parameter of every registered handler is the per-request value;
`command grep -l "ledger\.Reader" internal/api/*.go` lists, among non-test files, at most `router.go`
and the file that opens the views.
- [ ] Nothing in `internal/api` or `cmd/finwise`, test files included, calls a query method of the
reader: with the reader's wrappers temporarily removed in a scratch copy (the wrapper file moved aside and
the reader's `PotYields` deleted from `pot_yield.go`), `go vet ./internal/api/... ./cmd/...` still
compiles; the repository's own tree keeps the wrappers.
- [ ] HTTP level: a test handler that makes two ledger queries with a second invented snapshot renamed
over the path between them answers wholly from the first snapshot, and the next request answers from the
second.
- [ ] Authored level: a test handler that reads the app's database twice, with another connection
committing a change to what it reads between the two, gets the same value both times; the next request
gets the new value.
- [ ] With no app database configured the handler receives the empty authored view and every existing
test passes; no handler branches on whether a database is configured.
- [ ] `git diff --stat main -- internal/api/testdata` is empty, and `TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile`
passes without `-update`.
- [ ] A handler that asks the ledger nothing is answered normally when the snapshot file is missing; a
handler that asks it something is answered 503 `ledger_unavailable`, and
`TestEveryReadAnswersLedgerUnavailableForAFileThatIsNotADatabase` passes unchanged.
- [ ] After a request ends (answered, failed or panicked) the ledger handle it opened is closed and the
app database's connection is back in its pool: a test shows it for the three endings.
- [ ] The commit that changes the handler signature holds all 23 registrations, the handler type, the
router's call and the hand-written test handlers, and nothing that the package does not need to compile
and pass at that commit; `go build ./... && go test ./...` is green at that commit.
- [ ] `NewHandler` returns an error for a `Config` with no clock; `cmd/finwise/serve.go` passes the
host's clock and the app's database; `nowOf` on a context with no clock panics, and a test recovers the
panic.
- [ ] A source test fails for a `time.Now` in any non-test file of `internal/api`, `internal/ingest`,
