establishment's default line lists what was answered for the current month, and the other three what
was answered for the transaction's month; the panel asks for no month but those two.
- [ ] Right after the panel opens on a transaction, its line menu lists that month's lines and is not
empty over the prototype's dataset.
- [ ] After a revision bump with a transaction open, the panel asks again for the months it holds, and
its line menus and its menu of fixed tags show the new answer without the panel being reopened.
- [ ] A weekly queue whose items fall in two months has asked for both by the time each item has been
shown, and for no other month; each item's "Escolher outra linha" lists what was answered for that
item's month; after a revision bump the months still in the queue are asked again; with an empty queue
the tab makes no `filterOptions` call.
- [ ] The subscription screen asks for the current month while the screen's selected month is another
one, and asks again after a revision bump, its line menu then showing the new answer.
- [ ] Both menus of the settings screen, an establishment's default line and the lines linked to a
pot, ask for the current month while the selected month is another one.
- [ ] `POST /api/transactions/filterOptions` with a session answers 400 `bad_request` for `[]` and for
`["2026-13"]`, and 200 for `["2026-03"]` with the same body as before over both invented ledgers.
- [ ] `readCases` holds `transactions.filterOptions` with `["2026-03"]`; the two golden files are
renamed to `transactions.filterOptions.2026-03.json` with unchanged content (`git show -M --stat` of
the commit shows two renames and no changed line in them), and no other golden file changes.
- [ ] `TestArgumentBoundsFollowTheSchema` in `internal/contract/contract_test.go` asserts the bounds
1 and 1 for `transactions.filterOptions`.
- [ ] `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` are green with `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` unset, and the call
in `internal/api/realsnapshot_test.go` sends a month.
- [ ] `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` and `web/src/test/replay-sweep.test.ts` pass, the sweep with
no unrecorded call.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` exits 0 and its summary line reads `0 over 0.05%`: every screen
that opens a line menu (the transaction list and panel, the weekly review, a subscription, the
settings) and the budget screens still measure as the design, including the three states that open a
line menu, `inicio-menu-linha`, `inicio-linha-alterada` and `revisao-linha-escolhida`.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the report of the
work: `rename` made to rebuild the line from name and amount; `add` made to copy the id of the line
above; `cleanDraft` left dropping the id; the panel made to send the screen's selected month; the
panel's default-line menu drawn from the transaction's month; the panel and the subscription screen
left loading once; the queue made to send one month for every item; the settings made to send the
selected month; the list's filter left listing the menu alone; the month parsing removed from the Go
handler.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`

title: Editing the budget against a read-only backend asks the same refused question forever
description:
## What changes for the user
Against the real backend, which only reads for now, pressing "Editar budget" makes the app ask the server the same refused question about twenty-five times a second, without end, with the read-only message stuck on screen. Opening "Cenários" shows the read-only message before the person has done anything, and the screen stays blank where the scenario's impact should be. After this lands, pressing "Editar budget" shows the read-only message once and leaves the budget as it was, and opening "Cenários" does the same and returns to the budget.

## Outcome
A refused evaluation of a budget draft or of a scenario ends the editing surface that asked for it, with one read-only toast and no further request.

## Context
finwise's interface runs against a backend that is read-only for now. Every write and every evaluation of the contract answers a `read_only` error, and one function (`web/src/api/failures.ts`) turns that into a toast ("Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.") and a bump of the revision counter, so that every screen fetches again and none keeps showing a state the server refused. No call site catches errors itself, on purpose.

Two screens ask for an evaluation, which is refused like a write because the budget's arithmetic is not built on the server yet:

- `web/src/screens/budget/BudgetScreen.vue` watches the selected month, the revision counter and the budget draft together, and calls `api.budget.view(month, draft)` whenever one of them changes. In edit mode the draft is set, so the call is refused; the refusal bumps the revision counter; the watcher fires again with the same draft; and so on, forever. Measured in Chromium against the built backend over a real ledger: 127 refused calls in five seconds, still going.
- `web/src/screens/budget/ScenariosScreen.vue` calls `api.budget.evaluateScenario` as soon as it opens. That is refused once, the toast shows although the person only opened a screen, and the impact never arrives.

The decision taken for both, to be confirmed by the user: an editing surface that cannot evaluate ends itself. The budget leaves edit mode, discarding the draft it was just handed, and shows its read view again. The scenarios screen returns to the budget. Each shows the read-only toast exactly once. This follows the choice made for the read-only backend as a whole, that a refused change is one toast and the screen as it was, and adds no "unavailable" state of its own.

The fix belongs in the two screens: each recognises the `read_only` refusal of its own evaluation, ends itself, and lets the error go on to the central function, which shows the toast. The central function is not changed, and an error that is not `read_only` is not caught.

Tests already exist for refusals through mounted screens (`web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`, with `web/src/test/readOnly.ts` wrapping the stand-in so that every write and evaluation is refused as the backend refuses it). The sweep over the backend's recorded answers (`web/src/test/replay-sweep.test.ts`) tolerates a `read_only` refusal on the scenarios route because of this defect; once the scenarios screen no longer stays on a refused evaluation, that tolerance is removed.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Mount the Budget screen on the stand-in wrapped by the read-only helper and press "Editar budget".
2. Observed: `budget.view` is called with the draft again and again, each call refused, and the toast is shown each time.
3. Expected: one refused call, one toast, the screen out of edit mode, and no further call with a draft.
4. Mount the scenarios screen on the same stand-in.
5. Observed: one refused `budget.evaluateScenario`, a toast, and no impact on screen.
6. Expected: one refused call, one toast, and the route back at the budget.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After "Editar budget" over the read-only stand-in, `budget.view` is called with a draft exactly once, the read-only toast is shown exactly once, the screen is out of edit mode, and no call with a draft follows within the next ten bumps of the revision counter.
- [ ] After opening the scenarios screen over the read-only stand-in, `budget.evaluateScenario` is called exactly once, the read-only toast is shown exactly once, and the current route is the budget.
- [ ] Over the plain stand-in, editing the budget and opening the scenarios screen behave as before, and `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] An evaluation that fails with an error other than `read_only` does not end edit mode and still reaches the central function.
- [ ] The sweep over the backend's recorded answers no longer tolerates a refusal on any route.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, parity is unchanged, and both regression tests fail when their fix is removed.

## Tests
- Component, regression: a refused evaluation through the mounted Budget screen ends edit mode with one call and one toast.
- Component, regression: a refused evaluation through the mounted scenarios screen returns to the budget with one call and one toast.
- Component: another kind of failure does not end edit mode.
- Component: the sweep over the recorded answers, with its tolerance removed.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/screens/budget/BudgetScreen.vue`, `web/src/screens/budget/ScenariosScreen.vue`, `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/test/replay-sweep.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `web/src/stores/`, `bin/ci`

Two screens each learn to end themselves on a refused evaluation, with a regression test each, and one tolerance leaves the sweep.
close_reason: BudgetScreen.vue discards the draft when the evaluation of a draft is refused, and ScenariosScreen.vue returns to the budget when its evaluation is refused; both rethrow, so the central function still shows the one toast and no other kind of error is caught. Regression tests through the mounted screens over the read-only stand-in: before the fix the budget made 71 calls with a draft where one was expected and the scenarios screen stayed on its route; both fail again with their fix removed. The replay sweep no longer tolerates a refused call on any route; it answers the one scenario evaluation from the stand-in so that screen is swept drawn. bin/ci: CI green, 934 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%; no template changed.

title: Show the history of answered proposals, each approved one with its undo
description:
## What changes for the user
An assistant on the command line can propose changes to the person's finance data, and the person answers
each one in the app with a yes or a no. Once answered, a proposal leaves the screen. If the person later
wants to see what they approved last week, why they refused something, or to take back a change they
approved days ago, there is nowhere to look: only the change made last can be undone from a screen. After
this lands, the weekly review has a list of the proposals already answered, each saying what it changed,
who proposed it, when it was answered and how, and an approved one can be taken back from there while
nothing later depends on it.

## Outcome
A screen lists the answered proposals, newest first: approved, refused (with the reason the person gave,
when they gave one) and stale. An approved proposal shows the change it made and offers its undo; an undo
the journal refuses says so with the sentence the app already has for it.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person, over a ledger snapshot a separate collector
fills from the banks; what the person authors is kept in the app's own database. *A proposal* is a change an
agent asked for through a command line: a method of the app's API, its arguments and a reason the agent
wrote. An agent never writes directly; the app applies a proposal when the person approves it. A proposal
for the budget line of a transaction still pending shows in the weekly review's queue as a suggestion; every
other one shows on the approvals card of the weekly review, with a view of the values before and after.
*Answered* means approved, refused, or stale: approved after what it would change had changed, so that the
usual refusal was answered and the proposal was closed. *The journal* records every change to what the
person authored, so that it can be undone.

**Why it was left out of the first version.** Decided by the person on 2026-11-23: the first version of
proposals has no history. The agent reads the outcome of its own proposals through its command, and the
person undoes a change right after approving it, with the toast every write has. Whether a history is
missed is only known with use; this item exists so that the screen is not forgotten.

**What it waits for.** The storage of proposals, the approvals card's backing and the difference view do
not exist yet. They are specified by `finwise-th6` and built by the items written from it. This item was
written before them, so the names of the table, of the read and of the screen's parts are not known:
whoever picks it up reads those items first and restates the criteria and the blast radius below against
what was built.

**What exists that it will use.** `changes.undo` (`internal/api/changes.go`) undoes a change by its id,
whichever it is, and answers the refusal `stale_change` when the journal refuses (`internal/authored/undo.go`);
the sentence the person reads for it is "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito."
(`REFUSAL_SENTENCES` in `web/src/api/failures.ts`). The interface offers undo only for the change made last,
and no read of the API lists changes. The weekly review is `web/src/screens/revisao/WeeklyTab.vue`, with
`ApprovalsCard.vue` for the proposals that wait.

**Design.** The interface is ported from an HTML prototype (`design/README.md` says how), and the prototype
has no screen for this list. A design for it is needed before the screen is built, and it is the person's
to give or to approve.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A read of the contract answers the answered proposals, newest first, each with: what it proposed, in
the app's own words; the name its proposer gave; the reason the proposer wrote; the instant it was answered;
how (approved, refused, stale); the reason of a refusal when the person gave one; and, for an approved one,
the id of the change it made and whether that change can still be undone.
- [ ] The read answers an empty list, not an error, over a database that holds no proposal and for a server
without a database of its own.
- [ ] A proposal still waiting for its answer is not in the list.
- [ ] The screen lists them as designed and says in a sentence when there is none.
- [ ] The undo of an approved proposal calls `changes.undo` with its change; when the journal refuses, the
person reads the sentence for a stale change and the list is fetched again.
- [ ] The read has a case in the conformance suite, with a golden file over an invented authored state that
holds one proposal of each outcome, and the stand-in backend answers the same shape.
- [ ] The design parity passes for the new states on both viewports, with no limit raised.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: the person can open the weekly review, see what they answered and take back an approved
proposal from there.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/authored`: the listing over proposals of each outcome, newest first; a waiting one left
out.
- Integration, in `internal/api`: the read through the router; the undo of a listed change, accepted and
refused.
- Golden: one new file for the read over the invented authored state; none of the existing ones moves.
- Screen, in `web/src`: the list, the sentence for none, the undo and its refusal, over the stand-in backend.
- Parity: the new states on both viewports.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/review.ts`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/api/fake/`,
`web/src/screens/revisao/`, `internal/api/review_approvals.go`, `internal/authored/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `web/scripts/parity/states.mjs`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/changes.go`, `internal/authored/undo.go`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`,
`design/README.md`, `bin/ci`

One read, its statement in the store, one screen and its states. No write is added: the undo is the one
that exists. The file names are today's; the items written from `finwise-th6` decide where proposals live,
and this radius is restated against them before work starts.

title: Stop reading and interpreting the whole ledger on every call once its cost is measured to matter
description:
## What changes for the user
The app answers every screen by reading the bank's records from the start and working out what each row
means, each time. With the history the person has today that is fast enough that nobody waits; as the
history grows (a new month of purchases every month, for years) the time to open a screen, to save a budget
or to see a budget change while typing grows with it. After this lands, a screen opens as fast in the tenth
year as in the first, and a budget being typed answers as the person types. If it were wrong the person would
see it as a slowness that creeps in unnoticed, or, worse, as a speed-up that shows a number that no longer
matches the ledger.

## Outcome
This is a tracking bead. It holds the subject so it is not lost and tells whoever picks it up what was
decided, why it waits, what it will need from the write side and what must be decided first. It is not ready
to implement and should not be started until a measurement says it matters. It is finished when the
timings the write side's review took are written here, the person has said what is slow enough to matter,
and either this bead is closed as "not yet" with the date it is looked at again, or the implementation beads
exist, each written whole and depending on the write side being complete.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database*
(`finwise.db`) holds what the person authors. *Interpreting* a ledger is what `internal/txrules` does with
the collector's rows: it folds tax rows under their purchases, takes the movements of savings pots out,
marks movements between own accounts, bill payments, fees, refunds and unconverted amounts, and builds the
establishment key. *A snapshot swap* is the collector replacing the ledger file overnight.

**What was decided.** The cost of reading the whole ledger on every call is acceptable today and grows with
history, so it is deferred. The write side takes the timing of one write and of one draft evaluation on a
real snapshot, measured by the reviewer, in the reviews of the budget's arithmetic and of the transaction
writes, and that timing is what this bead waits for. (The plan states as its only open question the time of
one write and of one draft evaluation on the real snapshot.)

**Where the cost is, in the code as the write side leaves it:**

- *The ledger is reopened read-only on every call*: a handler gets a view with one handle and one read-only
  transaction on the snapshot, so every ledger query of a request sees one snapshot even if the collector
  swaps the file meanwhile. The reader opens the file per request; it is held nowhere.
- *Operations that span months interpret the whole ledger in one pass*: "all purchases here"
  (`transactions.applyLineToEstablishment`), the reimbursement candidates, and the card's own read, which
  also reach transactions older than the tracking start that were never indexed. A write resolves the
  transactions it names through the same interpreted read the lists use; the detail of one transaction
  interprets one month around it.
- *The count of what waits for review, on every screen* (added 2026-11-23, after the weekly queue landed):
  the frame of every screen and the home ask how many transactions wait for the person's review
  (`pendingCount` in `internal/api/pending.go`, answered by `shell.overview` and `home.summary`), and
  `pendingTransactions` there interprets the whole ledger whenever at least one review is kept, to leave
  out a review whose transaction the ledger no longer lists. It reads no ledger when no review is kept.
  It is one more cost to time with the others, on a database that has a review waiting.
- *The budget's arithmetic runs on the server*: the budget view sums a month's transactions into dispositions
  for every call, and the budget's edit mode and the scenarios screen call the evaluation on each change of
  the draft; those calls are not debounced today, and the plan adds a debounce only if the measured answer is
  slow enough to matter.
- *The index in the app's database* (`tx_index`) records observations to find a transaction's month, examples
  for the rules and its identity; it is never the source of any figure the screens show or sum. Using it to
  avoid reading the ledger would break that rule, and is therefore a decision, not an optimisation.
- *What the write side rejected, and why*, so it is not proposed again without the reasons: `ATTACH`ing the
  ledger to the app's database; copying the ledger into the app's database; opening a fresh ledger handle per
  query. The reason recorded for all three is that the reader hands out rows, never a connection, and the
  snapshot is swapped under it.

**Measuring, and what a measurement may say.** A real ledger is a person's whole financial history and this
repository is public. A real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name,
document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be
shown to the person running the test and goes into no file; the test runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Fixtures are invented. A duration is not a value of the ledger, but
the size of the ledger is: a timing is recorded alone, never beside a row count or a number of months.

**What an implementer must respect**: money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; a
cache must never show a figure that disagrees with the ledger the request opened, including across a swap;
every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant; every optimisation is proved by the
same checks that prove the thing it speeds up (golden files unchanged, the two invariants of the budget's
dispositions, the equality of the stand-in's answers over an empty ledger).

**Measured on 2026-11-23.** The write side's reviews had recorded no time per call, so the times were
taken that day: inside the server, over a real ledger, with a scratch database that held a budget and a
series of writes, on one desktop machine. Durations only.

| call | time |
| --- | --- |
| `review.closing` | 589 ms |
| `home.summary` | 575 ms |
| `review.weekly` | 474 ms |
| `settings.overview` | 386 ms |
| `savingsPots.list` | 339 ms |
| `netWorth.overview` | 327 ms |
| `budget.view` | 284 ms |
| `review.payday` | 195 ms |
| `transactions.detail` | 181 ms |
| `transactions.list`, one month | 180 ms |
| `card.overview` | 178 ms |
| `shell.overview`, asked on every screen | 177 ms |
| a write that looks a transaction up | 80 to 90 ms |
| `budget.save` | about 120 ms |
| `budget.evaluateScenario`, the draft | under 1 ms |
| one run of the ingest | well under half a second |

One reading of every transaction row took about 85 ms and interpreting the whole ledger on top of it 5 to
15 ms: the cost is the reading. The slow reads repeat it, up to six times in one answer. The pots list and
the net worth read the rows once and spend their time in the pots' yield history, which makes three passes
of its own.

## What must be decided first
Answered by the person on 2026-11-23.

1. **What is slow enough to matter.** A screen's read above 200 ms inside the server, and a write above
   150 ms, on the ledger and the machine of the measurement above. By that, seven reads are slow today, no
   write is, and neither the draft evaluation nor the ingest is. It is looked at again when the review of
   the first implementation item measures the same calls.
2. **What the review's timings were.** None per call had been recorded; the table above is the measurement.
3. **Which of the options is acceptable.** Removing the repetition, and only that: one reading of the
   ledger's rows per request, shared by every part of the answer, with nothing kept from one request to the
   next. Keeping the interpreted ledger in memory between requests is held back and decided only if a screen
   stays above 200 ms afterwards: it has to be invalidated when the snapshot is replaced, and what it can
   get wrong is a figure that disagrees with the ledger. Not taken: a debounce on the draft (the draft is
   not a cost on the server); interpreting incrementally; a cache in the app's database, since the index is
   never the source of a figure.
4. **How a cache is invalidated.** There is none to invalidate: nothing outlives a request.
5. **How it is verified.** No golden file moves and the conformance suites pass unchanged, which is the
   proof that every answer is the same; the times are taken again over a real ledger by the review, not by
   the implementer, and written as durations alone.

**The implementation items:** `finwise-vfw`, one reading of the rows per request; `finwise-c6t`, the pots'
yield history in one pass, for the two reads the first does not help, written with what is still to be
found out about its three readings.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The timings the write side's reviews took are written here, alone (no row count, no number of months),
and the person has answered item 1.
- [ ] Either this bead is closed as "not yet" with the date to look again, or every remaining item of "What
must be decided first" has an answer and the implementation beads exist, each written to the standard
(self-contained, checkable criteria) and depending on the write side's last piece.
- [ ] This bead changes no code: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` before and after, and no test is added, so
there is none to see failing.
- [ ] Done when: the cost is a measured number the person has judged, and either nothing is built because it
does not matter yet, or the optimisation is specified in beads that cannot show a figure different from the
ledger's.

## Tests
None: nothing is implemented here. The implementation beads must carry: the same answers (golden files,
equality over an empty ledger) before and after; a request across a snapshot swap that answers wholly from
one snapshot with the optimisation in place; the optimisation shown to be faster by a timing taken by the
review on the real snapshot, not by the implementer.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** none now (this bead edits only the tracker). When implemented, expect: `internal/ledger` (the
view and its lifetime), `internal/txrules` (what is interpreted and when), `internal/api` (the handlers that
interpret the whole ledger), possibly `internal/authored` if a cache is kept, and `web/` if a debounce is
added to the budget's edit mode and the scenarios screen.
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/txrules/`, `internal/api/budget_view.go`,
`internal/api/transactions*.go`, `internal/api/card.go`, `web/src/screens/budget/`

Not statable in a few lines until the options are chosen.
close_reason: A tracking item, and its own criteria are met. The times were measured on 2026-11-23 inside the server over a real ledger and are written in the item as durations alone. The person answered what is slow (a screen's read above 200 ms, a write above 150 ms) and which course to take: remove the repeated reading of the ledger's rows within one request, keep nothing between requests, and decide on anything kept in memory only if a screen stays slow afterwards. The implementation items exist: finwise-vfw and finwise-c6t. No code changed with this item.

title: Keep each transaction under a key of its own in the app's database, say what every listed transaction counts for, and answer the transaction list, detail and filter options with what the person authored
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the transaction list, the transaction panel and the filters show only what the bank sent: no
transaction is ever on a budget line, no tag, note or nickname appears, no history is listed in the
panel, and nothing a person could decide about a purchase (not counting it, splitting it, calling it a
refund) can show. This work is what lets everything the person later decides about a transaction be
kept and shown: once the writes that follow it land, a purchase put on a line shows that line, a split
shows its parts and what they still lack, a nickname replaces the bank's wording, and the panel lists
what was done to the purchase and offers to take back only what can still be taken back. On its own it
changes nothing on screen, because nothing writes those things yet. What the person would notice if it
were wrong, later and not at the moment it went wrong: a month's totals that leave a purchase out or
count it twice, a reimbursed purchase counted for more than it cost, a correction that vanishes when the
bank replaces a pending charge with the posted one, or a purchase shown on a line its month's budget
never had.

## Outcome
Migration `0003_transactions` adds the transactions' tables to the app's database: the index of
transactions seen (`tx_index`, `tx_ids`), each transaction's state (`tx_state`), its tags and split parts,
each establishment's row and fixed tags, and the history steps with the reasons the person gave. One
function resolves the transaction a write names through the same interpreted ledger read the detail uses
and creates or refreshes its index row, so every later transaction write shares it. A new package,
`internal/budgetrules`, holds `Dispose`, which puts every listed transaction in exactly one of twelve
dispositions and says what it adds to which budget line, guarded by a property test of two invariants.
One function in `internal/api` disposes a month by joining the ledger's rows with the authored rows.
`transactions.list`, `transactions.detail` and `transactions.filterOptions` answer every field the person
can author from those tables; on a server without the app's database, or with an empty one, they answer
byte for byte what they answer today. A third golden state proves the merged answers.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and the collector may swap the
file under it at any time. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package
`internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against it; everything the person authors is
kept there, and the server has one only when started with `--db`. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake
backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of
how writes behave, and its behaviour is the rule here except where this text says otherwise. *The
contract* is the TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` (`web/src/api/contract/`); *the manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it, with a schema for every method's arguments and
result. *A listed transaction* is one the API lists: a row of the collector's clean list (which already
hides a bank-pending row that has its posted pair) after `internal/txrules` has folded tax rows under their
purchases and taken the movements of savings pots out. *A budget line* has an integer id minted by the app's
database and a name that belongs to a budget version; *the budget in force for a month* is the latest
version starting at or before that month (a month before the first version uses the first). *The fees
line* is the built-in line `Tarifas e juros`, in no group, with a fixed id; it can be named in any month
whose budget has at least one line. *The current month* is the Brazil month of the request's instant
(`brday.MonthOf(nowOf(ctx))`), never the host's clock. *A golden file* is the committed, exact answer of
one call over an invented fixture.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.** None of it is in the repository when this text is
written; read each in the code as that work left it.

- The app's database ({{F1}}): `internal/authored` recognises, opens and migrates `finwise.db`. A migration
  is an SQL file embedded from `internal/authored/migrations/`, recorded by name and checksum in
  `schema_migrations`; every file not recorded is applied at start in name order, each in one transaction,
  after a copy of a database that already holds data is taken beside it with `VACUUM INTO`; a recorded name
  whose checksum differs is refused at start. Every SQL statement over the database is a registered
  constant: a test prepares each against the migrated schema and another fails on a statement that is not
  registered. Connections carry `foreign_keys(1)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`, WAL and
  immediate write transactions.
- The recorder, the journal and undo ({{F2}}): every change to an authored table goes through a recorder
  that works from a closed, hand-written registry of the journaled tables. An *attribute table* holds one
  row of independent facts per key and an effect is one column changing; in a *table of optional facts*
  every column has a default and a row at its defaults is the same as no row, so the first fact written
  about a key creates the row without owning it. A *set table* holds rows that are facts by existing and an
  effect is one row appearing or disappearing. A table can be *owned* by another: writing an owned row
  does not make the owner's change stale, and removing the owner removes and records its owned rows. A
  statement that inserts, updates or deletes in a registered table outside the recorder fails a test, and
  every table is either registered or on the named list of tables deliberately not journaled, which already
  names `tx_index` and `tx_ids`; writes to those happen in the same transaction as the change they
  accompany and are not effects. The recorder also offers a read-only function that says whether the
  inverse of a chosen part of a change would be refused, usable inside a read-only transaction.
- The views handed to handlers ({{F3b}}): a handler's third parameter is one value carrying a view of each
  store for the request. The ledger view is one handle and one read-only transaction, so every ledger query
  of a request sees the same snapshot. The authored view is one read-only transaction on the app's
  database, so an answer is wholly before or wholly after a concurrent write; without `--db` it is an empty
  view that answers "nothing authored", so read code has one path. Each slice adds to that view the reads
  of the tables it owns.
- Write dispatch ({{F4c}}): a write handler receives a recorder that already holds one immediate
  transaction and the facts of a change, and what it reads of the app's database it reads inside that
  transaction; it also receives the request's ledger view. `ledger_unavailable` is answered by a write as by
  a read, through the same classifier, when the snapshot is missing.
- The write conformance harness ({{F5}}): `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds invented, migrated
  databases from a clock handed in, one builder per group of tables added by the slice that owns the
  tables, and its builders go through the package's functions and the recorder, needing no exemption from
  either guard. Read conformance has a third state, the full invented ledger of
  `internal/api/fixtures_test.go` with an invented authored state, whose cases are a list of their own,
  `authoredReadCases`, with golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`; that list is
  kept out of the shape the interface's equality test scans for. The canonical dump of every journaled
  table is a function of `internal/authored`.
- The budget's tables and the line menu ({{B2}}): `lines`, budget versions per month and their lines, the
  fees line seeded, and one function of "the lines a month's budget has" (each line's id, its name in that
  version and its group; the fees line too when the set is not empty) from which the menu
  `transactions.filterOptions(month).lines` and every lookup of a line's name in a month come. The month
  argument of `transactions.filterOptions` comes from the contract change before it ({{B1}}).

**What the code is today** (each point read in the file named).

- `internal/api/transactions.go`: `registerTransactions` registers `transactions.list`,
  `transactions.filterOptions` and `transactions.detail`. `readTransactionsList` parses the query
  (`queryPeriod`, `periodOf` in `transactions_period.go`), loads the ledger context (`loadContext`:
  accounts, identities, bills, bank and account labels) and calls `interpretPeriod`, which reads the period
  widened by `taxPairingDays` (3) on each side, runs `txrules.Interpret`, fails the read when a row went
  nowhere (`checkPlaced`), and keeps the rows inside the period newest first. `readTransactionFilterOptions`
  answers every account, `Tags: []` and (until {{B2}}) `Lines: []`.
- `internal/api/transactions_wire.go`: `transactionFrom` writes one interpreted row. Today `Name` and
  `OriginalName` are both the ledger's name; `EffectiveAmount` equals `Amount`; `CountsInTotals` is
  `Movement == NotAMovement && !Unconverted`; `Refund` is the ledger's rule; `Line`, `ClassifiedBy`,
  `Confidence` and `Pending` are null; `BelowThreshold`, `ReimbursementIncome`, `Reimbursed`, `Excluded`
  and `Split` are false; `Tags` is `[]`. Its comment says what only the person can author is the
  contract's empty value, never a guess. `pendingReview` has the contract's four fields, all required.
- `internal/api/transaction_detail.go`: `readTransactionDetail` reads the whole clean list
  (`CleanTransactions(ctx, wholeLedger)`), finds the row by its provider id (`rowWithID`), then interprets
  only the month of that row widened by three days (`interpretMonthOf`), and answers the listed
  transaction with that id, or null when the id is unknown, is a tax row folded into its purchase, or is a
  pot movement. `detailFrom` answers `OwnTags`, `SuggestedTags`, `ReimbursementCandidates` and `History`
  empty, `Note` `""`, `Reason` `""`, `AskReason` false, `Justification`, `SplitParts`, `Reimbursement`,
  `Exclusion` and `RefundLine` null, `SplitRemaining` zero. `sectionsOf` gives the panel's sections;
  `counterpartyOf` answers `{key, nickname: null, defaultLine: null, fixedTags: []}` for an establishment
  or a person and nil for a movement.
- `internal/api/card.go` already interprets the whole ledger in one pass (`CleanTransactions(ctx,
  wholeLedger)` then `interpretRows(rows, around, wholeLedger)`); `wholeLedger` is in `shell.go`.
- `internal/txrules` already marks on each listed row (`types.go`, `interpret.go`): `Movement`, which is
  `OwnTransfer` (a PIX, TED or TEF to a document of the person's own identities, `movements.go`) or
  `BillPayment` (a card bill paid, from the card side in `cardrows.go` or the bank side by the text
  `PAGAMENTO DE FATURA`); `Fee`, a card debit typed `TARIFA`, the card credit `DESC ANTECIPA PARCELAS` that
  discounts instalments, and a bank row typed `PACOTE_TARIFA_SERVICOS` or `ENCARGOS_JUROS_CHEQUE_ESPECIAL`
  (`kind.go`); `Refund`, by rule and for card credits only (typed `ESTORNO`, a refund stem in the text, or
  a credit typed `OUTROS`); `Unconverted`, a foreign row with no value in reais, whose `Amount` is then in
  the foreign currency (`amount.go`); `Posted`, false while the bank reports the row `PENDING`; `Person`,
  when the other side's document has eleven digits; and `EstablishmentKey`, `doc:`, `name:` or `text:`
  (`counterpart.go`), which may be a document number and is never logged. `Amount` is signed cents,
  negative for money out, and includes attached tax rows.
- `internal/api/budget_view.go`, `spentOnFees`: the existing fees rule counts a row that is `Fee`, posted,
  not a movement and not unconverted, net of the credits that discount fees.
- The float guard (`TestNoSourceFileOfTheHTTPLayerTouchesAFloat` in `internal/api/reais_test.go`) and the
  source test that forbids `time.Now` were widened by earlier work to cover `internal/budgetrules` from its
  first file; `internal/txrules/purity_test.go` is the house pattern for a rule package that imports
  neither `database/sql` nor `os`.
- The stand-in: `rules.ts` (`contributions`, `effectiveAmount`, `isExcluded`, `toContract`, `allTags`),
  `transaction-detail.ts` (`toDetail`, `sectionsOf`, `counterpartyOf`, `splitRemaining`), `history.ts`
  (steps and notes), `model.ts` (`FakeTransaction`, `FakeHistoryEntry`), and the tests `rules.test.ts`,
  `writes.test.ts` and `panel-writes.test.ts`. Its `spentByLine` adds a seeded baseline and moves only the
  current month.

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

- `finwise.db` gives each transaction its own key and maps the provider's ids to it. Why: a pending row is
  replaced by a posted row under a new id; with a key of its own, carrying the person's work across is one
  mapping row instead of rewriting every table. Rejected: the provider's id as the key.
- Ledger rows and authored rows are joined in Go, by key, inside one request that sees one snapshot of each
  store. `finwise.db` keeps a small index of the transactions it has seen, used for identity, guards and
  the rules' examples, never as the source of a figure shown or summed. Why: the reader hands out rows,
  never a connection, and the snapshot is swapped under it. Rejected: `ATTACH`; copying the ledger into
  `finwise.db`; a fresh ledger handle per query.
- A transaction's line must exist in the budget in force for the transaction's own month; a line named by
  something with no month (an establishment's default line) is resolved in the current month. Why: the
  person decided that a transaction of a closed month can still be recategorised, split, excluded and
  linked (closing freezes the month's budget, not its transactions), and a line the month's budget lacks
  would count in no group of that month. Rejected: validating everything against the current month.
- Spending is summed from the ledger for any month, by Brazil day, and income received has a rule. This
  departs from the stand-in, which keeps a seeded baseline of spending and has no rule for income
  received. The departure is pinned by the property test of `Dispose` and named in the report.
- Migrations are recorded by name; names are assigned in advance, one owner each. This work owns
  `0003_transactions` and no other.

**The schema: migration `0003_transactions`.** The columns are the starting point; a column this work
proves it needs may be added, in this file only. Every table declares its primary key, `NOT NULL` where a
value is required, foreign keys to `lines` and `tx_index`, and a `CHECK` for every closed set of values and
for every amount that cannot be negative. The proof includes a test in which the database itself, with no
Go validation in the way, refuses a duplicate, an invalid value and a negative amount.

| table | columns | kind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tx_index` | `tx_key` (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`), `account_id`, `day` (`YYYY-MM-DD`, Brazil), `cents`, `establishment_key`, `bank_pending` (0 or 1), `first_run`, `last_run`, `evaluated` (0 or 1) | not journaled |
| `tx_ids` | `provider_id` (primary key), `tx_key` (references `tx_index`) | not journaled |
| `tx_state` | `tx_key` (primary key, references `tx_index`), `line_id`, `classified_by`, `confidence`, `pending_reason`, `pending_line_id`, `pending_confidence`, `ask_reason`, `note`, `exclusion`, `refund`, `refund_line_id`, `reimbursable`, `expected_cents`, `credit_tx_key` (unique, references `tx_index`), `credit_cents` | attribute table of optional facts |
| `tx_tags` | `tx_key`, `tag`, `position` | set |
| `tx_split_parts` | `tx_key`, `position`, `line_id` (nullable), `cents` (zero or more) | set; a part can keep its place and lose its line |
| `establishments` | `key` (the establishment key), `nickname`, `default_line_id` | attribute table of optional facts |
| `establishment_tags` | `key`, `tag`, `position` | set |
| `history_steps` | `id` (`INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`), `tx_key`, `change_id` (references `changes`), `kind` (a step or a note), `text`, `day` | set; restored under the same id |
| `history_step_reasons` | `step_id` (references `history_steps`), `reason` | set, owned by its step |

What the columns mean, as fixed already: in `tx_state`, `exclusion` is null for "counts", empty for
"switched on, no reason yet" and a text for the reason; `refund` is null for "as the ledger's rule says"
and 0 or 1 for what the person set; `expected_cents` is the amount the person expects back, or null when
they cleared it; `line_id`, `pending_line_id` and `refund_line_id` reference `lines`; a transaction is
pending when `pending_reason` is set, and `pending_line_id` with `pending_confidence` is its suggestion;
`ask_reason` says the panel is asking "why". `establishments.default_line_id` references `lines`. A tag's
`position` is the order it was added in and is never renumbered. The reason a person gives for a
correction belongs to its step but is kept beside it, in `history_step_reasons`, owned by the step: giving
a reason does not make the line change stale, and taking that change back takes its reason with it. The
reason a transaction's detail answers is the one on its latest step that has one; it is stored nowhere
else. `credit_tx_key` is the credit linked to a reimbursable purchase, unique because one credit pays one
purchase, and `credit_cents` is the credit's amount as the work that links reimbursements ({{T5}})
stores it. `first_run` and `last_run` are the collector runs in which the bank listed the row; no reader
statement reads the collector's run yet, so they stay null until the work that brings the database up to
date with each snapshot ({{R2}}) fills them. Which values `classified_by` and `kind` store, the exact keys
of the set tables, and how a position is numbered are the implementer's, within the `CHECK`s above.

The seven journaled tables are entered in the recorder's registry with the shapes in the table, and each
entry names the registered statements that read and write it. `tx_index` and `tx_ids` record observations,
not decisions: they are not journaled, an undo never removes an index row, and the index only grows.

**The index and the target of a write.** `tx_index` and `tx_ids` are what the app's database remembers
about the transactions it has evaluated or the person has touched. They serve four things: carrying the
person's work from a pending row to its posted replacement (the ingest, {{R2}}, maps the posted row's
provider id to the pending row's key, with no authored row rewritten), running the rules that classify new
transactions once per transaction (`evaluated`), knowing a transaction's month when a budget changes (the
clearing of lines a month lost, {{B4}}, reads the month from `tx_index.day` with no ledger read), and
finding the examples of an establishment. No amount shown or summed ever comes from the index.

This work writes the one function every transaction write uses to find what it names. It resolves a
provider id through the same interpreted ledger read the API lists transactions with, the one
`transactions.detail` uses for its target (the whole clean list, the row's own month widened by three
days, the listed transaction with that id), in the request's ledger view, so the write has the row's
current facts: its name, its establishment key, whether the other side is a person, whether it is a
movement, its amount, its day. An id that read does not list (an unknown id, a tax row folded into its
purchase, a pot movement) is unknown, and the caller decides what that answers (null where the result
allows it, `refused` / `not_found` otherwise). For a known id it then creates or refreshes the index row
inside the write's transaction: a provider id not in `tx_ids` mints a new `tx_key` and maps it; a known
one refreshes `account_id`, `day`, `cents`, `establishment_key` and `bank_pending` to the row's current
facts (if the bank reworded the row, the index row takes the new key; nothing authored moves). A row
indexed by a write is not marked `evaluated`: when the rules later meet it they mark it and leave it alone
because it already has a line or a review. Which interpreted amount `cents` holds is the implementer's,
as long as the ingest's pairing compares it the same way on both sides. The lookups of a write that
spans months ("all purchases here", the reimbursement candidates) interpret the whole ledger in one pass,
as `card.go` does, and index what they touch through the same function's second half. The sibling
transaction writes (the line writes, {{T2}}; tags, note and the establishment, {{T3}}; split, exclusion
and refund, {{T4}}) all call this function; none of them has a copy. A read never writes the index: it
runs in a read-only transaction, and a listed transaction with no `tx_ids` row has nothing authored.

One known interaction, owned by the ingest: the pairing of a vanished bank-pending row considers only
posted rows the index has never seen, so a posted row a write indexed first keeps its own key.

**What every listed transaction counts for: `budgetrules.Dispose`.** A new package of pure functions,
`internal/budgetrules`, that imports `internal/money` and `internal/brday` and nothing else (it opens
nothing, knows no HTTP and no `txrules` type, as `txrules`, `cardrules` and `potrules` do today). Its input
is plain values: for each listed transaction, its signed cents and the ledger's facts (unconverted, a
movement, a fee row, posted, the ledger's refund rule), and what the person authored (the line id, the
pending review, the exclusion, the split parts, the refund override and refund line, whether it is a
credit linked to a purchase, and for a purchase the linked credit's cents); and the month's budget, the
set of line ids with each one's group, plus the fees line's id. `Dispose` puts every listed transaction in
exactly one disposition and says what it adds to which line. Amounts below are magnitudes in cents. A
transaction is a credit when its amount is above zero and a debit otherwise, as the stand-in's
`contributions` divides them.

| # | disposition | condition, first match wins | counts |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | unconverted | the ledger has no value in reais for it | nothing |
| 2 | movement | a movement between own accounts or a bill payment | nothing |
| 3 | excluded | excluded with a reason | nothing |
| 4 | waiting | pending review | nothing |
| 5 | split | a debit with two or more parts | each part with a line adds its amount to that line; the rest (the amount less those parts, which is negative when they exceed it) is unassigned |
| 6 | fee | a fee row, charge or discount, that is on no line (as the existing fees rule defines it: posted) or that the person put on the fees line | a charge adds to the fees line; the credit that discounts it takes off |
| 7 | reimbursement | a credit linked to a purchase | no line; the smaller of its amount and the purchase's is applied inside the purchase, and any excess counts nowhere |
| 8 | refund | a credit that is a refund | reduces its refund line by its amount; with no refund line, nothing |
| 9 | income | a credit on a line of the income group | received on that line |
| 10 | other credit | any other credit | nothing |
| 11 | on a line | a debit with a line | its amount less the applied reimbursement |
| 12 | uncategorised | a debit with no line | nothing; its amount less the applied reimbursement is unassigned |

How the conditions read against the stored values. "Excluded with a reason": `exclusion` is a non-empty
text; switched on with no reason the transaction keeps counting. "Pending review": pending in the app's
database (`pending_reason` set). "A refund": the person's `refund` when set, otherwise the ledger's rule.
"Linked to a purchase": some purchase's `credit_tx_key` is this credit's key. A purchase's applied
reimbursement is the smaller of its linked credit's cents and its own magnitude, so its effective amount
never changes sign; a purchase with no link has none. "On a line of the income group": the line's group in
the month's budget is `rec`. A row the bank still reports as pending is listed and counts like any other;
the existing fees rule keeps counting only posted fee rows, so a bank-pending fee row on no line is not
disposition 6 and falls through to 10 or 12.

Two invariants guard the totals. For every debit of dispositions 5, 11 and 12: what it adds to lines, plus
what is unassigned, plus the applied reimbursement, equals its amount. For every month: every listed
transaction is in exactly one disposition, so the dispositions' counts add up to the number of
transactions the API lists and their amounts to the sum of the listed magnitudes. Both are a property test
over generated transactions in `budgetrules`, with a reimbursement smaller than, equal to and larger than
its purchase. The opt-in check of both over every month of a real ledger is the later end-to-end test of
the write side ({{O1}}), which calls the month function below; this work owes it that function and the
definition of an unconverted row's magnitude in the sum of invariant 2, stated in the property test.

The output's representation is the implementer's, with one constraint from its next user, the budget's
figures ({{B3}}): per transaction, its disposition, what it adds to or takes off each line id (a debit
adds, a discount credit and a refund take off, an income credit is received, and these stay
distinguishable), its unassigned amount and its applied reimbursement.

**Disposing a month.** One function in `internal/api` takes the request's views and a month, interprets
the month's listed transactions exactly as `transactions.list` does for that month (widened by three days,
then cut), joins each with its authored rows by key through `tx_ids`, takes the month's budget from the
lookup of {{B2}}, and calls `Dispose`. The budget's figures ({{B3}}), the shell's counts and the opt-in
real-ledger test ({{O1}}) call it; nothing else recomputes dispositions. A line id the month's budget does
not have cannot be stored once the clearing of lines a month lost lands ({{B4}}); until then, or in a
fixture, the read and the disposition must treat it the same way, and how is the implementer's, pinned by
a test, never a failed read.

**What the reads answer.** The list, the detail and the filter options answer from these tables, joined in
Go by key inside the request's two views. A listed transaction with no authored rows answers exactly what
it answers today.

`Transaction` (the list and the detail):

- `name`: the nickname of its establishment key when there is one, otherwise the ledger's name;
  `originalName` is always the ledger's name. One function answers the name to show for an establishment
  key, and the list and the detail use it; the card's lists are brought under it by the work on tags and
  nicknames ({{T3}}), and every later place that shows a name calls it.
- `line`: the name the transaction's line has in the budget of the transaction's own month; null with no
  line. In a period of several months each row is named by its own month's budget.
- `classifiedBy`: `Você` for the person, `Regra` for a rule, `IA` for the model, null for nobody;
  `confidence` as stored; `belowThreshold` false, because it is about the model's confidence only and there
  is no model yet.
- `pending`: null unless pending; then `reason`, `suggestion` (the suggested line's name in the month's
  budget), `confidence` and `justification` `""`. The contract's suggestion, confidence and justification
  are not nullable yet; making them nullable, and answering a pending row without a suggestion, is the work
  on the rules that classify new transactions ({{R1}}). No fixture of this work holds such a row.
- `tags`: the transaction's own tags in the order they were added, followed by the fixed tags of its
  establishment key in the order they were added, without repeats, as the contract says. The stand-in's
  `allTags` lists the fixed ones first; the server departs from it on purpose.
- `effectiveAmount`: the amount plus the applied reimbursement (a purchase of -300.00 with a linked credit
  of 150.00 answers -150.00; with a credit of 400.00, 0.00).
- `countsInTotals`: false for a movement, an unconverted row and a transaction excluded with a reason;
  `excluded`: excluded with a reason.
- `refund`: what the person set, or the ledger's rule when they set nothing.
- `reimbursed`: the purchase has a linked credit; `reimbursementIncome`: the credit is linked to a purchase.
- `split`: two or more parts.

`TransactionDetail`, beyond the above:

- `justification`: `""` for a pending transaction or one the model classified, null otherwise (as the
  stand-in's `toDetail`), until the model exists.
- `askReason` as stored; `reason`: the reason on the latest step that has one, `""` when none has.
- `counterparty` (only where `sectionsOf` shows the establishment or the person section, as today):
  `{key, nickname, defaultLine, fixedTags}`; `defaultLine` is the default line's name in the budget of the
  current month, null when that budget does not have it while the stored id stays.
- `ownTags`: the own tags alone, in order. `suggestedTags`: the known tags the transaction lacks among its
  own.
- `note` as stored, `""` by default.
- `splitParts`: null when not split, otherwise each part's line name (in the month's budget) or null and
  its amount, in position order; `splitRemaining`: the purchase's magnitude less the parts' sum, negative
  when they exceed it, zero when not split.
- `reimbursement`: null when the purchase is not marked reimbursable, otherwise `expected` (null when
  cleared). Its `link` (the credit's id, name, day and amount) and `reimbursementCandidates` are answered
  by the work on reimbursements ({{T5}}), which reads the whole ledger for them and owns their golden
  change in `full/`; here `link` stays null and the candidates stay `[]`, and no fixture of this work holds
  a link.
- `exclusion`: null when `exclusion` is null, otherwise `{reason}` (`""` while switched on with none).
- `refundLine`: the refund line's name in the month's budget, or null.
- `history`: the transaction's steps newest first, each `{id, text, day, reason, undoable}`: `id` the
  step's id as a decimal string, `text` and `day` as stored, `reason` its owned reason or null, and
  `undoable` computed by the recorder's read-only check over the units of this transaction that the step's
  change touched, inside the read's transaction, always false for a note. Taking a step back
  (`undoHistoryStep`) is the line writes' work ({{T2}}), which must agree with this flag.

`TransactionFilterOptions.tags` (the known tags): every distinct tag in `tx_tags` and
`establishment_tags`, alphabetically. The collation is the implementer's: deterministic, and pinned by a
test that includes an accented tag and an upper-case one. `accounts` stays as today and `lines` is the
menu of {{B2}}.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. A real
snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever
printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person
running a test and goes into no file; a test that touches a real ledger runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Nothing in this work needs a real ledger. Every fixture is
invented, and `-update` of the golden files refuses to run while `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set. An
establishment key under `doc:` is a document number: it is never logged. New files in `internal/api` log
nothing (`handler_silence_test.go` allows only `logging.go` and `router.go` to name a logging package).

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; the float guard covers
`internal/api`, `internal/authored` and `internal/budgetrules`. Every SQL statement over the app's
database is a registered constant. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English;
a design value in a component comes from a token (this work touches no component). The tables are read
only through the authored view in a read and through the recorder's transaction in a write.

**Failure paths that touch this work.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the migration fails | its transaction rolls back; the copy taken before it is beside the file; `serve` exits naming the path and the reason, never the content |
| the snapshot is missing | the three reads answer `ledger_unavailable` as today; a write resolving a target answers it too and records nothing |
| the snapshot is swapped during a request | the request finishes on the snapshot it opened |
| a transaction disappears from the ledger | its authored rows and its index row stay; nothing is deleted; it is in no list and no count until listed again |
| the bank rewords a row so its establishment key changes | an indexed transaction keeps what it has and its index row takes the new key; nothing authored is lost |

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`), each with what constrains it: the stored
values of `classified_by` and `kind`, the keys of the set tables and the numbering of positions, within the
`CHECK`s and the never-renumbered rule; which interpreted amount `tx_index.cents` holds; the output shape
of `Dispose`, within the constraint above; the magnitude of an unconverted row in invariant 2, stated in
the property test; the collation of the known tags, pinned; the treatment of a stored line id the month's
budget lacks, the same in the read and the disposition and pinned; whether disposition 6's "put on the
fees line" reads the line alone or also who put it there (a rule can put a row there through "all purchases
here"), pinned; file and function names.

## Acceptance criteria
Schema and index
- [ ] A database that held the journal's and the budget's tables gains the nine tables when opened; the
migration is recorded once under `0003_transactions`; opening again applies nothing.
- [ ] From a test, directly against the migrated schema, the database refuses: a second `tx_ids` row for
one provider id; two `tx_state` rows linking the same `credit_tx_key`; the same tag twice on one
transaction; a split part of -1 cents; an `expected_cents` of -1; a `classified_by`, `kind`, `refund`,
`ask_reason` or `bank_pending` value outside its set; a `line_id` not in `lines`; a `tx_state` row whose
`tx_key` is not in `tx_index`.
- [ ] The seven journaled tables are in the recorder's registry with the shapes of the schema table,
`history_step_reasons` owned by `history_steps`; `tx_index` and `tx_ids` are on the list of tables not
journaled; the test that every table is classified passes and fails when one entry is removed.
- [ ] Resolving a write's target for a listed id with no index row mints one `tx_key`, writes one
`tx_index` row with the row's account, Brazil day, cents, establishment key and `bank_pending`, and one
`tx_ids` row, adds no row to `changes` or `change_effects`, and leaves `evaluated` at 0; resolving it again
mints nothing; after the fixture ledger's row moves to another day the index row holds the new day.
- [ ] The resolution answers unknown, and writes nothing, for `no-such-transaction`, for `tx-foreign-tax`
(folded into its purchase) and for `tx-pot-transfer` (a pot movement), over the full invented ledger.
- [ ] A recorded write whose handler resolves a target and then fails rolls the index row back with the
change.

Dispose and its invariants
- [ ] `internal/budgetrules` imports only the standard library, `internal/money` and `internal/brday`; a
purity test fails on an import of `database/sql` or `os`, and the float and `time.Now` guards cover it.
- [ ] A table test has one row per disposition 1 to 12, including: a bank-pending fee row on no line, which
is not a fee; a fee charge the person put on the fees line while bank-pending, which is; a discount credit
that takes off the fees line; a refund with no refund line, which counts nothing; an excluded row whose
exclusion is `""`, which keeps counting; a credit on a `fix` line, which is an other credit; a split whose
parts exceed the purchase by 10.00, unassigned -10.00; and the first-match order (an unconverted excluded
pending split row is unconverted).
- [ ] A purchase of 300.00 linked to credits of 150.00, 300.00 and 400.00 has an applied reimbursement of
150.00, 300.00 and 300.00, adds 150.00, 0.00 and 0.00 to its line, and the 400.00 credit's excess of 100.00
counts nowhere.
- [ ] The property test passes over generated transactions with every flag combination, split parts with
and without lines summing below, at and above the amount, and reimbursements smaller than, equal to and
larger than their purchase: invariant 1 holds for every debit of dispositions 5, 11 and 12, and invariant 2
holds for every generated month; a failure prints what reproduces it.

The month function and the reads
- [ ] Over the full invented ledger with an invented authored state, the month function's dispositions for
2026-03 count as many transactions as `transactions.list` answers for that month and sum to the sum of
their magnitudes.
- [ ] On a server without the app's database, and on one with an empty app's database, `transactions.list`
(the five existing cases), `transactions.detail` (the eight) and `transactions.filterOptions` answer byte
for byte what they answered before; no file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` or `empty/`
changes (`git diff --stat` over the branch shows none) and `web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` passes
untouched.
- [ ] `authoredReadCases` holds at least `transactions.list` for 2026-03 and for `last-3-months`,
`transactions.filterOptions` for 2026-03, and `transactions.detail` for at least five ids, over an invented
authored state that holds: a line put by the person and one by a rule; a pending review with a suggestion;
a nickname; own tags and fixed tags that overlap; a note; a default line the current month has and one it
lacks; a split of three parts, one without a line; an exclusion with a reason and one without; a refund
override with a refund line; a reimbursable purchase with an expected amount; a history with a step that
has a reason, a step overwritten since, and a note. Each golden file is under
`testdata/golden/full-authored/` and none of these calls is written in the shape the interface's equality
test scans for.
- [ ] In those answers: a transaction with own tags `#b`, `#a` whose establishment has fixed `#a`, `#c`
answers `tags: ["#b","#a","#c"]` and `ownTags: ["#b","#a"]`; the nickname is `name` and the ledger's name
is `originalName`; `history` lists newest first, the overwritten step answers `undoable: false`, the note
answers `undoable: false`, the other step `true`; `reason` is the latest step's reason; the default line
the current month lacks answers `defaultLine: null`.
- [ ] A transaction whose line is renamed in a later budget version answers its own month's name in a
`last-3-months` list that spans both versions.
- [ ] The known tags list each tag in use once, in the pinned order, with an accented and an upper-case
tag in the fixture.
- [ ] Over a snapshot that cannot be read the three reads answer 503 `ledger_unavailable`.

Proof of the proofs
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the report: the
disposition order swapped (waiting before excluded); the reimbursement not capped at the purchase; a split
part without a line dropped from the unassigned rest; the posted condition removed from disposition 6; a
generated transaction left out of every disposition; the fixed tags listed before the own ones; a
renumbered position; `undoable` true for a note; a line named by the current month instead of the
transaction's; the index row minted twice for one provider id; the resolution reading a month that does
not hold the row; one `CHECK` and one uniqueness rule of the migration dropped.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the property test of the two invariants passes, and the
authored read cases answer every authored field from the app's database while `full/` and `empty/` are
unchanged.

## Tests
- Unit, over a temporary migrated database (`internal/authored`): the schema's refusals of a duplicate, an
  invalid value, a negative amount and a broken reference, with no Go validation in the way; every new
  statement registered and prepared; every table classified.
- Unit (`internal/authored`): minting and refreshing an index row, the map of provider ids, no index write
  recorded as an effect, the rollback with a failed change.
- Table (`internal/budgetrules`): one row per disposition and per tie of the first-match order, the
  reimbursement cap, the fee's posted condition, the refund with and without a line, ported where they
  exist from `web/src/api/fake/rules.test.ts` (`contributions`) and moved to cents.
- Property (`internal/budgetrules`): the two invariants over generated transactions and months, with
  reimbursements smaller than, equal to and larger than their purchase.
- Unit (`internal/budgetrules`): purity, no `database/sql` or `os` import.
- Unit (`internal/api`, over the full invented ledger of `fixtures_test.go` and a state built by
  `authoredtest`): the write-target resolution for listed, unknown, folded and pot ids; the month function
  against the list's count and sum; the tag order, the nickname, the line name per month, `undoable`, the
  known tags' collation.
- Golden, third state (`internal/api`, `authoredReadCases`): the list, the detail and the filter options in
  `testdata/golden/full-authored/`; `full/` and `empty/` unchanged.
- The existing conformance, golden and unreadable-snapshot tests, unchanged, and the gate once at the end.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/migrations/`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`,
`internal/budgetrules/`, `internal/api/transactions.go`, `internal/api/transactions_wire.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_detail.go`, `internal/api/transaction_target.go`,
`internal/api/transactions_authored.go`, `internal/api/month_dispositions.go`,
`internal/api/transactions_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/transactions_period.go`, `internal/api/card.go`, `internal/api/shell.go`,
`internal/api/budget_view.go`, `internal/api/fixtures_test.go`, `internal/api/conformance_test.go`,
`internal/api/reais_test.go`, `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`, `internal/txrules/`,
`web/src/api/fake/rules.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/rules.test.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/transaction-detail.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/history.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/model.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/writes.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/panel-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`,
`web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`, `internal/contract/contract.json`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/full/`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/empty/`,
`web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`, `bin/ci`

One migration; in `internal/authored`, the store of the nine tables (the index, the state and its set
tables, the establishments, the history), their registry entries, and the reads the authored view gains;
one builder file in `authoredtest`; a new rule package of two or three files; in `internal/api`, three
read handlers changed in place and three new files (the names are a proposal) for the write-target
resolution, the merge of authored rows and the month function. That is about thirteen code files in three
packages, which is why a split is proposed on the first line. The contract, the manifest, the interface
and the stand-in are read, not changed. No write handler is added: the writes that fill these tables are
the four slices that depend on this one. The difficulty is `critical` because `Dispose` decides every
total the budget will show, and a wrong disposition is silent.

## Recovery path
The migration only adds tables. If it fails, its transaction rolls back and the server exits; when the
database already held data, the copy the migration runner took before migrating is beside it
(`<name>.before-<UTC timestamp>`). To go back: stop the server; check the copy (`PRAGMA integrity_check`,
the application id); put it in place of the database with no `-wal` or `-shm` file beside it; start a
binary that does not carry this migration, since a database that holds a migration the binary does not
know is refused at start. Once the migration has been applied to a database that matters its file is
frozen; a correction is a new migration, never an edit.

title: Turn a ledger row into the transaction the app lists
description:
## What changes for the user
The bank's records are not the list a person expects to read. A card purchase and a bank debit carry opposite signs, a purchase abroad shows its price in another currency, the tax on it arrives as a separate row, paying the card bill looks like spending twice, and moving money into a savings pot looks like an expense. After this lands the app can turn those records into one line per purchase in reais, with the tax under its purchase, with transfers between the person's own accounts set apart, and with pot movements out of the general list. No record is ever dropped without being accounted for.

## Outcome
A Go package of pure functions, `internal/txrules`, that takes the rows the ledger reader returns for a period and gives back the transactions the app lists, each with its kind, signed amount in cents, Brazil day, counterpart and establishment key, plus a tally that places every input row in exactly one destination.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app over a SQLite ledger collected from the person's banks. A Go package, `internal/ledger`, already reads that ledger and returns rows faithfully, with amounts in integer cents and the raw provider fields parsed; it interprets nothing. This bead is the interpretation. It does no SQL and no I/O.

**The app's convention.** An amount is signed and negative means money out, on every kind of account. A day is `YYYY-MM-DD` in America/Sao_Paulo. The interface's contract for a transaction is `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`; its kinds and subtypes are the vocabulary this package maps to.

**Direction and sign.** The row's `type` (`DEBIT` or `CREDIT`) is only a direction, and the sign of the stored amount is inverted between account types: on a `BANK` account a debit is stored negative; on a `CREDIT` account (a card) a purchase is a positive debit and a payment or refund a negative credit. Direction comes from `type` together with the account type, never from the stored sign alone.

**Foreign purchases.** The stored amount is in the original currency. The value in reais is `raw.amountInAccountCurrency` when present. The app amount is the value in reais; the original amount and currency are kept for display.

**Day.** `date` is a UTC timestamp on every row; convert before taking the day. `creditCardMetadata.purchaseDate` exists on few rows, so `date` is the date.

**Kind.** Decided with the user: bank rows are split by payment method (PIX, boleto, and "Outros" for the rest: TED, TEF, debit, fees); card rows are those of `CREDIT` accounts. The kind is read from the account type, `raw.operationType` and `raw.paymentData.paymentMethod` together, because `operationType` alone lies: a bank row may be typed `OUTROS` and carry `paymentMethod` `PIX`. Vocabulary seen on bank accounts: `PIX`, `BOLETO`, `TED`, `TEF`, `CARTAO`, `FOLHA_PAGAMENTO`, `CONVENIO_ARRECADACAO`, `PACOTE_TARIFA_SERVICOS`, `ENCARGOS_JUROS_CHEQUE_ESPECIAL`, `TRANSFERENCIA_SALDO_RESERVADO`, `RESGATE_APLIC_FINANCEIRA`, `RENDIMENTO_APLIC_FINANCEIRA`, `OUTROS`; `paymentMethod` is one of `PIX`, `BOLETO`, `TED`, `TEF`, `OTHER` and exists only on bank rows. On card accounts: `PAGAMENTO`, `ESTORNO`, `TARIFA`, `PAGAMENTO_FATURA`, `OUTROS`, or none.

**Card rows typed `OUTROS`.** `operationType` cannot be the rule across banks: on C6 `OUTROS` is almost only tax, on Itaú it is everything the bank does not classify. Hiding only `PAGAMENTO_FATURA` would leave Itaú's bill payments counted as spending, and hiding `OUTROS` would drop real purchases. The groups, each row in exactly one:
- A tax row named after its purchase (C6): its amount is exactly 3.5% of a purchase with the same name on the same card within 3 days. It is attached to that purchase and leaves the list.
- An explicit tax row (Itaú): the description is `IOF INTERNACIONAL`. It is attached to the foreign purchase of the same day on the same card. The sources give no rule for a day with several foreign purchases: attach only when exactly one candidate exists, otherwise keep the row listed.
- A purchase abroad typed `OUTROS` (Itaú): an ordinary purchase.
- A bill payment seen from the card (Itaú): the description is `PAGAMENTO COM SALDO`. It is a movement.
- An early-payment discount: the description is `Desc Antecipa Parcelas`. The user confirmed it is a discount for paying instalments ahead; it is a credit under fees and interest.
- A credit with no keyword on the C6 card: the user confirmed these are refunds.
- A partial cancellation (Itaú): a refund. The sources give no keyword for it.

**Movements.** Listed, under their own kind, and never counted as an expense or as income by a caller: a bill payment (from the card side `PAGAMENTO_FATURA` or `PAGAMENTO COM SALDO`; the bank-account side has no written rule), and a transfer between the person's own accounts, recognised when the counterpart's document is one of the person's own in the ledger's `identities`. Savings-pot movements (`TRANSFERENCIA_SALDO_RESERVADO`, and Mercado Pago's `RESGATE_APLIC_FINANCEIRA` rows whose description starts with `Rendimentos`) leave the general list and are returned separately, per account, for the pot they belong to.

**Counterpart and establishment.** The ledger has no merchant on any row. A PIX or a boleto carries `paymentData.payer` and `.receiver`, each with a name and a document: the counterpart is the other party, its key is the document, and it is a person when the document has 11 digits and a company when it has 14. A card purchase has only its description: the display name comes from it and the key is the normalised text. Two descriptions that differ only in letter case, spacing or a trailing instalment marker such as `03/10` share a key. A document is another person's personal data: it is a key, it is never logged.

**What the sources leave open.** For each of these, write the smallest rule that is safe, state it in a comment, and report how many rows it matched on a real ledger, as a count only: the bank-account side of a bill payment; the keyword of a partial cancellation; the explicit tax row on a day with several foreign purchases; how far text normalisation goes. The safe default everywhere: a row no rule recognises stays in the list as an ordinary transaction of kind "Outros". Dropping it is the failure that matters.

**The tally.** Processing a period returns, beside the list, how many input rows were listed, attached to a purchase as tax, or returned as pot movements. Every input row id is in exactly one of the three.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A `BANK` debit of 50.00 yields -5000 and a `BANK` credit +5000; a `CREDIT`-account debit of 50.00 yields -5000 and a `CREDIT`-account credit +5000; each holds whichever sign the fixture stored.
- [ ] A purchase of 10.00 in USD with 55.00 in the account currency yields -5500 and keeps `1000` and `USD` as the original.
- [ ] A row dated `2026-03-01T02:30:00Z` has the day `2026-02-28`.
