`tx-foreign-tax` and `tx-pot-transfer` over the full invented ledger; a test write handler that looks up a
target and then fails leaves the index as it was.
- [ ] Over the full invented ledger with an invented authored state, the month function's dispositions for
2026-03 and for 2026-02 count as many transactions as `transactions.list` answers for that month and sum to
the sum of their magnitudes; a fee row put on the fees line by a rule is in the fee disposition.
- [ ] On a server without the app's database, and on one with an empty app's database,
`transactions.list` (the five existing cases), `transactions.detail` (the eight) and
`transactions.filterOptions` answer byte for byte what they answered before; no file under
`internal/api/testdata/golden/full/` or `empty/` changes (`git diff --stat` over the branch shows none) and
`web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts` passes untouched.
- [ ] `authoredReadCases` holds at least `transactions.list` for 2026-03 and for `last-3-months`,
`transactions.filterOptions` for 2026-03, and `transactions.detail` for at least five ids, over an invented
authored state that holds: a line put by the person and one by a rule; a pending review with a suggestion; a
nickname; own tags and fixed tags that overlap; a note; a default line the current month has and one it
lacks; a split of three parts, one without a line; an exclusion with a reason and one without; a refund
override with a refund line; a reimbursable purchase with an expected amount; a history with a step that has
a reason, a step overwritten since, and a note. Each golden file is under `testdata/golden/full-authored/`,
and none of these calls is written in the shape the interface's equality test scans for.
- [ ] In those answers: a transaction with own tags `#b`, `#a` whose establishment has fixed `#a`, `#c`
answers `tags: ["#b","#a","#c"]` and `ownTags: ["#b","#a"]`; the nickname is `name` on every listed
transaction of its key and the ledger's name is `originalName`; `history` lists newest first, the overwritten
step answers `undoable: false`, the note `undoable: false`, the other step `true`; `reason` is the latest
step's reason; the default line the current month lacks answers `defaultLine: null`; the excluded row with
an empty reason answers `exclusion: {"reason":""}`, `excluded: false`, `countsInTotals: true`.
- [ ] A transaction whose line is renamed in a later budget version answers its own month's name in a
`last-3-months` list that spans both versions.
- [ ] The known tags list each tag in use once, in the pinned order, with an accented and an upper-case tag
in the fixture; `suggestedTags` is that list without the transaction's own tags.
- [ ] Over a snapshot that cannot be read the three reads answer 503 `ledger_unavailable`.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against a deliberate break named in the report: the fixed
tags listed before the own ones; `undoable` true for a note; `undoable` computed over every unit of the
change instead of this transaction's; a line named by the current month instead of the transaction's; the
default line named by the transaction's month instead of the current one; the lookup reading a month that
does not hold the row; the month function interpreting the period without the three-day widening; the name
function bypassed in the list.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the authored read cases answer every authored field from the
app's database while `full/` and `empty/` are unchanged, and the month function's count and sum agree with
the list.

## Tests
- Unit (Go, over the full invented ledger of `fixtures_test.go` and a state built by `authoredtest`): the
  target lookup for listed, unknown, folded and pot ids, and its rollback; the month function against the
  list's count and sum; the tag order, the nickname, the line name per month, the default line per current
  month, `undoable`, the known tags' collation.
- Golden, third state (`authoredReadCases`): the list, the detail and the filter options in
  `testdata/golden/full-authored/`; `full/` and `empty/` unchanged.
- The existing conformance, golden, unreadable-snapshot and no-leak tests, unchanged, and the gate once at
  the end.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/transactions.go`, `internal/api/transactions_wire.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_detail.go`, `internal/api/transaction_target.go`,
`internal/api/transactions_authored.go`, `internal/api/month_dispositions.go`,
`internal/api/transactions_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/`
**Reads only:** `internal/budgetrules/`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/authored/authoredtest/`,
`internal/api/transactions_period.go`, `internal/api/card.go`, `internal/api/shell.go`,
`internal/api/fixtures_test.go`, `internal/api/conformance_test.go`, `internal/api/handler_silence_test.go`,
`internal/txrules/`, `web/src/api/fake/rules.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/transaction-detail.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/history.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/model.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`,
`web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`, `internal/contract/contract.json`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/full/`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/empty/`,
`web/src/test/empty-ledger.test.ts`, `bin/ci`

One package: three read handlers changed in place and three new files (the names are a proposal) for the
target lookup with the name function, the merge of authored rows, and the month function; one test file and
one golden directory, with the authored read cases added where the harness put `authoredReadCases`. About
six code files in `internal/api`. `card.go` is read, not edited: it moves under the name function with the
work on nicknames. No write handler is added. The difficulty is `critical` because the month function feeds
every total the budget will show and the target lookup decides which transaction every write lands on.
close_reason: transactions.list, transactions.detail and transactions.filterOptions answer with what was authored; lookupTarget resolves the transaction a write names through the list's own read and indexes it inside the write's change; disposeMonth is the one place a month's figures start from, feeding budgetrules.Dispose through one join whose every field is pinned; a transaction's line is named by its own month's budget; a step is undoable by the units of its change that belong to the transaction. No golden file of full/ or empty/ changed. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main (a type and a constant declared by both this work and the pot writes renamed on this side). Review: five independent mutations; three survived at first, all in the join (refund line, the person's refund mark, a linked credit still counting as income) and now fail tests, with all seventeen fields of the join mutated and caught. The implementer's twenty-five breaks each failed a test.

title: Count the pending reviews in the frame and the home, and give the month asked its variable limit and its weekly guide
description:
## What changes for the user
Today, over their real bank data, the home screen says the month's limit is R$ 0 of R$ 0 and shows no
week at all, the weekly review's strip reads the same, and the badge on "Revisão" never shows a number,
whatever budget the person keeps and however many purchases are waiting for them to say what they were.
After this lands the badge counts the purchases and credits that are waiting for an answer; the home
shows, for the month on screen, how much of the variable lines' caps has been spent, and one guide per
week of seven days saying how much can still be spent that week if what is left of the month's cap is
shared over the days still to come; the week holding today is marked as this week, a week not yet begun
shows a dash for what was spent, and a past month shows every week with what was really spent in it. The
weekly review shows the same limit, how much of it is used and this week's guide. If this were wrong the
person would see a badge that never empties, or counts something they cannot answer; a guide that tells
them to spend money the month no longer has; or the limit of the current month shown on a month they
went back to look at.

## Outcome
`shell.overview` and `home.summary` answer `pendingCount` as the number of transactions pending review
under the one definition the queue and the month's close also use. `home.summary(month)` answers `limit`
as the variable group's cap and spending in the month asked, and `weeks` as the weekly guide of that
month; `review.weekly(month)` answers `limit` (cap, spent, remaining, over, fill) and `week` (the current
week's guide, spent and fill) from the same figures. The pure package `internal/budgetrules` gains the
weeks of a month and the weekly guide, in integer cents. On a server without the app's database every one
of these answers is what it is today, and no golden file under `full/` or `empty/` changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, through `internal/ledger`.
*The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`, where everything the
person authors is kept; the server has one only when started with `--db`. *The stand-in* is the
in-memory fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it and its tests are
the only existing statement of how these figures behave, except where this text says otherwise. *The
contract* is the TypeScript interface `FinwiseApi` under `web/src/api/contract/`; *the manifest* is
`internal/contract/contract.json`, generated from it, which gives Go each method's route, class and
schemas. *A budget* is a list of versions, each valid from a month on; the budget in force for a month is
the latest version at or before it, and a month before the first version uses the first. Its *variable
group* (`var`) holds the lines whose amounts are caps (Mercado, Delivery, ...). *A transaction pending
review* is one the rules that classify new transactions could not decide: it waits in the weekly queue
for the person to say which line it goes on. *A month* is `YYYY-MM` and *a day* `YYYY-MM-DD`, both in
Brazil time (`internal/brday`); "today" and "the current month" are the Brazil day and month of the
instant in the request's context, never of the host's clock. *A golden file* is the committed, exact
answer of one call over an invented fixture. *The gate* is `bin/ci`, the exact checks CI runs.

**What earlier work provides.** None of the following is in the repository when this text is written;
each is delivered before this bead starts, and its interfaces are to be read in the code as that work
left them.

- The per-request views (finwise-jzw): a handler's third parameter carries a view of the ledger (one handle
  and one read-only transaction on the snapshot, so every ledger query of the request sees one snapshot)
  and a view of the app's database (one read-only transaction, or an empty view that answers "nothing
  authored" on a server without `--db`). The clock is a required part of the configuration.
- The third read state (finwise-tsr, in the directory finwise-fst added): read conformance runs over the full
  invented ledger with an invented authored state, with golden files in `internal/api/testdata/golden/full-authored/` and cases in a list
  of their own, `authoredReadCases`, which the interface's equality test does not find;
  `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds invented authored states, one builder per group of tables.
- The budget's tables (finwise-ef7): `budget_versions` and `budget_version_lines` (each line with its id, the
  name its version gives it and its amount in cents), the read of the budget in force for a month, and
  the one function that says which line ids a month's budget has (its lines, and the fees line when it has
  at least one). "A month whose budget has at least one line" is that set being non-empty.
- The transactions' store (finwise-jw2): `tx_index`, `tx_ids` (every provider id mapped to the
  transaction's own key, `tx_key`), and `tx_state`, which holds, among the rest, a transaction's pending
  review (`pending_reason`, `pending_line_id`, `pending_confidence`), with the `authoredtest` builders for
  them.
- The transactions' API side (finwise-tsr): the lookup of a transaction and the merge of a listed transaction
  with its authored state, in Go, by key, inside one request that sees one snapshot of each store.
- The dispositions (finwise-305): `budgetrules.Dispose`, the function that says what a transaction counts
  for: its disposition and the amounts in integer cents it adds to which line ids. A transaction pending
  review is disposition "waiting" and adds nothing; a purchase on a line adds its amount less any linked
  reimbursement; a split adds each part to its line; a refund takes its amount off its refund line; a row
  the bank still reports as pending counts like any other.
- The budget's arithmetic (finwise-jsx): `budgetrules.View`, whose variable group answers `subtotal` (the sum
  of the variable lines' amounts in the budget in force for the month) and `subtotalSpent` (the sum of
  what `Dispose` adds to those line ids over the transactions the API lists in the month, by Brazil day);
  and the percentage rule (P) of that work, one function in `internal/budgetrules`: for `x = n × 100 / d`
  with `d > 0`, `round½↑(x) = ⌊(200·n + d) / (2·d)⌋` with a floor division (half toward positive
  infinity, as JavaScript's `Math.round`), and `share(part, whole)`, which is 0 for a whole of 0 and
  otherwise that rounding held between 0 and 100.
- The ingest (finwise-82m): `ingest.Run`, the one function that brings the app's database up to date with a
  new snapshot. It evaluates every listed transaction dated on or after the month `finwise.db` was created
  in that was never evaluated and whose month's budget has at least one line, and puts in the queue what
  the rules cannot decide, with a reason ("Baixa confiança", "PIX para pessoa sem apelido",
  "Estabelecimento novo"). It also maps a posted row that replaces a bank-pending one to the same `tx_key`,
  so the person's work and a pending review carry over. (The projected run it starts from, read from the
  ledger, is finwise-j4z.)
- The ingest's callers (finwise-st4): `ingest.Run` is called at start, on a timer, by `finwise ingest`, and
  after a budget is saved or applied (after the save's commit and before it answers, because the
  interface refetches the pending count right after; an ingest that fails there does not fail the save).
  This is what fills the queue for real, and what this work needs: without the call after a save, a
  budget saved for a month would leave that month's new purchases out of the count until the next tick.

**What the code is today** (each point read in the file named).

- `internal/api/shell.go`: `readShellOverview` reads the accounts, the sync state and
  `reader.CleanTransactions(ctx, wholeLedger)` (for `firstMonthOf`), and answers `PendingCount` 0 and
  `ClosedMonths` `[]`; its comment says nobody has reviewed or closed anything yet.
- `internal/api/home.go`: `homeSummaryWire` with `Limit monthLimitWire{Cap, Spent}`, `Weeks []any`,
  `NetWorth`, `PendingCount int` and `PayAhead`; `readHomeSummary` parses the month with
  `onlyMonthArgument`, loads the pots without the yield (`loadPots(ctx, reader, false)`, which
  `TestTheHomeHandlerLoadsThePotsWithoutAYield` in `home_test.go` checks by reading the source: exactly
  one call, with `false`) and the card, and answers a zero limit, `Weeks: []any{}` and a zero pending
  count; its comment says the limit and the guides come from a budget nobody has made.
- `internal/api/review.go`: `weeklyLimit{Cap, Spent, Remaining Reais; Over bool; Fill int}`,
  `reviewQueue`, `weeklyReview{Limit, Week any, Queue, Approvals, Warnings}`; `readWeeklyReview` answers
  the zero limit, `week: null` and empty lists. The queue, `resolved`, the approvals and the warnings of

**1. Pending, one definition.** A transaction is pending when all three hold:

1. it is pending in the app's database: its `tx_state` row carries a pending review;
2. the ledger lists it now: one of the provider ids `tx_ids` maps to its key is among the transactions
   the API lists over the whole ledger in the request's snapshot (the same interpreted list
   `transactions.list` shows: a tax row folded into its purchase and a pot movement are not listed);
3. its month's budget has at least one line: the Brazil month of the listed row's day.

It is counted once per `tx_key`, so a bank-pending row and the posted row that replaced it count once.
The count `shell.overview` and `home.summary` answer is the number of such transactions in every month,
not only the month asked, as the stand-in's global count does; both methods answer the same number in one
state. A pending row the ledger stopped listing keeps its authored rows and is in no count; if it is
listed again it counts again. A pending review in a month whose budget ends with no line waits, out of the
count, until the month has a line again. A closed month's pending transactions still count (closing is
refused while they exist, which is the close's own rule).

The same three conditions decide the weekly queue and the month's close (other work: the queue finwise-rf3,
the close finwise-jro). They must be one function, used by all three, so a badge can never count what the queue
does not show. If the queue's work has already built it when this starts, use it; otherwise build it
here, where the queue will find it.

**2. The limit of the month asked.** For month M, with T(var) and the variable spending as the budget's
arithmetic computes them (finwise-jsx), in integer cents:

1. `cap = T(var)`, the sum of the variable lines' amounts in the budget in force for M (0 with no budget
   or no variable line). Not the current month's budget: the stand-in's is a departure this work makes.
2. `spent = Σ F(l)` over the variable lines l of that budget, where `F(l)` is what `Dispose` adds to l's
   id over the transactions the API lists in M, by Brazil day. These two are exactly the `subtotal` and
   `subtotalSpent` of the variable group `budget.view(M)` answers; they come from the same function, not
   from a second computation.
3. `home.summary`'s `limit` is `{cap, spent}`.
4. `review.weekly`'s `limit` is `{cap, spent, remaining = cap − spent, over = remaining < 0, fill =
   share(spent, cap)}`: a whole number from 0 to 100, 0 for a cap of 0, where the stand-in answers a
   fraction.

**3. The weeks of a month and the weekly guide.** The person decided this formula: the weekly guide is
what is left of the month's variable cap shared over the days still to come; a week's guide is the cap
less what was spent before it, times its days over the days to the month's end; one total over the
variable lines. Lost with that decision: equal shares per remaining week, which over-funds the short block
at the month's end, and a guide per line, which the contract and the screen do not have. The prototype's
own figures (500, 470, 400, 355, 142) follow no formula and are not a reference.

For month M with `D` days, today's day `t` (a Brazil day) and `C = cap`:

1. The blocks are the design's: block j (from 0) starts on day `s(j) = 1 + 7j` while `s(j) ≤ D` and ends
   on `e(j) = min(s(j) + 6, D)`. So 01–07, 08–14, 15–21, 22–28, and the days left, if any: a 28-day month
   has four blocks, a 29- to 31-day month five, the fifth of one, two or three days.
2. A block's label is its first and last day, each as two digits, joined by an en dash (U+2013, the
   prototype's `–`): `01–07`, `29–30`, `29–31`. A block of a single day is that day alone: `29` in a 29-day
   February.
3. The blocks exist as dates whether or not the month has a cap: "answered so far" in the weekly queue is
   counted over the block of the current month that holds today (finwise-rf3). They are a function of their
   own, taking only the month, in `internal/brday`; if that work built it first, or it is on `main` when this
   work meets it again, use it and change nothing in it. A second definition of the blocks anywhere is a
   defect.
4. With `C = 0` there are no weeks: `home.summary` answers `weeks: []` and `review.weekly` answers `week:
   null`. That is the case of a month with no budget, of a budget with no variable line, and of variable
   lines that are all 0.00.
5. `before(j)` = the variable spending dated on days 1 to `s(j) − 1` of M, as recorded in the ledger now
   (a sum of `F` restricted to those days; it can be negative only through refunds).
6. `base(j) = max(0, C − before(j))`: never below zero.
7. `n(j) = e(j) − s(j) + 1`, the block's days; `R(j) = D − s(j) + 1`, the days from its first day to the
   month's end, both ends included.
8. `guide(j) = round½↑(base(j) × n(j) / R(j))` to the cent: `⌊(2 · base(j) · n(j) + R(j)) / (2 ·
   R(j))⌋`. All terms are non-negative, so half up and half away from zero agree here.
9. A block has begun when M is before the current month, or M is the current month and `s(j) ≤ t`. A
   block of a month after the current one has not begun.
10. `spent(j)` = the variable spending dated on days `s(j)` to `e(j)` of M when the block has begun, and
    `null` when it has not.
11. `current(j)` is true only for the block holding today: M is the current month and `s(j) ≤ t ≤ e(j)`.
    A past or a future month has no current week.
12. `home.summary`'s `weeks` is every block, in order, as `{label, guide, spent, current}`.
13. `review.weekly`'s `week` is the current block as `{guide, spent, fill = share(spent, guide)}` (0 for a
    guide of 0.00, as the stand-in's), and `null` when M has no current block or no cap.

A consequence the formula carries and that is not a defect: the guide of a block not yet begun is worked
out from what has been spent so far, so it is the share that block would get if nothing more were spent
before it; it moves as the month goes. The guides of a future month, or of the blocks still to come in
the current one, therefore add up to more than what is left of the cap; the last block's guide is always
everything that is left.

**Where this departs from the stand-in on purpose** (each pinned by a test named in the report of the
work): the limit's cap follows the month asked instead of the current month's budget; spending is summed
from the ledger for any month instead of a seeded baseline; the weekly guide is computed instead of
seeded; `fill` is a whole number; pending means pending, listed by the ledger now and in a month whose
budget has a line, instead of every flagged transaction.

**Failure paths that touch this work.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the snapshot is missing | the three reads answer 503 `ledger_unavailable`, as today |
| a pending row vanishes from the ledger without a one-to-one match | it is in no count until it is listed again, and then counts again |
| a pending row is posted under a new id and paired | it counts once, under its key |
| a budget save removes the month's last line | that month's pending reviews leave the count; they return when the month has a line again |
| a save commits during a read | the read's authored view is wholly before or wholly after it |
| the snapshot is swapped during a request | the request finishes on the snapshot its ledger view opened |
| a server without the app's database | every answer here is today's |

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. A real
snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever
printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count, a pending count
included, may be shown to the person running a test and goes into no file; a test that touches a real
ledger runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Nothing here needs one: every ledger and
every authored state is invented. New files of `internal/api` log nothing, and the request log keeps to
verb, route, status, duration and error kind.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional
Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is
integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; the test that forbids floats covers
`internal/api` and the rule packages, and the one that forbids `time.Now` covers them too: today comes
from `nowOf(ctx)`. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant of
`internal/authored`, the only package that executes SQL against `finwise.db`; if reading the pending rows
needs a statement the transactions' work did not add, it is added there, registered and prepared by the
existing test. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; this work writes no
text a person reads beyond the week labels, which are digits and a dash. A design value in a component
comes from a token; this work changes no component. A conformance case that needs authored data is in
`authoredReadCases`, never in `readCases`, whose cases the interface's equality test replays on the
stand-in over an empty ledger. A golden file changes only with `go test ./internal/api -run
TestEveryAnswerMatchesItsGoldenFile -update`, which refuses to run while `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set,
and every changed golden file is read before it is committed.

guide, with its test. In `internal/api`, one new file for the pending definition (unless the queue's work
built it first, in which case it is read, not written), and the three handlers changed in place: the home's
limit, weeks and count, the frame's count, and the limit and week of the weekly review, leaving its queue,
approvals and warnings to the work that owns them. In `internal/authored`, at most one registered
statement that reads the transactions pending review, if the transactions' work did not add it. About five
code files. The contract, the manifest, the interface and the stand-in are read, not changed: no type
changes, and the screens already draw weeks, a null spent and a fill. The budget's arithmetic is called,
not changed.
close_reason: shell.overview and home.summary count what waits for review through the queue's one definition; home.summary answers the month asked's variable limit and its weekly guides, review.weekly its limit and current week, from pure rules in internal/budgetrules in integer cents. Verified: gate green on the branch merged with main; twenty deliberate breaks while writing it and five in review, each failing a named test.

title: Give or approve the design of the proposals' difference view and of the card's approve-all
description:
## Outcome
The person has given, or approved, a design for two things the interface does not have yet: the view
that shows a proposal as the values before and after, and the control that approves at once the waiting
proposals one sentence describes. With it, the item that builds them can port the screens and measure
them against a reference.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *A proposal* is a change an agent (an
assistant on a command line) asked for; the agent never writes directly, and the app applies a proposal
only when the person approves it. Proposals wait on the approvals card of the weekly review
(`web/src/screens/revisao/ApprovalsCard.vue`), each described by one sentence the app writes.

**Why a design is owed.** The person decided on 2026-11-23 that a proposal one sentence cannot describe
is shown as a difference, the values before and the values after: a budget proposal, whose argument is a
whole budget, and a line proposed for one or several purchases already on a line. They also decided that
an "approve all" approves only the proposals a sentence describes and leaves the others waiting to be
opened. The interface is ported from an HTML prototype (`design/README.md` says how a prototype becomes
tokens, reference screenshots and screens), a screen counts as ported when its states pass the parity
measurement on both viewports, and the prototype has neither this view nor that control. Building them
without a reference would be inventing a design.

**What the design must settle.**
1. Where the view opens from a card entry (in place, a side panel as the transaction panel opens, or a
   dialog), at 1440 and at 390 pixels wide, and the control that opens it.
2. For a budget proposal: whether every line is listed or only the lines that change; how an added and a
   removed line read; which totals are shown before and after (income, allocated, investment rate); and
   the month the budget holds from.
3. For a line proposed for one or for many purchases: what each row shows (name, day, amount, the line
   before and after, who placed it), and how twenty rows read on a phone.
4. Whether "Aprovar" and "Recusar" are offered inside the view, on the card entry, or both.
5. "Aprovar tudo": where it sits, its label, from how many waiting one-sentence proposals it shows,
   whether it asks for a confirmation, and how the toast lays out its three counts (approved, closed as
   stale, still waiting to be opened).
6. The names and the steps of the new parity states, and the changed reference of the weekly review's
   state, which holds three waiting proposals in the prototype's dataset.

**How it is delivered.** As a prototype, or an addition to the existing one, from which references can be
shot with `npm --prefix web run parity:reference`; `design/README.md` describes the path from there.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the six points above has an answer in a prototype or in a decision written into this item.
- [ ] The references of the new states exist for both viewports, shot from that prototype.
- [ ] Done when: the item that builds the difference view can port it against a reference without
choosing any of the six points itself.

title: Open every screen on the backend's recorded answers
description:
## What changes for the user
The backend and the screens are written in two languages by different hands, and each is tested against its own idea of the other. A field the backend names slightly differently, or leaves out, would pass both sides' tests and show up as a blank on the person's screen. After this lands every screen is also opened, in the gate, against the exact answers the real backend gives, so that kind of mismatch is caught before anyone sees it.

## Outcome
A test in the interface's suite serves the backend's recorded answers through the API contract and mounts every screen over them, for a ledger with every shape and for an empty one.

## Context
finwise's Go backend records what each of its `read` methods answers over two invented ledgers, as golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/<ledger>/<domain>.<method>.json`; a Go test keeps those files equal to what the handlers return, and they are generated only from invented data. The interface (`web/`) reaches a backend through the `FinwiseApi` contract and already has a sweep test that mounts every route over two states of its in-memory stand-in and fails on a thrown error, an unhandled rejection, or `NaN`, `undefined`, `Infinity`, `null` or `Invalid Date` in the rendered text.

The two sides agree on shape through a JSON Schema generated from the contract, and the Go answers are validated against it. A schema cannot say whether a screen holds on those answers. This bead closes that gap by reusing both existing pieces: the golden files as data, the sweep as the assertion.

**The replay API.** A test helper builds a `FinwiseApi` whose `read` methods answer from the golden files of one ledger and whose other methods reject with the contract's `read_only` error, as the backend does. A method whose arguments select among answers (a month, an id) answers from the file recorded for those arguments; the helper fails loudly when asked for something that was not recorded, so a screen that requests an unexpected month is a finding and not a silent `undefined`. The session methods answer unlocked.

**Where the files are read from.** The golden directory belongs to the Go side and stays there; the test reads it by path from the repository root. It is not copied into `web/`, because a copy can go stale.

**Two implementations, one first day.** The interface's in-memory stand-in and the Go backend each say what an empty ledger looks like, and nothing keeps them saying the same thing: a group label, a default threshold or the shape of an empty budget can drift on one side and every test of both sides still passes. Over the empty ledger there is no bank data to differ, so the two must agree exactly. A test compares, for every `read` method, the backend's recorded answer over its empty ledger with the stand-in's answer over its empty-ledger state, deep-equal, apart from a short written list of fields that legitimately differ (the clock's day, the wording of the sync state) with the reason for each. A difference outside that list is fixed on the side that departed from the contract's intent, and never by adding to the list without a reason.

**What a failure means.** A screen breaking over a golden answer is a real mismatch between the two sides. It is fixed where the fault is: in the handler when the answer departs from the contract's intent, in the screen when the screen assumed more than the contract promises. It is never fixed by editing a golden file by hand.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The replay helper answers every `read` method of the manifest from a golden file, for both recorded ledgers, and a missing file for a `read` method fails the test by name.
- [ ] The sweep mounts every route of `web/src/router.ts`, plus the transaction panel, a pot's page, an account's page, the card page and a subscription's page where the ledger has one, over both ledgers, with the same assertions as the existing sweep.
- [ ] A request for arguments that were not recorded fails the test with the method and the arguments in the message.
- [ ] A write through the replay API rejects with `read_only`.
- [ ] For every `read` method, the backend's recorded answer over the empty ledger equals the stand-in's answer over its empty-ledger state, apart from a written list of excepted fields, each with its reason; changing one label in either side makes the test fail and name the method and the field.
- [ ] Renaming a field in one golden file makes the sweep fail on the screen that reads it.
- [ ] The test runs inside `npm --prefix web test`, and so inside `bin/ci`, with no browser and no running backend.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the sweep passes over both recorded ledgers.

## Tests
- Component: the sweep over every route and both recorded ledgers.
- Unit: the replay helper's coverage of the manifest, its refusal of writes, and its failure on unrecorded arguments.
- The guard is broken once on purpose, by renaming a field in a golden file, and the failing screen named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/test/`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/router.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `bin/ci`

One test helper and one test file. If the sweep finds a mismatch, the fix lands in the handler or the screen at fault, in the same pull request, with a test beside it.
close_reason: A test helper serves the backend's golden files through the API contract and a sweep mounts every route, every listed pot, account and transaction over both recorded ledgers, failing on a thrown error, an unhandled rejection or broken text; a request for arguments that were not recorded fails by name. A second test requires the backend's answers over the empty ledger to equal the stand-in's, apart from a written list of excepted fields with a reason each, and fails on an excepted entry that no longer differs. The sweep found that a pot's page could not be reached from the list because its id holds a slash, fixed in the screen; the comparison found four places where the stand-in's first day departed from the backend's, fixed on the stand-in. bin/ci: CI green on the tree merged with main, 931 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%. The sweep still tolerates a read_only refusal on the scenarios route, which opens with an evaluation; a bug bead carries it.

title: Answer the frame, the accounts and the transactions from the ledger
description:
## What changes for the user
Until now every amount on screen is invented. After this lands, a person who starts the backend against their own ledger and unlocks with the PIN sees their real accounts and their real transactions: the right month, one line per purchase in reais, the tax under the purchase it belongs to, transfers between their own accounts set apart. What the app does not know yet (which budget line a purchase belongs to, tags, nicknames) shows as not filled in, never as a guess.

## Outcome
The backend answers six methods of the interface's contract from the ledger: `shell.overview`, `accounts.list`, `accounts.detail`, `transactions.list`, `transactions.filterOptions` and `transactions.detail`. Every answer is checked against the contract's schema, recorded as a golden file from invented data, and money leaves the server as an exact decimal.

## Context
finwise's interface talks to its backend through a contract described for Go by `internal/contract/contract.json`: for each method a route, a class, and schemas for its arguments and result. The HTTP layer (`internal/api`) already dispatches a `read` method to a handler registered for it, behind the PIN, and keeps a test-side list of reads still without a handler. The ledger reader (`internal/ledger`) returns typed rows in integer cents; `internal/txrules` turns a period's rows into the app's transactions (kind, signed amount, Brazil day, counterpart, establishment key, tax attached to its purchase, movements, pot movements set apart) with a tally that places every row. This bead joins them and is the first to show real data.

**What the rules expect of their caller.** `txrules.Interpret(rows, reference)` takes the reader's rows plus the accounts and the person's own documents, and returns the listed transactions, the tax rows it attached, the pot movements per account and the tally. Four things follow for this bead:
- A tax row is paired only with a purchase among the rows it was given, and a tax can fall up to 3 days from its purchase. Interpreting exactly one month would leave a tax listed on its own when the purchase is in the neighbouring month. Read the period widened by 3 days on each side, interpret, then keep the transactions whose day is inside the period. The month's tally is checked on the widened read; the cut to the period is checked by a test with a purchase on the last day of a month and its tax on the first day of the next.
- A movement (a bill payment, a transfer between own accounts) keeps one of the contract's kinds and carries a `Movement` field; it is not a separate kind.
- An attached tax is already inside its purchase's `Amount` and is also in `Tax`; it is never added a second time.
- A foreign row with no value in reais is flagged `Unconverted` and its amount is not in reais. It must not enter any sum, and the opt-in run over a real ledger reports how many there are.

**What is real and what is empty.** The backend is read-only and has no database of its own yet, so anything only the person can author comes back as on a fresh install. The contract was widened for that beforehand: a field with no honest value on a fresh install is nullable. The rule here is the same: a figure the ledger supports is real; anything else is the contract's empty value; nothing is invented.

| method | from the ledger | empty for now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `shell.overview` | today (the server's clock in America/Sao_Paulo), the first month with a transaction, the current month as the last, the sync state | pending count 0, closed months `[]` |
| `accounts.list`, `accounts.detail` | every current account with its balance, its bank, whether it has been idle for more than 30 days, and an account's transactions | the bucket an account belongs to |
| `transactions.list` | the clean list for the query's period through `internal/txrules`, newest first, filtered as the query asks | budget line, who classified it, confidence, tags, nickname, exclusion, split, reimbursement |
| `transactions.filterOptions` | the accounts | tags `[]`, lines `[]` |
| `transactions.detail` | the same base fields, the tax attached to the purchase, the original amount and currency, the instalment, the bill | history `[]`, notes, every section the person fills; `null` for an unknown id |

With an empty ledger (no account, no transaction) the first and last month are both the current month and every list is empty.

**The sync state.** `shell.overview.sync` is `ok` with the day and time of the last complete run, or a warning with a message when a connection is in trouble (a status other than `UPDATED`, an execution status other than `SUCCESS`, a last update older than 48 hours, or a consent about to expire). A message the person reads is Brazilian Portuguese and lives in one Go file with every other such string; everything else in the code is English. The stand-in's wording in `web/src/api/fake/` is the reference.

**Money on the wire.** The contract carries money as a JSON number in reais with decimals, negative meaning money out. The server holds integer cents. The conversion happens once, in a type whose JSON encoding writes the cents as a decimal literal with two places, so no float arithmetic ever touches an amount. `1999` is written `19.99` and `-6510` is written `-65.10`.

**No total of the month is computed here.** The contract's "spent" figures (the home summary's limit, the weekly review) mean what was spent on the budget's variable lines, and no transaction has a budget line yet, so those figures are 0 in later work and this bead adds no sum over the list.

**Conformance.** A test runs every handler of this bead over two ledgers built by the reader's fixture builder, one with every shape the rules know and one empty, and validates each answer against the method's result schema in the manifest with `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6`, a test-only dependency. The same answers are stored as golden files under `internal/api/testdata/golden/<ledger>/<domain>.<method>.json`; the test fails when an answer differs from its file, and `-update` rewrites them. Because a golden file is committed to a public repository, `-update` refuses to run when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set.

**A real ledger.** A test skipped unless `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set runs every handler over that file for every month it holds, validates every answer against its schema, checks that the tally of each month sums to its input rows, and logs counts only. No value from a real ledger is ever printed, logged or committed.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each of the six methods answers 200 with a valid session, and its answer validates against its result schema over both fixture ledgers.
- [ ] Renaming one JSON field of any answer type makes the conformance test fail.
- [ ] `transactions.list` for February 2026 includes a fixture row dated `2026-03-01T02:30:00Z` and its list for March does not.
- [ ] A fixture purchase with its tax row appears as one line whose detail carries the tax; the tax row has no line of its own.
- [ ] A fixture pot movement is absent from `transactions.list`; a transfer between own accounts is present with the movement kind.
- [ ] Over the empty ledger, `shell.overview` gives the current month as first and last, and every list method answers `[]`.
- [ ] `transactions.detail` answers `null` for an unknown id.
- [ ] A purchase on the last day of a month whose tax row is dated the first day of the next appears in the first month as one line carrying the tax, and the tax row appears in neither month.
- [ ] A snapshot file that exists but is not a SQLite database answers 503 `ledger_unavailable`: the reader returns a typed error for a snapshot it cannot read, and the HTTP layer maps it. Today that case answers `internal`.
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` no longer says that no backend exists, and says how to see real data at the desktop.
- [ ] `1999` cents is encoded as `19.99`, `-6510` as `-65.10`, `0` as `0.00`; no handler converts cents to a float.
- [ ] A fixture connection with a status other than `UPDATED` produces a sync warning whose message is in Portuguese.
- [ ] Running the golden test with `-update` and `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` set fails without writing a file.
- [ ] The pending list of reads without a handler no longer names these six methods.
- [ ] The opt-in test over a real snapshot validates every answer of every month and logs counts only.
- [ ] `go.mod` gains `github.com/santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema/v6` and no other direct dependency.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the opt-in run reports every month's tally summing to its input rows with every answer valid.

## Tests
- Conformance: every answer against the manifest's schema, over both fixture ledgers.
- Golden: every answer against its file.
- Unit: the money encoding; the sync warning; the query's filters and ordering; the cut of a widened read back to its period.
- Integration with `httptest`: each method through the router with a session.
- Integration, opt-in: a real snapshot, counts only.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/`, `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/ledger/safety_test.go`, `go.mod`, `go.sum`, `AGENTS.md`
**Reads only:** `internal/contract/contract.json`, `internal/ledger/`, `internal/txrules/`, `internal/money/`, `internal/brday/`, `web/src/api/contract/`, `web/src/api/fake/`, `bin/ci`

New handler, wire-type and test files in the existing HTTP package, its golden directory, and one test dependency. If a handler needs a ledger query that does not exist, it is added to `internal/ledger` as a new file with its test.
close_reason: The backend answers shell.overview, accounts.list, accounts.detail, transactions.list, transactions.filterOptions and transactions.detail from the ledger. Money is written from integer cents as a decimal with two places and a test forbids floats in the HTTP layer. A month is read three days wider and cut back, so a tax and its purchase across a month's end are one line. Every answer validates against its schema in the manifest over two fixture ledgers and is recorded as a golden file from invented data; the golden update refuses to run with a real snapshot set. A snapshot that is not a database answers ledger_unavailable. bin/ci: CI green. Over a real snapshot every answer of every month validated, every month's tally summed to its input, and every account was placed in exactly one bank; the built server was also called end to end against it. One departure from the bead: a bank account's bucket is a required field of the contract and is answered as available.

title: A refused month close folds the step it was started from
description:
## What changes for the user
In the monthly closing, pressing "Fechar o mês" while the app cannot save shows the message that nothing was changed, and the month does stay open. But the step the person was looking at folds shut, as if something had happened. After this lands a refused close leaves the screen exactly as it was before the click: the step stays open.

## Outcome
A refused or failed close of a month leaves the closing tab's open step open.

## Context
finwise's interface runs against a backend that is read-only for now: every write answers with a `read_only` error, and one central function turns that into a toast ("Somente leitura por enquanto. Nada foi alterado.") and a bump of the revision counter so the screens fetch again. No write call site catches errors itself, on purpose.

The closing tab, `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`, keeps which step is unfolded in its view store. Its `askToClose` sets `view.openStep = -1` before it calls the write that closes the month, so the step folds whether or not the write succeeds. Every other write on the screens changes local state only after the server answered, or not at all; this is the one place found where local state moves first.

The fix belongs in the screen: fold the step only once the close has succeeded. The central failure handling is not changed, and no error is caught here.

A test helper already exists for this kind of check: `web/src/test/readOnly.ts` wraps the stand-in so that every write is refused the way the backend refuses it, and `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts` already refuses a month close through a mounted screen and asserts the toast and the open month.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Mount the Revisão closing tab on the stand-in wrapped by the read-only helper, on an open month.
2. Unfold the last step, "Fechar o mês", and confirm closing the month.
3. Observed: the read-only toast appears and the month is still open, but the step is folded.
4. Expected: the read-only toast appears, the month is still open, and the step is still unfolded.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After a refused "Fechar o mês" through the mounted closing tab, the step that was unfolded is still unfolded.
- [ ] After a successful close on the plain stand-in the step folds, as today.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` still reports every state at or under 0.05%.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` and the regression test fails when the fold is moved back before the write.

## Tests
- Component, regression: a refused close through the mounted closing tab leaves the step unfolded.
- Component: a successful close folds it.
- Parity: the full run, unchanged.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/screens/revisao/ClosingTab.vue`, `web/src/api/refused-writes.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/screens/revisao/useClosingActions.ts`, `web/src/test/readOnly.ts`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`, `bin/ci`

One line moved in one screen and one regression test beside the existing refused-write tests.
close_reason: ClosingTab.vue folds the step only after closeMonth resolved; nothing is caught in the screen, so a rejected write still reaches the central failure handling. The regression test refuses the close through the mounted closing tab and asserts the step stays unfolded, and that a successful close folds it; it failed before the fix and again when the fold was moved back before the write. bin/ci: CI green, 878 tests. Parity: 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%; the template is untouched.

title: Read the ledger's rows once per request and share the reading among the parts of an answer
description:
## What changes for the user
Opening the home screen, the weekly review or the month's closing takes about half a second before
anything of the person's own machine or network is counted, and the same wait comes back after every
change saved, because the screen loads again. It will get longer as the bank history grows. After this
lands, those screens answer in a fraction of that, and every figure on them is exactly what it was.

## Outcome
Within one request, the ledger's transaction rows are read from the snapshot file once, however many parts
of the answer need them. Nothing is kept from one request to the next, so every answer still comes from
the file as it is at that moment. No answer of the API changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is an SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks and replaces by renaming a new file over the old one; the app only
reads it. A request's *view* of the ledger (`internal/ledger`, `(*Reader).View`) opens the file at its first
query and keeps one read transaction until the request ends, so that every query of one answer sees one
state of the file (`Views` in `internal/api/views.go`). *The rows* are what
`(*View).CleanTransactions(ctx, period)` answers (`internal/ledger/transactions.go`); with the period
`wholeLedger` it answers every row. *Interpreting* turns rows into the transactions a list shows
(`txrules.Interpret`). *The app's database* holds what the person authors; it is not part of this item.

**What was measured, on 2026-11-23**, inside the server and over a real ledger, with a scratch database that
held a budget and a series of writes, on one desktop machine. Durations only: no value or count of that
ledger is written anywhere. One reading of every row took about 85 ms; interpreting the whole ledger on top
of it took about 5 to 15 ms. So the cost is the reading, and the slow answers are slow because they repeat
it:

| read | time | readings of the rows | of which reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `review.closing` | 589 ms | 6 | 497 ms |
| `home.summary` | 575 ms | 6 | 489 ms |
| `review.weekly` | 474 ms | 5 | 407 ms |
| `settings.overview` | 386 ms | 4 | 320 ms |
| `budget.view` | 284 ms | 3 | 236 ms |
| `review.payday` | 195 ms | 2 | 162 ms |
| `transactions.detail` | 181 ms | 2 | 161 ms |
| `transactions.list` (one month) | 180 ms | 2 | 161 ms |
| `card.overview` | 178 ms | 2 | 157 ms |
| `shell.overview` | 177 ms | 2 | 158 ms |
| `savingsPots.list` | 339 ms | 1 | 80 ms |
| `netWorth.overview` | 327 ms | 1 | 79 ms |

A write that looks a transaction up reads the rows once and took 80 to 90 ms.

**What the person decided that day.** A screen's read is slow above 200 ms inside the server, and a write
above 150 ms. The repetition is removed first, and only that: one reading per request, shared, with nothing
kept between requests. Keeping the interpreted ledger in memory from one request to the next was held back:
it is a cache that has to be invalidated when the snapshot is replaced, and the failure it can produce is a
figure that disagrees with the ledger, which is the failure that matters in this app. It is looked at again
only if a screen stays above 200 ms after this item, and decided then. A cache in the app's database lost
too: the index of transactions is never the source of a figure.

**What this item should take away,** computed from the table as the time of every reading after the first:
`review.closing` and `home.summary` about 410 ms each, `review.weekly` about 330 ms, `settings.overview`
about 240 ms, `budget.view` about 155 ms, and about 80 ms from each read with two readings. That would put
every read of the table at or under 200 ms except the last two, whose time is elsewhere: the pots' yield
history, which is the subject of `finwise-c6t`.

**Where the readings are, on `main` at the time of writing.** Take the inventory from the code; these are
the ones found:

- rows read whole and not interpreted: `shell.go` (the first month), `accounts.go` (the idle test),
  `review_payday.go` (the salary account);
- rows read whole and interpreted: `listedLedger` in `transaction_target.go`, called by `pending.go` (the
  pending reviews, behind `shell.overview`, `home.summary`, the queue and the closing),
  `subscriptions_charges.go`, `settings_counterparts.go`, `reimbursement_candidates.go` and
  `transaction_line_writes.go`; `card.go` (`loadCard`); `pots_model.go` (`attachMovements`);
- rows read whole to find one transaction: `findListed` in `transaction_target.go`, behind every write that
  names a transaction and behind `transactions.detail`;
- rows read for one widened month: `transactions_period.go`.

One request reaches several of these, each reading for itself. `reimbursement_candidates.go` already shares
one whole listing inside one call with `sync.OnceValues` (`sharedWholeListing`); that is the same idea at a
smaller scope.

**What makes it safe, and what could make it wrong.** A request's view is one read transaction, so a second
reading of the same rows inside it answers the same rows by construction: sharing the first reading changes
no answer. Two things could: sharing a reading across two requests (a request must never see rows another
request read, since the snapshot may have been replaced between them), and a part of the answer changing
the shared rows in place (sorting or rewriting a slice another part reads afterwards). Where the one
reading lives, in the ledger's view or in `Views`, is the implementer's choice, and so is whether a month's
rows are taken from the whole reading when it already exists.

**What a write needs.** A write's lookup compares the snapshot it reads with the run the ingest took in
last, inside its own change, and the router tries the write once more over fresh views after a take-in
(`indexListed` and `requireTakenIn` in `transaction_target.go`, `withSnapshotTakenIn` in `writes.go`). The
second attempt must read the file again: a reading shared within a request's view dies with that view, and
the tests of `take_in_router_test.go` and `take_in_sequences_test.go` pin it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Within one request the ledger's rows are read from the file at most once, shown by a test that counts
the readings for `home.summary`, `review.closing`, `review.weekly`, `settings.overview`, `budget.view`,
`shell.overview` and `transactions.detail` over the invented ledger with an authored state in which a
review waits: one reading each.
- [ ] Two requests read the file once each, shown by the same count; and with the snapshot replaced by
another invented one between two requests, the second request answers from the new one.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is empty,
and the three conformance suites pass unchanged.
- [ ] A part of an answer cannot change the rows another part receives: a test changes the rows one caller
got and finds the next caller's as the file has them.
- [ ] The tests of `take_in_router_test.go` and `take_in_sequences_test.go` pass unchanged, and the second
attempt of a write after a take-in reads the snapshot the take-in left.
- [ ] Nothing outlives a request: no package-level variable and no field of the router, of the reader or of
the registry holds rows, shown by the test of two requests above failing when the reading is kept on the
reader.
- [ ] Each rule was seen failing once, by breaking it on purpose, and the record names the test that failed:
a second reading inside one request; the reading kept from one request to the next; a caller changing the
shared rows.
- [ ] The time of each read of the table is measured again over a real ledger **by the review, not by the
implementer**, three runs each, before and after, and written in the pull request as durations alone. The
review says which reads are at or under 200 ms and which are not.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: one request reads the ledger's rows once, no answer and no golden file changed, and the
review's timings are in the pull request.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/ledger` or `internal/api`, wherever the reading lives: one reading per view however
many times the rows are asked for; a new view reads again.
- Integration, in `internal/api`: the count of readings per request for the reads named above, through the
router; two requests; a snapshot replaced between two requests; a caller that changes its rows.
- Golden: none moves; the conformance suites of reads, authored reads and writes pass unchanged.
- Existing, unchanged: the take-in tests of the write side.
- Timing: none by the implementer; the review measures over a real ledger and prints durations only.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/view.go`, `internal/ledger/transactions.go`, `internal/api/views.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_target.go`, `internal/api/pending.go`, `internal/api/card.go`,
`internal/api/pots_model.go`, `internal/api/subscriptions_charges.go`, `internal/api/settings_counterparts.go`,
`internal/api/reimbursement_candidates.go`, `internal/api/shell.go`, `internal/api/accounts.go`,
`internal/api/review_payday.go`, `internal/api/transactions_period.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_line_writes.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/writes.go`, `internal/api/take_in_router_test.go`,
`internal/api/take_in_sequences_test.go`, `internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `internal/txrules/`, `bin/ci`

Two packages. If the reading is shared inside the ledger's view, the files of `internal/api` in the list may
need no edit at all, and the diff is the two files of `internal/ledger` and tests; if it is shared in
`Views`, each caller in the list changes by the line that reads. No contract type, no store function and
nothing of the interface is touched.

## Recovery path
Nothing stored changes. Reverting the pull request brings the repeated readings back and nothing else.

title: Journal every change to the app's database through one recorder and undo by inverse, refusing what was overwritten since
description:
## What changes for the user
Today nothing in the app can be changed, so nothing can be taken back. In the design the person sees
"Desfazer" in a message for eight seconds after each change, and again beside each step of a
purchase's history; in the prototype that button quietly puts the whole app back to an earlier
picture, wiping anything changed in between. This work builds what will stand behind those two
buttons: each thing the person changes is remembered as one change with who made it, taking it back
restores exactly that change and nothing else, and when what it would overwrite has been changed
again since, it refuses and says so ("Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito.")
instead of destroying the later edit. Nothing is visible yet, because no button writes until later
work. If this were wrong the person would see an undo bring back the wrong category on a purchase, or
erase a later correction without a word.

## Outcome
`internal/authored` gains the layer every later write goes through. A closed, hand-written registry
names the journaled tables in two shapes, says for a table of independent facts which of two kinds it
is, and says which table is owned by another. A recorder holds one immediate
transaction and one open change and is the only way a journaled table is written; every effect lands
in `change_effects`, and a change that records nothing and is never asked for its id leaves no trace.
Undo restores a change's effects by inverse in one transaction and refuses, changing nothing, when the
change is unknown, already undone, or followed by a later change still in force on anything it would
restore, even one that put the old value back. A change can be extended so one undo takes back both
writes. The same inverse works over a chosen part of a change,
recorded as a new change, with a read-only answer to "can this still be taken back". A canonical dump
of every registered table exists for proofs. Guards fail when a table is unclassified or is written
outside the recorder. No route and no handler is added.

## Context
finwise is a personal finance app for one person. The **ledger** is a SQLite snapshot a separate
collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. The **app's own database**,
`finwise.db`, is where everything the person authors lives; `internal/authored` is the only package
that executes SQL against it. **The stand-in** is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how
writes behave, and its behaviour is the rule except where this text says otherwise. The **journal** is
the record of every change made to authored data: each write is one change with an author, made of
effects, and can be undone.

**What exists when this starts.** The work that creates the database (finwise-9h2) has landed:
`internal/authored` recognises and opens `finwise.db` as a pool in which every connection has
`foreign_keys(1)`, `busy_timeout(5000)`, `synchronous(FULL)`, `journal_mode(WAL)` and immediate write
transactions; it offers a read-only transaction and an immediate write transaction; it applies
embedded migrations recorded by name and checksum; and every statement it runs is a registered
constant that a test prepares against the migrated schema, with a test that fails on a statement
outside the registry and one that forbids floats in the package. Its migration `0001_journal` created
the journal's tables:

- `changes(id, at, day, author, method, extended, undone_at)`: `id` is
  `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`, never reused; `at` the instant and `day` its Brazil day;
  `author` one of `person`, `rule`, `model`; `method` the API method that made the change; `extended`
  whether a later write appended to it; `undone_at` null until undone.
- `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`: one row per effect, ordered by `seq`
  within its change.
- `meta(key, value)`, which this bead does not use.

Read the package as it is before writing: file and function names are whatever that work chose. This
bead adds no migration and does not edit `0001_journal.sql`: every database that has started with it
holds its checksum and would be refused at the next start. If the recorder turns out to need a column
that file lacks, stop and say so in the report instead of editing the file or inventing a migration
name: migration names are assigned in advance, one owner each, and none is assigned to this work.

**The decision, and what lost.** Undo is the inverse of recorded effects, refused when what it would
overwrite has changed since; the same rule serves the undo of one history step. Why: the stand-in's
undo restores a snapshot of the whole state, which silently destroys later changes, and with money
refusing is the safe failure. What lost: snapshot restore; last writer wins; restoring a step over
later edits. This is a deliberate departure from the stand-in, where `createChangeLog`
(`web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`) clones the state with `structuredClone` when a change begins and
`undo` assigns the clone back, and where `undoHistoryStep` (`transaction-edits.ts`) assigns a step's
saved fields back whatever happened to them since. What the stand-in's tests say that stays true:
an unknown change and one already undone are refused (`writes.test.ts`, "refuses a change it does not
know, or one already undone"); one undo takes back a change together with the one that extended it
("takes back the establishment-wide change together with the one it extended"); taking a step back
does not touch what was done after it, and can itself be undone (`panel-writes.test.ts`, "taking a
step back"). The departure is named in the report together with the test that pins it.

**The registry and the two shapes.** All changes to authored tables go through the recorder. The
recorder works from a closed, hand-written registry of the journaled tables. Each entry says which of
two shapes the table has, its key columns, and how a key and a row are written as canonical JSON (keys
as an array in column order):

- an **attribute table** holds one row of independent facts per key (a transaction's state, an
  establishment, a subscription, a setting). An effect is one column changing:
  `(change, seq, table, key, column, before, after)`. The registry says which of two kinds such a
  table is.
  - In a **table of optional facts** (a transaction's state, an establishment, a pot's settings) every
    column has a default, and a row whose columns are all at their defaults is the same as no row: the
    first fact written about a transaction creates its row without owning it, so taking that fact back
    later leaves the others alone.
  - In a **table of things that are created whole** (a subscription), some columns are required, and
    creating the row is itself a unit: a later change to any column of it makes the change that
    created it stale, so undo never leaves half a row behind.

  A restore is computed for the whole row and written once, never column by column.
- a **set table** holds rows that are facts by existing (a tag on a transaction, a split part, a line
  in a budget version, a closed month, a history step). An effect is one row appearing or
  disappearing: `(change, seq, table, key, null, before, after)`.

A table that is not in the registry cannot be written through the recorder, and a test fails when any
statement that inserts, updates or deletes in an authored table is executed outside it. A **unit** is
what one effect is about: a table, a key and, for an attribute table, a column; in a table of things
created whole, the creation of a row is one more unit of the change that created it. So the registry
entry of an attribute table carries its kind, and the two kinds behave differently at exactly one
point. In a table of optional facts there is no such thing as creating a row: two changes to
different columns of one key are independent of each other and each can be undone without the other,
whichever of them came first and whether or not a row existed before. In a table of things created
whole, the same independence holds between changes to a row that already exists, but the change that
created the row cannot be undone while any later change to that row is still in force.

None of those tables exists yet; each arrives with its own migration in later work, which adds its
entries to the registry. So the registry this bead ships has no production entry, and everything here
is proved on scratch tables that the tests create and register. The recorder therefore takes its
registry as a value: the package's own in production, a test's in a test.

**A table owned by another.** Some facts belong to a row of another table without being part of it,
and the registry can say that one table is owned by another. The one the write side needs is the
reason a person gives for a correction: it belongs to its history step but is kept beside it, in a
table the step owns (`history_step_reasons(step_id, reason)`, created later with the transactions'
tables (finwise-jw2)). The point of keeping it beside: giving a reason does not make the line change stale,
so "apply to all purchases here" and the "Desfazer" of the message still work after it; and taking the
line change back takes its reason with it. Removing a row removes the rows it owns and records them as
effects of the same change, so they come back with it. The reason a transaction's detail answers is
the one on its latest step that has one; it is stored nowhere else. For the recorder that is three
requirements. Writing an owned row is an effect on the owned row's own unit and on no unit of the
change that made the owner, so neither undo nor extension of that change is refused because of it.
Removing the owner, by a recorded write or by an undo, removes its owned rows in the same transaction.
And when a recorded write removes an owner, the disappearance of each owned row is an effect of that
same change, so undoing it brings owner and owned rows back exactly. A foreign key with a cascading
action would delete rows the recorder never saw and never recorded.

**Tables deliberately not journaled, by name:** `changes` and `change_effects` (the journal itself),
`schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index` and `tx_ids` (what the database remembers about the
transactions it has seen: observations, not decisions), `lines` (a budget line's id, once minted,
exists for good) and `pin` (changing the PIN is not a recorded change and has no undo). Most of these
do not exist yet either; the list is written now so that a table added later which is in neither list
is caught. Writes to these tables happen in the same transaction as the change they accompany and are
not effects: undoing the change leaves them.

**A change.** A write handler receives a recorder that already holds one immediate transaction and
the facts of a change: author, method, the instant and the Brazil day (`brday.DayOf` of the instant;
the package never reads the host's clock). The change's row is written with its first effect, or when
the handler asks for the id because it must answer one; a handler that does neither leaves no trace in
the journal. It performs its recorded writes and returns; the caller commits. The change id is the
handle the API returns, as a decimal string; ids are never reused and are the same for the same
sequence of writes, which the golden files of later work rely on. Any failure rolls the whole thing
back. Authors are `person` (an HTTP session), `rule` (the step that brings the database up to date
with a new snapshot and classifies new transactions by rule) and `model` (reserved for a later nightly
model call). The journal is never trimmed.

That one rule about when the row is written gives the three endings the write side needs. Where a
method's result may be null, "nothing to do" and "no such target" answer null and record nothing: the
handler writes no effect and asks for no id, so no row exists. Where the result may not be null, a
write that changes nothing records an empty change and answers its id, whose undo is a no-op: the
handler asks for the id, so the row exists with no effect, and its undo succeeds. And the step that
classifies by rule records one change for a whole run only if anything authored changed; with nothing
to record, no change is written. It follows that a recorded write whose content equals what is already
there records no effect, and so by itself writes no row.

**Undo**, in one immediate transaction with foreign keys deferred to the commit:

1. Collapse the change's effects per unit (a table, a key and, for an attribute table, a column): the
   first `before`, the last `after`.
2. If the change is unknown or already undone, or a later change that is still in force has an effect
   on any of those units, refuse (the API will answer `refused` with the reason `stale_change`) and
   change nothing. The journal's order decides, not the value: a unit set from A to B, then to C, then
   back to B by later changes is not the first change's to take back. As a guard against a write that
   escaped the journal, a unit whose current content differs from that `after` is refused the same
   way. So is a restore that the database's own constraints refuse (a unique column whose old value
   another row has taken meanwhile): the state it would bring back is no longer possible, so the
   undo is rolled back whole and answered as stale, never as an internal failure.
3. Otherwise restore every `before`, in reverse order of `seq`.
4. Before committing, run the checks that other packages register with the engine: functions that
   look at the database inside the undo's transaction and say whether the restored state is one the
   app allows. None exists yet; the first two arrive with the budget and the closing of a month (the
   budget of a closed month must be what it was before the undo, and no transaction may be left on a
   line its month's budget lacks). A failing check rolls the undo back whole and is answered as
   stale. An undo never repairs by itself: it has no change to record a repair in.
5. Mark the change undone. Undo returns nothing and is not itself undoable.

A change is in force while it is not undone, so once the later changes are themselves undone, newest
first, the earlier one can be undone again. In a table of things created whole, for the change that
created a row, any later change in force to any column of that row counts as an effect on its
creation; in a table of optional facts nothing does, because no change owns a row there. In step 3
the order is the order of rows: the `before`s that fall on one attribute row are combined and that
row is written once, or removed once when the change created it whole. The reverse order matters for
what SQLite cannot defer, such as a unique value handed from one row to another inside one change,
and the criterion below about that case binds whatever the implementation does with a unit written
more than once. A restore that the database refuses, or that leaves a foreign key unsatisfied at the
commit, rolls the whole undo back.

`internal/authored` knows no HTTP. It reports a refusal as a typed error of its own. The `refused`
kind and its list of reasons are added to the API's contract by separate work (finwise-our); turning the
typed error into the wire answer `{"error":{"kind":"refused","reason":"stale_change"}}` (HTTP 409),
and the handler of `changes.undo` itself, belong to the write dispatch, the part of the router that
hands a write method to its handler and commits (finwise-2s5). The sentence the person reads, "Isso já foi
alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito.", lives in the interface.

**Extending a change.** One write of the API, "apply to all purchases here"
(`transactions.applyLineToEstablishment(changeId)` in `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`: "Extends
a line change to the rest of its establishment; undoing it undoes both"), adds to a change already
committed. It happens in one immediate transaction that requires the origin to be a live `setLine`
change, not yet extended, whose own effects still hold; it appends its effects to the origin, marks it
extended and returns the same id, so one undo takes back both. Anything else is `stale_change`. This
bead builds the mechanism, with the required method given by the caller: reopen a committed change as
a recorder, after checking that it exists, is not undone, was made by that method, is not yet
extended, and that its effects still hold, tested the way step 2 of undo tests them: no later change
in force on any of its units, and every unit still holding its last `after`. One case is not
staleness and is not decided here: an origin whose transaction is a person or a movement between own
accounts has no establishment to extend to and is answered `not_found`. That case and the handler are
later work (finwise-yfu, the writes that put a transaction on a budget line).

**One part of a change.** A transaction's history is a table of steps, each tied to the change that
produced it and of one of two kinds: a step that records what the change did to the transaction, and
a note (such as "rule created") that records that something happened beside it. Taking one step back
(`undoHistoryStep(id, stepId)`: "Restores the state before that step alone and drops the step from
the history") opens a new change that applies steps 1 to 3 to the units of that one transaction that
the step's change touched, then deletes the step. Because effects are per column, taking back "marked
as refund" leaves a refund line chosen later untouched, as the stand-in's test expects; and a step
whose columns were changed again since is refused instead of overwriting the later edit.
`HistoryEntry.undoable` is computed with the same comparison and is always false for a note, so the
panel offers only what can be taken back. A transaction's state is a table of optional facts, so this
holds in every case, including when the refund mark was the first thing ever authored on the
transaction: that first fact made the row without owning it. Being a recorded change, a step's undo
can itself be undone with `changes.undo`. Taking a line step back always leaves the "why" question closed (after
some corrections the app asks the person why; whether it is asking is part of the transaction's
state, and closing it is one more recorded write of the same new change). The steps table arrives with the
transactions' tables (finwise-jw2) and the handler with the writes that put a transaction on a budget line
and keep its history (finwise-yfu); what this bead builds is the mechanism they call: the same three steps
