over a subset of a change's units chosen by the caller, performed inside another open change so that
the restores are that change's effects, without marking the source change undone and with the
recorder still open for the caller's further writes; and a read-only function that says whether that
inverse would be refused, usable inside a read-only transaction.

**Canonical JSON, the dump, and floats.** `key`, `before` and `after` are canonical JSON, compared as
text. The form of a row and of a value is the implementer's, with three constraints: a key is an array
in column order; the form is deterministic (the effects of a write are later compared with golden
files, and the journal is never trimmed, so values written today are compared against content rendered
years later); and no number passes through a float. That last one has a trap the package's float guard
cannot see: decoding a stored value into `any` turns every number into a `float64` without the word
appearing in the source. Amounts are integer cents (`money.Cents`) and travel as integers. The proofs
compare a canonical dump of every registered table, in which a row of a table of optional facts at
its defaults is the same as no row. The write conformance harness that later proves every write of
the API can be undone (finwise-fst) needs that same dump for every journaled table, so it is a function of
the package, not a helper buried in a test.

**The statement discipline meets the recorder here.** Every SQL statement over the app's database is a
registered constant. A recorder that assembled SQL from table and column names at run time would run
statements no test ever prepared, so each registry entry names the registered constants that read and
write its table, and no SQL text is assembled per call. Scratch tables and their statements live in
test files, which the discipline does not cover.

**What later work will ask of it,** so the design can be checked against real use: one change that
writes many rows across several tables and is undone as one (saving a budget removes later versions
with their lines, parent and children, and clears lines from transactions' state; a bulk write over
many transactions; settling a pending transaction changes its line, its establishment's default and a
nickname at once); a set row whose other columns change while its key stays (a split part that keeps
its place and loses its line); set rows with minted ids restored under the same id (a history step);
a unique value handed from one row to another inside one change (a line name within a budget
version); and a count of the changes made by one method, not undone, on given days, read from
`method`, `undone_at` and `day`, which must therefore be written faithfully.

**Failure paths this bead owns.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept; the API answers `internal` |
| an undo meets a later change | `stale_change`; nothing is restored |
| two tabs, or a tab and the rule step, write at once | writes queue; each is its own change; an undo that lost the race is refused |

**Left to the implementer** (what makes this bead `spec:open`): the canonical form of a row and of a
value, within the constraints above; how a registry entry is represented, how it says which kind an
attribute table is and how it says a table is owned; how the creation of a row in a table of things
created whole is written in `change_effects`, within the columns that table has; whether a row of a
table of optional facts is deleted or kept when it returns to its defaults, the two being the same to
every reader and to the dump; the mechanism of the guard against
writes outside the recorder (a scan of the source, or a check at run time), as long as it fails on the
break named in the criteria; and how many random sequences the property test runs and how long they
are, as long as every run reaches every operation listed under Tests, a failure prints what
reproduces it, and the default `go test` run stays fast enough for the gate.

**Privacy and conventions.** No test here touches a real ledger; the tables are scratch and the
content invented, so a failing sequence may be printed in full. Work happens in the worktree it was
given and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of
a session, a work item or a plan in a commit message. Money is integer cents and no float may appear
in the money path. Every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant. Interface
text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; a design value in a component comes from
a token (neither arises here). The package logs nothing and prints nothing.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A recorded write to a table that is not in the registry returns an error and writes nothing.
- [ ] On a scratch attribute table of either kind, on a row that already exists, changing one column
records exactly one effect whose `tbl`, `key` (a JSON array in column order), `col`, `before` and
`after` are that unit's; changing two columns records two; writing the content already there records
none. In a table of optional facts, the first fact written for a key that has no row records that
column's effect and nothing that makes the change the owner of the row. In a table of things created
whole, creating a row is recorded so that the change is known to have created it.
- [ ] On a scratch set table, a row appearing records one effect with `col` null, `before` null and
`after` the row; a row disappearing records `before` the row and `after` null.
- [ ] A change opened with the instant 2026-12-01T01:30:00Z, author `person` and a method name stores
that method, that author and the day `2026-11-30`; an author outside `person`, `rule`, `model` is
refused; the id returned is the row's id.
- [ ] The row of a change is written at its first effect, or when its id is first asked for, whichever
comes first, and once. A recorder that records no effect and is never asked for its id leaves no row
in `changes` or `change_effects` after its transaction commits, and the next change gets the id that
one would have had. A recorder asked for its id that records no effect leaves one `changes` row and
no effect; the undo of that change succeeds, changes nothing and sets `undone_at`; a second undo of
it is refused.
- [ ] A recorder that fails after two recorded writes leaves the dump and both journal tables exactly
as they were; a recorded write and a plain write to a non-journaled table made in the same change
commit together and roll back together.
- [ ] Undo of a change restores the dump taken before the change, for both shapes and both kinds; for
a key of a table of optional facts that had no row before, the dump is equal whether or not a row at
its defaults is left behind.
- [ ] Undo is refused, with the dump and both journal tables unchanged, for: an id that does not
exist; a change already undone; a change one of whose units a later change still in force has an
effect on; a change one of whose units holds something other than its last `after` because a write
went around the journal.
- [ ] The order decides, not the value: after a first change sets a unit from A to B, a second sets it
to C and a third sets it back to B, undoing the first is refused although the unit holds B, the first
change's own `after`. Once the third and then the second are undone, the first is undone and the unit
holds A.
- [ ] A change that wrote one unit twice (from A to B, then to C) is undone when the unit holds C,
restoring A.
- [ ] In a table of optional facts, a first change writes one column of a key that has no row, a second
change writes another column of that key, and the first is undone: the undo succeeds, the first
column is back at its default and the second keeps its value. Undoing the second as well leaves the
dump equal to the one taken before either.
- [ ] In a table of things created whole, a change creates a row, a second change changes one column of
it, and undoing the creation is refused with nothing changed. Once the second change is undone, the
creation is undone and the row is gone whole.
- [ ] In a table of either kind, for a row that existed before both, two changes to different columns
of one key are independent: either is undone while the other is in force, and the other's column
keeps its value.
- [ ] A restore writes each attribute row once: on a scratch table of optional facts with a constraint
spanning two columns, a change that sets both columns in one recorded write is undone without the
database refusing any statement on the way; on a scratch table of things created whole, undoing the
creation removes the row without any statement emptying a required column first.
- [ ] After an undo, `changes` has the same number of rows as before it, the undone row's `undone_at`
is the instant given, and its effects are still in `change_effects`.
- [ ] A change that removes or creates a parent row and its children, recorded parent first and
recorded children first, is undone to the exact previous dump in both orders, with foreign keys
enforced at the commit.
- [ ] A change that deletes a row and then inserts another row taking over a unique value of the
first is undone without a constraint failure.
- [ ] An undo whose restore the database refuses (a unique value taken since by a row the change
never touched) fails and leaves the dump and both journal tables unchanged.
- [ ] Extension: a committed change made by the required method, not undone, not extended, whose
effects still hold by the test of undo's step 2, is reopened; the effects recorded then carry the
origin's id with `seq` continuing; the origin is marked extended; the id handed back is the origin's;
one undo restores the dump from before the origin. It is refused as stale, changing nothing, for: an
unknown id; an undone change; a change made by another method; a change already extended; a change one
of whose units a later change in force has an effect on, also when that change put the value back.
- [ ] Inverse of a part: over a caller-chosen subset of a change's units, inside another open change,
the selected units return to their `before`, the unselected ones keep their content, the restores are
recorded as effects of the open change, the source change is not marked undone, and undoing the new
change puts the selected units back. It is refused, changing nothing, when a later change in force
has an effect on a selected unit, and is not refused because one has an effect on an unselected unit.
- [ ] The read-only check agrees with the inverse of a part: in the property test, for every state
reached, it says "can be taken back" exactly when the inverse then succeeds, and it runs inside a
read-only transaction.
- [ ] Owned rows: writing a row of a table owned by a set table does not make the change that created
the owner stale, for undo and for extension; undoing that change removes the owner and its owned rows;
a recorded removal of an owner that has owned rows records one effect for the owner and one for each
owned row in the same change, and its undo restores owner and owned rows to the exact previous dump.
- [ ] A column set to 9007199254740993 (2^53 + 1, which no `float64` holds), then changed, then
restored by undo, holds 9007199254740993 again, and the journal's `before` and `after` for it hold
that integer exactly.
- [ ] Every table of the migrated schema, SQLite's own `sqlite_` tables aside, is either in the
registry or in the list of tables deliberately not journaled, which names `changes`,
`change_effects`, `schema_migrations`, `meta`, `tx_index`, `tx_ids`, `lines` and `pin`; a table in
neither, or in both, fails a test.
- [ ] A statement that inserts, updates or deletes in a registered table and is executed outside the
recorder fails a test.
- [ ] With two handles on one file: after a write through one handle commits a change to a unit, an
undo through the other handle of an earlier change to that unit is refused and nothing is restored;
an undo begun while another write transaction is open waits for it and then decides on what that
write left.
- [ ] The property test passes: random sequences of recorded writes over scratch tables of both
shapes and both kinds of attribute table, in which write then undo returns the exact previous dump,
undo after an interfering write is refused and changes nothing, also when later writes put the old
value back (A to B, then C, then B), a first fact is taken back from under a second in a table of
optional facts, the creation of a whole thing is refused while a later change to its row is in force,
and a parent and its children are restored whatever their order.
- [ ] The package's existing tests still pass with the new statements: every new constant is
registered and prepares against the migrated schema, and no file of the package uses a float.
- [ ] `internal/authored/migrations/0001_journal.sql` is byte-identical to what it was, and no file
outside `internal/authored/` is changed.
- [ ] The report names the test that pins the departure from the stand-in: an undo that would
overwrite a later change is refused, where the stand-in restores its snapshot over it.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, and the report names the break used for each: step 2
removed altogether (an interfering write is then overwritten); step 2 deciding by the value alone (the
A, B, C, B case is then undone); the guard on current content removed (a write that went around the
journal is then overwritten); a later change counted although it was undone; the creation of a row
in a table of things created whole not treated as a unit (the creation is then undone under a later
change); the first fact in a table of optional facts treated as owning its row (taking it back is
then refused once a second fact exists); an attribute row restored column by column (the database
refuses a statement on the way); the change's row written when the recorder opens (a handler that
does nothing leaves a row); the restores run in forward order; the collapse keeping a unit's first
`after` instead of its last; `undone_at` not set (a second undo succeeds); foreign keys not deferred;
the "not yet extended" check removed; the owned rows left behind when their owner goes, or removed
without being recorded; a number decoded through `any`; a write to a registered table added outside
the recorder; a table left out of both lists.
- [ ] On a scratch table with a unique column: a change moves row A's value away, a second change gives
that value to row B, and undoing the first change is refused as stale with every table left exactly as
it was, not reported as an internal error.
- [ ] The engine accepts registered checks that run after the restore and before the commit, inside the
same transaction: with a check registered on a scratch table that refuses a given restored state, an undo
that would produce that state is refused as stale and every table is exactly as it was; with the check
accepting, the same undo succeeds. The undo of one transaction's part of a change (the history step's
undo) runs the same checks.
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, the property test passes, and an interfering write makes
undo refuse with nothing changed, also when it put the old value back.

## Tests
- Property, over scratch tables created and registered by the test in a temporary database (an
attribute table of optional facts, every column with a default and a constraint spanning two of them;
an attribute table of things created whole, with required columns; a set table; a table owned by the
set table; and a parent and child pair joined by a foreign key): random sequences that every run
takes through both kinds of attribute table. For optional facts: a first fact on a key with no row,
then a second fact on another column by another change, then the undo of the first, after which the
second survives. For things created whole: the creation of a row, then a change to one column of it,
then the undo of the creation, which is refused. And through: a write on an existing row of each
kind, a set insert, a set delete, a set row whose other columns change, an owned write, a parent with
children in both orders, a change that records nothing, an empty change, an extension, an inverse of
a part, an interfering write, a unit taken from A to B, then C, then back to B by three changes, and
an undo; after each undo the canonical dump is compared with the one taken before. A failure prints
what reproduces it.
- Table: the refusals of undo and of extension, one row per cause, the later change that put the value
back and the write that went around the journal among them; a later change that was itself undone no
longer refusing; the three endings of a change (no trace, an empty change, a change with effects); the
collapse (A to B to C); per-column independence in both kinds of attribute table, including a first
fact taken back from under a second in a table of optional facts; the creation of a whole thing
refused while a later change to its row is in force, and undone once that change is.
- Unit: the journal rows a change leaves (`changes` and `change_effects`, field by field); the
integer 9007199254740993 through write, change and undo; a unique value changing hands; a restore the
database refuses.
- Unit, two handles on one temporary file: an undo that lost the race to a write; an undo that waits
for an open write.
- Unit, guards: every table classified; no write to a registered table outside the recorder; the
package's statement and float scans over the new files.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/authored/`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/migrations/0001_journal.sql`, `web/src/api/fake/changes.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/history.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/transaction-edits.ts`, `web/src/api/fake/writes.test.ts`,
`web/src/api/fake/panel-writes.test.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/changes.ts`,
`web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`, `web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`, `internal/brday/`,
`bin/ci`

One package: the registry, the recorder, the journal's statements, undo with its two variants, the
canonical form and the dump, and their tests; six or seven new code files and no edit outside
`internal/authored/`. It is one package, and `size:L` only by that count of files. The migration file
is read and not edited. `internal/api` and `cmd/finwise` are not touched: nothing calls the recorder
until the write dispatch exists.
close_reason: internal/authored has the journal: a recorder that is the only way a journaled table is written (Set, Create, Put, Delete, ID, RestorePart), Change, Extend, Undo, CanRestorePart and the canonical Dump, over a hand-written registry of attribute tables (optional facts, things created whole) and set tables. Undo is decided by the journal's order, then by what each row holds, then by the database's constraints and the registered checks; every refusal changes nothing. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main. Review: eleven independent mutations; nine failed tests, two survived at first (a column and the whole row of one thing written in one change: a wrong restore, and a wrong refusal) and now fail two deterministic tests and the property test on 200 of 200 seeds. The implementer's thirty breaks each failed a test, three after a fix to the guard or a new test.

title: Let a write read the app's database in its own transaction, let a handler extend a change, and release the write lock when anything panics
description:
## What changes for the user

Nothing the person can see yet: no screen and no answer changes. This finishes the one door every later
save goes through, so that the saves built next (the budget, the settings, a transaction's line) cannot be
built on a gap. Without it, three things would go wrong later and silently: a save that checks something
and then writes could decide on a state another save changed in between; "apply to all purchases here"
would have no way through the door; and one crash inside a save or an undo would leave every later save
waiting five seconds and failing, until the server is restarted.

## Outcome

A write handler reads the app's database through a view of its own transaction and sees its own writes. A
handler that acts on a committed change receives the request's ledger view and can extend a change as well
as undo one. A panic anywhere inside a journal transaction (a write, an extension, an undo, a registered
check) rolls it back, so the next write gets the lock at once. The router checks the arguments of every
handler shape against the manifest, and a test holds that for the shape that acts on committed changes.

## Context

The dispatch of writes is built (`internal/api/writes.go`): a `WriteHandler` gets `Writes{Ledger,
Recorder}` and runs inside `(*authored.Database).Change`, which the router commits; a `JournalHandler` gets
a `Journal` (today only `Undo`) and runs with no transaction of the router around it, because the engine's
`Undo` and `Extend` each open their own immediate transaction (`journalTransaction` in
`internal/authored/recorder.go`) and would otherwise wait for a lock their own request holds. Three gaps
were found while it was reviewed.

**1. A write cannot read.** The recorder writes (`Set`, `Create`, `Put`, `Delete`) and answers the change's
id; it reads nothing. Every read of the app's database is a method of `*authored.View`
(`internal/authored/view.go`: one read-only transaction, `TrackingStartMonth`, `LastBackup`, and each later
domain adds its own). A write handler that must look before it writes (is the month closed, does this
line exist in that month's budget, what is stored now) has nothing to look with. A second, separate view
would be wrong: it would not see what the same request already wrote, and it would read outside the write
lock, so two requests could each check and then each write.

The decision: the recorder hands out a view over its own transaction, `(*Recorder).View() *View`, so that
a read is written once, as a method of `*View`, and works unchanged in a read handler and inside a write.
`Writes` gains `Authored *authored.View`, set by the router to that view, beside `Ledger`; a helper shared
by a read handler and a write handler then takes the two views and does not care which it serves. Closing
that view must not end the write's transaction. After the change has ended, a read through it answers the
closed-view error. While the recorder has failed, a read through it answers that failure, because the
transaction is then in a state no effect describes. Rejected: read methods on the recorder itself (every
read would be written twice, and the two copies would drift).

**2. A handler of the journal shape has no ledger and no extension.** "Apply to all purchases here"
extends the change that set one transaction's line: it must find the other purchases of that
establishment in the ledger and append their effects to the earlier change, so that one undo takes back
both (`(*Database).Extend(ctx, origin, method, write)`). `Extend` opens its own transaction, so that
method cannot be a `WriteHandler`; it has to be of the journal shape, which today receives neither the
ledger view nor `Extend`. The handler itself arrives with the transaction's line writes; what is built here
is the shape it will use: the journal shape receives the request's ledger view, opened at its first query
and closed at every ending of the request, as a write's is, and the `Journal` interface gains `Extend`.
Inside the function given to `Extend` the handler has the recorder, and through it the view of point 1.
What a journal handler returns is still encoded after the engine's call committed, so its result must be
one that cannot fail to encode; that stays as it is.

**3. A panic leaves the write lock held.** `journalTransaction` rolls back when the function it runs
returns an error and commits when it returns nil. When that function panics, neither happens: the
connection keeps its immediate transaction, nobody ends it, and every later write waits out the five
second busy timeout and fails, until the process is restarted. The dispatch works around it for a write
handler by turning the handler's panic into an error before it reaches `Change` (`callWrite`). That covers
one caller and one place. A panic in a registered check during an undo, in the function given to `Extend`,
or in the engine's own code is not covered, and neither is any later caller of the package (the job that
brings a new snapshot in will call `Change` with no router around it). The fix belongs where the
transaction is opened: `journalTransaction` rolls back when the function panics and lets the panic go on
unchanged. `callWrite` stays, because it is what makes the request answer `internal`.

One guard of the dispatch that no test holds, found by a deliberate break in review: with the check of the
arguments against the manifest skipped for the journal shape alone, every test passes, because the one
journal handler that exists checks its own argument as well. The next one may not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Inside `Change`, a read through `recorder.View()` made after a recorded write sees that write, while
      a view of the database opened before the change does not; after a rollback neither sees it.
- [ ] `recorder.View().Close()` leaves the change open: a recorded write after it succeeds and commits.
- [ ] A read through that view after the change ended answers the closed-view error, and one made after a
      recorded write failed answers that failure; neither begins a transaction.
- [ ] The same holds inside the function given to `Extend`.
- [ ] `Writes.Authored` is that view: a scratch write handler that writes a scratch row and then reads it
      back through `writes.Authored` answers the value it wrote, in one request.
- [ ] A scratch handler of the journal shape that extends a change made by a scratch write handler appends
      its effects to that change: the journal holds one change, and one `changes.undo` puts both the
      original and the appended effects back.
- [ ] An extension the engine refuses (the origin undone, made by another method, already extended, or with
      a later change in force on a unit the extension wrote) answers 409 `refused` / `stale_change` and
      the canonical dump is unchanged.
- [ ] A journal handler receives the request's ledger view: one that queries it answers from the snapshot,
      one that queries a missing snapshot answers `ledger_unavailable` with nothing changed, and the view
      is closed at every ending of the request (answered, refused, failed, panicked).
- [ ] Arguments that do not match the manifest never reach a handler of the journal shape: a scratch
      journal handler that checks nothing is called zero times for each malformed body, and the answer is
      `bad_request`. The test fails with the check skipped for that shape.
- [ ] In `internal/authored`: after a panic inside the function given to `Change`, inside the function
      given to `Extend`, and inside a registered check during `Undo` and during `RestorePart`, a `Change`
      on the same database succeeds within 2 seconds, the canonical dump equals the one from before the
      panicking call, and the panic's value reached the caller unchanged.
- [ ] Through the router: a panic inside an extension's write answers `internal`, keeps nothing, and the
      next write gets the lock within 2 seconds.
- [ ] The existing tests of `internal/api` and `internal/authored` pass, `changes.undo` answers as before,
      and no golden file changes.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once against the code before its change or against a deliberate
      break, and the report names which.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: a write reads its own transaction, a journal handler can extend a change and query the
      ledger, and no panic inside a journal transaction makes the next write wait.

## Tests

- Unit, `internal/authored`: the recorder's view (sees its own writes, survives its own close, refuses
  after the end and after a failure), also inside an extension; the four panics, each followed by a write
  under a 2 second deadline.
- Unit, `internal/api`, over the scratch journaled tables of `authoredtest`: the write handler that reads
  what it wrote; the extending journal handler and its undo; the refused extensions; the ledger view of a
  journal handler and its closing; malformed arguments against a journal handler that checks nothing; the
  panic inside an extension.
- Golden: none changes. No real ledger and no real database is opened.

## Blast radius

**Edits:** `internal/authored/recorder.go`, `internal/authored/view.go`, `internal/api/writes.go`,
`internal/api/reads.go`, `internal/api/changes.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/authored/undo.go`, `internal/authored/journal.go`,
`internal/authored/authoredtest/scratch.go`, `internal/api/router.go`, `internal/api/errors.go`

Two files of the engine and three of the dispatch, with their tests beside them. No migration, no table,
no statement that writes, no contract type, nothing under `web/` and nothing in `cmd/`. `changes.go`
changes only as far as the journal shape's signature does. If the scratch support needs one more helper, it
is added in `authoredtest` and named in the report.

## Recovery path

Nothing stored changes shape and nothing is migrated. Reverting the commits brings back the dispatch as it
is today.
close_reason: A write reads the app's database through a view over its own transaction (Writes.Authored, (*Recorder).View()), sees its own writes and reads under its lock; the journal handler shape receives the request's ledger view and its Journal gains Extend; journalTransaction rolls back when the function it runs panics, so no caller leaves the write lock held. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main. Review: three independent mutations, all failing tests; the implementer's ten breaks each failed a test.

title: Make the Patrimônio screen, the pots list and a pot's page fetch again whenever something is written or undone
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the Patrimônio screen, the Cofrinhos list and a pot's page each load what they show once, when
they open, and keep showing it after anything changes until the person leaves and comes back. Every other
screen that shows what the person can change refreshes by itself after a change or an undo. Once the
person can choose a pot's bucket and the budget lines it feeds, these three would keep showing the old
bucket, the old group and the old net worth right after the choice, which reads as if it was not kept.
After this lands the three refresh by themselves after every change and every undo, without the page
going blank while they do, and a page left for another pot never shows the first pot's figures. What the
person would notice if this were wrong: a pot in its old group after choosing a new bucket, a net worth
that only moves after leaving the screen, or a pot's page briefly showing the pot that was open before.

## Outcome
`PatrimonioScreen.vue`, `CofrinhosScreen.vue` and `CofrinhoScreen.vue` watch the revision counter beside
what they watch today and fetch their answer again whenever it moves, keeping what they show until the new
answer arrives and ignoring an answer that arrives after a later request was made. Each has a screen test
that proves it, over the stand-in. Nothing they render changes, and the parity check still passes on
every state of the three screens.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person; its interface is `web/`, Vue 3 with
Pinia and vue-router. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under `web/src/api/fake/` that the
design prototype runs on, created with `createFakeApi`; it already answers every write these screens are
affected by (`settings.setPotBucket`, `settings.toggleLinkedLine`, `changes.undo`). *The revision counter*
is the Pinia store `web/src/stores/revision.ts` (`current`, `bump()`): every write and undo of the
interface bumps it, and its own comment says "What shows data a write can change watches it and fetches
again, so a write does not have to know who is looking." *The parity check* is `npm --prefix web run
parity`, which builds the interface on the stand-in and measures every ported screen, state by state
(`web/scripts/parity/states.mjs`), against the design's reference screenshots on two viewports in a real
browser; it is not part of the gate `bin/ci`, and the repository's rules ask that it be run for any change
that touches a screen and that its output go in the pull request body.

**Why now.** Every screen that shows what the person authored must fetch again when the revision is
bumped. Five places do not today; two of them (the transaction panel's and the subscription screen's line
and tag menus) are fixed by the work that gives the line menu its month (finwise-m9q). These three are the rest, and
the writes that change what they show are a pot's bucket and its linked lines (finwise-7ss: the pots' writes
and the reads that count a pot by its bucket). This work needs none of that: the stand-in already answers
those writes, so it can land first.

**What the code is today (each point read in the file named).**

- `web/src/screens/patrimonio/PatrimonioScreen.vue`: `api.netWorth.overview().then(...)` once at setup,
  into `overview`; the template renders nothing until it is set.
- `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/CofrinhosScreen.vue`: a `watch` on `() => view.showClosed`, immediate, that
  calls `api.savingsPots.list({ includeClosed })` and keeps the answer only when `includeClosed ===
  view.showClosed` still holds.
- `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/CofrinhoScreen.vue`: a `watch` on the route's `id`, immediate, that clears
  `pot` and `missing`, calls `api.savingsPots.detail(requested)`, ignores the answer when `requested !==
  id.value`, and sets `missing` for a null answer ("Cofrinho não encontrado.").
- The pattern already in use: `web/src/screens/assinaturas/AssinaturaScreen.vue` watches `[id, () =>
  revision.current]`, clears what it shows only when the id changed (`requested !== previous?.[0]`), and
  ignores a stale answer; `web/src/screens/inicio/InicioScreen.vue` and `web/src/screens/config/ConfigScreen.vue`
  watch the counter too.
- Their tests: `web/src/screens/patrimonio/patrimonio.test.ts` (mounted with `mountAt`),
  `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/cofrinhos.test.ts` and `cofrinho.test.ts` (mounted with `mountRouted`, the
  latter with a `prototypeState()` it can change), all over `createFakeApi` with the prototype dataset.
  Over that dataset the pots list's group heads are `Reservado`, `Investido` and `Sem balde` (the
  stand-in's pot `sn` has no bucket and a balance of 500.00), and the page of `rfp` has the subtitle
  `Mercado Pago · Reservado · 120% do CDI`. In the stand-in a pot with no bucket counts in no part of the
  net worth, so giving `sn` a bucket raises that part and the total by 500.00.

**The rule for each screen.** It fetches again on every move of the counter, as well as on what it watches
today. While the new answer is on its way the screen keeps showing the one it has: only a change of the
pot's id clears a pot's page, as today. An answer is shown only if it is still the answer to what the
screen is showing now: the pots list compares its option, as today, and a request it has since replaced;
a pot's page compares the id; the net worth screen keeps only the answer to its latest request. The
backend is faked at the API boundary with `createFakeApi` in every test, never with an inline stub.
Nothing rendered changes, so no style, token or text is touched.

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic,
Conventional Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit
message. Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; this work adds no
interface text. A design value in a component comes from a token; this work adds none. Money is integer
cents on the server and no float may appear in its money path; this work touches no amount. Every SQL
statement over the app's database is a registered constant; this work runs none. Nothing here needs a
real ledger: the tests run over the stand-in's invented dataset.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] On the pots list, mounted over `createFakeApi`, `settings.setPotBucket("sn", "Disponível")` through
the same API followed by `revision.bump()` changes the group heads from `Reservado`, `Investido`, `Sem
balde` to `Reservado`, `Investido`, `Disponível`, without a remount; `changes.undo` of that change and
another bump bring the first heads back.
- [ ] On the Patrimônio screen, the same write and a bump make the `Disponível` card and the total each
grow by R$ 500,00 without a remount.
- [ ] On the page of `rfp`, `settings.setPotBucket("rfp", "Investido")` and a bump change the subtitle from
`Mercado Pago · Reservado · 120% do CDI` to `Mercado Pago · Investido · 120% do CDI`; between the bump and
the answer the page still shows the pot (its `h1` is `RF Pets`), not an empty page.
- [ ] On a pot's page, an answer for the first pot that arrives after the route has moved to a second pot
is not shown; on the pots list, an answer for the option no longer selected is not shown; on the
Patrimônio screen, an earlier answer that arrives after a later one is not shown.
- [ ] Each screen asks its read once more per bump, and not more (counted on the fake API's method).
- [ ] The existing tests of the three screens pass unchanged.
- [ ] `npm --prefix web run parity` passes every state of the three screens on both viewports; its output
is in the pull request body.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, against the watch on the counter removed from its screen, and
the stale-answer tests against the comparison removed; each break is named in the final report.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, `npm --prefix web run parity` passes with its output in the
pull request body, and each of the three screens shows a changed answer after a bump without a remount.

## Tests
- Screen test (`web/src/screens/cofrinhos/cofrinhos.test.ts`, over `createFakeApi` with the prototype
  dataset): the heads after a bucket change and a bump, and after its undo and a bump; a stale answer for
  the other option ignored.
- Screen test (`web/src/screens/patrimonio/patrimonio.test.ts`, same fixture): the `Disponível` card and
  the total after the change and a bump; an out-of-order answer ignored.
- Screen test (`web/src/screens/cofrinhos/cofrinho.test.ts`, same fixture): the subtitle after the change
  and a bump; the pot kept on screen while it reloads; an answer for a pot the route has left ignored.
- Screen test, all three: one read per bump.
- Parity: `npm --prefix web run parity`, output in the pull request body.
- Each guard is broken once on purpose and the failing test named in the report.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/screens/patrimonio/PatrimonioScreen.vue`,
`web/src/screens/cofrinhos/CofrinhosScreen.vue`, `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/CofrinhoScreen.vue`,
`web/src/screens/patrimonio/patrimonio.test.ts`, `web/src/screens/cofrinhos/cofrinhos.test.ts`,
`web/src/screens/cofrinhos/cofrinho.test.ts`
**Reads only:** `web/src/stores/revision.ts`, `web/src/screens/assinaturas/AssinaturaScreen.vue`,
`web/src/api/fake/`, `web/src/test/mount.ts`, `web/src/test/mountRouted.ts`,
`web/scripts/parity/states.mjs`, `bin/ci`

Three screens' scripts and their three test files, in one module; no template, style, store, contract or
backend change. It is `verify:gate` because only the parity check, outside `bin/ci`, proves that nothing
rendered moved.
close_reason: The Patrimônio screen, the pots list and a pot's page watch the revision and fetch again once per bump, keep what is on screen while the answer is on its way, and drop a late answer. bin/ci green on the branch merged with main; parity 174 checked, 0 over 0.05%; hosted check passed. Review: the stale-answer comparison inverted fails the screen's tests; the implementer's breaks failed ten, four and three tests, after rewriting a test that had passed under one of them.

title: Put transactions on budget lines one by one, in bulk and for a whole establishment, keep each step in the transaction's history, and take one step back without overwriting what came after
description:
## What changes for the user
Today choosing a line for a purchase, in the list or in its panel, answers that the app is read-only, and
so do "Confirmar" on a suggestion, the "Por quê?" field, picking a line for a selection, "Todas" in the
toast that offers to apply a line to every purchase at the same establishment, and "Desfazer" beside a step
of the purchase's history. After this lands each of them is kept: a purchase put on a line counts on that
line, its panel lists "Você alterou para Mercado" with the day, the reason typed in "Por quê?" stays beside
that step, "Todas" moves every other purchase at that establishment that can go on the line and says how
many, and one "Desfazer" in the toast takes back the line and everything "Todas" did with it. Taking one
step back from the history restores what that step changed and nothing else; if the purchase was changed
again since, the app says "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito." instead of silently
throwing the later change away, which is what the prototype does today.

## Outcome
Six methods stop answering `read_only` on a server with its own database and are answered by handlers:
`transactions.setLine`, `confirmLine`, `setReason`, `setLineForMany`, `applyLineToEstablishment` and
`undoHistoryStep`. Each line is resolved in the budget of the transaction's own month. A line written by
`setLine`, `confirmLine` or "all purchases here" leaves a history step with the stand-in's text; a reason
is kept beside the latest step without making its change stale; "all purchases here" extends the change it
starts from, so one undo takes back both; and taking a step back is a new recorded change that restores
only that step's units of that one transaction, refused when they were changed since, with the panel's
`undoable` flag agreeing with it. Every case is in the write conformance harness with its golden effects.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is a SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it, and the file may be swapped
under it at any time. *The app's database* is `finwise.db`, owned by the Go package `internal/authored`,
the only package that executes SQL against it; the server has one only when started with `--db`, and
without it every write answers `read_only`, as today. *The stand-in* is the in-memory fake backend under
`web/src/api/fake/` that the design prototype runs on; it is the only existing statement of how writes
behave, and its behaviour is the rule here except where this text says the server departs from it. *The
manifest* is `internal/contract/contract.json`, the generated description of every API method. *A listed
transaction* is one the API lists: a row of the collector's clean list after `internal/txrules` has
folded tax rows under their purchases and taken pot movements out. *A budget line* has an integer id minted
by the app's database and a name that belongs to a budget version; *the budget in force for a month* is
the latest version starting at or before it. *The fees line* is the built-in `Tarifas e juros`, in no
group, with a fixed id; it can be named in a write in any month whose budget has at least one line. *The
current month* is the Brazil month of the request's instant. *An establishment key* is the identity of an
establishment or a person (`doc:`, `name:` or `text:`, from `internal/txrules/counterpart.go`); under
`doc:` it is a document number, never logged. *A golden file* is the committed, exact answer of one call
over an invented fixture.

**What this builds on, delivered by earlier work.** Read each in the code as that work left it.

- The recorder, the journal and undo (finwise-wi4). Every change to an authored table goes through a recorder
  working from a closed registry of journaled tables; *the journal* is `changes(id, at, day, author,
  method, extended, undone_at)` and `change_effects(change_id, seq, tbl, key, col, before, after)`. A *unit*
  is what one effect is about: a table, a key and, for an attribute table, a column. In a *table of optional
  facts* (a transaction's state, an establishment) every column has a default, so two changes to different
  columns of one key are independent and each can be undone alone. A table can be owned by another:
  writing an owned row does not make the owner's change stale, and removing the owner removes and records
  its owned rows. The change's row is written with its first effect or when the handler asks for its id;
  a handler that does neither leaves no trace. The recorder offers three mechanisms this work calls:
  *extending* a committed change (reopen it as a recorder after checking that it exists, is not undone, was
  made by the method the caller requires, is not yet extended, and that its effects still hold; append
  effects with `seq` continuing; mark it extended; hand back its id); the *inverse of a part* (the steps of
  undo over a caller-chosen subset of a change's units, performed inside another open change so the
  restores are that change's effects, without marking the source change undone); and a *read-only check*
  that says whether that inverse would be refused.
- `changes.undo(changeId)` (finwise-2s5), in one immediate transaction with foreign keys deferred to the
  commit: (1) collapse the change's effects per unit, the first `before` and the last `after`; (2) if the
  change is unknown or already undone, or a later change that is still in force has an effect on any of
  those units, refuse with `refused` / `stale_change` and change nothing; the journal's order decides, not
  the value (a unit set from A to B, then to C, then back to B by later changes is not the first change's to
  take back), and as a guard against a write that escaped the journal, a unit whose current content
  differs from that `after` is refused the same way; (3) otherwise restore every `before`, in reverse order
  of `seq`, and mark the change undone. Undo returns nothing and is not itself undoable.
- Write dispatch (finwise-2s5): a write with a registered handler on a server with the app's database has its
  arguments validated against the manifest's schema (a mismatch is `bad_request`), then runs inside one
  immediate transaction with a recorder holding one open change (author `person`, the method's qualified
  name, the instant, the Brazil day `brday.DayOf` of it); the dispatcher commits, and any failure rolls
  everything back, including when the five-second wait for the lock runs out (`internal`). A handler
  refuses with the kind `refused` and one reason of a closed list (HTTP 409); this work produces
  `stale_change`, `not_found` and `unknown_line`. Where the contract's result allows null, "nothing to do"
  and "no such target" answer null and record nothing; where it does not, a write that changes nothing
  records an empty change and answers its id, whose undo is a no-op. A test file lists the writes still
  without a handler, `writesWithoutHandler`. Handlers are plain functions with no `net/http` type in their
  signature. Each handler also receives the request's ledger view, one handle and one read-only
  transaction, so every ledger query of the request sees one snapshot (finwise-jzw).
- The write conformance harness (finwise-fst): every write has cases in a mode. *A recorded change*: the answer
  validates against the manifest, its effects match a golden file
  `internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/<domain>.<method>[.<slug>].json`, and undoing it returns the
  canonical dump of every journaled table to the dump taken before. *Nothing to do*: no row is added to the
  journal. *An extension of an earlier change* (`applyLineToEstablishment`): undoing it returns the dump
  taken before its origin. *A refusal*: 409 with its reason and no table changed at all, the index
  included. A list names the refusal reasons that have no producer yet; the slice that first produces one
  removes it there and adds its case. The no-leak test runs every write case.
  `internal/authored/authoredtest` builds invented authored states.
- The budget's tables and line lookup (finwise-ef7): one function of "the lines a month's budget has" (each
  line's id, its name in that version and its group, and the fees line too when the set is not empty), from
  which every lookup of a line's name in a month comes.
- The transactions' tables and the index (finwise-jw2): `tx_state(tx_key, line_id,
  classified_by, confidence, pending_reason, pending_line_id, pending_confidence, ask_reason, note,
  exclusion, refund, refund_line_id, reimbursable, expected_cents, credit_tx_key, credit_cents)`, an
  attribute table of optional facts, one row per transaction; `establishments(key, nickname,
  default_line_id)`, the same kind; `history_steps(id, tx_key, change_id, kind, text, day)`, a set table
  whose `kind` is a *step* (it records what its change did to the transaction) or a *note* (it records that
  something happened beside it); `history_step_reasons(step_id, reason)`, owned by its step. The index
  (`tx_index`, `tx_ids`) gives every transaction a key of its own, `tx_key`, and maps each provider id seen
  to it; it records observations, is not journaled and is never undone.
- The reads that merge what the person authored, and the lookup of the transaction a write names
  (finwise-tsr). *The target lookup* is the one function every transaction write uses to find what it names:
  it resolves a provider id through the interpreted ledger read `transactions.detail` uses for its target,
  in the request's ledger view, answers unknown for an id that read does not list (an unknown id, a tax row
  folded into its purchase, a pot movement), and creates or refreshes the index row of a known one. *The
  name function* answers the name to show for an establishment key (the nickname, otherwise the ledger's
  name). And the detail's `history` answers each step with `undoable` computed by the recorder's read-only
  check, always false for a note.

**What the code is today** (each point read in the file named).

- `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`: `setLine(id, line): Promise<LineChangeResult | null>` ("Null
  when nothing changed: the line is the same and no review was waiting"), where `LineChangeResult` is
  `{changeId, establishment: {key, name} | null}` ("null for a person or a movement, where it makes no
  sense"); `applyLineToEstablishment(changeId): Promise<ChangeResult & { changed: number }>` ("Extends a
  line change to the rest of its establishment; undoing it undoes both"); `setLineForMany(ids, line):
  Promise<ChangeResult>`. `web/src/api/contract/transaction-detail.ts`: `confirmLine(id):
  Promise<ChangeResult | null>` ("Accepts the model's classification as it stands, or its suggestion for a
  pending one"); `setReason(id, reason): Promise<ChangeResult>` ("The optional answer to 'why' after
  correcting the model, kept on the history step"); `undoHistoryStep(id, stepId): Promise<ChangeResult |
  null>` ("Restores the state before that step alone and drops the step from the history");
  `HistoryEntry.undoable` ("True when taking this step back restores a previous state").
- `internal/api/router.go` refuses every `write` with `read_only`; `internal/api/transactions.go`'s
  `registerTransactions` registers the three reads.
- The stand-in: `transaction-writes.ts` (`setLine`, `applyLineToEstablishment`, `setLineForMany`,
  `decided`, `nameOf`), `transaction-edits.ts` (`confirmLine`, `setReason`, `undoHistoryStep`),
  `history.ts` (`record` saves the listed fields before applying and pushes a step whose `restore` holds
  them; `note` pushes a step with no `restore`), `changes.ts` (`begin(origin)` keeps the transaction, the
  line and the establishment key of a line change so `originOf` can extend it; `undo` assigns back a
  snapshot of the whole state), and the tests `writes.test.ts` and `panel-writes.test.ts`.
- The interface already sends these writes. `web/src/components/transactions/useLineChange.ts` sends
  `setLine` from a line menu; on a null answer it does nothing; otherwise it bumps the revision and toasts
  `Linha alterada para <linha>.` with "Desfazer" when `establishment` is null, or `Linha alterada para
  <linha>. Aplicar a todas as compras em <nome>?` with "Só esta", "Todas" and "Desfazer"; "Todas" sends
  `applyLineToEstablishment` with the change id and toasts `<linha> agora vale para todas as compras em
  <nome>: <changed + 1> alteradas.` (`alterada` when `changed` is 0) with "Desfazer" on that same change id.
  `useTransactionActions.ts` sends `setLineForMany` for the selection and toasts `<n> transações agora estão
  em <linha>.` with "Desfazer". `web/src/components/transaction-panel/panelActions.ts` sends `confirmLine`
  from "Confirmar" (shown in `LineSection.vue` while `justification` is not null), `setReason` from the
  "Por quê? (opcional)" field (shown while `askReason`, sent on change with the field's value) and
  `undoHistoryStep` from a history step. No file under `web/` changes in this work.

**Decisions already taken, with what lost.**

- Undo is the inverse of recorded effects, refused when what it would overwrite has changed since; the same
  rule serves the undo of one history step. Why: the stand-in's snapshot restore silently destroys later
  changes, and with money refusing is the safe failure. Rejected: snapshot restore; last writer wins;
  restoring a step over later edits.
- A transaction's line must exist in the budget in force for the transaction's own month; a line named by
  something with no month is resolved in the current month. Why: the person decided that a transaction of
  a closed month can still be recategorised (closing freezes the month's budget, not its transactions), and
  a line the month's budget lacks would count in no group of that month. Rejected: validating everything
  against the current month. So no write here is refused because the transaction's month is closed.
- Where a result type allows null, an unknown target answers null; `not_found` is for results that cannot
  be null. Why: the screens already treat null as "nothing happened". Rejected: refusing every unknown id.

**The rules common to the six writes.**

1. *The target.* Each write resolves the transactions it names through the target lookup, in the
   request's ledger snapshot, which also creates or refreshes their index rows. An unknown transaction
   answers null for `setLine`, `confirmLine` and `undoHistoryStep`, and `refused` / `not_found` for
   `setReason` and `setLineForMany`; nothing is recorded either way.
2. *The line.* A line named by a write on a transaction is resolved by its name in the budget in force for
   that transaction's own month, through the line lookup of the budget's tables; a name that budget does not have is refused with
   `refused` / `unknown_line` and nothing is recorded. The fees line is accepted under `Tarifas e juros` in
   any month whose budget has at least one line, and refused in a month whose budget has none, where no
   name is accepted. The line is stored by id.
3. *Settling.* Putting a transaction on a line (`setLine`, `confirmLine`, `setLineForMany`, "all purchases
   here") sets its line, sets who put it there, clears its confidence and clears its pending review (reason,
   suggested line and suggested confidence), as the stand-in's `decided` does. Who is the person, except
   for the transactions "all purchases here" moves, which are put there by a rule.
4. *History steps.* `setLine`, `confirmLine` and "all purchases here" add a step (kind *step*) to each
   transaction they put on a line, tied to the change, dated the change's Brazil day, with these texts
   (Brazilian Portuguese, constants in `internal/api/messages.go`, the one file that holds what the server
   writes for a person to read): `Você alterou para <linha>`, `Você confirmou <linha>`, `Regra aplicou
   <linha> (você pediu para todas em <nome>)`. `setLineForMany` and `setReason` add no step, as in the
   stand-in. The step's insertion is one more effect of its change. The other groups of transaction writes
   that keep steps (split, exclusion and refund, finwise-9je; reimbursements, finwise-ilt) land in parallel and need
   the same function to add a step; if the tree holds none when this work starts, write it once in
   `internal/authored` beside the history tables and use it, never a second copy.
5. *The snapshot.* Every write here resolves its transaction in the ledger, so with the snapshot missing
   each answers `ledger_unavailable` through the same classifier a read uses, and nothing is recorded; a
   write that fails halfway keeps nothing and answers `internal`.
6. *Registration.* Register the handlers in a registration function of this work's own files, the way
   write dispatch registers a write handler, instead of adding lines to `registerTransactions`, which the
   sibling slices landing in parallel would edit too.

**`setLine(id, line)`.** Null when the transaction is unknown, or when the line is the same (the same line
id) and nothing was pending; this is decided after the line is resolved, so an unknown name is
`unknown_line` even when the transaction already has a line. Otherwise it settles the transaction by the
person and asks "why" (`ask_reason` true) only when it corrected a line the model had set or settled a
pending one (`classified_by` was the model, or a review was pending), as the stand-in's
`transaction.by === 'IA' || !!transaction.pending` does; otherwise `ask_reason` is false. Still settling a
pending review when the line is the one already set is not null (stand-in: "still settles a pending review
when the line is the one already set"). It adds the step `Você alterou para <linha>`, with the line's name
in the transaction's month. It answers `{changeId, establishment}`: `establishment` is `{key, name}` for an
establishment, with `name` from the name function (the nickname when there is one), and null when the
other side is a person or the transaction is a movement. A movement or a person can still be put on a line.

**`confirmLine(id)`.** The line is the transaction's line, or, when it has none, its pending suggestion.
Null when the transaction is unknown or has neither. Otherwise it settles the transaction on that line by
the person and adds the step `Você confirmou <linha>`; `ask_reason` is left as it is. The stand-in records
the change and the step even when the line, who and the review were already what confirming sets; so does
the server, which then records the step as the change's only effect. The line comes from what is stored,
not from an argument, so no `unknown_line` arises.

**`setReason(id, reason)`.** The result cannot be null: an unknown transaction is `not_found`. The reason
is stored, as sent, on the transaction's latest history step (the one with the highest id, whatever its
kind, as the stand-in's `history.at(-1)`), as that step's owned row in `history_step_reasons`, replacing
the reason it had. Because the row is owned by the step, giving a reason does not make the line change
stale: the "Todas" and "Desfazer" of the toast still work after it, and taking the line change back takes
its reason with it. The reason a transaction's detail answers is the one on its latest step that has one
and is stored nowhere else, so a reason given to a transaction with no step at all has nowhere to go: the
write records an empty change and answers its id (the stand-in instead keeps a `reasonText` on the
transaction). The same reason as the one stored is an empty change. Whether an empty reason is stored as
an empty text or removes the owned row is the implementer's: the stand-in keeps `""`, and either way the
detail's `reason` answers `""` when no step has a non-empty reason; one test pins the choice.

**`setLineForMany(ids, line)`.** The whole list is validated before anything changes: repeated ids count
once; one unknown id refuses the call with `not_found`, and one transaction whose month's budget lacks the
line refuses it with `unknown_line`, with nothing recorded and no table changed, the index included (the
refusal rolls the transaction back). Each transaction's line is resolved in its own month's budget, so one
call can put transactions of two months on lines of the same name with two different ids. Which refusal is
answered when a list holds both an unknown id and a transaction whose month lacks the line is the
implementer's, pinned by a test. Each transaction is settled by the person; `ask_reason` is not touched and
no step is added. An empty list records an empty change. This is a departure from the stand-in, whose
`changeMany` skips the ids it does not find and applies the line whatever the month.

**`applyLineToEstablishment(changeId)`, "all purchases here".** It extends the change it names, in one
immediate transaction, through the recorder's extension mechanism with the required method
`transactions.setLine`: the origin must be a live `setLine` change, not undone, not yet extended, whose own
effects still hold (no later change in force on any of its units, and every unit still holding its last
`after`). Anything else (an unknown id, an undone change, a change of another method such as
`setLineForMany`, an extended one, one overwritten since) is `refused` / `stale_change` and changes nothing.
A reason given since is an owned row and does not count against it; neither does a later write to another
column of that transaction, such as its note. The origin's transaction is resolved again in this request's
snapshot; when it is a person or a movement it has no establishment to extend to and the answer is
`refused` / `not_found`, as it is when the ledger no longer lists it. Then, appending to the origin:

- the establishment's default line (`establishments.default_line_id` of the origin's establishment key)
  becomes the origin's line, stored by its id, even when nothing else moves (stand-in: "remembers the
  establishment default after Todas, and forgets it on undo"). This never refuses: the line is stored
  whatever month the origin transaction is in and whether or not the current month's budget has it,
  because a default line acts only in a month whose budget has it (the rules that classify new
  transactions apply it only there, finwise-82m) and a read shows it only while the current month's budget has
  it. The writes that set a default line by name (`setDefaultLine`) resolve that name in the current month;
  this write names no line;
- the whole ledger is interpreted in one pass, as `internal/api/card.go` does, and every other listed
  transaction of that key moves to the line when it is in the same direction as the origin (purchases for a
  purchase, credits for a credit, by the sign of the amount, a zero amount counting as a purchase as in the
  stand-in's `contributions`), is not a movement (txrules' `Movement` is neither a transfer between own
  accounts nor a bill payment), is not a refund (the person's setting, or the ledger's rule when they set
  none), is not unconverted, is not split (two or more parts), is not excluded with a reason, is not already
  on the line, and whose month's budget has the line (the fees line: whose month's budget has at least one
  line). Transactions of any month qualify, closed months and months before the app started asking about
  transactions included; each is resolved and indexed through the target lookup. Each moved transaction is
  settled by a rule, keeps its `ask_reason`, and gets the step `Regra aplicou <linha> (você pediu para todas
  em <nome>)`, where `<nome>` is the origin's establishment by the name function. A pending one has its
  review cleared (stand-in: the pending count goes down);
- the origin is marked extended and the answer is `{changeId: <the origin's id>, changed: <how many
  moved>}`. One `changes.undo` of that id takes back the line, the default line, every moved transaction
  and every step.

The stand-in moves every transaction of the key that is not on the line, whatever its direction, month or
kind; the server departs on purpose in four ways, each pinned by a test: it keeps to the origin's
direction, it skips movements, refunds, unconverted, split and excluded transactions, it skips months
whose budget lacks the line, and it refuses an origin that is not a live, unextended `setLine` change.

Left to the implementer, each pinned by a test: how the origin's transaction and line are found (from the
origin's effects or its step; a `setLine` change touches one transaction); which version's name `<linha>`
carries in a moved transaction's step when its own month's budget names the line differently (the rule
that a transaction shows its line's name in its own month's budget points to the moved transaction's
month).

**`undoHistoryStep(id, stepId)`.** Null, recording nothing, when the transaction is unknown, the step id is
not one of its steps (`nope`, an id of another transaction's step), or the step is a note. Otherwise it
opens a new change (method `transactions.undoHistoryStep`) that applies the inverse of a part: undo's steps
1 to 3 over the units of that one transaction (its `tx_state` columns and its set rows) that the step's
change touched, leaving the establishment's row and every other transaction alone; then it deletes the
step, whose owned reason goes with it and is recorded too. A step whose units were changed since by a later
change still in force, or whose units no longer hold the step's change's last `after`, is refused with
`refused` / `stale_change` and nothing changes, instead of overwriting the later edit. Because effects are
per column, taking back "marked as refund" leaves a refund line chosen later untouched (stand-in: "does not
touch what was done after it"). Taking a line step back always leaves the "why" question closed: when the
step's change touched the transaction's line, `ask_reason` is set false in the same new change, as the
stand-in sets `restore.askReason = false` in `setLine`. The answer is the new change's id. Being a recorded
change, a step's undo can itself be undone with `changes.undo`, which puts the units and the step (with its
reason) back under the same step id. After it, `changes.undo` of the step's own change is `stale_change`.
For a step that "all purchases here" wrote, the step's change is the origin's, and only that transaction's
units are restored (stand-in: taking back the step on another purchase of the establishment returns it to
the line and classifier it had). The steps written by the rules that classify new transactions (finwise-82m,
`Regra classificou como <linha>`) are taken back the same way. `HistoryEntry.undoable`, delivered by the merged reads (finwise-tsr), is
computed with the same check, so it is true exactly when this write would succeed.

**Where this departs from the stand-in on purpose**, each pinned by a test the report names: undo by
inverse with refusal instead of snapshot restore, a history step changed since cannot be undone, a rule's
step can be taken back; the line menu and line validation follow the transaction's own month; bulk writes
are all or nothing; "all purchases here" keeps to the origin's direction and skips movements, refunds,
unconverted, split and excluded transactions and months whose budget lacks the line; `setReason` on an
unknown transaction is `not_found` where the stand-in answers a change; a reason with no step to hold it is
kept nowhere.

**Failure paths that touch this work.**

| what goes wrong | what happens |
| --- | --- |
| the snapshot is missing while writing | the write answers `ledger_unavailable`; nothing is recorded |
| the snapshot is swapped during a request | the request finishes on the snapshot it opened |
| a write fails halfway, or waits out the lock | one transaction: nothing of it is kept, the index included; `internal` |
| an undo or a step's undo meets a later change | `stale_change`; nothing is restored |
| "Todas" after the line change was undone, changed again or already extended | `stale_change`; nothing changes |
| "Todas" when a later change still in force has an effect on something "Todas" would write (the establishment's default line, or the line of one of the transactions it would move) | `stale_change`; nothing changes. The recorder refuses it by itself (`Extend` checks, after the handler wrote, that no later change in force has an effect on a unit the extension wrote): effects appended under the earlier change's id would otherwise sort before a change that came first |
| two tabs, or a tab and the ingest, write at once | writes queue; each is its own change; an undo that lost the race is refused |
| the process stops between a write's commit and its answer | the change is stored; the interface says the result could not be confirmed and refetches |

**The cost of the whole-ledger read.** "All purchases here" interprets the whole ledger on every call, as
the card's read already does; that cost is accepted today and grows with history. The time of one
`applyLineToEstablishment` and one `setLine` over a real snapshot, against a scratch app's database, is
measured by the review, not by the implementer, and recorded on the pull request.

**Privacy.** The repository is public and a real ledger is a person's whole financial history. A real
snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is ever
printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the person
running a test and goes into no file; a test that touches a real ledger runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. The review's timing uses a scratch app's database in a temporary
directory and reports durations only. Every fixture of this work is invented, and `-update` of the golden
files refuses to run while `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` is set. New files in `internal/api` log nothing; the
no-leak test's list of strings must cover what the new write cases carry (a line's name, a reason, an
establishment key, a step text).

**Conventions.** Work happens in a git worktree of its own and ends at local commits: atomic, Conventional
Commits, no attribution lines, and no mention of a session, a bead or a plan in a commit message. Money is
integer cents and no float may appear in the money path (this work moves no amount). Every SQL statement
over the app's database is a registered constant, prepared against the migrated schema by a test.
Interface text is Brazilian Portuguese and everything else is English; the Portuguese this work adds is
the three step texts, in `messages.go`. A design value in a component comes from a token (this work
touches no component).

## Acceptance criteria
The examples run on the fixtures' clock (2026-03-20, so the current month is 2026-03) with an invented
authored state from `authoredtest` holding three budget versions: from 2026-01 without the line, from
2026-02 with it named `Mercado`, and from 2026-03 with the same id named `Feira`. The single-transaction
cases use the
full invented ledger of `internal/api/fixtures_test.go` (`tx-pix-out` is a PIX to a person,
`tx-own-transfer` a movement, `tx-pending` bank-pending, `tx-refund` a card refund, `tx-unconverted` an
unconverted row). "All purchases here" needs one establishment with many rows, which the full ledger does
not have, so its cases use a ledger built for the test with `ledgertest` (as `card_test.go` builds its
own): under one establishment key, two purchases in 2026-03, one purchase in 2026-02, a purchase in
2026-01 (whose budget lacks the line), a credit, a refund credit, an excluded purchase, a split purchase, an
unconverted purchase and a purchase already on the line.

- [ ] With `--db`, the six methods answer 200 with results that validate against the manifest; none of
them remains in `writesWithoutHandler`; without `--db` each still answers `read_only` before its body is
read.
- [ ] `setLine` on a 2026-03 purchase with `Feira` stores that line's id, `classifiedBy: "Você"`,
`confidence: null`, `pending: null`, adds the step `Você alterou para Feira` dated 2026-03-20 and answers
`establishment: {key, name}` with the establishment's nickname as `name` when it has one; with `Mercado` it
is 409 `refused` / `unknown_line`, and on the 2026-02 purchase `Mercado` is accepted and `Feira` refused.
- [ ] `setLine` answers null and adds no journal row for an unknown id, a folded tax row (`tx-foreign-tax`),
a pot movement (`tx-pot-transfer`), and the same line with nothing pending; with the same line and a
pending review it answers a change and the review is cleared.
- [ ] `askReason` after `setLine` is true when the transaction was pending or classified by the model, and
false when it had a line by the person or a rule; `establishment` is null for a person (`tx-pix-out`) and
for a movement (`tx-own-transfer`), and both are still put on the line.
- [ ] `Tarifas e juros` is accepted by `setLine` in a month whose budget has a line and refused with
`unknown_line` in a month whose budget has none.
- [ ] `confirmLine` on a pending transaction with a suggestion puts it on the suggestion with
`classifiedBy: "Você"`, adds `Você confirmou <linha>` and leaves `askReason` unchanged; on one with neither
a line nor a suggestion, and on an unknown id, it answers null with no journal row.
- [ ] After `setLine` and `setReason("é do apartamento")`, the detail answers `reason: "é do
apartamento"`, the newest step's `reason` is that text and the older step's is null; `applyLineToEstablishment`
on the `setLine` change still succeeds; then one `changes.undo` returns the canonical dump to the one taken
before the `setLine`, reason row included.
- [ ] `setReason` on an unknown id is 409 `refused` / `not_found`; on a transaction with no step it answers
an empty change; the choice for an empty reason is pinned by a test.
- [ ] `setLineForMany(["a","b","a"], line)` settles both once; with one unknown id it is `not_found`, and
with one transaction whose month lacks the line it is `unknown_line`, each with the canonical dump, the
index and the journal unchanged; its undo restores each transaction's previous line, classifier and review;
it adds no step.
- [ ] `applyLineToEstablishment` on a `setLine` change of one 2026-03 purchase of that key moves exactly
the other 2026-03 purchase and the 2026-02 purchase (whose month's budget has the line under another name),
and none of the 2026-01 purchase, the credit, the refund, the excluded, the split,
the unconverted purchase or the one already on the line; it answers the origin's id and `changed: 2`; the
default line is stored; each moved
transaction answers `classifiedBy: "Regra"`, `pending: null` and the step `Regra aplicou <linha> (você
pediu para todas em <nome>)`, `undoable: true`.
- [ ] Over a credit origin it moves only credits of the key; with every other transaction already on the
line it answers `changed: 0` and still stores the default line. Over an origin in 2026-02 whose line the
current month's budget does not have (a fourth version or a fixture built for the case), it still answers
a change, stores the default line by id, and `counterparty.defaultLine` then answers null.
- [ ] `applyLineToEstablishment` is 409 `refused` / `stale_change`, changing nothing, for an unknown id, an
undone `setLine` change, a `setLineForMany` change, a change already extended, and a `setLine` change whose
transaction was put on another line since; it is `not_found` for a `setLine` change on a person or a
movement. A later `setNote` on the origin's transaction does not make it stale.
- [ ] In the extension mode of the harness, one `changes.undo` of the extended change returns the
canonical dump to the one taken before its origin, default line, moved transactions and steps included.
- [ ] `undoHistoryStep` on a `setLine` step restores the transaction's previous line, classifier,
confidence and pending review, sets `askReason` false, removes the step and its reason, and answers a new
change id; `changes.undo` of that id brings back the line, the step under the same id and its reason;
after the step's undo, `changes.undo` of the original change is `stale_change`.
- [ ] `undoHistoryStep` on a step whose transaction was put on another line since is 409 `refused` /
`stale_change` with nothing changed, and the detail answered that step `undoable: false` just before; on a
step whose transaction only had its note changed since it succeeds, and the detail answered `undoable:
true`.
- [ ] `undoHistoryStep` on one transaction's step of an extended change restores only that transaction
(the origin and the other moved transactions keep the line, the default line stays); it answers null for an
unknown transaction, an unknown step id, another transaction's step and a note.
- [ ] A property test over random sequences of these six writes and `changes.undo` on the fixture keeps
`HistoryEntry.undoable` equal to whether `undoHistoryStep` then succeeds, for every step of every state
reached.
- [ ] Each of `setLine`, `confirmLine`, `setReason`, `setLineForMany` and `undoHistoryStep` has a
write-conformance case in the recorded-change mode with its golden effects file under
`internal/api/testdata/golden/writes/` and the undo check; `applyLineToEstablishment` has one in the
extension mode; `setLine`, `confirmLine` and `undoHistoryStep` have nothing-to-do cases; the refusal cases
cover `stale_change`, `not_found` and `unknown_line`, and any of the three still in the list of reasons
without a producer is removed from it.
- [ ] With the snapshot file missing, `setLine` answers 503 `ledger_unavailable` and no table changes.
- [ ] The commits change no file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/full/`, `empty/` or `web/`.
- [ ] The no-leak test runs the new write cases and fails when a handler of this work is made to log one of
its arguments.
- [ ] The time of one `applyLineToEstablishment` and one `setLine` over a real snapshot, against a scratch
app's database, is measured by the review, not by the implementer, and recorded on the pull request as
durations only.
- [ ] Every new test was seen failing once, each against its own deliberate break, named in the report: the
line resolved in the current month instead of the transaction's; the same-line check made before the line is
resolved; `askReason` set on every correction; the bulk write validating inside its loop; "all purchases
here" ignoring the direction, then moving a refund, then moving into a month that lacks the line; the
extension accepting a `setLineForMany` change; the reason written into `tx_state` so it makes the line
change stale; the step's undo restoring the whole change instead of that transaction's units; the step's
undo skipping the staleness check; `askReason` left as restored after a line step's undo.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`
- [ ] Done when: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`, "all purchases here" still works after a reason was given and
one undo then restores every row, and a step changed since is refused with nothing changed.

## Tests
- Conformance, recorded-change mode (Go, the harness's lists), over the full invented ledger and an
